IF YOU KEEP YOUR BOAT IN A BOATYARD
By "Barnacle",

If you keep your boat in a boatyard for the winter, there are a few small points that are worth bearing in mind,

When you lay the boat up for the winter, check her over thoroughly and decide what work will have to be done ready for the next season, If there are any jobs that you cannot tackle yourself, let the Yard Manager Have a list of them immediately telling him the date by which you would like them finished. Then he can fit the work in with his winter programme and you can be reasonably ‘ sure the boat will be ready on time. If you do not let the Manager know about the jobs until Easter, the yard may be so busy that they will not be able to do them for you for some little time, Also with sail repairs, let the sailmaker have your instructions as early in the winter as possible.

Be explicit in your instructions, If you merely say "Stop the garboards leaking", you might find yourself with a bill for an assortment of new floors and frames, put in a ripe old boat that was not really worth repairing. If

3

you are not certain of the amount of work that will have to be done to effect a repair, explain the problem and get an estimate from the Yard Manager before authorising any work to be done. If the Manager tells you the boat is not worth repairing or spending money on, accept his judgement, find a mug who will buy the boat off you, and get yourself'a better one, Judging by the number of people one sees working on rotten, unseaworthy old tubs, there are still plenty of mugs about who believe a rotten boat is a bargain if it is
cheap.

While you are working in the yard, remember there may also be other owners working near you. Don't start raising dust until you have made sure that nobody near you is putting on varnish or enamel, and if you are washing cut a boat, be careful where all the water goes — you can soon turn 2 boatyard into a sea of mud to the great inconvenience of fellow workers.

If you borrow any tools, be sure you return them to their owner as soon as you have finished with them. If you ow tools and want them to remain in reasonable condition, unless you are confident of the borrowers abilities, never lend saws, other than hacksaws, chisels, planes or paintbrushes, and if you are an habitual borrower of tools, don't expect to borrow these items from an owner who takes any pride in his work, If you move or borrow any yard equipment for the weekend, be sure you put it back where you found it before you leave, and if you borrow any tools from the Professional Shipwrights, take care of them and hand them back in good order, Remember you are there only for your own pleasure, but it is the professional's livelihood.

If you keep your boat in a boatyard, you will be expected to buy paint etc. from the yard. local yards rents are not high, and most rely on the work on the laid up boats and profit on the sale of paint and gear to show any profit at all. If you think the yard are overcharging you, then take your boat to another yard. You will probably find his prices even higher!
Remember that the local yards are all very good to owners in letting them work on their own boats — there are plenty of boatyards that will not let owners do the work, and just imagine what your local garage owner would say if you drove in and asked him if you could respray your car and put a new engine in in his garage!

When dealing with the yard shipwrights, remember your manners. Most of them are skilled craftsmen, probably more skilled at their trade than you are at yours, and if you try to impress them with whet a superior person you are, they will merely laugh at you (when you have gone) for being the conceited ass that you are,

“NATIONAL BOAT SHOW 1960.

By moving to Earls Court, the organisers of the Boat Show have gained in space, and better still have obtained a pool wherein a few yachts may lie with their proper dignity. It is safe to predict that next year the upper floor of the building will also be in use and we shall again have the pleasure of looking down at the larger exhibits, as at Olympia.

Traditionally~built yachts of beautiful finish were on show in greater size
and splendour than ever - and inevitably at greater price. Newer techniques such
as moulded ply and fibreglass are more interesting in that they are more subject to development. Ian Proctor's "Alpha" is a notable example of a dinghy designed to require the absolute minimum of maintenance, with glass fibre hull and foam-- filled buoyancy by the Bristol Aeroplane Co., metal spars and Terylene sails and
cordage. She is expensive to begin with, but quite cheap if you include 5 - 10
years! maintenance- free life.

The News Chronicle is sponsoring the "Audacity", a very attractive 35 ton centreboard cruiser designed by Laurent Giles. Of cold-moulded construction = ww again with the co-operation of the aircraft industry she has the shape of a genuine yacht, yet taking size into account her price is competitive with the Tucker range of tea-chest boats. She deserves to share in the success of the News Chronicle " Enterprise".

The second generation of modern catamarans is with us. No longer can anything be sold that has two hulls; among day-sailers were three or four which could give a "Shearwater" a hard race. Three interesting cruising cats were shown; unconventional- unconventional to look at, but notably comfortable in a seaway, by accounts even from confirmed single-hull sailors. Nor are they in continual danger of capsizing - the Hawaiian 40 ft "Waikiki Surf" has crossed the Pacific frequently. For those really determined to capsize through sheer overdriving, Michael Henderson has the answer in " Golden Miller" which uses a masthead float and a little ballast to ensure self-righting from any position.

by _"BARNACLE" .

tf you are going to repaint and fit out a boat, you will need a certain number of tools. They are not many, and they are not expensive, so there is not much excuse for not having then.

first of all, remove old paint and muck from the hull you will need some scrapers, a good scrub>ing brush and bucket. The good old triangular serapers take a lot of beating, and for a high finish or awkward corners, special scrapers can be made up from broken vower hacksaw blades or old files. A file or stone for sharpening the scrapers will also be needed. A plastic bucket is
the obvious choice - 1 think who only point in favour of a galvanised bucket is
that you can lower it over the stern of your boat as an emergency brake without fear of pulling out the handle. brush for brushing out the inside of the boat, and some form of dustpan will be needed, unless you can borrow a vacuum cleaner. When cleaning out the inside of the hull, be careful to remove all dust, etc. from the limber holes. It may pay to make up a special little tool for this job, especially if the boat is an old one and the limber holes are partially blocked by an accumulation of old paint.

having cleaned all the old paint off the hull, you will probably need a putty knife. A stainless steel table ‘knife with a whippy blade makes a fair substitute, and can be handy for awkward corners.

Sheets of glasspaper are obviously needed, and can usually be purchased at the boatyard. If you want a good finish, don't skimp the sanding off, and then remove all dust thoroughly with a brush followed by a damp sponge.

Most essential of all are paint brushes. You will find it pays to get good brushes and take care of them, and keep separate brushes for different -jobs. Never use the varnish brush for any coloured paints, and try to keep one brush for each colour paint used, as it is very difficult to remove all the paint from a brush, and it is most annoying to find the white enamel is slightly tinged with green. A separate brush for priming paint is advisable, and separate brushes for black varnish and anti-~fouling are obviously essential. The black varnish brush need never be cleaned out. When you have finished with it, wrap it up in a polythene bag and leave it. It may harden up by next season, but ten minutes

Cont'd

Page 4.

work on an odd piece of wood with the brush well saturated in black varnish will soon soften it again. Whilst on the subject of painting, never try to apply paint thickly. several thin coats will harden better and give a much better looking finish. Also, whenever possible, start by painting the lightest colour first and finish with the darkest. Remember that anti~fouling must be put on within 24 hours of launching. Varnish is best done last of all, to try and get better weather. Again, several thin coats well smoothed down are infinitely better than one or two thick coats. For cleaning ay out brushes you will need an assortment of tins and old rags and some turps. The more tins and rags you can collect by fitting out time the better. When using varnish it pays to pour a small amount into a small clean tin you can comfortably hold in your hand ( an old enamel mug is ideal, or a teacup), rather than pour out a lot, and then either have to waste the surplus or: pour it back into the can.

For rigging the mast you will need at least a screwdriver, a pair of pliers and a good sharp knife.

There should not really be any specific use for a hammer at fitting out time, but it is almost certain you WILL need one somewhere. If the boat needs any structural repairs, you will need a larger tool kit, but so long as you have a good saw, a medium size plane, a large and a small chisel and means of drilling holes, you should be able to cone with most of the routine maintenance. if your boat is carvel built it will pay you to get one or two caulking irons of your awn, otherwise the yard shipwrights will usually lend these, together with rivetting dollies, large clamps, etc. when they are needed for special jobs.

CAVEAT EMPTOR. By BARNACLE "

If you are thinking of buying a second hand boat, you will be faced with a great number of decisions, some obvious and others not so obvious.

The first two things to decide are the type and size of boat you want, and the total amount of capital you are prepared to invest. Having settled these points you can start looking round the market. You may find several possibles. Let us have a look at the alternatives that may present themselves. Firstly there is the newish boat, probably at the top limit of your size range. This boat will depreciate in value as she gets older, but against this maintenance bills should be low. If the boat is of a type of which several have been built over the years, you will be able to get an idea of the average rate of annual depreciation over the class. If you buy this boat, be sure she is what you want, as if you start altering radically the accommodation or sail plan you will see little, if any return for your money and labour when you come to sell.

Next comes the older boat, may be slightly larger and slightly cheaper, but still basically sound. She may need minor repairs to bring her into really good order, but nothing serious. Her value will not change much over the years, but maintenance will be more; anything from 5/~ to £5 per hours sailing each year, depending on the standard you set and the amount of sailing you do. This boat will probably, over the years, be the cheapest to buy, as if you take care of her, you will be able to sell her for approximately what you paid.

The third alternative is a really old beat, at the top limit of your size range, and the bottom limit of your price range, needing quite a lot of work to get her into reasonable condition. If you are prepared to put a lot of time ard labour into the job, she may prove a good buy, but any large sums of money you spend on her will be completely thrown away, as maintenance will probably be heavy and no amount of money and work will increase her capital value very much.

Lastly there is the possibility of buying a real old wreck with only a couple of season's use left in her. She will be very cheap, and you can sail her to pieces, regarding the money spent as a dead loss, apart from what you may get from a scrap merchant for any lead, copper, etc., she may have If you buy a boat of this type, mind she doesn't fall apart under you when you are sailing, possibly drowning you, and certainly losing anything you might have sold as; scrap

Whatever size and age boat you buy, be sure that the initial cost plus all repairs, alterations etc. is within your price range, and represents a reasonable value for the boat. lost of the'bargains" one sees advertised are bargains for the vendor only. Beware of unusual types of boats which will have only a limited resale market and in particular, beware of conversions.

On buying any boat over about three tons,get a good professional surveyor.
Avoid fisherman and longshoreman - their ideas of a sound boat are usually
optimistic to say the least,and in the more expensive classes, the possession of a favourable surveyors report will often help if you want to borrow money to buy the boat. No matter how small the boat you intend buying, get an independe~.t opinion on her unless you are very well acquainted with all the ills likely to affect a boat. When contemplating buying a larger boat, it will probably pay you to get a friends' opinion before engaging a surveyor, as he may find some defect sufficient for you to reject the boat without the expense of a full survey. There are several good books on the market dealing with the surveying and repairing of old boats, and anybody about to invest in a second hand boat would be well advised to read as many of these as possible. No matter how new a boat is, treat it with suspicion. Even a month old boat may have cracked a rib or two, or she may even have been so badly built that the original owner would not have
her.
Never forget that it is entirely up to you to see that you are getting value for your money. A very few owners may take pity on your lack of funds and let you have a good boat cheap, but these owners are extremely rare, you are most unlikely to meet one. Also, most yacht brokers are acting for the vendors, so treat their remarks with a grain of salt, they want their commission. As they usually value their good reputations they probably won't lead you right up the garden path. One last point to watch, having found a boat at a price you can afford. make sure you can afford to run it when you have paid for her. The larger or older the boat, the more will be your annual maintenance bill.
Finally, always remember - The surveyor and his report.
"Barnacle"

ON LEARNING TO SAIL. BY "BARNACLE"

There may be some new members who have joined the Club this season, hoping to learn to sail.
Learning to sail is not easy. Like riding a bicycle, swimming or walking , it cannot really be taught, but can be learnt only by experience, efter the first few basic principles have been mastered. I do not like naming specific books for people to read, but for once I am going to make an exception and recommend all who wish to learn to sail to buy, read and learn Peter Heaton's book "Sailing".
Having read the book, a person of reasonable intelligence should be able to handle a docile type of boat on a reasonable day, with a competent person aboard to sort out any mistakes before anything serious happens. The finest place to take the first few voyages is the Norfolk Broads. You will probably do some very stupid things, that on a tidal estuary would have serious consequences, without coming to any real harm, and at the end of a week you should have a fair idea of how to handle a boat. If you cannot manage a holiday on the Broads, the next best thing is to find a boat owner who will take you out once or twice, letting you do as much as possible of the handling of the boat. It is not reasonable to expect the owner to let you take the boat away from or pick up a mooring surrounded by other boats, but you can take a couple of empty cans and sinker down to the Doubles and practise picking up moorings to your hearts content. Once you can get a boat on and off its mooring, can sail it on a run without gybing every five minutes, and have a reasonable idea of when a reef is needed, get out on your own, or with another learner, then you will have to make your own decisions. If the boat is of a reasonable tyne, and you do not go too far from Heybridge at first, you should not come to any great harm, and you will rapidly gain confidence, which is what really counts in sailing. Whilst you are Learning, keep away from other boats, particularly racing boats, as much as possible, until you know what you are up to, and keep away from moorings.

When you are certain you are master of your boat, try racing it. You will probably find that you are sailing very badly indeed, and racing,you will have a real incentive to improve your sailing, whereas you could spend years pottering round the creeks without even realising how badly you are sailing.

Be wary of people who offer to teach you to sail, particularly if they expect you to pay for tuition. They will not teach you any more of the theory of sailing than you could get from Heaton's book, in fact they will probably teach you less; and in any sailing club there ought to be at least a few members who will go out with you for your first few sails until you are competent to take a boat out on your own. Experience is the only real teacher, and her charges are sometimes fairly severe in the way of soakings and damaged boats, but you will find that there is often a difference between the theory and practise of getting a boat off a lee shore, or righting a capsized dinghy. The cheapest way to really learn to sail is to join a club and mix with those who sail. Not only will you be able to find people willing to go out with you; you will also be able to profit by the experiences of others. If you see a boat in difficulties, work out for yourself what mistake they have made, and what remedy they should adopt; then if you ever find yourself in similar circum-~ stances you will know the correct action to take.

What is the Officer of the Day?

This club, in common with most other sailing clubs, keeps a duty roster of members to take charge of the dey's racing. This is done because members who are keen enough to serve in this capacity will also generally be active sailing members; it would be unreasonable, even if any one were so public-spirited, to keep hin out of racing for a whole season. Active racing members, especially, should be prepared to take their turn of duty, rather than just hope for someone else to do it for then.
"Officer of the Day means just what it says: he is, for the day, the executive officer of the Sailing Committee, responsible for all matters requiring immediate decision. He may be an ordinary member of the club, and the whole hierarchy of flag-officers may be racing, but to-day he is in charge. He may ask or accept advice from whomsoever he wishes, but he makes the actual decisions of what course to set, whether to shorten it because of a change in conditions, er even if conditions are too rough for racing at all..If there are exceptional circumstances he may postpone the start from its advertised time; for example, if a competitor is unable to reach the line on time for reasons beyond his control~ but all this is subject to his discretion and no one else's, But note the word "discretion''; should he wield his great powers in a tyrannical manner, competing helmsmen may (later) protest to the Sailing Committee; who will, w however, support him in all reasonable cases.

Duties of the Officer of the Day.

The Officer of the Day should be at the Clubhouse an hour before the advertised time of starting the first race

Preparatory.

He must decide the course to be sailed. The start should be to windward whenever possible; helmsmen may be consulted if desired about which course is suitable for the conditions, and how many times it shovld be sailed. He must take the cannons, cartridges, flags, megaphone, course boards and Race Book from the Sailing Secretary's office and set them up on deck in readiness. Exactly five minutes later, the "preparatory" gun is fired, and simultaneously the "Blue Peter! is broken out. If any boat is (wholly or partly) over the starting line, a second (recall) gum is fired. WHAT RIG?. BY "BARNACLE",

Qn rigging a boat, one if confronted with two main alternatives, Gaff or Bermudan? There are of course, also the alternatives of sloop, cutter, ketch, yawl, or schooner, but the points I om going to mention here apply equally to all these. There are also the the alternatives of lug and Gunter rig for small boats and much less widely used, wishbone rigs. #ifty years ago, Bermudan rig had many snags and very few people would use it on a cruiser, but nowadays it is far more reliable proposition. hollow masts, scientifically and lightly stayed, with a well designed track and a halliard winch enable one man to deal with a large cruisers mainsail in a manner which would astound the Victorian yachtsman. Aerodynamically, the Bermudan sail, with its long, tight luff end high aspect ratio is much more efficient proposition on the wind than a gaff sail, but off the wind its efficiency falls off, although with a well stayed mast, a wonderful assortment of headsails of large area can be used.
Nowadays, the windage of a Bermudan mast is less that of a gaff mast for a boat of comparable size, as it has only the sail to support, and no heavy gaff, If the gaffer has a fidded topmast and not a pole mast, its windage will be even more increased.
The centre of gravity of a gaff mast is usually a little lower than that of a Bermudan, but the mast itself is heavier and gives a greater overturning moment when the boat heels. With sail set and topsail uo, the centre of gravity of the gaff rig is considerably higher then that of a comparable Bermudan Rig. even today, there are a surprisingly large number of people who maintain that a Bermudan mainsail can be hoisted and lowered only when the boat is head to the wind. This is the most utter piffle. If the mast track and slides are in good order and well greased, the sail can be raised or lowered on ANY point of sailing, though on a run care must be taken to avoid getting the headboard under the shrouds. I should hate to try hoisting a fifteen toppers gaff mainsail on a run, with a hundred pounds of gaff crashing from side to side as the boat rolls! Recent circumnavigators have shown uo fairly clearly the fact that Bermudan rig is slowly but steadily ousting gaff from the position of the best rig for the long distance cruiser. Le Toumelin found that "Kuruns" gaff jaws chewed into his mast in an alarming manner, and he was forever putting up chafing pieces. Tom Worth and Eric Hiscock both chose Bermudan rig for the boats they had built for their circumnavigations.
Humphrey Barton proved that two men, neither young, can sail a well designed bermudan rigged boat direct from England to low York, and "Samuel Pepys" "Cohoel! and others have shown the speeds at which Bermudan rigged boats can be sailed over long distances, mainly downwind.
Ease of handling" is a common advantage claimed for gaff rig, but I fail to see how two halliards (usually rigged with different purchases) are easier than one, end what could be simpler for reefing than to ease away on one halliard and wind the sail round the boom with a worm gear = no fighting with maddened, sodden canvas no reefing pennants to reeve; and above all, no reef points to forget to untie when letting out the reef. Anyway, it would seem that gaff rig is not all that easy to handle for very few people now go to the trouble of setting the topsail, which is indisputably the most efficient sail on a gaff cutter.
Un small boats, gunter rig is often a useful com>sromise, as it enables one to use short spars, which can all be stowed inside the boat, as on the "Heron! whilst still having most of the features of Bermudan rig. Lug rig is easily stowed away and hoisted, but tends not to be quite so efficient as gunter rig, bit one cannot really make comparisons here as there are such a wide variety of different shaped lug sails in use today, some of which are very efficient indeed. fn conclusion, it would seem that if one is after efficiency and ease of handling, Bermudan rig is a must, but fortunately, most of us sail for pleasure, and I hope it will be many years before gaff rig disappears, for what makes a finer sight than a full rigged cutter with jackyard topsail and a bowsprit a third the length of the hull.

NAVIGANS June.
CONVERSIONS BY BARNACLE.

Quite a lot of people convert boats these days, and maybe some of you are contemplating so doing. ‘hint very carefully before you do, for you might waste a lot of time and money.
Sone types of conversion are worth doing and worth doing well, but most are not. One popular misconception is that a good cruiser can be easily and cheaply made from a ships lifeboat. A little thought will soon show the truth here. A ships lifeboat is very carefully designed and built for one purpose and one purpose only the saving of life. 1t is not intended to sail or motor fast, or indeed at all in any Direction other than downwind, and nothing you can do will make a good sailing boat out of a lifeboat. If you build up the topsides and make a motor cruiser, you will probably finish up with a dangerously unstable boat A short walk round Heybridge Basin will reveal several glorious examples of this type of marine death trap. Also, ships'lifeboats come on the market only when they have reached the end of their useful life, or when the ship is rebuilt or scrapped.
reasonable conversions have been made from lifeboats at reasonable costs, but they are exceptional, end they have all required a lot of time and work, almost as much as building a new boat, and their final value is not high Host boats were originally designed and built for a specific purpose, and any attempt to convert them to any radically different use will usually end in
failure.
The three types of conversion which are worth tackling are the barge to to houseboat, smack to yacht, and ex-racer to cruiser. The first mentioned is very well worth while if you can find a sound barge at a fair price. Since Ionides day, many have been converted to excellent homes, and sailed regularly round the Thames Estuary by their proud omers, but the heyday of the sailing barge has now alas gone, and it would not be easy to find one in good enough condition to to worth spending a lot of money.
Very good yachts can be made out of old fishing smacks, but give the hull @ thorough survey before you start-Inshore fishing from small smacks is a dying
industry, and the boats are dying with it - most are dead and few of those still
in use have a great expectation of life. Decks . BY "BARNACLE"

One part of a cruiser which often receives much less consideration than it deserves is the deck. ALL too often one sees and hears of otherwise good boats getting a bad name due to an inadequate deck.
A-cruisers deck must be much more than just a ton to the hull. 14 must be capable of withstanding severe shock loads from breaking waves and falling crew, 1t must keel» water out of the boat, and it must be capable of carrying quite a lot of the sailing stresses,
Also it must be strong enough to hold fairleads, a lashed down dinghy, mooring cleats and other fittings, though all these items have special local strengthing the deck must still play its part in transmitting the loading to the remainder of the hull structure. Finally, it must be surfaced and laid out to make it safe to walk on, and easy to get about without fear of slipping or
tripping.
There are tures main methods of decking a conventionally built cruiser, Viz. laid caulked planks, tongued and grooved planks canvassed over, end plywood sheets. All three methods need adequate deck beams to support them, and within
reasonable limits, the more camber the better - a lot camber may make the deck
seem awkward when the boat is on a mooring, and things left on deck may roll overboard, but when the boat is sailing heeled well over the camber is a distinct advantage. Also, the whole deck structure is better able to resist the impact of breaking seas,
All three methods require good hanging knees on as many of the beams as possible, laid or canvassed decks also require good lodging Knees, particularly in the way of the mast. A plywood deck does not require lodging knees, but it must be very well fastened to the deck beams and topsides.
The tongued and grooved deck is the easiest and cheapest to fit, and with good non slip deck paint on the canvas should »rove quite adequate. The life of the canvas is very limited, and once it begins to go, troubles start. Any water getting under the canvas will almost certainly run along between the wood and canvas and leak out yards away from where it entered, (usually over the middle of a bunk, or over the toilet), this makes the leaks hard to trace, and often signs of rot in the deck are the first indication that the water is seeping along it. Once a canvassed deck starts rotting, it will spread the rot to the hull and cabin sides very rapidly.
& well kept laid teak deck is the envy of all who behold it, and should last the life of the boat. However, it must be given frequent attention, and washed over every day in hot weather if it is to remain tight. A laid deck, whether of teak or pine, shovld never be varnished ( unless you really want to slide overboard), and most paint finishes will get slippery when they are wet. The seams must be left well filled with marine glue, for once a laid deck starts*w leaking the water will run along the caulking like a wick, ond although a teak deck is not likely to rot, the beams on which it is laid can and will rot quickly once regular leaking starts. All »lanked decks work as the boat sails, and often leak as well, but dry up when the boat stops sailing hard. A bit of lateral give in the deck is not altogether a bad thing, as it enables the boat to "“wrigele+ through and over rough seas.
A plywood deck should be ‘almost leakproof, particularly if all the sheets forming it are scarpled together with a good resin glue, but such a deck is not so easily fitted to a boat with extreme shear as a planked deck, as the ply sheets object to the double curvature involved. One big disadvantage of a ply deck is that it can work only at the edges. This greatly reduces the possibility of leaks, but also greatly increases the strength required in securing the deck to the hull.
It is not easy to achieve a good non slip finish on a ply deck without using a “loaded! paint. Of these, probably the best is epoxied resin loaded
with sand - it is hard on hands and knees if you do slip, but slipping is not
Likely.
One of Britain's leading offshore racing skippers has expressed the opinion that in a few years plywood will render planked decks as obsolete as the old "planked on edge! gaff cutters for ocean racing, and it certainly seems that a ply deck can offer many advantages. Plywood is really the only satisfactory

deck material for surfacing with fibreglass, as a planked deck will very soon work and split off the fibreglass.
whatever type of construction used, the deck must be at least as strong as the topsides of the boat, if not stronger, for when sailing it has to do just about the same work, and it does not have the benefit of the extreme double curvature found in the hull to give it extra strength.
Next month I hove to be able to mention some points to watch concerning deck Layout.

Barnacle. DECK LAYOUT.

‘Deck Layouts vary enormously from boat to boat, even on recognised None designs! like the local Blackwater Sloops, which can be seen with full width cabins and low foredecks, full width cabins and raised foredecks with and without forehatches, and low decks with a narrow coach roofs. So far, I. have not seen one with fully raised topsides and reverse sheer, but one day perhaps one will be built. .The performance of these boats is not greatly affected by the differences in deck layout, but the accommodation and ease of handling is most certainly affected, as(stupidily enough! ) is the handicap rating.
Each type of deck layout” has its own peculiar advantages. and disadvantages, and when buying a boat a lot.of thought is needed to decide which are the’ most important factors. A full width cabin and raised foredeck give the best internal accommodation, make the cabin seem Far mere Specious than it really is, and’ also provide the easiest deck to lay, the 7° “4 likely to leak and the strongest. against this, picking up moorings is not quite so easy (unless a star type. buoy is used) and the windage is increased ( so slightly as not to matter). Also a flush deck of this type gives good space for sunbathing and carrying a small dinghy. Safety on deck is greatly increased by liferail all around, and particularly by & pulpit.
4& full width cabin and lowered foredeck gives fairly good accommodation inside ns hull, and so long as reasonable bulwarks are fitted, provides a safe little well for anchor and handsail work. On a boat of reasonable freeboard, a pulpit is a desirable feature. The greatest disadvantage of this type of deck layout is its tendency to leak at the break of the cabin front. When sailing hard in rough water the nearly vertical flat surface of the cabin front is hit hard end often by fairly»solid lumps of water, and it will not be long before some annoying leaks develop, particularly if the bulwarks are faired up to cabin top level in a smooth curve. No matter how large a scupper is cut in the bulwark, water will still be trapped in the corner, thus aggravating the leaks (which ard almost certain to appear over the bunks). Snags with both the above types of deck layout are the height from cockpit floor to cabin top and the difficulty of finding a really good position for jib sheet cleats and winches. If they are on the cabin top they are liable to get horribly in the way, and if they are on the bulkhead, they are quite likely to catch in your trouser leg as you step down into the cockpit. Then it is a question of which is the stronger, the cleat or your trousers! Either way you will most likely finish up head downwards in the cockpit Cont'd Page 3

or if the boat is sailing herd, overboard. A low deck with raised cabin set inboard looks very nice, and without liferails, provides the safest deck for working on, but it ruins the accommodation on a small boat and is liable to be a prolific source of leaks and eventually rot. It is the most difficult type of deck to lay, and also the WEAKEST Ts The longer the coachroof, the less the transverse strength of the deck, and if the coachroof is extended forward of the mast some really hefty knees will be needed to take the sailing forces.
For ultimate strength, ease of -laying and maximum accommodation, full reverse sheer is the best tyne of deck, but it is advisable to fit a small doghouse to break the monotony of the otherwise bare deck to keen water from running straight down the main hatch and into the cockpit. On the size cruiser considered her a flush decked normal sheer boot would be impracticable as it would give no usable space down below. If you went 2 really effective means of keeping the inside of the boat wet, and reducing the strength of the foredeck, then fit forehatch . It will also help trio uo the unwary when they go forward, but will serve no useful function on e smell cruiser. Several designers claim you can stand in the hatchway to deal with headsails, but if the foredeck is so unsafe that this is necessary, then the boat should not be at sea. A forehatch on a larger boat does provide a quick means of disposing of redundant headsails, but on boats of under five tons it is just as quick to push them through the main hatch. If the interior layout has been well planned they can easily be stowed away from there, For maximum ease of handling the deck should be kept as clear as possible. boxes or belaying »pins should be provided for halliard falls, and mooring* abouts should be kept as close as possible to the edges of the deck. sheets should run either along the deck edges or along the cabin sides whenever possible. Fairleads right in the middle of the side deck are often nice for use with certain headsails, but are a nuisance when going forward in a hurry. Ventilators should be fitted where they will not be tri>.ed over, and where they will not foul sheets, or
mooring warps - not always an easy job on a small cruiser.
Unless the deck has a very good non skid surface and a generous camber it is a good idea to fit two teak strips along the foredeck to provide an angle in which to tread when the boat is heeled well over, but don't forget to break then at intervals so they can't trap water.

With the season drawing to a close one can reflect a little on the performance of the "elements" this year. Mother nature has a very great effect on our pastime, and in some respects 1960 bore strong resemblance to 1958 in its antics. Those of us who viewed the synoptic charts daily with their long string of depressions while the proverbial Azores "high!" struggled in vain, hopefully reminding ourselves that it couldn't last, but it did; the meteorological term "depression" has a truer ring about it at times than the originators could have anticipated. But to a more practical outlook, it behoves all of us who venture upon the water whether in a dinghy or a cruiser, to learn something about what is colloquially called " the weather ", and to read and interpret the signs in the sky. Meteorology can be a fascinating subject, one does not have to go in to the subject deeply, just enough to be useful for our purpose. We do not anticipate having to prepare "teephi" diagrams or worry about adiabatic lapse rates before we venture forth, these are for the professional meteorologist, but to under- stand the behaviour of depression and anticyclones, to recognize a frontal system as it passes through, and a squall if it makes a beeline for you. There is an excellent pamphlet written by Lt.Com. Rantzen just for people like us. Although the writer like many other people has noted the climatic changes that have occurred over the years and now commented upon in the appropriate quarters, the main interest still is what is it going to be like tomorrow or " what will it be like when I'm down the other end of the river’.

Helmsmanship and Seamanship.
By Barnacle.

The last few years has seen the rapid growth of an entirely new breed “TM
of "sailors" - the "dinghy boys". Many dinghy sailors are absolutely first rate
seaman, but, alas, there are many others who cannot be called seaman at all. Having learnt how to persuade their fragile little plywood box along at something approaching its maximum speed, and picked up a few of the racing
rules (often far to few) off they go - a menace to themselves and to everybody
else on the water.
Having won a race or two they consider themselves fine helmsmen, as maybe they are, but, they also consider themselves seamen, and that they most certainly are not. One has only to stand on Maldon Quay for half an hour to
observe them at their worst - having got their boats into the water, and sail
up, off they go (if the wind is in the right direction!) If the wind is onto the Quay, then the fun starts (if you can call watching their boat damaging antics fun) they will try anything sooner than paddle well clear before hoisting sail, then after the race they frequently ram the quay hard rather than get their sails off and blow in under poles. Put them ashore on a nicely shelving lee shore, with a few moored boats about, and one is all set for a first class pantomime, These little tricks may be all’ right with their ultra light weight. plywood boats in calm sheltered waters, but some day, having learnt their bad vw habits, they may try similar tricks with a cruiser weighing 20 tons, in rough breaking water. Then the Coroner's verdict will be "Death by Misadventure" and not "Suicide" as it should be, and the insurance company will have a heavy claim to settle.
Their knowledge of boat maintenance is often as sketchy as their knowledge of boat handling. Rigging is something one buys from a yacht chandlers — knots are something one might have to use on a big boat, and splicing is a magic art learnt only after a couple of hundred years at sea. Damage to the hull can be
repaired only by the boatyard, or, a far more dangerous attitude, - " Where's
the hammer and the tin tacks - I'll soon patch that!'.
There are many other things about which these charming people know nothing. They know more or less what the weather is doing at the moment, but why, and what it is likely to doing the near future is a complete mystery to them. Many of them have never heard of the International Regulations for Preventing Collisions at Sea, let alone read them, then they wonder why the owner of the eleven ton yawl cursed them so heartily as they wriggled out from under his bowsprit. They do not realise that a boat of any size is very restricted in the upper reaches of the river, and they expect a large and heavy yacht to turn in an impossible distance or stop dead.
Navigation, chart reading, signalling by morse or flag wagging, buoyage systems, and the wealth of maritime lore and tradition are all closed books to then.
But worst of all, they are utterly lacking in common courtesy and good
manners on the water.
Not all these horrible undesirables sail dinghies. They are to be found

Cont'd Page 3.

PAGE

in even greater numbers among the "Marine Motorists" particularly the owners of little outboard runabouts, and they are certainly to be found sailing larger racing cruisers.
Now I have deliberately been sarcastic and painted a very black picture. I know of no dinghy owner who has all the faults listed, but there are many who have one or more of these faults, and it is up to all of us who race dinghies to see that our behaviour on the water cannot offend others, and to endeavour to broaden our Knowledge of nautical matters. There is much more to sailing than just racing round a few buoys near the clubhouse, and much of it is easily learnt.
To learn the other persons point of view, what could be better than to cadge a sail with him?. A day trawling down river, or crewing on a cruiser racing from Mersea to Burnham will not only be instructional, it will be jolly good fun.
I hope sincerely that no one reading this will take offence — I am commenting on a very noticeable and very regrettable trend, not " getting at " anybody, and I hope that anybody who might think he is being " got at " will reread the article in the spirit in which it is written.

Unfortunately the end of another season is upon us, and most of us are thinking of laying up our boats. Judging by the sad and sorry sights one sees along the river every winter, it would pay a good many people to think a trifle harder about the business of laying up. No boat is improved by being left just

as she was at the end of the last sail, with paint beginning to flake off, damp bilges, damp sails and odds and ends of gear scattered all over the place. If the hull is to be left afloat, it should be stripped as far as possible, and covered over so as to leave adequate ventilation without letting in the rain and snow. If it is impossible to arrange for an adequate cover, try and give the whole boat a coat of paint or varnish before leaving her, This will almost certainly be in a very poor state by the spring, but the paint underneath will not have suffered. Some owners haul out their boats in the Autumn and give them a coat of emulsion paint all over, then when they come down to fit out, their topsides are in really good condition. If you are laying up ashore, rake certain the inside of the boat is dry before you put the cover on. It is not enough merely to pump and sponge out the bilges. The whole of the boat must be thoroughly washed with plenty of fresh water to remove all traces of salt. All floorboards and bunk boards should be taken up and scrubbed, and lockers should be emptied and left open. Floorboards should be left up for the winter, and all ports and ventilators fully opened so that the whole of the hull is well ventilated. Mechanical fittings such as pumps and winches should be well cleaned, again taking great care to remove all traces of salt, then they can be greased and left for the winter. Qn removing the mast it should be examined very carefully to see whether it needs any repairs, then after labelling and removing all the rigging the mast,boom, spreaders and any other spars should be given mw coat of varnish before being stored away in a dry shed. When stowing away the spars make certain they are well supported so they can't bend. All wire rigging should be examined for signs of trouble and carefully coiled and stowed away. If possible the rigging should be well oiled before it is put away, but if this cannot be done it should be taken out and oiled during the winter. A small boats rigging can be stored in a large biscuit tin, then if a spare tin is kept handy the rigging can be taken out and oiled one or two wires each night and then put in the second tin so you can be certain that each wire does get oiled. This process can advantageously be repeated two or three times during the winter. If a large enough diameter drum can be readily obtained, all the wires can be coiled down in it, a quart or so of linseed oil poured in and the lid sealed on. Then if the drum is rolled over every so often all the wires will get well oiled with no more trouble than kicking the drum round the store shed. Looked after this way ordinary galvanised wire will last indefinitely, but if it has been neglected and allowed to rust, you won't get much life from it. Ropes should be well washed, and about the easiest way of doing this is to coil them all in a large tank, put a hose in and run fresh water through them for a day or two, after which they should be hung up to dry before being finally coiled, and stowed of %y for the winter. Sails deserve more care than your best clothes, for they are“Tar more expensive, and one day your life may depend on the condition of your sails. If you can't manage to wash, dry, repair and store your sails properly, then hand them in to the sailmaker, He won't charge much, and you can be certain your sails will be well cared for. All small parts like blocks, jamb cleats etc. Should be taken off the boat and taken home for the winter. It is quite surprising how much work can be done at home at odd moments, then if you have laid up the hull, spars and rigging properly, your fitting out in the spring will take only two or three weekends, so their is no reason why even the larger cruisers should not be ready to sail by Easter. If, however, you have been lazy and com skimped the work at laying up time, you must expect to be faced with a lot of unnecessary hard work in the spring, and the replacement of gear that would otherwise have been good for several more seasons. Also, never forget that if you once let your boat really deteriorate you will never be able to get her back Lo good condition, and her resale value will fall.

A Note on Tidiness.
By Barnacle

Has your boat got a proper place for everything and everything in its place? If not, why not? ,On @ boat it is essential that there should be a place for every item of equipment carried, otherwise chaos will result. A locker or cupboard under the aft deck is not enough - it will merely confine the chaos to a smaller area. One has only to look into a badly stowed food locker aboard a large cruiser after an inadvertent gybe to realise what an unholy mess can be caused by a few broken jars and upset packets. If the crew have any tendencies towards sea-sickness, such a mess will most certainly be the last straw for them, and it can be avoided so easily. Once one item in a locker works loose it will bang about knocking all the other things out of their places, breaking whatever it can until finally the entire contents of the locker fling themselves against the door, break it open and land in the bilges.
In the cool of the evening, can you readily lay your hands on a dry sweater, or is it stuck down the bottom of your kitbag under a load of useless junk? Usually when you want anything on & boat you want it in a hurry: so as far as possible all stow2ge systems should be arranged so that nothing is covered by something else.
Binoculars and camera should be kept ready to hand at all times, out should be kept dry and in a place where they are not likely to get
1 damaged.
Untidiness below on a boat usually results in @ great deal of inconvenience and unpleasantness, but untidiness on deck can have serious, even fatal consequences. An improperly stowed anchor can very easily punch a hole in 4 boats planking, and a badly stowed warp will tend to foul everything, maybe even your legs, throwing you overboard and holding you there, head under water with your feet secured to the deck by a fine old tangle. Serve you jolly well right. Next time, if there is a next time, perhaps you'll stow your warps properly. There is only one way of stowing a warp so you can be certain that it will run out clearly whenever you need it, and that is the flat "Flemish Flake". The men on the grain barques rounding Cape Horn did'nt risk their lives in the scuppers flaking down the falls of sheets and braces merely to make the boat look tidy, they did it bed32use their safety depended on the smooth running out of those falls. A snarled up main brace could mean the sails would be taken aback and the masts broken, and it was only by flaking down the ropes neatly that the men could guarantee that they would run out freely when needed. yet. Boathook and fenders should be handy when manoeuvring in the — vicinity of other boats, but ther must be so placed that they cannot foul the jib sheets or the anchor warps. Often when kedging a boat against the tide, using a dinghy to lay out the anchor, one is tempted not to bother to coil the warp properly as you haul up to the ked¢ge, but the mess you can get into if a turn of the kedge warp catches a flake of the bower anchor, or if you merely drop the whole lot straight into the dinghy will soon make you wish you has'nt been so lazy. It may seem a waste of time spending five minutes on the foredeck in: . pouring rain coiling down & warp that is to be used again directly, but it is far less of a waste of time than spending half en hour in the dinghy trying to sort out a tangle. If you manage to sort out the tangle without letting go of the anchor or losing an oar or rowlock, only your temper will suffer, but there is & great risk of losing an oar whilst struggling with the wet, muddy rope, and then you are in a
pickle.
Even the most unlikely things can cause trouble. One offshore racer found herself in serious difficulties when a worn burgee halliard broke and the loose end wrapped around the main halliard in 4 rising gale, preventing them from reefing. Accidents like this can occur so quickly, and the only possible way of preventing them is to aim at absolute perfection throughout the whole boat. If you race, the nearer you can get to perfection, the better will be your chances of winning.

"ODDS AND ENDS"

When working on a boat, one often runs into unexpected problems, which can tax ones ingenuity to the utmost.
One minor one, which seems to baffle many people, is getting a good coat of paint or varnish on the underside of a wooden handrail on a cabin top without getting paint a11 over the whole cabin top. Masking with newspaper and sellotape is the obvious and easy way of keeping the paint clear of the coachroof, but does not help in getting it onto the underside of the rail.

An old toothbrush can provide an excellent, although slow way of doing this, or a piece of thin plywood or metal can be used to hold the bristles of an ordinary brush up against the underside of the rail. Neither method is very easy or quick, but both will give a good finish 1f done.with care. A toothbrush with a bent handle is often the only way ot getting paint behind bilge stringers and other internal fittings.

The inside of a centreplate case is another brute to deal with, but this can usually be done adequately without removing the plate by securing 2 piece of rag or thin plastic sponge material to the end of 3 long thin strips of metal. It will prove a messy, but effective method. The mess can be kept off the inside of the boat by judicious use of paper, canvas or polythene sheet, and off the operators hands by a pair of cheap plastic gloves.

Some people suffer terribly from cold hands when sailing or working on their boats early in the season. Those who heave tried wearing gloves will know that they do not help as they soon get soaked, but have you tried a pair of woolen gloves with rubber or plastic gloves over, with the storm cuffs of an oilskin jacket pulled down well over them? The gloves must be well chosen for fit, and feel a little clumsy at first, but one soon gets used to them, and mooring up and sail stowing is infinitely more easy than with numbed fingers.

Many people would rather put splice in the ends of their mooring ropes then a whipping, but are put off by the fear that the end might not pull freely out of a ring bolt when casting off. This fear is groundless if the splice has been properly tapered off to finish, taking anything up to a dozen tucks cutting away a few fibres from each strand after each tuck. If the resultant splice still feels too bumpy, than make the first three tucks eg inst the Ley in the usual way, “né finish off tucking with the lay going round and round the same strand 38 in % wire splice. Plastic ropes can be dealt with in exactly the same way, but it is advisable to put in -t least a couple more tucks thin with natur2l fibre, and to serve tightly over the whole of the finished splice, not forgetting to stretch the rope “s much as possible before: s serving. when buying rope always remember that the best is cheapest in the long run. Sisal con not be relied on after one . years use, hemp or monills should least four or five years if well cared for, but nylon, terylene or polythene can be fitted and for- gotten so long as they are not likely to get chafed.

Melon is ideal 1 for anchor and-TMooring ropes, dinghy painters, personal lifelines and s2il tiers, but should never be used for halliards or sheets which ire normally cleated *s it stretches so much. Many people us? nylon sheets deliberately so that they will stretch when a sudden puff hits the sails, and this might be quite
+4
a good ides, but other people prefer a "hard" sheet with no "bounce"

4/

When tying a knot in nylon be very careful to tie a good knot, for nylon can prove very slippery, letting the knot come un- done, and if a fair strain is put on the rope a badly tied knot can pull so tight as the rope stretches that it is impossible to undo it once the strain is off the rope. A new natural fibre rope that refuses to coil neatly can be tamed by towing it astern for a mile or two, but many sisal warps will not coil well until they have been used a number of times, then just as you've got it into a perfect coil, vou will probably notice it's beginning to rot and chafe dangerously! Never rely on an old rope for a warp, halliard, sheet or dinghy painter. Replace it and use up the old one for something else. A flat turks head in old rope makes a very good teapot stand if small, or small mat; a longer warp can be flaked down and to a canvas backing for a doormat: a pair of rope soled sandals can be made out of an old halliard; the tiller and rudder can be decorated with turks heads, or more fenders can be made from your old warps; or you con keep it lying round to practice- time tying knots until you are confident you can always manage to tie a bowline properly in a muddy warp, using only one hand, and in total darkness. When you can manage a bowline under these conditions, try 3 fishermen's bend!

STABILITY. by Barnacle.

There is Probably: more muddled re about a boats' stability than about anything else concerning boats. It has been said that the twin drop keels, ( in one design of cruisers ) gave her double the stability, fortunately, it was not stated of what the stability was doubled. Also, many people consider that outside ballast gives more stability than inside. Both statements have some elements of truth, but both are such vague generalities as to be almost
meaningless.
There is one thing, and one thing only that determines. a boats stability, and that is the relationship between its centre of gravity and centre of ‘buoyancy. If this relationship is the same for two boats of equal weight at equal angles of heel, then the boats are equally stable, whether they have one _or twenty drop keels, whether the ballast is lead, iron, concrete or shingle and whether it is outside, in the bilges or half way up the mast.
The stability of a boat can and does vary a great deal according to the
‘angle of heel. Many racing have very little stability at small angles of heel, ‘but once they begin to dip their deck edge their stability increases rapidly, whereas boats like dinghies have a high initial stability, but lose it as they heel until they finally become unstable and capsize. The various classes of catamarans provide some fine examples of this tyne of behaviour. wy On a cruiser, the stability of a given hull at any angle of heel up to that at which the deck touches the water can be increased only. by lowering the centre of gravity, which can be most easily achieved by replacing iron and inside ballast with lead hung below the keel. An equally stable hull of different form can be designed, with inside ballast, by changing the lines such that at a given angle of heel the centre of buoyancy is higher up the hull. The stability of a boat at a small angle of heel has a great effect on its performance in rough water, and it is not generally a good thing to aim for a high initial stabil-ty achieved by using a hull form where the position of the centre of buoyancy moves rapidly as the angle of heel changes, as such a boat ‘will roll with every passing wave, straining its mast and rigging, whereas a boat which relies on a low centre of gravity for its stability will remain fairly steady. At greater angles of heel stability can be readily increased by increasing the freeboard. Although this raises. the centre of gravity slightly, it raises the position of the centre of buoyancy by greater amount, but when applying a high freeboard to achieve good ultimate stability, a very careful eye must be kept on the effects at small angles of heel of raising the centre of gravity, as it is quite possible to achieve negative stability at angles of about twenty degrees.
‘Once @ boat heels over so far as to get. water*on deck, the position of the .centre of buoyancy may well be lowered with increasing angle of heel, so good freeboard will help greatly by increasing the angle to which a boat must heel before water comes on deck.
On watching an ocean race, the two most noticeable features of the more modern boats are their ‘“high freeboard and the simplicity ape of their rigging and
deck —
Many people think that raising and lowering a Boats: centreplate will have a great effect, but not much, as.will readily be appreciated when it is realised that even on a lightly built boat with a heavy plate its weight is rarely more than about a tenth of.the. total all up weight, and: its centre of gravity moves through only about thirty to thirty three inches, so She the centre of gravity of the whole boat is lowered by only a few inches.’
All calculations concerning. stability. can be rendered virtually meaningless by the effects of Waves, and it is quite possible for an "uncapsizeable"TM boat to be turned upside dow by unusual waves, as happened to Voss, Wray, Miles Smeaton and doubtless to many others. FREE BOARD. BY "BARNACLE
moon -— om

Last month I dealt briefly with the effect of freeboard on stability, end this month I propose to consider a few more aspects of this controversial topic. <A sailing boat of given size must displace a given amount of water, and her weight must equal that of the water displaced. Almost all conventionally built boats have to be ballasted down to their marks, and the lighter the hull can be incorporated in.the ballast, thus giving greater stability and driving power. One way of keeping hull weight down is to keen the hull as small as possible for a given displacement, and since the length and breadth of the hull above water cannot be altered, this means keeping down the freeboard. This low freeboard gives an added bonus in that windage is also reduced, but it has very many snags. Accommodation below will be reduced, and at more than slight angles of heel the deck edge will be under water, and there will be the added drag of the rigging cutting through the water sléwing the boat down. Also any weight of water on deck is liable to find its way below. and designers of modern offshore racers are giving ample freeboard to keep their boats as dry as possible. The. extra windage is of little account as it is still small compared with the sail area, ond is often masked by the waves, The conventional sheerline owes its origin to two factors, the difficulties of building other shapes, ond the uses to which the boats were put. Primitive man's hollow tree trunks and basket work coracles_ had flat sheerlines,
but as’ soon as boats began to be built with planks, the .
conventional sheer resulted, since it is ist virtually impossible to get any worthwhile beam into’a boat without finishing up with a hollow sheer, for otherwise the planks yy would be impracticably broad in the centre and narrow = at the ends. .
The when boats were used for commercial, purposes, the hollow sheer had its uses. The high bow was needed to keep the seas off the deck, and a high stern to keep out following waves, but amidships the deck was low to facilitate cargo handling, and to keep the weight of the guns as low as possible. Later, the fishing boats from which our present day yachts are descended had a high bow so they could lie safely to their gear during rough weather, and low freeboard amidships so the nets could be hauled over the bulwarks. The present day designer, able to build his hulls of a single sheet of moulded plywood. or fibreglass can readily produce any sheerline he wishes, and he has not got to worry about keeping guns low or the
difficulties of hauling a ton of. fish over the side, so he has a free hand to |
produce the sheerline of greatest benefit to the yachtsman. A first essential is to keen the seas off the deck as much as possible, and since it is usually in the vicinity of the chain plates that the heaviest water comes aboard, due to the difficulty ‘of sailing a-boat any closer into true running seas, it is there that the greatest freeboard will be needed. The stem must be kept to a reasonable height, but the stern can be lower, as long experience has shown that a boat with
bad lines aft will be liable to be pooped in a following sea, and that 6a keep the . water of the deck the stern would have to be impracticably high, so the current dl trend “is to keep the stern small, to offer the least resistance to the impact of a following sea,These requirements have resulted in the "powder horn" sheer of the MK.2 silhouete and the reverse sheer of the "Debutante"; both very practical
sheerlines offering the best chances of dry deck, together with the worthwhile |
bonus of more room below. Another bonus is that the overall strength of the hull is increased as the curve of the deck is in opposition to that of the keel,
and
the hull is better able to resist the sagging strains of heavy seas breaking on deck. Many people have some very peculiar ideas about reverse sheer, ond imagine that it makes a boat more liable to bury its bows. When sailing a Debutante heeled over it certainly looks as if she is going to bury her bows, as the weather deck edge slopes down to the stem head at a very odd angle, but in fact she has quite a high stem and is less likely to bury her bows than a small cruiser of similar size and more orthodox design. Another great advantage of reverse sheer is that water which finds its way onto the foredeck tends to rm off over the sides instead of all running aft and trying to flood the cockpit. The difference in comfort between reverse and conventional sheer is most noticeable if you ever happen to be to leeward of a couple of otherwise similar boats going well in a good breeze — I had it brought home to me when I noticed a Buchanan designed boat, I think it was a Yeoman, beating up off Bradwell with ‘water Swilling along both Side decks and the crew ll huddled in the cockpit, whilst on a Helen of Troy class boat with its foot or more extra freeboard the owners wife or daughter was lying in the sun on the lee side deck, although both boats were heeled to about the same angle. Wave tops licked the covering board of the Helen of Troy, but she kept her deck dry, and maling due allowance for the difference in size seemed to be going every bit as well as the Yeoman.

BEAM. By "Barnacle".

Having briefly discussed freeboard, let us now consider a few aspects of that other controversial dimension, beam.
Many British yachtsm\¥en seem to consider that the beam of a boat should be kept as Low as possible, and they are to be seen sailing with their boats heeled over at absurd angles in the lightest of winds, or sitting below without room to stretch their legs. They are prepared to put up with these discomforts because a reduction in beam means a reduction in wetted area and their boat will be faster (or so they hope). In fact this is not true, as many American yachts have shown by beating the best British designs, boat for boat, in offshore races. Two of the reasons for this success are their greater initial stiffness, which enables better use of their sail area to be made, and their less violent motion which results in less crew fatigue on a long race. Also on the current handicap formula a moderate beam will help to reduce a boats rating, and certain designers are at last beginning to take advantage of this. One reason for the popularity of the "plank on edge" in this country was the use of the Thames Measurement formula to assess a boats rating. Since this formula uses beam squared as a multiplying factor it was obviously highly desirable to keep beam as low as possible. The tonnage given by this formula rises steadily as beam varies between about a quarter and a half the length, but once the beam exceeds three quarters of --. the length, the tonnage drops off rapidly until a circular vessel achieves a Thames tonnage of zero; — very handy for avoiding harbour dues, but of little other
value! - In fact, if you really want to baffle harbour masters, build yourself a
boat whose beam is greater than its length, then they*1l have to pay you to moor it in their harbours as it will have a large negative Thames Tonnage. (But mind they don't charge you on your register tonnage, which will be considerable!) This most peculiar tonnage rule, with its evil effect on design, was copied from the rule for ass&essing a merchant ships tonnage, i.e. the number of tons of wine she could carry. At the time this rule was evolved most ships were of very Similar form, so simple measurements of length, beam and depth, with a constant correction factor for A hull form, gave quite accurate results. Then it was noticed that the depth was usually about half the beam, and since it was awkward to measure depth, as the hold had to be cleared, half the beam was substituted in the formula. This was the signal for depth to increase and beam to decrease.
On a cruising boat, good beam gives good initial stiffness, and more room below decks. On a beamy boat it is often possible to decrease headroom quite considerably without making the boat seem cramped, as the only time headroom is of value is when you want to stand upright, and when sailing it is usually impossible to do this anyway, whereas it is very pleasant to be able to sit down and stretch ones legs out full length.
Not only does greater beam usually give a stiffer hull more capable of standing up to its canvas, it also gives a wider base for the rigging, thus reducing stresses in the mast and shrouds and enabling the boat to carry its canvas longer in a blow. Colin Archer exploited this to the full, and many people are convinced that boats of his design, or that general tyne, are the finest in the world. The impression of solidity and safeness one feels on their incredibly broad decks has to be experienced to be believed.
Now that the Americans have so clearly pointed the way, many of our best ey designers are using greater beam, and the modern racing cruiser can also be a comfortable roomy floating home. Bikes:

an le wee a by "Barnacle"

Archaic Rule though it is, the Thames Measurement Tonnage still gives a fairly good idea of a cruiser's potential accommodation, «t least for the smaller sizes of boat. Since the aft measuring point is the aft side of the rudder post, it conveniently ignores any "dered" space in a lone counter; it takes no account of depth, which in any normal boat. does not greatly effect the number of people who can cruise in reasonable comfort, end it .axes no allowance for ch:rt space, bosun's stores etc., “which often reduce register tonnage to an absurdly low figure. Displacement tonn-re offers no guide et all, when a two-berth Blackwater sloop displaces f.r more than a five-berth, class 2 ocean racer!

Before considering actual sis let us be quits clear whet "accommodation" really means. A boat which is going to do any cruising et all must offer bunks 6 feet 6 inches long and et least twenty inches wide, possibly tapering in at the foot, for each person; a galley with at least two burners capable of Being used whilst the boat is sailing or rolling in a not too sheltered anchorage, and a flat surface et least a foot square on which to prepare meals;
y]

Qn . flat surface on which charts can be laid; and a decently installed toilet. Only when a Do:.t has all these features can she be said to have "accommodé tion for so many ,people". any well-designed cruiser offering "full accommodé tion" hou:d have a permanent chart table which does not form a general working surface, and a toilet shut off in a separate camp:rtment. Adequate storage space for lamps, warps, spare gear, clothes, food end drinking water are obviously essential on any cruiser.

Unless the boat is extremely bluff in the bows, it is not possible to get comfortable bunks within three feet of the stem, nor can they go within two feet of the rudder—post unless the cockpit is far too for aft and excessively cramped. After all it is hardly fair to call a boat a six~berth cruiser if only two people can squeeze into the cockpit. Quarter berths or other partially "buried" bunks must have full sitting headroom over at least two feet of their length.

From these requirements it is obvious that twenty to twenty-one feet overall length (or length to the rudder post) is the minimum into which four berths can be squeezed, with the toilet unscreened and a "bare minimum" galley, using two quarter berths, midships galley, and two settees running up into the bows. Any reasonably—-proportioned t.enty-footer is going to be about 3 tons Thames, and boats below this size can offer accommod: tion for two only. Ab separate compartment for the toilet needs another two to three feet on the length, putting us in the 4-5 ton class. Five bunks can be fitted into twenty-seven feet, using two quarter berths, galley opposite chart table, two settee berths, and toilet and pipe cot in the fo'c'sle. By now we are in the 7-ton range, and a trifle cramped. The extra: space needed to get a second pipe cot into the fo'c'sle expands our boat into a ten-topper, unless we put the toilet opposite the galley (a very bad place for it, as a1ybody who has experienced this arrangement will know) and use a folding chart table over the foot of a settee.

Above about twelve tons, beam end depth have increased to the size where one can contemplate a permanent bunk behind a settee back, or a pipe cot hung above a settee, and it is no longer possible to generalise about size and accommodation. Note that these figures are minimum sizes for a given amount of accommod:tion aad not average. Boats as large as twenty tons often offer accommodation for only three or four (but very spacious accommodations) Some designers try nd cheat by offering such tricks as chart tables folding down over the head of a quarter berth rendering the berth unusable, and gelle.s consisting of a single primus in a box under the bridge deck, or, even worse, a two-burner celor-gas stove screwed to a bulkhead. If only those designers could be compelled to spend wet, stormy month aboard their creations with a full crew of fairly sensitive strangers} The supply of "small cruisers" would almost completely cease!

Potted Pilot. By T.W. Hallam.

Introduction.

If, as has been said, Navigation is an exact science, then Pilotage may I think be truly classified as an Art. Its aim is to enable the intrepid mariner (that's you,) in your vessel, (that's your little ol! tore-out) to sail in safety from point to point around our coasts and
estuaries.

There have been, of course, @ number of excellent books written about the subject,from Homer's Odyssey to the North Sea Pilot Book, Part IV of England, Berwick to the North Foreland).
(Hast Coast Most of these however have been written with the assumption that the user's vessel is 2 300-Ton full-rigged ship, drawing up to eighteen feet. In view of this it is not surprising that pilot books tend to be the gloomiest books written since the Book of Job.

Even those very excellent books written specifically for yachtsmen,

-5-

such as Jack Coote's Fast Coast Rivers and Commander Irving's Yachtsman's Guide to the Thames Estuary, have in mind yachts with a draft up to eight feet or thereabouts. The fantastic increase in the last ten years in the number of small boats, and dinghies, drawing at the most three feet, has I think created a demand for Sailing Instructions of quite a different nature. Many long, and in some cases dangerous, passages for e small boat can be shortened and made safer by using short cuts prohibited to the larger cruisers. It is with this in mind that the writer will try over the next few months to compose a series of articles on pilotage specifically for the owners of the smallest class of vessel.

Normally each article will divide into two parts, the first part being a discussion on pilotage as a general subject, and the second part a specific sat of Sailing Instructions for a particular part of the as warming however; on no account co..st, river or harbour. A should the sketch charts accompanying the Sailing Instructions be used for navigational purposes. Always use proper charts.

Tools of the Trade.

These may be as simple or as elaborate as the desires of the pilot might dictate. First in importance comes the lead line. This consists essentially of a length of well~stretched line with a lead weight at one end and a number of marks along the length to indicate depth. The old-time professional seaman's lead line was long, twenty fathoms, and was marked in a logical, although at first sight rather bewildering system, using pieces of leather and bunting. For our purpose a five fathom length would be ample, with a weight of about three pounds, and marked in fathoms (every six feet to you, mate!) by means of knots; one for one fathom, two knots apaced an inch apart for two fathoms, three for three fathoms and so on. I actually use one knot again for five fathoms on the assumption on that I can tell even on a dark night the difference between six feet and thirty feet of line. Don't put the ‘mots too far apart or you might make a mistake one dark and dirty night. Here, having got you thoroughly tangled up in thirty~-odd feet of recalcitrant line, is where we say, like the old-fashioned movie serial,

SHORT ROUTE TO BRIGHTLINGSEA

To avoid going the long way pound the Bench Head Buoy (Black Conical) when sailing from W. Mersea or Bradwell to Brightlingsea, the following short cut can be used.

Taking the Nass Beacon off VW. Mersea as the point of departure, head due East for 1 mile, when a Green Beacon surmounted by a Triangle will be seen. This marks a wreck and should be left to port about forty yards, Continuing on the same course for 2 miles, a Green Conical Wreck Buoy is taken as the next mark. Give this a fairly wide berth, at least two hundred yards, and leave to port. From here there are two alternative courses. For vessels drewing only a foot or two or if the tide is not approaching low water, alter course to 52° Magnetic end head for No. & Port Hand Red Can Buoy in the River Colne. Alter course up the Colne between the lines of Port Hand Red Can Buoys and Starboard Hand Black Conical Buoys. Should however the tide be low or the vessel draw more than two feet, continue from the Green Conical Wreck Buoy along the same course of Magnetic to the Inner Bench Head-Red Can Buoy with Light-Flashing Red and thence up the
Colne.
Except for the area around the Wreck Buoy ‘x:own as the Hills one might expect to find not less than three feet at any state of the
tide.
