BALANCE By "Barnacle",

The balance of a boat is most important, and yet it is a subject on which one finds a surprisingly wide variety of different views, many of apparently equal merit. The first essential is that the hull should be balanced, i.e. that on heeling she should keep a straight course.» Endeavours to fulfil this requirement have led to some terrible hull shaves. Obviously cylindrical hull will be so balanced, but is hardly likely to make a successful boat, whereas a boat with fairly flat floors and a very broad stem ought to be violently unbal- ended, but this does not always prove to be the case. One of the simplest methods of getting a rough idea of a hull's balance is to check the fore-and-aft p.sition of the centre of buoyancy et various angles of heel. Any great movement of the centre of buoyancy will indicate lack of balance. Theories such as the balanced diagonal theory and Admiral Turner's Metacentric Shelf Theory are both invoked in the design stages, the former usually with great success. The latter is not much in evidence these days, as it does not always result in a good hull design.

Disposition of inside ballast will also affect a boat's balance, and quite often moving a few hundredweight of iron will turn a hard- mouthed brute of a boat into an easily-handled vessel, with a considerable- exable increase in speed. This increase in speed is due to the fact that a well—balanced hull needs little or no helm to keep her on course, wherees.an unbalanced hull which is always trying to turn, often requires a considerable helm angle to hold her, and this helm angle greatly increases the forward resistance of the boat.

Once a nicely~halanced hull bas been achieved, the sail plan must also be balanced, and it is here that theory and practice diverge hope- lessly. The centre of lateral resistance of the hull is easily found, as is the centre of effort of the sail plan with all sails sheeted-in flat to the centre~line of the boat, It is generally accepted that this centre of effort should be forward of the centre of lateral resistance, but there is no guide to how far forward. One very nicely balanced five-tender ( a very well-known design) has the two centres coincident, whilst one of the leading Bast Coast designers always ains a getting the centre of effort twenty-five per cent of the waterline length for- ward of the centre of lateral resistance, and his boats also balance very well.

When one looks down on 2 boat beeting to windward, the centre of effort must be forward of the C.L.R., since it swings forward and outward as the sails set off the centre-line, and it also moves to leeward as the boat heels over. This «means two tuming couples are acting, one tending to cause the boot to luff, and the other opposing this tendency.

Unfortunately theory leaves us floundering at this point, as there are too many variable factors involved, but most designers manage to produce the desired result.

All the designer's hard work can be rendered useless by careless sail- trimming, and one often finds old boats with modified rigs which balance very badly indeed. One pitfall here is the fitting of longer bowsprits and larger headsails on hard-mouthed boats, the theory being that since the boat is always trying to tum head to wind the greater sail area forward of the most will blow her head off. This is all very well con- sidered statically with the boat upright, but all too often when sailing heeled the extra sail area forward depresses tie bow, producing even worse weather helm. If you own a beet with bad weather helm, it is often possible to cure it by spending a week-end shifting ballast and playing with the headsails.

Another source of lack of balance is a hole in the rudder or deadwood. A bedly designed propellor installation can utterly ruin a poet's perform-— ance, and this is the reason why so many designers prefer to mount aux- auxiliaries on one quarter, where they function nearly as well as a central engine, without affecting the boat's sailing performance. An added bonus is that it is easier to get at the propellor to clear weeds or fouled-up ropes. "BARNACLE"

Tools: of the Trade The Lead Line (Cont'd)

You will remember I suggested last month that the lead line should be well stretched. This is most important, not only for stability of measurement but also, and of rather more importance, so that the line will coil easily. Most people have had the experience of trying to coil up a piece of new rope. It is like fighting with a boa-—constrictor, in the end one is lucky to come out of the contest unchanged. The addition of the knots to the lead line just makes the whole thing more intractable Distressing for a moment, and ignoring the bloke who just shouted "keep to the point" the easiest way to coil up a new rope is to chuck the whole coil overboard, hanging on of course to the bitter end, and coil up as it is pulled in, taking the twists out as they appear over the rail.

To coil up one ond in the left hand, slide the right hand along the rope, straightening it as you go, almost to arms length, then bring that length of rope in the form of a coil back to the left hand giving the rope a twist in the direction of the ley of the strands. Transfer from right hand to left and carry on. You will find that the twist is done most easily between the thumb and first finger of the right hand as it moves back towards the left. This will give coils of equal size and of about twenty inches diameter.

To stretch the lead line before marking, tie one end to a fixed object and pull on the other with a tackle. Wren it is taut drench it with water. Keep it in that state for a few hours, then let it dry tightening the tackle as it slackens.

Another and rather easier way is to tie a bucket on one end, make the other ond fast to the boat, chuck the bucket overboard, end tow it on. the end of the line for few hours.

A much easier type of line to handle, and one which is much more disinclined to tangle is the round sennit or plaited line. You know the sort of line Mum hangs her clots on in the garden. This is not, however, easily obtained in small sizes.

When not in use. keep the lead line coiled down in a box in the cockpit or for example under a thwart. This will ensure that when you want it in a hell of a hurry, as you usually do, it is available and you don't have to spend five minutes untangling it. Another my way is to carry it wound between two cleats a couple of feet apart. On my own boat it is kept wound on a kevil or long cleat about two feet long fastened through the stanchions inside the rail. There is it out of the way yet constantly available.

Now how to use the lead line. This is always good for a laugh! We read of the loadsman in the old time ship-of-the-line standing in the chains and swinging the lead round his head in ever increasing circles like a sort of Ouzlam Bird in reverse ;car, then letting it go to fly forward, the lead, that is to say, not the leadsman. into the water, the line sliding

through his fingers until bottom was reached whereupon he would chant "By the Hark Nine" or some such remark. Remembering that the lead must have weighed anything up to ten pounds or more, I often wonder what he chanted when he forgot to let go. I bet even Captain Hornblower laughed!! No, your way of using the lead will be a much more decorous affair, although in @ small boat still with distinct possibilities as 2 mirth-maker.

The Entrance To Bradwell Creek

This has always had a somewhat justifiable reputation for difficulty, although once known it is comparatively simple, Sailing Directions given in most pilot books are now however somewhat in error due to the erection of the Nuclear Power Station, Some marks have been removed and other replaced,

Approaching from the west, keep parallel to Pewit Island and well out, about half a mile from the island, This means at the present time you will be passing quite close to the ships which lie in the river. Keep on this line until about two hundred yards west of the Power Station cofferdam barrier wall, This is a most unmistakable object which resembles a pier and lies about a quarter of a mile east of the entrance,

Turn south and head towards the shore. When in line with and about two hundred yards from the west end of the barrier wall a square wooden post will be seen in a south westerly direction, distance about two hundred yards, This post, which carries water temperature monitoring equipment for the Power Station, is on and near the end of the spit which runs in a north easterly direction from the eastern end of Pewit Island, Head for a point due east of, and thirty yards from, this post, From this point turn and sail towards the post in a westerly direction keeping south of the post and passing it close to, about eight to ten yards, From here on the southern and eastern side of the spit which is quite steep to, is marked by withies. The channel is narrow and is most shallow at the outer end,

Follow the withies in, keeping them to starboard and very close, a few yards, on no account straying to the south and east of them, The mud flat extending from shore between Power Station and the navigable channel of the creek is extensive and dries out six feet above L.W, Ordinary Spring Tides, As the channel turns towards the south a pair of leading marks will be seen on the sea wall. Keep these in line until Bradwell Quay itself is opened up then turn and sail along the line of moored vessels running parallel to the
quay.

There is generally three to five feet depth of water in the creek at L.W.0.S,T, The best place to anchor however if staying the night is in the area of the last bend in the creek before the quay.

The would~bo purchaser or builder of 2 small boat is now confronted with a bewildering variety of hull construction methods, all of which suffer from various disadvantages tages so that it is extremely difficult to choose between them. I propose to mention a few salient points on each method, some of which are not always obvious to the new
owner.

Our first major division is between round bilged and hard chine boats, with the various multi-chine types as an intermediate stepping
ok

Round bilged hulls divide into plunked and moulded types, each of which divides down even further.

Fir d round bilge type let us consider clinker building. The edition:1 was of building a hull and e very good method it is too. too difficult but it may need some moulds or bulkheads on which to shape the hull. Many clinker hulls are built without any form of mould, the shape of the hull being governed solely by the shape of the planks. One advantage whilst building is hat the ribs can be steamed into place after the hull is rivetted up, but 2 major snag is that each plank must be cut to its correct shape, no edge bending being Permissible permissible, and the lands of the planks must all be planed off to the correct angle. This means that clinker built boats need time and care in building ond may oc wasteful of timber. The final result is a Strong. — flexible hull with an almost indefinite life. The only seems to be caulked are those between a garboards and the keel. between the Lands of the planks can be taken up by hardening the fastenings. Damaged planks can bo replaced and new ribs can be fitted easily leaving repairs which are completely unnoticeable and which do not affect the strength of the hull in any way. The flexibility of a clinker hull ina seaway makes for speed and a long life, .the only risk being splitting the lands off the planks, but this is unlikely to occur if the boats built of good timber. Many people claim that the lands of clinker planks help to keep down odd dollops of water which would run up smooth topsides and onto the cool:.

For many years the only rival to clinker building was carvel.
Since the planks are fastened only to the frames and not to each other all the framework must be heavier on a carvel null and the ribs must be fitted first. When using grown frames this is no disadvantage and little material is needed beyond that required for the hull, but if bent frames are to be used then a full set of moulds and ribbands must be made. Where more than one hull is to be built these are of little account, but for a one-off job they do take time and money. Carvel planking is economical of timber as the planks can often bo oige bent by up to two feet; it does not require a high degree of accuracy in fitting, like clinker; and it is delightfully easy to rivet up. A c:rvel built hull needs caulking and stopping, but is far easier than clinker to repair. Weight for weight it is not as strong 2s clinker, but for all sizes of cruisers the extra weight required makes little difference, and carvel built hulls usually outlast all other types “ith their flexibility and case of repair.

The third planked round bilge method is edge fastened strip. This. is a method sometimes quoted us being ideal for amateur construction, but a closer look at what is involved soon shows that for most hulls clinker or carvel would be simpler. A full set of moulds is needed, but no ribbands.
The number of string involved in th. construction is fantastic and all must be planed on all Your owen 30 without 2 good machine planer the job becomes hopelessly tedious and ‘ng. Buying the strips ready planed with the differing radii ro make & good job would put the cost up far too much and there would be is difficulty of keeping the strips separated according to their radii. Having planed up the mile or so of strip needed, there is the fun of restening it, with about four times as many nails as a clinker hull, all driven blind. Far more of the time involved in fastening is spent drilling then rivetting and rooves cost far less than nails so the fastenings for a strip built hull will cost more and take longer to fit then for carvel or clinker. Having planked out to the

turn of the bilge, the ends and edges of the bottom strips heave to be trimmed off parallel to the shear line ready to take the topside planking, a job to cause far more cussing than anything met with on. any other type of planking. The final result is a light, strong, rigid hull, rigid because all the seams must be glued to ensure a watertight hull, and this rigidity leads to cracking; if the hull is overstressed in any way. Such a crack would be the devil to repair, but woe betide you if you inadvertently hole the hull. Short of completely rebuilding the entire hull above the level of the hole it is absolutely impossible to restore it to its original condition and a glued in patch is likely to st up stress concentrations which might lead to further troubles.

The Potted Pilot by T. YW. Hallam

Part 3

Tools Lead Line (Continued) of the Trade -the
* * *

In the small cruiser the best position from which to use th lead line is the lee side of the cockpit. This ensures that there is no danger of it becoming fouled up with any projection on the bottom of the boat, the keel or centreplate for example, or even as has been known the rudder Hold the lead line with two or three coils in your outboard hand with the lead dangling free on a couple of feet of line. The rest of the coils are held in the inboard hand. Swing the lead with an underhand motion a couple of times to get the rhythm, then let it go to fly forward, those coils held in the swinging hand being released at the same moment but the line itself still being retained in the hand in such a manner that the line is free to run. As the line tightens release as many coils as are necessary from the inboard hand. By this time the lead will have entered the water somewhere level with the dows. As the lead sinks more line will run out but at the same time the boat will be overtaking the lead. The power of the swing should be such that the lead reaches the bottom just before the line becomes vertical in the water. The amount of energy you will expend will depend upon the speed of the boat and the depth of the water

When the lead reaches the bottom a slight but distinct thump will be felt in the fingers of the swinging hand, which you will remember, still has the line running through it. Fingers are extremely sensitive instruments, and can detect even in deep water this thump and the slight slacking of tension in the line as the lead hits the bottom.

You will now be able to read off the depth either visually or by feel from the knots, which will be in the region of either wielding or holding hand Coil up the line again retrieving it as quickly as you can and make another cast.

This brings us face to face with a cardinal truth. Unless at ree

anchor one sounding utterly useless. Two or three at least are required, preferably more. One sounding merely tells you the depth of the water over
oe

that one particular pimple or depression on which the lead has landed. A number will give you the trend of the soundings; whether the water is becoming shallower or deeper, and whether this change in depth is fast or slow, thus indicating a steep or shallow change in the contours of the sea bottom.

The lead line as a pilotage instrument can be used in a number of ways. Perhaps the most obvious is to give adequate warning of the time to go about when tacking near the shore. Another way is to use the lead s a blind man uses a stick, tapping along a kerb. At night, or in fog, when sailing on a river or estuary, one can sail towards a known bank until in say a couple of fathoms, then follow the two fathoms line along, feeling ones way with the lead. The existence of a spit or a swatch will be apparent, thus giving by reference to the chart an indication of ones position; but more of this later on in the series when we consider the technique of pilotage proper.

The lead line is probably the most useful and certainly the cheapest tool of the pilots trade. It is also unfortunately the least used by most yachtsmen. This is probably due to the fact that using it is possibly the quickest way of getting water up ones sleeve. The amount of water brought on board by the lead line as it is retrieved is almost unbelievable. A few casts and ones hands and sleeves are soaking, no fun in the winter.

There is another implement which can be used for depth sounding, the possession of which in days gone by was the hall mark of the East Coast yachtsman, the sounding pole. This, a light wood or bamboo pole between six and twelve feet long, marked off in feet by alternate white and black bands, would be displayed proudly in the rigging, stamping the owner as a genuine hairy chested ditch crawler. Its use had its lighter moments too. The sight of old Charlie trying desperately to get into Bradwell Creek at

Cont'd on page 6

a quarter to closing time on a Saturday evening, wielding his sounding pole like a demented drum-major was usually sufficient to clear the public bar of the Green Man.

Although the sounding pole has largely fallen into disuse now- nowadays, I am sure that a shorter version, say five feet long, would be if anything more useful to the dinghy, or any Light craft cruiser, owners. It could be used single handed easier than the lead and could double as a boat—hook or a spinnaker pole.

HULL CONSTRUCTION - 2 by "Barnacle"

Last month we dealt with three methods of planking a round bilge hull with solid wood. First, this month, let us look at clinker-ply, or glued clinker. This is an elegant way of producing a light, strong dinghy, and has most of the advantages and disadvantages of normal clinker. Since the plywood strakes have adequate transverse strength, it requires no ribs, but this great advantage is offset by the fact that all seams are glued, producing a rigid hull which is more liable to be cracked. For a boat which is to give any real service, all strakes should be rivetted es well as glued, since it is an unfortunate fact that the modern resin glues do not always behave the same way on a boat immersed in sea water as they do immersed in a laboratory beaker. For rapid production of light, shapely yacht tenders this method is just about ideal.

Next in the possible methods of producing a round bilge hull we can consider wooden moulding. This can be many layers of thin veneers bonded to form 2 single sheet of shaped plywood, or two or three skins laid at angles (I am lumping such constructions as vee root, slim strake and double diagonal under the heading of moulded hulls). At first sight these methods seem very well suited to amateur construction, but a little further consideration shows that there will be nearly as much work in building the mould as in building a more conventional hull, and then to achieve good results considerably more than a casual acquaintance with modern resin glues is needed. One or two skins are not too bad, but the third, fourth and fifth get extremely tedious. No, this is a method best left to the factory. And what about the result? Strong;, light, very shapely, and rigid, ideal for a short term proposition, but perhaps not the thing in which to invest hard earned savings in the expectation of realising your money in ten years time.

At this point let me clear up possible misunderstandings about my use of the word rigid. It has been pointed out to me that the topsides of 2 glued-strip hull can move in and out as much as those of a carvel hull. Admittedly, but that is NOT what I meant by rigid. They have no movement at all in the fore and aft direction; the very direction in which movement is essential to give to a pounding from a heavy sea. Old sailor men always swore hat Eastwoods brick barges went fastest in a heavy sea when they worked the most, and the Lowestoft and Southwold "Yolls'' used to carry a saw to cut through the thwarts so their clinker hulls could work even more, when they wanted to get along quickly in a North East gale.

Lastly in the round bilge hulls we have fibreglass. This is no proposition for the amateur. A mould involves more work than building a hull by any other method, and then the knowledge of practical chemistry required is considerable if the best results are to be achieved. A fibreglass hull has most of the advantages and disadvantages of a moulded wooden hull, except that it cannot rot, worms won't eat it, and the topsides need not be painted although the bottom of a cruiser will still need antifouling. On the other hand ultra violet light will degrade the resin, other ageing effects may occur, and a cheap moulding may delaminate. One is also faced with an unusual surface finish worry, that of one side being beautifully smooth and the other very rough indeed. Some firms overcome this by using inner and outer mouldings so all the rough surfaces are hidden One point with regard
to fibreglass dinghies - always buy a dinghy with wooden floorboards and
thwarts screwed in and not moulded in place. The fibreglass may appear to have a good non-skid surface when dry, but when it gets wet it is about as safe to stand on as a sheet of wet ice, and it is extremely fatiguing rowing a dinghy when one is continually sliding around on the thwarts. On any
fibreglass boat always beware of moulded-in wooden components - these are
almost certain to rot very quickly. Some moulders use pieces of wood moulded in place to form a support for a rib in the fibreglass This is frowned on in the better moulding shops, but it is the fibreglass rib that supplies the strength and not the timber, so it is not too serious if the wood does rot. A moulded in keel, gunwale or thwart which rots is a different story.

And what if you damage a moulded hull? Some people may recall a glue advertisement showing a Flying Fifteen that had been run into. The

would be far beyond the repair capabilities of the average holes can be patched, but on wooden mouldings it is extremely difficult, if not impossible, to restore them to their original condition. The patch can nearly always be made so it cannot be seen, but there is still a risk of weakness where patch and original join, as it is impossible to get the actual strand h of glass to cross this joint so there must be a difference. in strength at this point.

HULL CONSTRUCTION - 3

To finish off this series let us consider the various chine hulls.
These are by no means confined to dinghies and small cruisers, as some quite large hulls are built with chines, including spritsail barges.

Building a hard chine hull (single or multi-chine) is usually quick, far quicker than any other method, but it requires more accurate workmanship, and the fairing off of keel, chines and frames is harder than anything met with on a round bilged carvel hull. The hull may be planked and. caulked, it may be clinker, or it may be ply skinned. All are somewhat easier and quicker to build than the equivalent round bilge hull, particularly ply, where the boat is changed from a skeleton to a complete hull ina week end.

Most of the troubles with chine hulls occur in the design stages, as it is possible to bend a flat sheet of normal plywood only into a cylindrical or conical shape. Any compound curvature or twist is not possible. This has fooled many people who imagine that all they have to do to design 2 hard chine hull is to draw a series of straight sided sections. Alas, nothing could be further from the truth, for the sections, particularly in the bows, are quite well curved, ss are the keel and chines. In fact a well designed hard chine hull, skinned with sheet ply, can be nearly as shapely es a planked or moulded hull, whilst costing far less to
build.

Many people have attempted to "prove! that chine hulls are not as good as round bilged hulls, whilst others have wasted just cs much time trying to prove the reverse. In fact each has its advantages and disadvantages, which do not greatly affect the sailing performance of the boat, 9 except in the case of sailing barges
& oS chine hull
where the long was
decidedly superior to a round bilge.

Ply skinned chine hulls do have stress concentrations along the keel, chines and deck edge, but these are not usually likely to cause serious trouble on a well designed hull, whilst clinker and carvel chine hulls behave exactly like round bilge hulls, and are as easy to repair. A plywood skinned chine boat can be restored to its original condition after being holed by replacing the entire ply panel involved, but its life expectation is probably not so good as that of a planked hull, although marine plywood is steadily improving.

To summarize, (most difficult) for an amateur built hull wanted quickly; hard chine, plywood skinned. For a hull not wanted quite so quickly, involving less care in building and with the best possible expectation of life; round bilge carvel. For small dinghies; clinker ply, and for a light, long lasting hull requiring that bit more care in building; normal clinker. For those rich types who can afford to buy a new racing boat whenever they want to; a moulded hull, either ply or fibreglass.

Tools of the Trade (continued) Part 4.

So far we have been considering methods of depth sounding using equipment that is traditional, and in the main, cheap. There are, however, more esoteric, and more @xpensive ways of doing the same job. Electronic Depth Sounders, or Echo Sounders are becoming the fashion nowadays. Priced between £35 and £150, and fitted in Some cases with ane@udio alarm to tell the pilot when a particular depth is reached, they are undoubtedly

fascinating things to play with. They do the job quite efficiently too, in fact they are probably nearly as food aS a weight on the end of a piece of line! They cost a bit more of course, but no doubt this is off-set by the joy of fiddling with a piece of electronic apparatus. Tf I had that amount of money to spare I would prefer to spend it on a new dinghy, :r a new mainsail, or even, perish the thought, to paying my
creditors!

For those who would be serious about. this matter, however,the Echo Sounder works as follows. An ultra- sonic signal is generated, usually in the range of 20 KC/S to 50 KC/S. This is fed to a transducer fastened to the bottom of the boat. The signal radiated from the transducer is reflected by the sea bottom, the reflected signal being picked up by the transducer and fed to the receiver section of the set., Then it is compared time-wise with the tr:nsmitter signal. The speed of propagation through water being known, the time lag between the transmitter end récsiver signals will give the depth of water. The result of this computation is displayed either one meter calibrated in fathoms or feet, or on a rotating noon lamp type of display. The advantage of this equipment is that a continuous visible display of depth is presented, together with, in some cases, an audible warning signal when a pr.-determined depth is reached, thus enabling the helmsman to give more attention to actually sailing the boat. This is more important perhaps when racing rather than cruising.

The disadvantages are cost, and the maintenance of a piece of comparatively complicated electronic equipment which by the very nature of the environment in which it lives is bound to add to the normal task of maintaining the boat and its equipment,

We have considered, at some length, méans whereby we determine the depth of water in which we are sailing. The next point is to consider the tools necessary to ensure we know in which direction we ere going. Tae most

important of these is the steering compass.

This is an essential part of the boat's equipment.
It is, moreover, usually quite expensive and cannot be ré.laced easily, unfortunately, by any contrivance mads out of bits of sticks and string. The normal ship's compass has a card which is graduated in points and half points. There are thirty-two points, ¢isnt in each quadrant. Starting at North and going clockwise, those in the North to Bast quadrant are as follows:- North, N. by E., N.N.&., N.t&.by N., Neites N.E. Dr Bey E.N.E., Hobby N., East Those in the other quadrants follow the same pattern, the cardinal points changing as we swing through the quadrants. A recitation of the full thirty-two in order, is known as “boxing the compass" and is soméetiing every sailing man should be able to do instinctively without having to stop and think. Try if after 6 few pints in the Jolly Sailor. You will probably get it mixed up with that rather improper story about a railway porter. They don't call us rude seamen for nothing!

As a full circle is normally divided int» 369° and there are thirty-two points, it follows that there are 111i” to each point and just over 54° to a half-point. This last, incidentally, is just about the amount of leeway a boat makes when on the wind, and is a common unit of
measurement.

What is the value of -our boat? Its true value, not the exorbitant price you may have paid for it. This is a very tricky question to answer properly, although in many cases one could reply "the amount she will fetch in free sale on the open market". a, however, dues not apply to boats built for spécialsurposes, whose

a
real value may be many times what they cov.ld hope to
fetch
on an open market.

Let us have a look wt some of the factors which help to determine a boats value. Unlike cars, age is of little help, and condition must be taken as the main factors It is possible to find quits good brats, eighty years old, in far better condition than similar forty year olds.
The next consideration is the vessel's pedigree; her designer, and racing record. Hers one hes to tread warily as some of the best designers have their off days, whilst some almost unknown people have designed first class boats. If it is a dinghy you are buying, the best guide is the size of the class. The higher the sail numbers the more likely you are to get a quick sale at a good price. Avoid unknown "ore designs‘ like the plague. They may have many brilliant features, but their second hand valué will be low because there will be only a limited market for them. Likewise, never buy a racing dinghy without a valid measurement certificate. She may be out of class, and if she is, her value will probably be halved. Also, if you already own an unmeasured class dinghy, get it measured. It is pointless owning a racing machines that can never be entered for open events, and even if you don't want to race, ou may want to sell the boat one day, and you will lose far more than the cost of the measurer's fee.

POTTED PILOT - Part 5 by T.W. Hallam

Tools of the Trade

The Steering Compass (Cont'd)

In its usual form the instrument consists basically of a card to which is affixed a magnetic needle or system of needles, this assembly being mounted on a pivot inside a bowl. The bowl is filled with a liquid, as described last month, the liquid being a mixture of distilled water and alcohol. The liquid will cause a drag on the card and damp out any tendency towards violent oscillatory motion set up by the movement of the boat. One must remember that the earth's magnetic-field is not very strong, and it is quite easy to cause an undamped or dry point compass card to spin completely round, causing it to require several seconds to come to rest. Whilst this may be acceptable ina compass which is used on land and can be set dows on a solid object until the card comes to rest, it is obviously completely useless in a boat’ where the motion never ceases.

The card is calibrated, usually in points, half and quarter points, although degrees may be used and are sometimes marked on the card in addition to the points. A line is marked on the glass top of the bowl, known as the "Tubber's Line". The compass must always be installed such that this " "Tubber's Line" is exactly parallel to the fore and aft centre-line of the boat. The line is sometimes replaced by a graticule or a pointer, but the principle is the ‘same. :

The compass must be fitted in such a way that it remains horizontal even when the boat heels or pitches. This is achieved by mounting it on two pivots fore and aft in a ring, which is in turn pivoted athwartships in another ring or cradle. These are known as gimbals.

The. position of the compass in the boat is something that requires some thought. It follows that as it is a magnetic instrument that any ferro-magnetic material, iron or steel, or any electric magnetic instrument or component, such as & radio loudspeaker, or indeed even a piece of wire with current flowing through it, will cause an inter-action with the magnetic needle and: affect its reading, Put it then, as far away from any local ww ironworks 2s you can, and don't forget the iron tiller, if you have one, nor that rusty heap of old iron under the cockpit floor, the thing you proudly call "my auxiliary engine" although you know, and I know, the thing hasn't coughed since the day auntie left the sea cock open on the thunderbox, and flooded the whole boat.

More about compasses and positions next month, so don't rush out and buy one yet.

Thirslet Creek

Thirslet Creek (pronounced locally as "Thistly") is a little used but very useful haven in which to anchor for shelter when the wind-is any- where between South through Jest, round to Worth. With a South Westerly wind blowing hard on a flooding tide that »part of ‘the Blackwater between Osea Island and Mersea can be most uncomfortable and under these circumstances Thirslet Creek is a good shelter.

It runs into the big flat on the north side of the River Blackwater Opposite Stone, in a jesterly direction from the entrance, which is opposite St. Lawrence Bay. On the south side of the entrance is a steep -— to spit known as Thirslet Spit, marked with, at the .moment, two beacons. One is

Page 7

the original Thirslet Beacon and lies over at an angle of about forty five degrees, the other a new post carrying water temperature monitoring equipment for Bradwell Power Station.

The creek is about 150 to 200 yards wide along most of it's length
and has an average depth of water of 9 to 14 ft. for the first half mile, shallowing to about 5ft. for the next quarter mile after which it narrows and _ peters out to a mere ditch. an oyster fishing watch boat is anchored just inside the entrance on the North Side, and care should be taken not to anchor in the vicinity of any oyster beds, usually marked by withies.

In the recent circular in 'Navigans' quite a large number of members gave weekend cruises aS :n interest. Those who own cruisers should bs well equipped for this type of Sailing, but dinghy owners will neéd to make special prepare. tions. Unfortunately the Blackwater Estuary is not very well endowed with good waterside campsites, so to avoid cruises becoming a monotonous series of visits to the same site, owners will be well «-advised to prepare tnreir boats for sleeping aboard, either aflvuat or aground.

One advantage of sleeping aboard is that less extra gear is needed, and what ther. is, does not have to be carried ashore. The first requirement is a cover. A dinghy with a gcoseneck about four feet above the keel can have a strut made to hold the boom horizontal, and a canvas cover lacing down over the topsides, preferably with end flaps which can be
laced across - when sleeping =board an anchored, floating
boat, she will usually lie head to wind so only the forward end of the cover need be closed. For maximum comfort inflatable mattresses (inflate with them in position so they round odd knees etc.) and quilted terylene sleeping bags will be found hard to beat, but for the impecunious (and hardy) a couple of blankets with polythene sheet under and over will serve. Lifejackets of the padded type 6r a kit beg stuffed with clothes will make a good pillow.

For sleeping aboard with the boat aground on a hard beach you will need four (or more) bilge chocks, which can be quite light plywood boxes, and shovld fit under the beat from keel to chines, Obviously an anchor and warp will be needed - the longer the warp the better. Half inch or three quarter nylon should adequate, and will ultimately prove cheaper than kemp or sisal, as well as being cleaner to handle. A plastic bucket will bs found essential. Quite a 1bt of gear can be stored in it, and if necessary it can be used to bale out in an emergency.

For cooking, it is hard to beat a primus stove, the portable Calor gas stoves are attractive, but if you run out of gas you may not be able to set a replacement cylinder, but paraffin is sold almost everywhere. If the stove is to bs used with the boat afloat a gimbal is highly desirable. Tin plated kettles and saucepans etc., will last a season and are quite cheap, but it is advisable to get plastic plates and cups and stainless steel cutlery. Food, spare clothes, cigarettes etc. can all be stowed in polythene bags, so start collecting these now. Don't forget containers for paraffin and drinking water. A stove full of fuel will be ample for a weekend, and two gallons of water is quite enough for two people for two days.

Lighting can be electric, by candles or paraffin lamps, but mind you covert If you intend to go below Osea don't forget your chart and some form of compass, an? make sure you have a good pair of cars or paddles aboard.

Moorings by “Barnacle"

All too many people these days take a very casual attitude
towards moorings - if there is a wéll painted buoy floating
gaily on the surface, it “MUST be a good mooring - they
never think that the chain might be rusted away to only a few thou of métal, and ropes might be rotten so the sorry story of boats adrift, boats up on the sea wall, and boats holed by drifting into old wescks, continues. if “you value; your boat, never leave it untended on a mooring you have not inspected yourself.

A good mooring comprises a ground or span chain of heavy links securely fastened to two substantial roots, with a lighter riding chain secured to its centre by a swivel and suitable shackles, the swivel well greased, and the shackles securely wired. A single root mooring can be used in isolated cases, but to avoid a vertical pull on the root a much larger scope or chain must be used, so a single root mooring should never be used where several boats are to be moored in line. Where really close moorings are desired, double riding chains should be used, starting from points roughly a third of the way along the span chain, and uniting just below the surface, with a swivel to the short single chain to which the boat is secured. Such a mooring can not foul the hull or centreplate under water, but ensures that the boat swings through little more than twice its own length as the tide turns.

The roots should sé substantial, and dug well in - a half
hundredweight concrete block allowed to settle in the mud is not a good root. Old barge and.1ors with their upper fiukes cut off, old centreplatés buried three fest in the mud, crossesof old air raid shelter angle iron, old cartwheels well creosoted and carefully buried all provide good roots. The easiest to lay is a demolition contractor's ground anchor -a gigantic iron corkscrew, which goes down about five feet, but these must never be allowed to take a nearly vertical pull.

Buoy ropes should be spliced round thimbles and shackled to the chain and the buoy, as chafe will otherwise sever the stoutest of ropes in a season, and should be strong enough to hold the boat when nsecéisary.

The whole mooring should bc inspected every year and during the winter should either be taken up or the buoy and ropé removed and the chain allowed to sink into the mud. CENTRE PLATES - Another hint

Owners of centre-plate yachts which take the ground between tides are almost sure to be troubled at some time or other through their plates becoming mud-bound; in fact, so serious is the problem that it has caused many owners to turn to keel boats or to seek moorings at which they remain always afloat. Of course, all manner of suggestions have been advanced for overcoming the difficulty but none is really satisfactory.

In the case of a certain yacht which suffered acutely from this difficulty, a solution was to pass the end of the boom-crutch through the chain slot in the top of the centre-board case, and give a direct push to the plate as far aft of the pivot bolt as possible. Generally a long shove was more effective than sharp hammer blows or gigging with the tackle.

Contd. on Page 4.

Page lh.

In very dry weather, when the mud was really solid, the first job on arrival on board, was to pour water into the case and keep it filled whilst hoisting sails and preparing for casting off. By the time all was ready and the moorings about to be let go, the plate always responded to a good steady push from one or two members of the crew.

A COVER FOR A CRUISING DINGHY

If you intend to use a dinghy for cruising it is worth getting a proper cover made, but if you intend to sleep aboard only in extraordinary circumstances such as being caught out in a flat calm and pouring rain and unable to reach a campsite ashore, then quite a simple cover can be improvised.

My first cruising on the Blackwater and Colne was done in a 12 ft. lugsail dinghy with no decking at all, and at night we used to lash the yard and boom together, support one end on the mast thwart and hoist the other to a suitable height with the halliard. The sail was then spread over and lashed
round under the boat - an operation that could only be done with
the boat ashore. The result was draughty and the sail got F covered in mud, but at least we had somewhere dry to sleep. f Later I borrowed a larger, flat bottomed boat with wide side deck” and with her we supported the aft end of the boom by lashing the tiller to the end of it and spread a rectangle of old canvas over, holding it in to the cockpit coamings with a lashing all round. This was tolerable with the wind abeam, but if we were afloat and lay head to wind a howling gale blew in at the open fore end of the crude cover.

When I eventually saved enough to buy "Melody" I decided she was worth fitting with a proper cover, and got Mr.Taylor to make one for me at a cost of about ten pounds. For this cover, the boom rested in the scissors crutches on the aft deck, and the cover came down to about the middle of the side decks, lacing onto a row of small clips screwed to the shear strake below the rubbing strake. Inside the cover a flap hung just inside the coamings and laced to clips under the carlines. With.the front lacing round the mast and tent type doors aft lacing down to the sheethorse the result was almost completely draughtproof. ww

Owners with "all over" covers made to fit the boat with thé boom lying from the goosensck to the aft deck could easily sew a couple of triangular extensions to the cover so it will reach the hull when the boom is raised, either by a support, or the topping lift or main halliard taken to the boom end fitting. (If the main halliard is not long enough, use the kicking strap as an extension). A cover so modified might not fit over well forward, but it should be draughtproof.

For a dinghy that is having a cruising cover specially made, arrange the doom as high as possible, with a wooden or
metal support at the aft end - you could rely on the topping
lift, but sooner or later it will slip or break and the boom will fall on your head. The best method of holding down the cover is to lace or clip it to hooks outside the hull, but where this cannot be done it can be held with lines passing under the hull, or a “drawstring” round below to rubbing strake.

For real luxury, the cover can be spread like a Mansard roof by using a pair of oars for the lower ridges, held apart

by spreaders (tiller and tiller extension, jib whisker pole etc. could be modified to serve a dual purpose) and held up either by lacing to the cover or tying below the boom. The Spreaders then form handy clothes racks etc. One warning - make sure the main sheet is well out of the way, as it can be
an infernal nuisance hanging from the boom - I used to coil
"Nelody's" on top of the boom before putting the cover on.

You will find a cover which can be fitted from inside the
boat well worth its cost - no more muddy feet, sleep wherever
you can find fairly calm water and with all your gear handy. If you really use the space in the boat you will find yourself far better off than you would ashore in a tent which is probably less than half the size of even a small dinghy.

Anchoring | by "Barnacle"
Having dealt very briefly with the subject of moorings, let us now turn our attention to anchors and anchoring. For the cruising mar there are three types of suitable anchor; Danforth, C.9.R. and Fisherman, the relative merits of which are thoroughly discussed elsewhere (if I mention Heaton again Someone will think I'm a relative of his). Every boat should carry at least main and kedge anchor, so if you really can't decide which type of anchor will suit you best, then try one ef each. The main anchor should be ready for immediate use whenever the boat is cruising in coastal waters. This does not mean lying under the aft deck, with a tangle of filthy old rope on top of it. It means secured to the foredeck in such a manner that it can be let. go ina matter of seconds, with a stout warp or chain secured to it, the warp or chain so stowed that it will run out freely, and with the bitter end made fast to the boat. For those of you who had not realised it, this is the origin of the saying
"right to the bitter end" - it's the end (of the cable) made
fast to the bitts -- or which should be made fast to the bitts:
It comes expensive if you habitually forget to secure the bitter end. The warp or chain should never be made fast to the bitts in such a manner that it cannot be undone quickly - one day you might have to slip your anchor ina hurry. Most textbooks advise a lashing that can be cut with a knife, but there is a danger here that the lashing will rot or chafe, and you may have the mortification of seeing the end of your highly expensive chain, which you thought was so well secured, disappearing through the roller fairlead. Nos A far better way is to secure the bitter end to a Stenhouse slip, an inexpensive little bit of ironmongery which will hold as strongly as the rest of the chain, and can be readily knocked open with the first heavy object that comes to hand if ever you do have to slip your chain.

If you are sailing singlehanded it is quite good practice to lead your anchor cable through the roller fairlead on the stem head, then back outside everything to the cockpit, where the anchor can be stowed away .on the grating. (Although most boats give the lone sailor enough time to nip up forward and deal with
a properly stowed anchor).

If your main anchor is a C.9.R. or Danforth it is easy to stow and always ready for use, but that does not apply toa Fisherman. These can be brutes to stow, and the generally accepted method is to lay the flukes flat on deck with the stock outboard, one end sticking up vertically. To prevent this end catching stray jib sheets, fishing lines etc. (as it certainly will, if you give it half a chance) it is best stowed alongside a shroud or liferail stanchion to which it can be seized, or better still, protected by a piece of plastic tubing of suitable diameter slid over the stanchion or shroud. Whilst on the subject of Fisherman anchors, make sure the pin is securely home, and WIRE it in place. A lashing here, like a bitter end lashing, gets neglected, and if the pin comes out, the anchor is practically certain to drag.

When cruising it is quite a sound idea to have the kedge anchor ready for immediate use as well as the main. Warp is nearly always used for the kedge anchor, and see that it is of ample length. Thirty fathoms is the MINIMUM that should be carried on a two and a half topper. For larger boats, wire can be used, but it is awkward to stow; the drum off a Kelvin sounding machine, complete with its wire, comes in handy here. A kedge warp need not be terrifically heavy rope, but be sure it is properly coiled away, and in good condition.

Contd, on Page 7

Page 7

Always put out enough warp or chain when anchoring. Three times the depth at high water is the usually quoted figure for a Fisherman anchor, up to five times for a C.9.R. Remember these are MINIMUM figures, and twice as much won't hurt a bits “Most boats are very, very badly supplied with chain
and warp - after all, a C.%.8. on twenty fathoms of chain
can not be relied upon to hold in more than four or five fathoms of water, and since we have a two fathom rise and fall of tide in these parts it means you must be in only two fathoms of water if you wish to anchor safely at low tide.

When anchoring for more than an hour or two, or in the vicinity of other boats, the kedge should bdé laid out down tide of the main anchor. Very few boats carry enough chain to do this the easy way by dropping back on the main anchor, laying the kedge overboard, and then hauling back to a point midway between the anchors.so a trip in the dinghy will have to oe made. If you value your life do this properly, with the anchor slung over the dinghy's transom with a slippery hitch, and the warp properly coiled down well clear of your legs. If you get tangled up with the anchor or warp and fall out of the dinghy your hopes of survival will be very
slight. _ |

In heavy weather it is nice to be able to lay out a third anchor Somewhere up wind, but not in line with the main or kedge. Should the wind blow across the tide, you will be putting a severe strain-on anchors laid up and down tide in the usual manner, and they may well start to drag, whereas quite a small anchor laid up wind will prevent this. Ll believe the Royal Navy regard a boat as properly moored only when she has three anchors out ina "crow's foot", In any event it is comforting to have a third anchor aboard. It can spend most of its time out of the way in the bilges, but it may save your boat in an emergency. Another comfort is an anchor buoy secured to the crown of the main anchor by a line which need be no more than a third the length of the cables. Then, if you foul your anchor you can pick up the buoy, and by hauling on the buoy line upend the anchor clear of whatever has fouled it. A useful substitute for a buoy is a tripping line made fast to the crown of the anchor, stop.ed onto the main cable with cotton and its end siezed to the cable about half way up.

Finally, when letting go an anchor, first wait until your boat is moving astern over the ground, then, if you have a Fisherman anchor, pay out the cable carefully so it cannot foul the anchor. A C.Q.R. or Danforth can be let go more abruptly, but do not be too careless.

The eLeering Compass

A type of compass which is popular in small craft is the ex-aircraft grid steering compass. These instruments are obtainable at. most surplus stores, varying in price from about fifteen shillings to five pounds, depending upon condition. and, perhaps most important of all, the type of shop from which it is purchased. There are two models, a five inch diameter and a seven inch diameter. Both work on the same system which

although the same in principle as the ordinary marine compass, differs in application. The grid-compass has .a dead beat card carrying a wire graticule in the form of a "T" with the centre of rotation at the position where the stem joins the cross bar thus :-

The North Seeking pole of the magnetic system being in the direction shown.

The glass cover to the bowl has a set of graticules in the form of a boxed "T" thus:

Contd.on Page 7

Page 7

and the rim marked off in degrees, North being on the side away from the stem of the "T", This cover is rotatable by hand and has facilities for locking. The bowl carries a short white pointer against the edge inside.

The compass is mounted so that a line between the pointer and the centre of rotation is parallel to the centre-line of the boat, the pointer being on the forward side. To use the instrument, the cover is rotated so that the course to be steered in degrees is level with the little pointer, and locked. The boat is stscered on to a course such that the "T" on the card coincides with the boxed "T" on the glass. The boat is now Sailing through the water on the course set up on the cover, or grid ring. Note that I have said "through the water", it does not follow that the boat is actually moving over the sea bed in the direction it is being steered, due to leeway, tidal drift etc. of which moré soon.

These compasses were designed for aircraft and were quite expensive. The shape of the graticules overcomes to a large extent the problem of parallax and even if the compass is not gimballed, can still be uséd with a reasonable angle of heel, say ten degrees.

A very useful and comparatively cheap compass for small boats is the "Sestrel Minor" costing in its basic
form £2,16.-
This has a card of about two inches diameter in a perspex bowl. The card has vertical graduatiors around the edge, and with the addition of a sighting ring and a handle, can be used as a hand bearing compass.

Other popular compasses arse on the market varying in price between about £8 and £80. The two mentioned above however are probably the most attractive to the average nard-up small cruiser man,

One difficulty which arises with some compasses is the formation of bubbles under the glass. This is caused by the continued expansiors and contractions of the damping fluid, evaporation of the alcohol from the fluid, or just plain leakage. These bubbles tend to upset the damping action on the card and Should be removed. This can be a rather agifficult process if not tackled in the right way. The method I have used is to unscrew the filling cap and gently suck with the mouth, holding the instrument at a slight angle, orifice upwards. The bubbles will gradually move towards the rim until they form into one larger bubble at the filling hole. Top up with distilled water and screw the cap down tightly. Don't try drinking the fluid, it doesn't test#a bit like gin even if it does contain alcohol:
Incidentally, the grid steering compass does not suffer from this trouble as a rule. Being designed for use at high altitudes it has bellows type expansion chamber built in to it. Contd.on Page 8

The steering compass must be mounted in such a position that it can easily be seen by the helmsman in whatever position he may be. This, in a small vessel is not easily done. On larger vessels with wheel steering it is usual to have the compass mounted in a housing called a binnacle in front of the wheel. The binnacle consists of a box with a glass window, having facilities for illuminating the compass card, all mounted on'a stout pillar. The cockpit of a small boat has no place for such a monster. it is usual “therefore to mount the compass on the after cabin bulkhead. A common method in pre war days was to mount the compass inside the cabin behind a window in the bulkhead, thus protecting the instrument from the weather. This is a reasonable way for the ordinary compass but would be too difficult an arrangement for a grid steering compass. The latter should be mounted in a position which gives the helmsman eas; access to it for course setting. The insides of the after cockpit coaming under the tiller is a good place provided that there are no heavy galvanised iron fittings, such as cleats, in the vicinity. If your vessel has a bridge deck at the forward end of the cockpit it may be possible to mount the compass under a hinged glass or perspex window, but again, look out for the large lumps of 1Pon. Don't forget that galley equipment is often ferrous in in nature and tends to be very portable. If you must lose your temper when the stew burns, don't fling the ladle at the helmsman, it might end up near, the compass.

RIVER BLACKWATER TO RIVER CROUCH USING THE RAYSAND CHANNEL
These sailing instructions are suitable for shallow draught vessels drawing two or three feet at all states of the tide except at Low Water Ordinary Spring Tides and about an hour on each side. Deeper draught vessels should make an extra time allowance depending upon their draught.
Sail down the main channel of the River Blackwater until Cast Mersea Church lies on a bearing 355° Magnetic. Turn towards the south using this bearing as a back bearing for about 21 miles, until the Buxey Beacon (tall post with T shaped topmark) bears 160 Magnetic, Alter course to due South ; (180°) Magnetic and continue for about miles until the vessel is in line with the line of buoys R.Y.V.S. marked D.Z., marking the limit of the bombing range. On securing your boat by "BARNACLE"

You may have read and digested all in my two previous articles and yet still lose your boat from its mooring or anchor, How can this be? A glance over the foredecks
of a row of boats will soon show you - note the old bvawley
with its heavy oak posts passing down through the deck to the keel, and the chain with two or three turns round the post; then note the luxury motor cruiser of comparable Size, probably built by a firm with more experience of aircraft, caravan or furniture making than boat building - e Firm whose employees sec the sea only from Blackpool Pier on Bank Holidays. The motor cruiser will probably be provided with a beautiful little chromium plated cleat nearly big enough to take Mother's linen line, and there might be as many as four one inch number six screws holding the cleat to the deck planks. Some firms with a little more imagination might even go so far as to put one anda half inch eights through into a deck beam, making the cleat just about secure enough to take the weight of the anchor, if you can manage to pass the chain or warp round the grossly undersized cleat!

The minimum that should be relied on in the way of a mooring fixture is a cleat or eyebolt large enough to pass a hand under, through-bolted to a solid timber running from the stem head under all foredeck beams back to the mast, with solid blocks between the timber and deck planking in the way of the fittings. Not only should there be such a fitting on the foredeck, there should also be at “east one on the aft deck so that the boat can be secured alongside a quay or staging. It is most regrettable that in the present boom in sailing there are firms with no good reputation to lose, and with absolutely no knowledge of the requirements of a good cruising boat, who will sell boats which cannot possibly be properly secured to a mooring, and it is even more regrettable that some of these firms are producing boats which should never be taken off their
moorings! - Boats with no provision for hand starting the
engine, with no cable locker, no clips for fire extinguishers, nothing that any even moderately cautious skipper would regard as essential. Possibly the best thing that could happen to such a boat is for it to go adrift in the first real
blow and wreck itself - let us hope with no one aboard
other than the manufacturer or salesman-demonstrator.

Having ensured that your boat is provided with adequate posts, cleats or rings to secure to, and sufficient warps to anchor properly, warp the boat safely round a boatyard or through a trot of moorings, or secure her alongside a quay, the next essential is:fenders of some sort. I doubt whether there has ever been a boat with too many fenders.

Fenders come in all shapes, sizes and materials,all of which have their advantages and disadvantages. Inflatable plastic fenders might get punctured, but until they do they are a joy to use; coir fenders are very good until they get wet and dirty, and then a sodden lump on deck, oozing muddy water all over the places is a real nuisance. Solid rubazote or similar
fenders are very good, but watch them - like the solid expanded
plastic mooring buoys they come fitted with a natural fibre rope which very soon rots and you losé your nice new fender
or buoy. Then there is the poor man's standby - old tyres.
Thesé mark the paintwork after a time, but it is only a
discoloration - the wood is not damaged. They can be
obtained very cheaply, often free, and the only other disadvantage is that they must be provided with holes to allow the water they collect to drain out.

Page 11

When mooring alongside another boat be sure you have sufficient fenders out to avoid damaging no either hull
matter at what angle they may come together, and if ina berth that will dry out, make sure that the heights of the fenders are such that the boats are still adsquatéely protected even if one settles lower in the mud than the other. In particular, watch the corners of transom sterns - they can give another boat a nasty dig. “When mooring alongside a piled quay or staging, hang two or three fenders over your topsides with a stout spar or plank between the fenders another piles so that if your boat moves forward or aft the fenders will still be effective. Also, whenever you moor alongside put sufficient fenders out on your exposed Side to protect your boat against the cheerful clot who comes along without any fenders and leaves his boat alongside yours.

Finally, always remember to bring all your fenders on deck when sailing -— nothing looks more slovenly than a boat Sailing along with a row of fenders out.

The Cruising Yacht's Tender "Barnacle"

A tender for a cruising yacht can be anything from a diminutive fibreglass bathtub up to a thirty foot high-speed launch, but in this article Ij~ropose to mention only a few points relevant to tenders to yachts of ten tons and under. Ideally, a cruiser's tender should be of such size that it can be carried aboard its parent boat, but Since it should also be capable of carrying all the crew safely, it must all too often be towed. Six feet Long is the smallest practical size for a pram dinghy to carry two people, and a dinghy this size can usually be carried aboard a four topper, but the four topper may well have a crew of four! Up to about the five ton mark the cruiser owner will be well advised to carry a folding dinghy aboard, and keep a decent size dinghy at his home port, leaving it on the mooring when he goes out.

Much has been said and written on the relative merits of pram and stem dinghies, but since a six foot pram dinghy has easily the carrying capacity of an eight foot stem dinghy, these arguments are of academic interest only to the small cruiser owner who must try to squeeze his quart of gear and crew into a pint pot of dinghy.

More conflicting requirements for a tender are that it must be light to tw well, or hoist aboard, and it must be strong to withstand the inevitable abuse it will get.
Clinker ply, with rivetted seams, appears to be the cheapest and easist way of obtaining a suitable hull, which will be stronger and easier to build than a hard chine ply skinned boat. If you build your own dinghy, fit the gunwhale timbers outside the top strake instead of in the usual position inside. This method has three tremendous advantages: it helps to keep stray wave tops out of the boat, it leaves more room inside and gives a wider spacing to the rowlocks, and it makes it possible to tip every drop of water out of the boat when she is ashore.

Inside, the dinghy should have non-skid bottom boards, adequate thwarts which leave ample room for legs an inch or two longer than average, and if at all possible, there should be at least a small watertight locker to hold gear which must be kept dry. The rowlocks should be secured to the boat with plastic line, and there should be either a couple of little leather pockets or clips in which they can be stowed when not in use. When towing the dinghy, oars or paddles should also be securely lashed in, preferably to a thwart. Bottom boards should bs held in place with a turn button, and the baler should, like the rowlocks, be tied in with plastic line so that the whole dinghy can be turned upside down and shaken without the loss of any gear.

At least two stout towing painters should be fitted and a dinghy which is to be hoisted aboard should also have a strongly fitted ringbolt or clips in the stern. All round the topsides of the dinghy should be fitted a substantial fender; an old bass warp used to be nearly universal, but these days far better rubber or plastic fenders can be bought for very reasonable prices. Underneath, the dinghy should be provided with stout oak bilge keels, preferably shod with bronze strips, so that the bottom will not get torn out when she is dragged up and down shingly beaches. A dinghy which is to be carried upside down on the deck of the parent craft can have these bilge keels fitted in the form of twin handrails - most convenient when walking round the dinghy, and also very handy for tying on dirty dishcloths etc. hung out to dry -

Contd. on Page 8

Page 8 Pg

(they don't look nearly so bad as when they are tied to the ship's liferail). Some people who have to move their dinghies up and down concrete hards fit them with small wheels, either oné nouséed in a hollow in the central skeg, or a pair at the ends of the bilge keels. This certainly simplifies moving the dinghy ashore, and does not really make any difference to the performance afloat. .

If at all possible, a dinghy should be provided with ample well fitted buoyancy, preferably solid framed plastic, and all yachts' tenders should be clearly marked with the name and port of registry of the parent boat. Remember, the first visitors will probably see of the yacht that is your pride and joy (or it SHOULD be!) is the dinghy, so keep it smart and in good order,

Picnic Cruise

The turnout for the first picnic. cruise of the season on Sunday April 29th was most gratifying. The weather had been rather unpromising, and with a stead N.E. wind prevailing, of a distinctly polar temperature, the prospect of spending several hours on Osea Hast Point did not commend itself. Nevertheless, 21 hardy souls in eight boats made the journey and in general had an enjoyable day.

The number of people w:io took part would have been larger had not Avril decided, with that streak of femininity common to all boats, that SHE was going to have her picnic on Northey Island, regardless of where her crew aimed to go, and this she promptly did. Unfortunately she was carrying the galley stores, but we. were able to take off all the vital tea making equipment and water supply, thus averting grave possibilities of mutiny within the club.

Once at Osea driftwood was collected, a camp fire was soon ablaze and tea was promptly being dispensed. After lunch old man 'Sol' gave us a peep or two and we were able to enjoy some sailing in each other's boats. Unfortunately, just as we were thinking of returning, one of. the party had the misfortune to capsize on a lee shore but thanks to a rescue crew who went to their aid in Mike Newston's Silhouette, things were put to rights. The unlucky pair soon recovered from an icy ducking thanks to the "camp fire" and hot coffee. A whip round enabled them to be rigged out in dry clothes. This incident delayed our return, but the last boat arrived back at 9 pem. as dusk was falling.

I would like to thank all those who turned up for the agent in spite of the unfavourable weather.

Thanks are also due to Mike Newston who willingly took a crew in his Silhouette to help the capsized boat, and to Fenton Rylance and Alan Pratt who made up the crew. Mike, at the time, was not a club member but I hope that he has now applied, or will be persuaded to do so.

The Best from your Boat

I do not intend to enter into any controversy over the type of dinghy that you should have, because this depends on'too many factors and people have individual ideas about boats in rather the same way as choice of motor car.
;

I aim to help you to get the best out of whatever boat you have bought. Remember that ina competitive class a 1% increase in speed probably makes a difference of about 6 places so that as a rule it is minor things that will give you a lst compared with 6th or 7th.

You will find that in most fleets it is the best main- tained dinghy that is consistently in the front and there is no other answer to this than time spent on your boat, getting everything to the best state within your power.
Surface finish is not so important as people think. It only makes a difference when it is blowing fairly hard. The smoothness of your dinghy contours on bottom and topsides is very important, and all bumps and crevices should befaired in so that you have a nice flowing line. This will involve you ina considerable amount of time with filler cement and sandpaper. Do not forget things like your rudder and centre plate, because these account for a good part of your wetted area.

Having got your hull, centreplate and rudder into as good a shape as you can, next we come to the mast and rigging. Here you must abide by your class rules but get your mast as light as you can within these rules. Also get the best aerodynamic form that the rules will allow. The rigging should be kept as simple as the class rules will allow and most important, in good condition, it is false

economy to save 5/-d. on rigging and lose a £20 hollow mast. If you have mast tangsto hold your stays make these of stainless steel. There have been a number of cases lately of small s. shackles giving way, you can now buy tested shackles and it is money well spent to use these in important places if you cannot afford to use them everywhere. It is much cheaper in the long run to use stainless steel stranded wire instead of galvanised iron or solid stainless steel.
If you are using Terylene rope for halliards remember that this must be pre-stretched.

We will leave sails for the moment as these are important enough to warrant a complete article of their
own.

Now we come to the inside of the dinghy. Remember that your job when racing is largely a matter of concentration, therefore you should be as comfortable and relaxed as circumstances will allow. Both you and your crew may have to move very quickly at times so you should keep the floor of the boat as clear as possible so that you can move without falling over the odd rope or fitting. Arrange your sheet leads and plate tackle to intrude as little as possible and yet be immediately to hand in emergency. If you have self-bailers see that these are under the centre thwart. If at all possible and in most cases with a little ingenuity, you can arrange to have clear deckspace where you and your crew sit. Your crew cannot be expected to give of their best if they are sitting on a fairlead or some other deck fitting!

Using the Yachts Tender by "Barnacle"

These days a horribly large number of yachtsmen are drowned when they fall out of their dinghies, and one has only to watch them to see why.

Let me quote a personal experience. Seven of us, having enjoyed a convivial evening at the “Green Man" piled aboard a twelve foot stem dinghy to take the last of the ebb tide down Bradwell Creek to a twenty ton cutter anchored near the mouth. With such a load aboard the top of the open dagger plate case was below water. What fun: Never mind - the ever ingenious skipper sat on the top of the case, stopping about half the flow of water. Two of us baled, two rowed, and we all sang with the joy of living, until we grounded on the far side of the creek. With seven of us aboard there wasn't really room to row straight, so many willing hands hindered each other in hoisting the (luckily small) lugsail, and one gallant soul leapt over the transom to push us off the mud. Unfortunately for him it was the bow that was aground, not the stern and he went in up to his armpits. fee rudder could not be found, so we steered (?) with the oars, and eventually reached the cutter, but not before a gybe all standing had caught the mainsheet round one man's neck and nearly strangled him. Arrived at the cutter all seven of us leant out to grab her, and the dinghy capsized beneath us, leaving us hanging from bobstay, whisker shrouds and bulwarks to scramble aboard as best we could. Fortunately somebody had held on to the painter, so the party was soon under way again with a swamped dinghy lying under our counter. What fun:

What mad, suicidal folly - I still go cold when I
think of how incredibly lucky we were. To be drunk in charge of a dinghy is every bit as dangerous as to be drunk in charge of a car. But even sober, sedate yachtsmen load their dinghies until they have only an inch or two of freeboard rather than make two safe trips.

Whilst this may be permissible in shallow water when the tide is rapidly departing and all aboard are fully aware of the risks being taken it is never justifiable in deep water or where there is any sea running. It is amazing how few people seem to be able to step straight into or out of the centre of a dinghy. When ferrying passengers it is usually best to get the stern of the dinghy against the up-tide face of a jetty or staging so they can step straight in, but this is not always possible, and is of course impossible when boarding or léaving a tide rode yacht. On all occasions the skipper should be first into and last out of the dinghy and he should be constantly on the alert to move over and keep the dinghy balanced whilst passengers are getting in or out.

When coming alongside a tide rode yacht, always try to approach from the weather quarter, and see that all aboard the dinghy know clearly who is going to catch hold of the boat on arrival. This should always be the foremost person in the dinghy, even if she first touches aft. If the passenger in the stern of the dinghy grabs the yacht's rail the tide will lever the dinghy away from the ship's side, and if the passenger still hangs on, the dinghy will turn right round, making it almost impossible to get her properly secured, whereas if the foremost person catches on with one hand, then passes the painter round a cleat, stanchion éto., the wind and tide will hold the dinghy alongside the yacht.

When approaching from up-tide on a strong tide, swing the dinghy round before she gets level with the parent yacht, and approach from the bows with the dinghy travelling stern first.

Again it must be the foremost hand in the dinghy who catches
on.

One sure way of capsizing a dinghy sooner or later is to consistently board and leave it with it held alongside the transom or end of a counter stern of a tide rode yacht. The tide will be trying to steam the dinghy away from the yacht, and if you step too near'the side against the yacht the run of tide under the dinghy may well flip it over on top of you.

Whenever you step from a dinghy to a yacht or staging, take care not to kick or push the dinghy away from beneath
you - it takes a little care and practice to step cleanly into
the centre of the dinghy, but it is an art that is well worth
learning.

Finally, ship your oars and slip out the rowlocks before you come alongside, not after you have torn a gash out of the topsides. Never step in or out of a dinghy with
the rowlocks fitted - if they catch in your turnups or socks
you can have a nasty spill. .

The weather forecast for Whit Monday was not good, at least for those who listened at 3 o'clock. The rest, reading only the National Press, were probably much happier as they set out from 'Mamgu' in the early hours (9.30!) Luckily the first guess proved right and there were not more than a few spots of rain during the day. Avril, once again, showed her versatility as 23 Club boat. Having gone aground last time on the wrong island, she determined to snow us that she could run to Osea Without her jib. Unfortunately she overshot, and the crew were most grateful when the Rescue Launch supplied the missing sail and they could tack back over the ebb, to the camp-fire, tea and biscuits.

The morning was rather.a lazy one, but Robbie Sims was hard at it all day on the Rescue Launch engine. Our thanks are very much due to him for taking over the job at tae last moment, At 1,50pm. the Launch came alive, and gave no further trouble all day; Jack and Robbie started the race from the Osea Pier line, and followed us round with ease. The course set was of 12 miles, down to the furthest Stone Club buoys, up to the Doubles and back to the Pier for the finish. Most of the race was a gentle reach in the light Northerly breeze, and Mr. Payne, sailing ' Rainbow' single-panded, was obviously happy with the conditions. He finished well up among the Fleetwinds and was an easy winner on handicap, thus reversing last year's result when wy conditions were all against him. John Tillotson did particularly well in his father's: boat, coming home a very good second.

Far cad -way day most used knot is the bowline, loon which will not slip» and is easily untied, it can be used to secure = noorins warp to a ring s:olv or post, tie on a personal lifeline, secure a fender,prevent the ship's cat from wandering(tied in his lifeline and NoT in his tail as suggested by one member.) and I must confess I have even used it to secure the warp to the kedge anchor. Don't be satisfied with your ability to tie a bowline until you can manage it in 1 wet, slimy, muddy warp,in total darkness and in any position,possibly with 2 jerking load on the rope.

The other knot used frequently in mooring is the clove hitch, as it is so simple to form a couple of loops in the rope and slip it over the end of a most, but it is many years since-I tied a clove hitch by passing the rope round the post- if I can't slip a clove hitch over the end I invariably put in the extra turn 2nd make a rolling hitch_ much more secure. :
