Sunshine, fresh breezes, a dash of rain on Monday afternoon, added to a splendid sunset as well as sunrises for those who were stirring, all combined to make a memorable weekend of sailing and camping for the club. Mersea Stone again was the choice this year for the base of operations and what better choice could there have been.

The expedition was led by Phil Luke of Great Baddow. In all, eleven boats put in at the camp-site over the Bank Holiday weekend, the little armada being composed ef two Sharpies, one Torch, four Enterprises (two of which arrived on Sunday), one G.P., one Fleetwind, Karolin a self-contained camp in herself, and last but by no means least, Avril, in all her glory.

As most club members will recall, Avril 's explorers became stuck in the mud on the first picnic cruise. We are proud to announce that Avril did not become stuck in the mud this time. Alas, she.became stranded on the hard at Brightlingsea, overnight on
Saturday, having been assured by the locals that the tide was favourable. Thus it was
that her skipper and crew spent their first night at camp aboard Avril.
The boats arrived at intervals throughout Saturday, the first adventurous souls having put out on the early morning tide. As the day progressed, tents were added to the splendid location, the last ones going up shortly before midnight, salved with all the necessary good fortune from Avril in her predicament at Brightlingsea. By
Sunday there were ten tents in all, eleven including "the smallest room".

THE BEST FROM YOUR BOAT,
Part 2, Sails.

It’ is only in the last 3 or 4 years that we in this country have abandoned the idea that a good sail should be cut flat and should have very little flow,The Continentals have proved us wrongin this, and most dinghies will go very much faster Rj under any condition with a lot of flow in botno mainsail and foresail., A good mainsail should nave a large shelf along the boom, and be very baggy just aft of the mast. There are two ways of doing this, you can, if you have a long purse,buy your 39ils from Paul Elvstrom who builds the shape into the sail by the way he cuts the widths of cloths still keeping the luff and foot straight.This is by far the best way, but it is out of the price range of most of us.

The common way of getting flow into'a sail is by shaping the luff ané the foot, so that before the sails are put onto the spars they have shaped luff and foot, which, when they are fixed to straight spars puts flow into them,

The. way you use your new sails is very important as you w can completely ruin a new sail in its first hour:of life. -We will deal first with the treatment of a cotton sail. It should ideally, be set first on a nice sunny diy, with a moderate breeze. Pull un the luff just hand taut, do not attempt to sweat the sail up the mast, the same is true along the boom, it should only be hand taut on the outhaul, A cotton sail needs 24 hours use before it is stretched and during this time you should continually take uv the slack on boom and mast as the sail stretches. Do not sheet the sails in hard during this 24 hours, it is best to keep the boat reaching with a beam wind backwards and forewards, At the end of 24 hours sailing time you can then sweat up the luff of the sail but do not pull out the outhaul as tight as it will go on stretching slightly for another 24 hours or so. NEVER in this period of 9 sails life reef it, if you do, it will newér recover, also — try not to get it wet.,It should be aired after use and carefully put away dry. You should,even after careful stretching, treat your sails very carefully if you capsize, especially in salt water, Rinse them in fresh water,dry and air them before storing. y Well cared for cotton sails will give 5 years first class racing.

a Coming to terylene sails the requirements are somewhat different.Cotton sails are carefully stretched and they retain
the stretched ‘shape for the rest of their life, Terylene on
the
other hand is elastic,and while you can ruin a terylene sail by the way you set it ,the damage is not permanent.You
must
therefore be very fussy about tension on luff and foot each time you set sail. The amount of tension you put on them will determine how the sail sets, and by varying the tension you can give the sail the best shape for varying weather conditions, You will .after a, little experimenting, find out the right tension so that the sail will have no creases in the wrong places. As you increase the tension you will flatten the sail.

Make certain that your battens are the right length, and if you have
a leach line, have this as loose as possible con- Sistent with the sail: setting,

If they have become wet with salt water, wash them in fresh water and dry them as you would for cotton sails before putting them away. Please, if you have a good set of sails either cotton or terylene, do look after them for sailmaking is some- thing of a black art, and excellent sails are few and far between. SPLICES AND ROPES' ENDS. "Barnacle",

_ As one looks round 2 boatyard these days one sees plenty of roves with unravelled ends, steadily getting shorter and shorter, and perfect horrors to tie good knots in. This should not be, as it is so easy to prevent an end from unlaying. If for any reason you have to cut a Warp and have not time to do anything about the raw end, slip a thumb knot in it to stop it from unlaying until you have tine to do something About it- cither whip or splice it.

Whipping is neat and tidy 2nd is easily done, but the plain whivping-is not ' a good bst' as a permanent finish. Far better, is the sailmakers' :whipping which cannot pull off the end. A third recognised whipping is the West Country whipping, but I have never seen it used, or known 2nyone who has, so it can , probably, well be forgotten.

A back svlice.can always be put in the ends of a warp if it is well tapered ett, and it provides a neat end to the rope, but it does stiffen it and may make it difficult to tie 2 zsood knot near. the end of the rope.

Eye splices, both with and without thimbles, are needed all over 2 boat, 28 Without doubt, it is far and away toe neatest way of putting a loon in the end of 1 rove, and should be used whenever 2 permanent loop is needed. Examples , such as the end of the lanyard on the ship's bucket, and the tails of halliard falls ,where they shackle onto .blocks or wire parts, come readily to. mind. Splicins is fascinating work, and once learnt, the beginner is often tempted to put splices in places, where they should not really be used, _ Simply for the fun of making them. When learning to splice don! t make the mistake of trying to start on codling, thinking that the small stuff is. easier- it isn't. Codline is often so tightly laid that it is a real brute to tuck and a single splice say take four or five times as longs 2s one in something like two inch hemp. Rope is expensive, and continually practising splices can soon get through quite a le length, so it is advisable bo start learning on an old mooring rope. “hen practising , don't bother to make vast numbers of tucks, but concentrate on setting the start of the splice correct, When anlicing cotton and synthetic fibre ropes it is necessary to whin or seal the ends of the strands before starting the splice, but this is not so for sisal or hep. Once the back splice and eye splice have been mastered there are other splices, but they are seldom used now, 2nd are worth learning only for their interest.

Page 14,
There is quite a range of fancy knots that can be tied , using the individual strands of a rope, to produce a decorative ring round the end of 2 rope. Some of these can be used in Place of a crown knot to start a back splice, and others are> finished off by relaying the rope beyond the knot and putting on 2 sailmakers' whipping. These knots are well worth learn- — ing so that you can finish off the ends of your mooring warps in 2 distinctive, easily identified manner. Unfortunately it is very difficult to mako a neat job of these fancy finishes in synthetic ropes, whose strands do not hold their lay very well, and it is next door to impossible in cotton.
However, sisal and hemp take these fancy knots well, and it is a pleasant way of passing a Warm windless after- noon sitting on deck doing a bit of ropework, You may complain that I have not actually told you how to do any of the knots and splices, Certainly not- they are very well described and illustrated in almost every textbook on sailing, and in ‘Scouting for Boys', and-it is not ny intention in these two articles to write about a subject that has already been covered thoroughly, but merely to emphasise certain, not so obvious, points which are often neglected in the textbooks,

SAILING COMMITTEE

As noted in last Month's ‘Navigans', Rescue Launch policy was high on this months agenda. Most members will be aware of the troubles that Roy and his helpers had to overcome last winter and at the beginning of this season. Thanks to their efforts we are now able to rely on the Launch and to consider the finer points of its use.

1.CREW. The Launch has several tricky points of operation, so only members on the lists below may take charge of the boat except in extreme emergency. Those on the rota list have undertaken to be present in turn on “"Programmed"days. New recruits to either list are eagerly sought, and will be quickly taught the essential points.

Rota List. R,Wellstead, A.S. & J.Bigden, R.Sims, I. Wheeler,
J.Littlewood, R.Drury.
Mon-Rota List. E.Baker, A.Pratt, F.Darney.

2.Note. The Launch will be manned by Rota Crew on all Race & Picnic Deys and on the last day of Camping weekends. On other days requests for the services of the Launch should be made to the 0.0.D. If he decides it necessary, a coxn.. from either list above will take out the launch with a scratch crew.

3. Race Days. The Launch will be ready with the engine tested half an hour before the Race, but will not leave its mooring unless required by the 0.0.D. If the launch is not available, and it is "red Flag", weather, courses will be restricted to above Hilly Pool.

4. Picnic Cruises. The Launch will accompany the Cruise as Rescue or Committee Boat or Tug only. It will not be used as a fishing boat or for Joy Rides.

5. Camping weekends. The Launch will not accompany the campers,
but will be manned at Heybridge on the last day. If weather conditions (storm or calm) require it, it will be sent as far as Stone to act as Rescue, Tug or escort.

6. Any defects or running repairs on the Launch must be reported immediately to the Club Coxswain.

7. At all times the launch is under the authority of the 0.0.D. whose decision on its use or non-use is final. The launch is out of bounds to members not on Rescue Duty.

Good Books. Lately

New and again one picks up a book which is manifestly not one's cup of tea at all, only to become so captivated by it that it is virtually impossible to lay it down unfinished. "BY GEMINI" is preciesely that kind of book. The wrapper shows an outboard cruiser on a pline, the "gal" at the wheel waving one hand like the model in a washing machine ad., and paying even less attention to her controls; and the blurb informs us (if we need to be told) that the author, Ann Davison, is the first woman to sail Across the atlantic single-handed. She also appears to be a rather engaging extrovert who writes in order to do what she likes, and does what she likes in order to write about it. It is what she does and the candour with which she reviews it that are of relevant interest to readers of "Navigans".

Shortly after her arrival in America, the idea arose in her mind of making a trip through the States and crystallised into the round trip from Miami to Miami by way of the atlantic Intracoastal waterways, the River Hudson and its related canal system. leading into the Great Lakes, the Rivers Illinois and Mississippi to the Gulf of Mexico, which is here

described, Throughout an incubating period of five years, she cherished the nation of doing this in her 25 ft. sloop, "Felicity Ann"; Which had brought her across the Atlantic and only with reluctance did she concede the unsuitability of this boat for negotiating narrow inland waterways, canal locks, and bridges of which there would be nett 2 few in si« tncusanc miles. "Power corrupts; and absolute power corrupts absolutely‘ Let anyone who doubts take the "Maggie" and feel how sweetly she turns in her own length, 360 degrees in the revolution of the wheel, and so let the yachtsman “appreciate the candour. of Ann Dawson's narrative of her conversion from, emergency use of an auxiliary with maximum speed of five knots to outboards, Which she rated as "fast" at anything over ten miles an hour, and her eventual acceptance of twenty miles per hour as merely normal and comfortable. It is this simplicity indeed that lends
weight to her comments on the conditions existing in the New Jersey Waterways, where narrow, winding channels amid shoals offer something that is in essence comparable to what we are familiar with in the Thanes Estuary and the description of fishermen moored to buoys' as well as in tke fairway, of water-skiiers hurtling in and out shedding as they go, chunky deep sea fishers churning their way through it all, should be prescribed reading, in its context, for all who sail in little ships.

Many other points of interest are commented upon. Moorings
and facilities offered, for-instance, held charm for the Old World reader: it, is not unusual how fine an electric point presumably where one Would expect to find a stand pipe on a Broads staithe; and one would have liked some assessment of the charges made for the amenity. Navigation across Georgian Bay theough who area known as Thirty Thousand Islands presented baffling problems, until the author happened on a sequence of painted markers which showed up well and from which she successfully took direction. She later learned she had navigated. some 60 miles through a National Park area on bird sanctuary signs at 20 miles an hour. The Drainage Canal had its moments too: barge tows over 1,000 ft. in length, leaving a 5 mile wake; and the Mississippi current brings flood debris down at a rate of 9 knots and makes it necessary to plane upstream to a mooring in order not to be swept away. Emergence into the Gulf did not bring immediate betterment. A perfect anchorage on a steeply shelving beach, not far from a grocery and marine store, seemed an ideal hideaway, Morning found the boat hanging on her anchor line, pointing skyward, the occupant of one berth standing on her head and the other comfortably on her feet. In this Looking-Glass Land a strong offshore wind may effectively drain these coastal areas.

Recommended for the Christmas Stocking as well is the library list, for both tke unpaid crew and the skipper, for sheer fun and for some very useful light on a subject we shall have to face sooner or later and ought to look at bedtimes.

Sod's Law, . by "Barnacle".

Most, if not all of you must have met this law in one of its numerous forms at some time or another, and being unable to think rof anything better on which to discourse this month I propose to mention a few of its better known twists and corollaries, if only to let off a bit of steam and air some old, old grievances.

How many of us have set out for a day's sail on eoe of those mornings when the wind doesn't seem to knew quite what to do, and having been headed by gusts between N. and S.E. all the way down to the Colne, eager for lunch with the consoling thought that at least an Easterly wind will blow us home. Then, bloated With good food we lie down for an hour or two, lulled to sleep by the quiet slap of the wavelets on the planks, the not so quiet sounds of a host of transistorised radios all blaring forth different programmes and the not at all quiet cries of marine motorists as they roar up and down the river. A couple of hour's rest (?), and then what de we find? A South Wester, either force one or Force five, with another horrid. beat all the way home!

This is, of course, Sod's law which tells us quite clearly that if we have removed from the boat any of the tools which have been lying aboard untouched for the last six years, then this is the day when we are really going to need that one tool. (For. bed also read oilskin. bathing costume, signal flag, spare lamp glass, spare sail etc.etc.etc.)

Mr. Sod was, I feel sure, at one time a shipwright. It is truly remarkable that presented with a vast expanse of decking several square feet in area; beneath which is hidden one screw head three eighths of an inch in diameter, our dear friend informs us that if we were to drive a single nail into that expanse of decking, then we shall certainly hit that one solitary screw head! Far worse of course is the occasion when we have a fitting to secure with three or more screws, for then Mr. Sod gees to great pains to ensure that it is always the last screw which fouls the hidden obstruction, leaving the unpleasant alternatives of moving the fitting over (usually to the next hidden obstruction) or leaving out the last screw to the detriment the neat appearance of the boat, and possibly tke strength as well.

Mention damaged dinghies, and you have hit upon Mr. Sod's favourite field. The fiendish ingenuity he displays in arranging that the cracked rib is always the one which involves removing thwarts, knees and a host of other fittings before it can be replaced whilst the next rib, which could be whipped cut in five minutes, is undamaged, must be seen to be believed.

Mr. Sod's sailing weekends are spent touring all recognised anchorages and laying a profusion of old chains and cables across the places which we all knw to be good clear anchorages. It is also at his instigation that Trinity House remove the one buoy on which you always rely, at the very time when you've left your binoculars at home and damaged the compass.

The Sod differntial factor which has to be applied to all published tide tables must also be familiar to all - but how helpful it would be if there was only some constant in the formula. The nearest approach to it is the fact that if you are hoping to get your deat afloat the height of the tide will be four inches less than you need. Conversely, of course, if you've left the beat aground and unmoored in the certainty that she won't float, then this is the time for a really good freak high tide, fully six inches above predicted heights. As to the time of high water factor, Mr. Sod does save us some worry by assuring us that no matter what method you've used to calculate it, you'll be at least a quarter of an hour out.

COMMODORE'S COMMENTS

There are three things of note to which I should like to draw your attention this month.

Firstly, the Laying Up Dinner and Dance, This takes place on Friday,
8th November at 7 o'clock for 7.30; and this year, for the first time, will

Secondly, we have during the week November 4th to 8th, the election of committee members for the M,A.S.C. main committee. All details are on the posters around the establishments,

Finally, a word about power vessels, The Committee have decided that power boats of the non planing type are acceptable; defining these as vessels with outboard or inboard engines which at all times act as displacement craft, As there are bound to be border-line cases, each application will be treated

If the hull is to be clinker planked, it is planked next, each strake carefully cut and fitted, screwed to the main backbone of the hull and rivetted to its neighbour, gaps being left in the neat rows of rivets for the ribs, which are fitted when the hull is fully planked. If the hull is to be carvel planked, the ribs must be fitted first as the planks are not secured to each other but only to the frame of the hull. When bent ribs are being fitted, there must be something available to hold them to the correct shape. On a clinker hull the planks do this very nicely, but as we have just seen, the planking of a carvel hull cannot be done until the ribs are in, so a series of ribbands - long, even grained softwood strips - are run round the outside of the moulds where the planking will eventually lie, widely spaced where there is to be little curvature in the ribs, closing to may be as little as an inch or two apart where the bends are to be sharp.

Each ribband is well fastened to the stem, transom and moulds, and the whole framework is now checked to see that all curves are fair.

By this stage the hole for the stern tube will probably have been bored if the engine is to be mounted centrally, and much of the work on the rudder mountings will be done. If the boat is to have a centreplate, the case will have been fitted to the keel before the moulds were erected, and the plate will probably be in. Floors, either plate or grown wood may have been fitted to the keel, and in some cases they may be used to form the lower portions of some of the moulds. Other boats will not have the floors fitted until the hull is planked.

At the top of the hull the beam shelves and clamps, breasthook and quarter knees will be fitted, all located by sockets cut in the moulds.

Motor slowly against flood right clear of entrance, turned into wind and with Frances at the helm I started to make sail. The engine stopped and I tried briefly to start it, no go. Our situation was not critical and I proceeded to make all sail and press on for Hurst narrows. The seas were quite large and we had the wind (4-5?) to our starboard quarter. Most alarming for crew who had to take the helm whilst I inspected plugs, spark and fuel flow. All seemed O.K. so I swung it over and it started after a few turns. Having got it to go I shut off, and turned petrol off and confirmed with crew that we would make for the Solent, we made across the bay, well clear of the shore as wind was W.S.W. (lee shore). Decided to go to west of Shingles Bank, but on approaching we could see clear water (relatively) right into Hurst narrows. The wind had backed slightly to South and we ran in towards the narrows. Seas had been up to 10-11ft high, 60 ft long. Quieter water under lee of Shingles but very confused on main channel side, breaking etc. Unfortunately the wind backed again forcing us to enter the very heavy seas and we cut diagonally across the tide towards the Island side where we found some shelter. Here we gybed and ran over towards the quiet water near Keyhaven. Ran straight up Solent on the port gybe.

Saw a large wishbone schooner tacking against wind and flood off Yarmouth. She was making heavy weather and was last seen running up Solent (Lymington) under bare poles! However, a Brixham trawler was carrying full working sail and made good progress. MARK handled well despite the strong winds and vicious seas. The dinghy towed on a fairly short painter and gave no concern apart from twice having to be pulled alongside to have the rag stuffed back into the dagger trunk. When we anchored I baled out about 2" of water. Just after 3 [?] p.m. we entered Newtown Creek, dropping mainsail just inside. We motored in and dropped hook on the windward bank. The cook made a welcome lunch and it is now 4.30 [?] p.m. as I write up the log. We intend to make way and spend the night somewhere in the Beaulieu River.
Motored out of Newtown, set mainsail and ran up Solent against first ebb. MARK seemed easier with just mainsail, but showed a tendency to broach in the short wind-over-tide seas. Made our way over to mainland side and entered the Beaulieu River via the Swatchway 7' 6" on tide gauge and the island was either gone or underwater (very high tide). Tomorrow should confirm its existence. Sailed up the river (engine for tacking and dead-beat sections).

Motored right up passing Swan of Beaulieu and Mary Helen at Gins Farm, sailed right up within the last two reaches of Beaulieu itself. Crew was enchanted with river and agreed it was like Pin Mill only Bigger, Better and much more opulent. Passing conducted tour steamer gave us a snippet of useless gen. A large country house (Babycham Director?) just past Gins has solar-heated outdoor swimming pool, reflector system. At the top end of the river we downed sail and crew motored us down as I made ship tidy, warps, fenders and jib off. We moored alongside Gwenda, long lean cruiser. Alongside her was CHORISTER, yes, the same vessel! Have not had a chance to chat her yet, hope to do so tomorrow.

We had poached egg and cuppa after making fast, then I scrubbed the Newtown mud off the anchor. Had Gwenda's owner and crew aboard muchly admiring "little" MARK, who has about twice as much accommodation! Lord Montagu does the river proud. Dinghies not to stay more than four hours (parking tickets?) Ashore phoned Beechcroft 9-15 p.m. Pint lager and lime in B.H. [?] next to Master Builders, filled water bottle in bar. Drank outside, lovely evening.

Aboard at 10 p.m. washed (crew, as Skipper is writing log!) Hope to make Hythe by lunch time, Bembridge by evening tomorrow ready for big jump-off Tuesday or as soon as B.B.C. say it's fit.

CLUB EVENT

Despite the frosty weather a fair number of members turned up at the college on Thursday 16th January to hear John Scarlett's contribution to the winter programme. This talk was devoted to boat maintenance and repair and was divided into two parts, the coffee break forming a convenient dividing line.

In the first part John dealt with general maintenance, pointing out that it is an all-—the-year-—round job and not just a case of a few hours work at laying-up and fitting-out. He also pointed out how insidious water can be in delaminating ply and rotting planks. The maintenance of sails and rigging followed, particular stress being given to the storing of cotton sails and the treatment of galvanised rigging. At this point we were reminded of the forthcoming.talk by Mr. A.G. Taylor, the well known Maldon sail-maker, scheduled for 12th March which should give everyone a greater insight into the subject of sails.

The next point was the all-important one of paint, with a strong warning against allowing the excessive build-up of old paint on a boat.
Obviously
a case of a lot of paint covering a multitude of sins ! The pros and cons of enamel versus polyurethane and epoxied resin paints was then discussed, one of the points being made that the latter two are just as effective at keeping water in as keeping it out-! Fibre glass sheathing also appears to have the same doubtful virtue.

A brief outline was then given on the manufacture of marine ply with the note that the magic sign BS.1088 is open-to a very wide interpretation.

The second part of the talk covered actual repair work, from minor delamination of ply up to the replacement of large portions of the boat.

Htos

—

Also included was the replacement of damaged planks in clinker and carvel hulls and replacement of damaged ribs, the whole repair procedure in all cases being very fully illustrated by sketches shown via the epidiascope.

JG. Reeve.

STEAMING THE RIBS
BY "BARNACLE"

It is early morning in the boatyard. The skeleton of the new boat seems to fill the building shed, with its multiplicity of struts and braces securing it to the roof beams. A wisp of smoke rises as the boy lights the fire under the steam chest boiler, and splintering noises show he is busy smashing up the last remains of an assortment of old dinghies, rotten cabin tops and broken masts, ensuring a good supply of fuel for the day*s activities.

Some of the shipwrights are wriggling their way round inside the framework of the new boat, marking off the run of the ribs with chalk and pencil marks on the ribbands, whilst others gather round the circular saw and planer, feeding into them the boards of wet, green oak, delivered freshly cut to the yard the previous day. As the ribs emerge from the planer they are checked, and any with small knots or wavy grain are rejected and the rest are laid out with the grain in the best direction for bending, and chamfers are planed on the inner corners. If the grain tends to run out, the outer corners may have their sharp edges removed to reduce the risk of splitting when they are bent.

By the time the first batch of ribs are prepared, steam is probably up in the boiler. Some yards have very good steam chests, others are a trifle on the crude side. In the latter case, the boy will probably be stopping up the worst of the leaks, surroundéd by a fine haze of steam. When the steam chest is nicely hot. the first half dozen or so ribs are fed in, the chest is closed and the ribs left to stew for about half an. hour, depending on their size. Like most forms of cooking an overdone rib is nearly as bad as one that is underdone.

Even when the ribs are ready there will be no signs of hurry, but just try working with the shipwrights ! From the time the steam chest is opened until the rib is in place not a second will be wasted. Two men are ready inside the frame of the hull, whilst others wait outside. The chest is opened, emitting a pleasant cloud of steam, a rib is grasped (by a well gloved hand) and withdrawn and passed to the first man outside the boat. The rib feels bone dry, very hot and surprisingly rubbery. The man outside the boat will rapidly give the rib any necessary sideways bend, passing it over the top and down inside the ribbands, outside the shelf timbers to the men inside the hull who locate its lower end in the socket in the keel and push it firmly into position against the ribbands. The men outside watch carefully, and as soon as they notice it is not touching a certain ribband a clamp is screwed on to pull it into place. Meanwhile the men inside the hull are tacking the rib to the ribbands, and maybe too the keel with wire nails. The rib usually lies snugly in place alongside the beam shelf, but occasionally it is necessary to tack it here as well. Then the next rib is taken from the chest and the drill repeated. Quite often. two or more teams are working on different parts of the hull simul- taneously. As ribs are taken from the chest, others are put in, alternate batches often being marked by hammering a tack into the ends so there can be no doubt which have been in the longest.

Work is always started in the middle of the hull where the beam is greatest, and carried on into the stern where there are usually the sharpest . curves so that any ribs that break or refuse to bend properly can be put

Conteces

-5-

in up in the bows where the ribs are shorter and with little curvature, but this must be done very quickly before the timber cools off too
much.

Oak or rock elm (not to be confused with ordinary elm) are the woods chiefly used for steamed ribs. Both can be obtained with good straight grain in the required lengths, and both take steaming well, the rock elm being the easier to bend when hot. The whole secret of steaming is plenty of hot steam, under pressure if at all possible, and cook the wood for the right time. Amateur attempts with a bit of drainpipe over a driftwood fire will usually succeed fairly well, in fact the wood will bend quite well if it has been immersed in boiling water, but it is far and away easier to handle if it has been properly steamed in a good chest with no water touching it.

ADMIRALTY CHARTS THE CRUISING YACHTSMAN

A valuable item in the cruiser's inventory should be an adequate set of charts corrected up to date. The standards applied by the Admiralty Chart Agents are necessarily high: alterations are continually being made, and cancellation is. ruthless after a very few years (maybe three or four), with the result that several pounds! worth of charts are reduced to the status of lampshade material.

Sailing on cancelled and uncorrected charts really has nothing to recommend it, and the obvious solution is to do one's own corrections, fairly regularly, and above all, well before time of sailing. After all, the familiarity thus gained with the chart numbers as well as their range and content is something that will pay off later in confidence and facility and so increase one's scope and enjoyment of cruising.

Members of this club are well based to enjoy a pretty wide range of cruising possibilities from creek-crawling (remember Arthur Ransome's "Secret Water"?) to going foreign, even if it does involve crossing one or.two of the main shipping lanes. For general purposes the cruising area available can conveniently be taken as bounded by a line from Dungeness to Boulogne on the one hand and from Happisburgh to Den Helder on the
other.

From the Catalogue of Admiralty Charts (1964 Home Edition, price one shilling from any of the Agents ) one can compile a basic and comprehensive selection of large and small scale charts to cover this area according to requirements. (The nearest official supplier of local charts is May and Brett Ltd., 118 High Street, Maldon).

Starting from scratch, the yachtsman's requirement will be a large ‘scale chart of home channels and nearby harbours. The rule, "as large a scale as possible", holds good at every stage and for every size of vessel. Admiralty charts covering a large stretch of coastline have the advertised disadvantage that marks close inshore are not shown. For example, No. 1610 (North Foreland to Orfordness) bears the following
Caution:

"Certain buoys, lights and wrecks in the inner waters are not shown on this chart. All buoys and wrecks are omitted westward of the heavy pecked line. For these the larger scale charts must be
consulted."

This pecked line zigzags between Walton-on-the—Naze and Westgate—on~ Sea, and passes outside all of the swatchways which would normally be used by yachtsmen.

3

The alternative large scale charts covering lesser areas in detail are unwieldy on the small boat (minus chart table and maybe even without cabin). To overcome this difficulty the Admiralty has recently issued a series of Yachting Charts showing small inshore areas on a large scale, backed with its authority and presented on a sheet small enough to be handled in a dinghy, giving on the reverse side sailing directions, yacht repair facilities and local yacht clubs, with additionally a transparent cover to fit —- all at a price about half the average full
size production. With Nos. 5389 (W. Mersea to Maldon) and 5388 (Approaches
to Rivers Colne and Blackwater) the yachtsman can comfortably explore the home estuaries, and they will be sufficient also for most cruiser races organised by the Blackwater J.R.C. The series covers every popular yachting centre from Great Yarmouth to Dover. The Yachting Chart for Burnham is No. 5390 and (surely excellent value this!) for Approaches to Harwich with the Rivers Stour, Orwell and Deben it is No. 5387. It has to be borne in mind that for this admittedly cheap series corrections are not provided, although there 12ppears no reason why yachtsmen should not insert their own.

However, when the yachtsman wishes to make a passage from one centre to another, the next difficulty arises: even between the Blackwater and the Crouch he is going to be off his charts for a small distance, and between the Blackwater and Harwich he is going to be off for quite a large distance round the Naze. Then the need for a larger chart end at least an improvised chart table makes itself felt. For Burnham via the inner channel (the Raysand colloquially 'raisin') local knowledge is probably better than any charts; otherwise you go by the Spitway and on to Ne. 1975 (Thames Estuary — Northern part). For passages to the Stour
Nos. 1975 and 2052 (The Naze to Orfordness) give coverage, as well as
including the whole of the lovely Orwell and Deben estuaries. Exploration of these is made easier if one supplements the charts with Jack Coote's book, "East Coast Rivers", which gives details of channels and anchorages (illustrated by photographs and diagrams ) and a mass of information about
shore facilities. |

A crossing of the Thames Estuary calls again for something over ard
above No. 1610 in view of the warning quoted above. No. 1975 will see
you out of the Blackwater but covers only half the crossing and has to be
used in conjunction with No. 1607 (Thames Estuary - Southern part), which
will take you as far as Leigh, the Medway, Whitstable or Ramsgate. Here you may at choice use either Yachting Charts Nos. 5391 (Leigh Creek),
5392 (Medway), 5393 (Whitstable) or 5394 (Ramsgate) for entering harbour,
or else (for Ramsgate) the full size No. 1828 (The Downs) which has the advantage that it goes as far as Dover.

For the Suffolk and Norfolk coast to Happisburgh (variously Haisborough and Ha'isboro' where, according to Bob Roberts at least, even the fishes will put you on course in "windy old weather"), Chart No. 1543° (Haisborough to Orfordness) will give you coverage for passage making and includes a plan of Southwold harbour where it is needed. For entering the harbours of Great Yarmouth and Lowestoft one has a choice (dependent on the size of sheet one is prepared to handle) between the two Yachting Charts Nos.5385
(Yarmouth) and 5386 (Lewestoft) and the full size No. 1536 (Approaches to
Gt. Yarmouth and Lowestoft). If the latter can in fact be accommodated, it has the advantage of exceptionally large scale insets of both these fairly busy working harbours.

So far we have covered less than half of our designated area. Charts for the North Sea passage and cruising on the other side are as large a subject again and best dealt with in later articles.

In the meantime, for the benefit of members wishing to keep those valuable investments up to date, it is proposed to offer month by month a brief reference list of the Admiralty Notices to Mariners affecting our area with a note of the chart numbers concerned. If the club could provide a subscription to this publication (cost: 1 guinea per annum which in fact is simply the cost of postage ) in order to make the stock available, a really worthwhile service would be rendered (Committee for the attention of??).

"The seasons came quickly while I worked. Hardly were the ribs of the sloop up before apple—trees were in bloom. Then the daisies and the cherries came soon after. Close by the place where the old Spray had now dissolved rested the ashes of John Cook, a revered Pilgrim father. Se the new Spray rose from hallowed ground. From the deck of the new craft I could put out my hand and pick cherries that grew over the little grave. The planks for the new vessel, which I soon came to put on, were of Georgia pine an inch and a half thick. The operation of putting them in was tedious, but, when on, the calking was easy. The outward edges stood slightly open to receive the calking, but the inner. edges were so close that I could not see daylight between them. All the butts were fastened hy through bolts, with screw—nuts tightening them to the timbers, so that there would be no complaint from them. Many bolts with screw—nuts were used in other parts of the construction, in all about a thousand. It was my purpose to make my vessel stout and
strong. : _ '

Now, it is a law in Lloyd's that the Jane repaired all out of the old until she is entirely new is still the Jane. The Spray changed her being so gradually that it was hard to say at what point the old died. or the new took birth, and it was no matter. The bulwarks I built up
of white—-oak stanchions, fourteen inches high, and covered with seven- eighth-inch white pine. These stanchions, mortised through a two inch covering board, I calked with thin cedar wedges. They have remained perfectly tight ever since. The deck I made of one-and~a—-half-—inch by three—inch white pine spiked to beams six by six inches, of yellow Georgia pine, placed three feet apart. The deck.inclosures were one over the aperture of the main hatch, six feet by six, for a cooking galley, and a trunk further aft, about ten feet by twelve, for a cabin. Both of these rose about three feet above the deck, and were sunk sufficiently into the hold
to afford head—room. In the spaces along the sides of the cabin, under the deck, I arranged a berth to sleep in, and shelves for small storage, not forgetting a place for the medicine-chest. In the midship hold, that is, the space between cabin and galley, under the deck was room for provision of water, salt beef eke, ample for many months"

A MAST IS MADE

BY "BARNACLE"

Many club members have built their own boats, but few of them have made the mast and even fewer have been faced with the job of making a hollow mast.

From the outside all masts look pretty much the same, but the tall tapering mast of a modern.ocean racer is one of the most complex examples of woodworker‘'s skill to be found. These days few boats of any size have solid masts, and those do often have them laminated out of many separately pieces to produce the strongest possible spar. Hollow masts can be made in two halves, carefully carved out and glued together, or they can be built up box fashion from selected planks. For masts of small to medium size the former method is tote preferred as the mast can readily be made to any desired shape, and the wall thickness can be kept uniform. Larger masts have to be built up -.because of the amount of timber that would be wasted were they hollowed out of solid, but where the various boards have been glued up to form the two halves they are often carved inside to give a uniform wall. A third method of producing a hollow spar is to roll a tapered tube of thin veneer, with plugs at the ends and any cross tree stations. (The McGruer method). This produces an incredibly light, strong spar, but also an incredibly expensive one! "Melody's" boom is an original McGruer spar, the Maldon smack "Fly" has a hollow gaff made

from the Mcgruer boom from the King of Spain's class racer. Anybody With lots and lots of spare time and money might like to have a shot at this.method of construction.

The method most likely to interest us is the two halves carved from solid. A mast made this way should always be started with one over—size piece of timber. Sitka spruce is nearly always used, and a fine timber it is. A good forty foot length will have the grain running straight from end to end without knots or waves, and it is a much lighter wood than B.C. pine.

Firstly the single baulk of timber is cut lengthwise into two halves, one of which is turned endwise, and the two are then marked to ensure that they are kept in the same relationship. When buying timber for a hollow mast from a reputable firm of boat builders timber merchants it can be ordered in the two halves, with one half reversed and clearly marked, but it is far safer to order one piece and cut it yourself.

This halving and reversing is so important because it ensures that the two sides of the mast will be of equal strength and that any wanders in the grain cancel out. Having halved the baulk the freshly cut faces are planed FLAT AND SMOOTH. This is one job where even the best machine planing is not considered good enough by the experts, and much care is taken to get a perfect joint face. The fore and aft profile is then marked on each half, sawn, and planed to finished size. The length of all the hollow sections between the crosstree: plugs are marked all round each half, a table of saw depths and fence settings drawn up and the hollows roughed out on the circular saw. This job cannot be hurried. The more taper there is to be on the spar the more cuts must be made, and some of the cuts have to be made parallel to the front and some parallel to the back, so the halves frequently have to be turned end for end. Eventually the machining is finished and the hollows cleaned out by hand with roundsoled planes and gauges.-. Working on spruce demands very sharp iron if the wood is not to be torn. When the hollows are fairly smooth, and the correct size to template, recesses are cut for any sheave boxes, masthead light wires are laid up in the hollows and the halves are glued together and held with may be as many as sixty clamps. Spar glueing is an "all hands" job in the boatyard, and is not something that can easily be done by a couple of amateurs.

When the glue has set the sides of the spar are planed off to profile then the corners are removed to a predetermined depth (most yards have marking gauges which mark the correct amount to remove to convert a rectangular spar to octagonal ), the resulting octagon has its corners removed and so on until the spar reaches its final round or pear shape.

"Ironmongery" is fitted, the spar is sanded smooth and varnished, and another mast is ready for the attention of the rigger.

INTRODUCTION

The following pages are not a "SHIP'S LOG", they are the "WORKING DIARY" of a fortnight's summer holiday on my brother's converted ship's boat "AaRK".

It had been arranged that Vic and his family should spend a fortnight in the summer aboard AaRK and Vic had decided to go further afield than last year when he tookherup to Woodbridge. Christchurch in Hampshire was chosen for a number of reasons, it represented a bit. of a "voyage",
it entailed some navigation and also most important of all, it is a lovely landlocked harbour with facilities for his young children.

My mother lives thirty miles from Christchurch in a town called Romsey, and Frances and I were to meet Vic and Family there.

I shall not touch on Vic's holiday, except to mention that he left Heybridge Lock on a Saturday morning and walked into Mother's house on the Monday evening, three days to Southampton. The following day he took AaRK to Christchurch and hence did the trip in four days.

British Railways had a fire at Waterloo and we caught a dubious long slow train to Eastleigh and so to Romsey. ‘Delight, Vic was waiting at Romsey Station. Frances was so glad to see him despite being her b—brother-—
in-law

ANY FOOL CAN SCREW

By "Barnacle"

. Recently during a discussion, a would be boat builder remarked that any fool can neil er screw two pieces ef wood together, the truth of his ‘remark’ lies in his emission of the word properly.. Nailing add screwing appear to be such simple jobs that people with little experience often tend to think that they require no thought or care, and then they wonder why the wood splits, the screw shears off, or the fastenings do not hold.

When screwing two pieces of wood together, the first things to decide are the seize and number of the screws to be used. These depend on the seizes of the components being fastened, the type of timber used, and the load to be carried, and can be determined only from experience. Many people tend to use too few screws of too large a size, and often use too short a screw. Soft woods such‘as pine or spruce need fastenings at closer centres than hardwoods like oak, and the screws can with advantage be longer than would be used for oak. The widths of the timbers involved affect the diameters of screws used — as a very rough guide it is seldom safe to use larger than

-5-

number six screws into three quarter of an inch, eights into inch and tens into inch and a quarter. This apparently small screw size is adopted so that the centres can be staggered so adjacent screws are not run into the same line of the grain. Screw length, as well as being affected by the type of timber used, depends on whether the screw is to be in shear or in tension — screws in tension being longer than those in shear. Also, it is usually good policy to increase the diameter of a screw in tension to get the advantage of the larger head area.

Difficulties in driving screws are almost entirely eliminated by drilling the correct sizes of clearance and pilot holes, and in the sizes of screws used for small boat work, this does mean the correct size and
not something that looks vaguely right - the margin between a screw which
binds solid before it is right home and a screw that strips out under load is only two or three drill sizes different. A frequent reason for splitting the outer piece of wood is failure to cut a proper 90° countersink for the screw head. Quite often in soft wood the screw will bed itself in nicely, but every so often there is a weakness in the timber and the wedging action of the head will split it open. The thread of the screw should be greased particularly if it is to be run into oak or elm, and the screwdriver used must FIT the slot of the screw. A screwdriver bit in a carpenter's brace is the best tool to use, as it is easier to Spin it quickly to run the screw in than it is to use a normal screwdriver, and the tremendous leverage ensures that the screw is done up tight, whilst the "feel" of the tool avoids the risk of shearing off the screw head as can happen if a spanner of tommy bar is applied to a heavy screwdriver. "Pump" action screwdrivers are very good for digging unsightly marks in the timber surface unless cross head screws are used, and they completely.lack the tightening power of a brace. Brass or
steel (galvanised) screws should not be used on boat work - brass screws
will de-zincify in a year or two, and although the screw may look quite sound it will have no strength. Stainless steel, gunmetal or silicon bronze screws are more expensive, but if a little care is used in fitting them, each screw can be relied on to carry its full load for many, many years, and should repairs be necessary, they can be unscrewed and often used again whilst a mild steel screw will have rusted, and a brass screw
is liable to shear off. |

Nailing has been revolutionised by the "anchorfast "and " gripfast" barbed nails. Used properly, these nails are excellent, but they are expensive, and their biggest snag is that once hammered home they can be undone without damage to the timber. All but the smallest sizes should have pilot holes drilled, and in some cases it is advisable to drill a clearance hole in the material that is to be nailed down. These barbed nails will resist all strains as well as screws; in fact they are often used as an alternative to screws, but they have not the power to close a gap on fastening that a screw has.

Once one has decided to screw two pieces of wood together, one has only to decide on the number, size and material of screw to use, whereas if one is to nail, one has also to decide on the type of nail to be used, and whether to clench or nail blind. Also one has to decide whether or not a pilot hole will be needed, whether to use oval nails with the grain of the upper or lower piece of timber if the grains cross, and whether to clench with or across the grain.

The correct angle at which the nails should be skewed when nailing blind is often overlooked — nails hammered in square to the surface of the timber can pull straight out under load, whereas pairs of nails driven in to form Vees can be pulled out only with great difficulty.

One final point on nailing - when using galvanised nails, take care
not to damage the galvanising. If the nail is going to end up minus half its zinc, you might as well use cheaper ungalvanised nails in the first
place.
"Barnacle."

WHO PINCHED THE ANCHOR

While serving in H.M.S. Anthony, a destroyer of some 1,300 tons,
belonging to the 3rd Flotilla Meditteranean Fleet, the ships company had
the rather unique experience of being caught up in an unsolved mystery.

It happened during the Spring Cruise of 1931, four of our destroyers
were lying at anchor off St. Tropez in a very picturesque bay which that
part of the French Riviera abounds in. le were at open ancktor, that is,
one anchor down and free to swing in any direction s6:.i about two cables
length separating each ship, (1,200 feet to the layman) when the signs of
a storm arose one evening. The Captain ordered steam to be raised, and
the second anchor be prepared to be dropped under foot a traditional
precaution which steadies the swinging
of the ship and prevents a bumping
and boring match with the next in line.

After dark weather conditions became steadily worse so orders were
given to"let
go second anchor", ‘which duly went out of the Hawse Pipe
and away into the unknown. A stiff off shore breeze kept the weather.
anchor really biting in for most of the night, then as dawn began to
break so did the blow. By daylight things had calmed down nicely, the
Captain gave orders to weigh second anchor and return to normal harbour
routine.

Cable work on destroyers was always tedious, plenty of hand-draulic
attached to various items of cable bashing as I called it. So when steam
was put on the capstan it made life much easier. Slowly the cable began to
tighten, link by link it came in over the lip of the hawse pipe with a
grouching grinding noise of steel to steel, there was only one speed for
the capstan engine — flat out:-— and only one speed for the cable — dead
slow, the gear ration took care of that.

We had six shackles out, that is, 75 fathoms of it, so there was a
good twenty minutes work before we expected to see the anchor break surface.
Bach shackle as it came in was reported to the Bridge by the Cable Officer
using coloured hand flags, slowly the cable was stowed in the cable locker
by its own weight as it piled in heaps down below. The colour
df flag No.l
was duly held up, and everyone there began to sigh "oh well, nearly home"
when suddenly a loud voice from the Capn of the Focstle rang out "Anchors
Gone Sir"! To everyones amazement, there was the cable dangling just
above the water line and rising steadily up towards the hawse pipe with
nothing on the end!

The Cable Officer then gave the order "Stop Capstan' and préceeded to
look over the side for ONE BROWN LSNNOX 30 CWT BOW ANCHOR quoting the
Ship's Rate Book — a sort of catalogue of every item carried.

-7T-

Everyone present sensed the next remark which was made, the Cable Officer "Where the ** ** ** is it, Capn of Focastle? The bluejackets in the vicinity began to snigger sensing some witty remark by one Petty Officer Bloggs "Somebodys pinched the thing Sir", "Put yourself in the First Lieutenants report" came the reply. Justice had to be done.

Destroyers in those days didn't carry diving apparatus, or divers, so a request was duly made by radio to our nearest ship who carried the gear. It happened to be H.M.S. Royal Oak lying at Golfe Juan, who sent their 42 foot launch and equipment in a most obliging manner taking some 3 hours to accomplish the fifteen or so miles "round the corner".

When diving began, some speculation as regards finding self same anchor was running high, the odds changed from hour to hour as the bubbles from both divers made a wide arc over the surface, they spent
about four hours down there - ene of our chaps who went in the launch
as relief pumping party aware he saw them sitting on the ocean bottom Playing cards! Anyway they finally surfaced with no results, the unusual muddy boots being the only proof that they had at least gone down to the ocean floor.

So after we had fixed them up with a welcome meal they returned to their battlewagon, leaving Petty Officer Bloggs feeling chocker block!

On the messdeck, the usual arguments arose as to who should pay for the anchor, and the cost of the divers (who in those days got double pay for each hour while diving), how much did it cost to buy a new one and so on. It was even suggested that P.O. Bloggs should re engage for his pension which meant "sign on for another 10 years". To enable him to get out of "being in debt to the Crown".

Shortly afterwards the Court of Inquiry took place in the Captain's Cabin, and a verdict of "Lost by Accident" was passed, everyone felt sorry for the Capn of the Forcastle when the Cable Officer said to him "You couldn't have shackled it on P.O. Bloggs!

He had the last say when replying to that accusation, "Well Sir how did it run out and take the cable with it if it wasn't shackled on?". No reply to that one and as far as I know no positive reason was ever established why the anchor disappeared.

NOTE: All you would be Mariners watch out for Davy Jones, who knows he might have pinched it!

TORPS.

The Anchor's value per Naval Rate Book was in the region of £20 - made of pig iron — quite cheap stuff.

On Thursday 13th February the programme consisted of a showing of member's slides, photographs and films. Brian Partridge was in the chair and he introduced the show with a brief talk on the various points to be noted when photographing boats. —

Members provided many interesting and varied shots of sailing in various parts of the country and abroad, including what must now be historic pictures of Mamgu taken on open day some three years ago.

Thursday 27th February brought us the long awaited films of the
America Cup races of 1958 and 1962. These films were loaned to the club
by Mr. Oren Aisher and were presented to him by the New York Yacht Club in recognition of his services to yachting. These films are in great . demand and apparently we were very fortunate to obtain ‘the loan of them. In lending these films Mr. Aisher does not make any charge but requests that a collection be taken for donation to the R.Y.A. Olympics fund (a very worthy cause for all interested in sailing).

Unfortunately on the night we chose the College projectionist was not available but Mr. A.C. Stock volunteered to fill the breach with the proviso that he wasn't fully experienced. However, aided by members of the club and ‘after a number of false starts (including the rewinding of one film which the last borrowers had neglected to do) we were all set. During all this manoeuvring of yards of film etc. our Commodore very gallantly ad-libbed to keep the party going.

The first film dealt with the 1958 series of races and included a brief history of their origin with particular mention of Sir Thomas Lipton and the part he played in keeping them going. We were shown the whole sequence of operations from the building and launching of the competing boats to the eliminating contests to find the American representative. The film finally ended with the series of races between challenger and challengered which resulted in America retaining the cup.

The Australian Challange of 1960 formed the subject of the second film where we saw them in training, at one point having a fair amount of trouble with the spinnaker! However, by the time the races were due they had mastered the art effectively. Unfortunately, as we know, the Cup still stays in America despite their gallant efforts with Sceptre.

These were two remarkable films and one left the College that night with possibly a tiny little bit of envy and perhaps with a feeling that dinghy sailing on the Blackwater'is maybe a little tame.

After the film showing the collection taken amounted to £4. 3. 104. This sum was made up to 6 guineas by the Club and passed to the R.Y.A. Olympics fund.

J.G.e Reeve.

Tuesday 13th August

Awoke gloomy, and the tide went out.
Greased propshaft, water pump, and had a good breakfast. The radio has packed up and we must take it ashore and find suitable shop somewhere. It was O.K. last night and dead this morning.

Washerwoman did the dhobey, cleaned and polished below decks and generally tidied up. Went ashore at noon, to find buses ran to Newport every 12 min. However we found a good radio shop and bought new batteries which worked 100%? Not sure. Had lunch in Pilot Boat Im, Beer, Lobster Salad with wizard dressing, it was all jolly good. Saw Sam working on club Redwings after lunch an odd sight all lined up on the beach together. Everyone of them identical even up to the little yellow racing flag at the mast head.

Returned to AaRK and scrubbed decks, washed down topsides and at teatime when the tide came in I sailed the dinghy once round the harbour. An education, one hand on the tiller and mainsheet. One foot, foresail sheet, one buttock to hold down the dagger board and the other hand to push

-9-

the shroud out and keep the mast from going by the board! Must get proper rigging some time. After tea we went ashore and refilled all the water carriers, had a beer and bought the "Evening News" for weather forecast. Back aboard and just got the dinghy lashed on deck as dusk fell. Supper poached egg and sweetcorn then sorted out charts, courses and log whilst waiting for 11 p.m. weather forecast. Set alarm for 5-20 a.m..- Cool showery, with some sun. 11 p.m. watch O.K. Lovely sunny day, cool.

of Bembridge against the flood. Off the entrance fort made sail and shut off engine. Light winds, set compass course for Nab Tower, (visible!) and did some chart work, see separate sheet. Aa,b Broad reach up to Nab and beyond changing to run, set jib on boathook and ran steadily on compass course. The wind was steady moderate and we had fair sunshine. I was pleased with my rudimentary navigation i.e. compass course to entrance was accurate, 25 miles ETA within 10 min.

Found entrance easy and were shepherded to mooring alongside yachts on Quay by B.R. men 4/- charge and 2/~ tip. Supercilious customs official came alongside to ask details of vessel. Greased stern gland and made a cup of coffee (no food since bacon sandwiches 6 a.m.).

Frances wrote letters to Mother Vic, I put 1 gall. of mix in tank and dipped it. There is now more in the tank than when we left Christchurch! Not bad, about 130 miles. I am now going to wash and brush up, put on cleaner clothes and go and FEED (also get petrol, milk if possible). Forecast 9.00 p.m. W-SW light variable.

SUNDAY, JUNE 21st,196h. ww. 41-15 Meg 964
MARCONI REGATTA DAY CRUISER EVENT. ENTRY FEE 2/6

This event will be in the nature of a seamanship or obstacle race and is open to all boats equipped for. cruising and towing a dinghy. Gntrants should anchor off the Marconi Sailing Club site at Stansgate Abbey point on the South bank of the R. Blackwater before 2-30 p.m.

All boats should anchor between a line from the extension of the concrete hard just up river from the cottage on the seawall, and the club race starting line marked be metes at the gun emplacement on the seawall at the Ramsey Wick end of the site, and Goldhanger Spit Buoy.

Boats must be left with all sails lowered. Headsails may be hanked on stays, with halliards and sheets on, but must be tied down to the deck. (Sails with Wickham—-Martin gear must be lowered.) The mainsail must have at least two tiers on, but no cover, and the boom must rest in the normal gallows or crutch. Entrants should be prepared either to Slip or recover their anchors. Dinghies are to be drawn up on the beach clear of the water, below the cottage on the seawall.(Beach Marshals will adjust the positions of all dinghies at 2-40 p.m. so all are the same distance from the water, but the marshals will NOT turn dinghies round.) All crew members must be ashore.

The event will start at 3-O p.m., when the sailing instructions Will be handed out. All crew members must be in the clubroom for the start, unless instructed otherwise on the day by the Officer of the Day.

Entries, with fee, should be sent to the M.S.C. Sailing Secretary,

N.F.Tovey, [redacted], 14,[redacted]., Great Baddow, Chelmsford, Essex

up to the Thursday before the race, and will be accepted in the clubroom from 2-0 p.m. onwards on the day. Entrants should be prepared to use any or all equipment one ‘could reasonably expect to find aboard cruising yacht; entrants unable to complete any portion of the event will not be disqualified, but will be given a time penalty. Enbrants are advised to bring an anchor and warp for the dinghy in addition to the normal kedge, and a marker buoy. No limit will be placed on the size of crew, but there must be a minimum of two, any bear in mind that all the crew must be ferried out to the boat in the dinghy after the start, and the dinghy must be towed in the race.

It will help the sailing committee if owners can send in their entries well in advance. The handicapping details required will be those on the other side of this form. Boats which have a T(H)OF given by the Blackwater Joint Racing Committee or the Old Gaffers Association should just quote the T(H)C# unless there has been some alteration to the boat since the figure was issued.
A second prize will be given if there are more than six entries, and a third prize if there are more than nine.

_ The object of this event is a pleasant day out, with a bit more point than "just pottering", and for those new to sailing, a chance to see how well fitted they and their boats are for cruising.
The
more entries there are, the more fun all can have, so please tell all your friends about this event, and tell them about the event described on the other side of this sheet, an event intended to attract the "family man" who prefers to use his boat for a week end out rather than as a day racer.

During the weekend of July 4th and Sth, it was pleasant to have the clubhouse to ourselves again after the spate of Open Meetings and Regatta day. One of the few early arrivals was Brian Partridge with his camera, He hopes that some of the photographs he took of tu; barges will be published in the Marconi magazine at a later date.

The barges were soon forgotten in the preparations for a

than 10 entries, which must be nearly a record. The general procedure was for each “Lady" to find a man with a boat and then, by fair means or foul, persuade hin to accompany her in the race. It was not so much a question of having right of way, but rather a question of “can 1 get out of the way?"- Fortunately, there were no serious accidents and everyone seemed to enjoy their

It was just eleven o'clock as we slipped our moorings from Webb & Feesey's yard, the chimes of a clock mingling with the put—put-put of our motor as it echoed amongst the wooden buildings to starboard in the still night air. -Our destination? fkochester, on the Medway, and Folk Dancer, the latest addition to Jack Mill's charter fleet, was ours from Friday night until midday Monday. There was Dave Smith, myself (barely recovered from being a wanted man, by the “essex police the previous weekend), Ian, and Johnny, on his first sea trip.

With the ebbing tide and our 8 h.p. auxiliary we were soon past Osea, then, anchoring for a quick five minutes to pick up some gear at Stansgate, we were off again, the bright lights of Bradwell power station our guide. we watched astern, fascinated by the occasional fluorescent sparkling of sea creatures in the
wake.

The.twin red lights on the ends of the barrier wall off Bradwell became slowly visible and then it was time to turn the 5 tons of Folk Dancer towards the lights of West Mersea. “My sensations this morning were vastly livelier than those of yesterday at the same hour. My limbs were supple again and my head clear. Wot even the searching wind could mar the ecstasy of that plunge down to smooth seductive sand where I buried greedy fingers and looked through a medium blue with that translucent blue, fairy—-faint and angel-pure, that you see in perfection only in the heart of ice. Up again to sun, wind, and the forest whispers from the shore; down just once more to see the uncouth anchor stabbing the sand's soft bosom with one rusty fang deaf and inert to the "Dulcibella's" puny efforts to drag him from his prey. Back, holding by the cable as a rusty clue from heaven to earth, up th that bourgoise little maiden's bows; back to breakfast with an appetite not to be blunted by condensed milk and somewhat passé bread. An hour later we had dressed the ‘“Dulcibella" for the road, and were foaninze into the grey void of yesterday, now a noble expanse of wind-whirped blue, half surrounded by distant hills, their very outline vivid in the rain-washed air.

I cannot pretend that I really enjoyed this first sail into the open,: though I was keenly anxious to do so. I felt the thrill of.those forward leaps, heard that persuasive song the foam sings under the lee-how, saw the flashing. harmonies of see and sky; but the.sensuous perception was3.deadened by nervousness. The a. yacht looked s.aller than ever outside the fiord. The sone of the foam seened very near, the wave-crests aft very high.. The novice in sailing clings desperately to the thought of sailors - effective, prudent persons, with a typical jargon and a typical dress, versed in local currents and winds. I could not help missing this professional element. Davies, as he sat grasping his b-loved tiller, looked strikingly; efficient in his way, and supremely at hoe in his surroundings; but he looked the amateur through and through as with one hand and (it seemed) one eye he wrestled with a array-splashed chart half unrolled on the deck
beside him. all his casual ways returned to me - his casual talk
and that last adventurous voyage to the Baltic, and the suspicions his reticence had aroused." ‘

WHERE SHALL WE STOW IT?

By "DaAh*ACL Ss"

towing away all the necessary gear is a problem which all who cruise must solve. Those who erely hurl everything into a large locker or onto the cabin sole are asking for trouble, either in the form of breakages or soaked clothing. at first glance there would not appear to be much storage space even on quite large cruisers, but a thorough examination of the boat will usually reveal more than enough space to stow everything nece«sary for at least a fortnight's cruise.

one vital word here is ‘necessary". The novice cruiser is easily detected as he staggers aboard with two or three large kitbags bulging with stuff that will not be unpacked until he gets home again. All people differ in the 3quantity of clothes they need aboard to keep then happy for a fortnight, so vou must learn BX experience how much you really Need. Then add one thick, long “eater and don't take any more than that amount.

On board clothes are best kept in canvas kit bags or holdalls if the boat has not got special netting racks or lockers. One very fine eleven topper has the main saloon partially lined, with Clothes lockers built into the lining behind the bunks.

Drinking vater is the biggest headache of all to stow, but if the boat was designed and built for cruising the designer should have solved this problem for you. If you are converting an old boat, it is best to make every effort to build in a tank as low dower as possible. sometimes this proves impossible, and then probably the best solution is that used by “sopranino”" — a fairly large number of small screw top containers, either aluminium or plastic, which can be wedged into odd corners.

In a planked hull they can he stood along the bilge stringers and held against the side of the hull by shock cord. fuel for c@oking stoves presents a similar croblez, and for many years I
_PXiried all liquids in glass bottles - screw tog for fuel and
“flip top" (Corona) for potable liquids. Meths was always put in clear glass screw top bottles, and paraffin in coloured bottles, and the only occasion on which the system let us do’n was when we made a very peculiar tasting pot of tea with lemon "Corona" in mistake for water. After: this, only coloured fizzy drinks were
carried!

Tinned food takes up quite a lot of room, but is very easily stowed down in the bilges, remembering to paint an identifying symbol on each tin and remove all paper labels so they won't soak off and clog the bilge pumps. .several types of tins need no labels
- sardines, milk, herrings and corned beef can all be identified
by their shape.. If four separate coszpartments are available, all soups can go in one, fruit in another, meat, stews, etc., in the third and odds and ends in the fourth, and ther none of the tins will really need labelling other than “specials” like steak and kidney puddings which must be cooked in the tin, With such tins it is advisable t. slip the label into the ship's log book for reference to the cooking instructions when you cone to use it.

Bread, butter, packets of oatmeal, rice, etc., need a locker, although they ca” be kept in special tins with tight fitting lids
- National Dried Milk tins are good for this, and given a coat of
cellulose paint and neatly labelled they will last several seasons. Tea, sugar, etc., can be carried quite safely in glass jars with screw top lids, fitted into a specially made rack and held in with a length of shock cord. Polystyrene containers would be better, but there don't seem to be any available with good screw tops.

3

* * *

Cutlery is a pest, and the only solution is a proper tray, stowed either in the bottom of a locker or fitted in slides as a little draper. It is not a bad idea to fit one or two small drawers in odd spots such as under the side decks, under the foredeck at the forward end of the cabin, or under a footstep to hold odds and ends like primus prickers, spare torch bulbs, money, car keys etc.,
etc.

Crockery should really have a special locker, but in its absence mugs can be hung from hooks along the beam shelf and plates wedged in behind a bunk mattress. Saucepans and frying pans can stow on or under the preferably lashed down, and there should be room behind the stoves for the kettle, watches are best fitted into a little clip ou a handy frame behind the galley. Soap and other washing utensils really need a little watertiszat
locker of their own - if you buns them all in a polythene bag it
gets a trifle unpleasant in time.

Cameras, and binoculars, etc., should have a place of their a own as I said in an earlier article, and if nothing better can be found a length of netting hung under the coachroof or deck beams will keep them tolerably safe. 8 golden rule in stowing gear aboard is try to keep the weight as low as possible, and try to avoid putting too much in thetends of the ship. A few lengths of shockcord, see pieces of netting and a couple of shelves and you will be surprised how much can be stowed away neatly and safely in even the smallest of cruisers or cruising dinghies.

For the first time (I believe), an all-—Marconi crew took part in the Hast Anglian race from Harwich to Jstend on August Bank Holiday week-end. Arthur Adam, Maggie 4dam, Alan ry and John Littlewood sailed KAZARKA into 6th. place in clasS , 7th. overall — 4 seconds behind the first non-class boat. = There were 45 starters.
The race started from a line off Harwich
Pier in a force
2-3 northerly breeze. Most of the yachts set spinnakers as soon as the starting gun was fired and there was some close jostling at the Guard buoy just after the start. The dinghy sailors had their rule books at the ready}

. The wind faded as the afternoon wore on, and the field bunched again; evidently the leaders ran out of wind first. As the tide strengthened, even ‘the big boys found they could make no progress, and the whole fleet kedged within an area scarcely more than a mile square, just inshore of the Sunk Lightship. Uncomfortable; a nasty jobble left over from stronger winds earlier, and sails banging about unless they were taken off.

We were kedged for an hour or so}; a study of the chart revealed many old wrecks on the bottom and we wondered how many of us would foul our anchors on then. Our own seemed to be holding remarkably well on a warp only 2% times the depth, which had us worried — but it came up easily when wanted. A class x yacht,
anchored on chain, seemed to be indifficulties - we last saw
them with 7 men tallying on in an effort to recover theirs. Svimnaker agains. wind North Force 1 -— 2, no relation to the forecast S.i/.-W. force 5 yet. Conditions showed the advantage of having an anti-snarl net set under the spinnaker to keep it from wrapping round the forestay. At the start we saw a few boats had these, but we hadn't; had to have a nifty deck-hand (J.L.) to free the tangles before they were too serious. One or two boats, we found afterwards, were right out of luck; a "Stella" came in to Ostend with her spinnaker still tightly wrapped on the stay, and had to send a man up to take off the forestay.

The wind gradually freshened as dayli: ht came and went round more to the W.; a Folkboat -—- “BLU# MOON’ -—-— was within half a mile to leeward —— Jest Hinder Lightship 1% miles to starboard. Towards 6 o'clock BLUE: MOON handed her spinnaker and presently we did the same. lt was by now about force 5 and we were going as fast under Genoa. ‘ent storming on through a rising sea; sometimes all we could do to hold the course, but didn! t want to lose time sail-—changing with a rival so close. The Ostend

skyline presently showed up, but was difficult to identify; partly because none of us was familiar with it, partly because the most "conspic." building is a new block of flats, not yet mentioned an the chart. It will be a useful seamark when its position
is
shown. As we approached , became clear; the details we
finally
rushed between the pierheads into the sheltered water, with BLU MOO almost overlapring. Motored up to the yacht basin, which was already tight-packed with the earlier arrivals. “Breathe in, ladies!" Next after us, 40 minutes later, came our friend MUONSTONS, FB 167, from Maylandsea. ‘e give her time, but only a few ainutes; she was 8th. in class

The yacht basin at Ostend is a very sociable place when full —- in our "trot" the way ashore was over some 20 other yachts of all classes. #xcellent opportunity for discussing each other's notions for anti-chafe gear, etc. I was aost impressed with GkiNaADS's spinnaker boon, with both ends heavily sheathed in leather to take the wear from the forestay on “shy” reaches. Arising at 10 a.m. (plenty early enough for a Sunday morning), we fixed our plan of action for the day. The return passage would be much easier — to push out of the Medway against the last of the flood. We would then have the whole of the ebb to take us up the coast to the Spitway, where we should arrive soon after half tide. This should give us enough water to get through. With luck we would be at Mersea by seven.
After a quick breakfast, we cast off, the engine helping us on our way back. It was a dull overcast day and the air was thick with the smell of oil from the refineries. The wind had moderated from yesterday to a force three. we moored onto the dockyard wall at Sheerness to replenish our petrol supply. After a brief exchange with a puzzled gatekeeper at the dockyard we were in Sheerness High Street, looking for a garage. I wondered why people were looking

Ye tacked over to the barrier fence at Shoebury, Southend pier being distantly visible to port. Then back to the Oaze buoy,
lunching on the way. Our speed past the measured mile - six knots,
The tacks were broad and by half past two we were back in the Swin, with half the journey_over. The navigator (it wasn't me — I was doing the washing up!) was making a good job of it. "Half an hour on the north tack and we should reach the S.E. Maplin." And sure enough in half an hour we were turning east by the Maplin buoy. “Quarter of an hour east and we. will be at the °./.Swin." Once more he was right almost to the minute. “Now you can carry one bit if you like towards that wreck" (pointing to some masts sticking out of the water). Suddenly there was a bump, sending the plate in my hand crashing to the floor — then another bump. Running out to the cockpit I realised we were aground. "“everybody on the shrouds.” Leaning our weight out we tried to free the keel. Motor revving, sails down, nothing happened. “We'll try to push her round." But to push thirty feet of boat round in four feet of water I found rather difficult. The stark truth dawned on us — we were aground!

There was little we could do. “Half past three, low tide six, we should be off by eight" said Ian. "Charming", I thought. We lay on our bunks, watching the coats hanging more and more sideways as we went over.
