COMMODORE'S REPORT 1964

This season, one of the best sailing summers within memory, has, for the Marconi Sailing Club, been one of very nixed consequences indeed.

On the material side the Club's successes have been outstanding. The consolidation of the previous years intensive building efforts has led to an increase of membership to the point where your committee has had to freeze the intake of Non Marconi Members, and start a waiting list. And this in spite of the newly imposed entrance fee.

Our Numbers now stand at 513 subscription paying members.

It should be noted that I have said subscription paying members. This means I have not included any children of family members with the exception of those who are members of the Cadet section.

I think you will all agree that this is a most creditable figure, one which takes us into the company of the really important clubs in the area,

We have during the year purchased two boats and have been & presented with a third. —-

The "Fisherman Fourteen" was purchased early in the year, and has proved its worth time and time again. As a pulling dinghy it is a maid of all work. Fitted with the outboard engine it has been used as both an inshore rescue launch and as an offshore launch on- big days. The cost incidentally of this engine has now been 70% recovered by the "four bob" donations to the’ Fund.

A month or so ago we collected our new Rescue Launch, a 16 foot open Swedisn launch, powered by a single cylinder Albin engine.

This boat although seven years old is almost as new, having had only a season's use in that time. In fact for the last two or three years it has been laid up in a barn up in the Peterborough area, from whence it was collected.

The monies for these two purchases were borrowed temporarily from the M.a.c.0. and I am very happy to be able to report. that as you can see from the balance sheet, it is anticipated that we
will be in a position to repay nearly £400 of the total of £439.5s.
0d.

It should not be overlooked that the W.4.5.C. General Committee, and the Chairman Mr. Millett has shown great faith in both the ability of the Club to raise these amounts of money, and in the honesty of intentions of the section.

A number of dances and social evenings have been held at our Stansgate Club House. SAILING CLUB GOSSIP COLUMN

At the beginning of January a few members of the Club were still sailing at Maylandsea Bay Yacht Club. The five Sundays allotted for their Winter Series were all good sailing days with moderate wind and some sun.

BOOK OF The MONTH

Extract from “Safety in Small Craft" by D, A. nayner, published by Adlard Coles Limited

Marine disasters so often grow out of the breakdown of some small item of ship's gear, or result from some minor error of

3.

-4-

judgement, and they grow with frightening rapidity to overwhelm those whose lack of foresight or inexperience has allowed the chain-reaction to start. I can still recall very vividly the occasion when the pin of a cheaply bought shackle that secured the halyard to the topsail yard parted. I had, if I remember correctly, bought it at a convenient wireless shop. It had not come from the ship chandlers, but we were all very young and pence saved had appeared important.

The head of the yard, falling down the lee side of the sail, threw a quite unfair strain on the wire traveller which held the heel of the topsail yard to the mast. The wire parted and fouled the halyard which jammed the block at the masthead. One of the crew, feJ., went up the mast to clear the block. another, cast off the halyard and stood by the mast looking up. His brother, J.i.,the better to see what was happening aloft, stepped back and overboard.

With one ‘tan at the masthead I could not gybe the ship round to pick up J.2). Instead, to remain near him, I put the ship about. But I'd have taken more than the topsail halyard off the pins at the base of the mast. The jib sheets fouled the aan and the raffle, and for once that ship missed stays and hung in the wind, which was now coming down both sides of the flapping mainsail. It caught the damaged topsail and ballooned it out to drag the ship back on the same tack.

Fortunately all this happened on a day of little sea and light breeze and with the whole of the Irish in which to play. Within 10 minutes the masthead vas cleared, the topsail down on deck and J.iue, fortunately a strong swimmer, was back aboard. But, had it been blowing hard or had we not had sea-room in which to manoeuvre, the answer might well have been different. It must have been a very salutary lesson for me to have remembered this one incident so vividly after all those years, and I still recapture the feeling of helplessness as event followed event without ay having any idea of when things would stop happening. Perhaps it was the more of a lesson, because it occurred when the gramophone was on the cabin-top and when we were all lying about on deck with little clothing and less care.

The responsibility of a captain towards his crew is exactly the same whether they number 2 or 200, granted that in the smaller ship the strain of command may be less, but the charge for her crew's safety remains and cannot be delegated. It should be a sobering thought.
P. G. Luke

The correspondence has been urging the merits and de-merits of two classes of boats, and I have no brief for either. In my humble opinion, a new class just grows spontaneously, and not be dictated. I believe that at the present time, sailing under the Club burgee are some seven or eight G.P.14,'s, and of these (I am open to correction on this) only two, at any one time, raced in the handicap class last season. nevertheless, I am quite sure that had, say, 5U;. of these boats turned out regularly, the sailing secretary, upon request, would have been willing to institute a points series of races for the class. engendered, and it would possibly have encouraged the helmsmen to carry the name of the club into open events in their class, paving the way for the adoption of the class. This has not been the case, but perhaps next season may see the matter pursued on these lines. This does not necessarily apply to GP.14's alone, but to any other class of boat which has sufficient representation in the Club to warrant, and wanting, a points series of its own.

I feel that the only way in which the executive of a Club can exercise any jurisdiction over the classes sailed is by restricting the admittance of new members whose dinghy does not conform, at the present time there is a considerable rable 'menager ie fleet', and from the representation of this fleet in the handicap class, one can only conclude that the owners of these boats are quite happy to take their pleasure sailing individually, as opposed to racing. BOAT SHOW REPORT

It is 7 or 8 years since the London Boat Show transferred from Olympia to the larger premises at Warwick head; the organizers must now be wondering where they can move to accommodate the overwhelming mass of "beds" which almost prevents access to the exhibits. May I propose Farnborough aerodrome for 1966?

Part II
The ship, the plan and the crew

Late in 1963 1 decided to buy a Butch "CoNPaRstTTM class yacht - a 42 ton sloop built of fibre, with a generous amount of wood in her internal fittings gee class offered ample accommodation for two or three people with th — to take four or five for occasional week-ends; a ‘H.H. standard of seaworthiness; sound construction and low maintenance, This last point was much appreciated by my wife, as lower maintenance equates to a longer Sailing season.

We determined to collect her ourselves for two reasons, the first - economy - we found on investigation not to be a valid one; the cost of getting her shipped to Harwich would be vary little more than the fares of the crew to Holland. The second reason, that it would be the finest possible way of starting a cruise in Holland, proved amply justified. some years previously I had taken a fort-night's cruise there in a chartered yacht, but how much better to do it again in a boat of my own! The crew was to be my wife and myself for the first week, with Alan Pratt joining us for the second week to assist on the North Sea passage, since Maggie had had no off-shore experience at that time.

This plan meant that more than the usual amount of preparation was necessary; delivery trips are often made in a Spartan manner, but to enjoy a fortnight abroad we needed more equipment. Much of it I was able to adapt from KaZakka's predecessors or preferred to make from scratch to my own design work on this began several months before the nominal handing-over date - April lst, 1964, the date offered entirely seriously by the agent. Compasses needed to be overhauled, and an improved gimbal was made for the Pll steering compass; a compass light had to be made (the luminosity of RAF compasses becomes weak after twenty years). We required a stove that could be used under way; and after much thought a sat of gimbals was devised for our camping stove (an Optimus 22) incorporating an efficient fiddle-rail to hold two pans in place. An external door and other modifications were added to a Beolit transistor radio to assist its use for D/F bearings. Charts were obtained from Dutch sources for the inland waterways, as well as Admiralty charts for the North Sea crossing. Altogether, over 2 cwt. of gear was assembled and dispatched in advance by air freight.

Taking delivery

Friday, april 43rd, saw the saster/owner and mate arrive at Conyplex N.V., Alkmaar on a wet, wintry morning. A beautiful, blue- hulled yacht was lying in the canal opposite the yard; her mast was not yet stepped and two men were still working aboard. On her stern we read KAZAKK.A — Maldon.

We met the yard manager, Herr Burger. “Yes, everything would be ready in an hour or two...an inventory to check? Yes...Spinnaker gear? ‘Was that on the order?...Oh dear, our mistake...
We have a spare pole and we will post the halliard on in a few days...Five parcels for you at this address? No! They haven't come...by - air freight? I will ring Rotterdam airport."

After some minutes he turned back to us. "They are at Rotterdam - in the Customs shed. 'Personal effects' they do not understand, Can you go to Rotterdam?" Rotterdam is 90 km. south of Alkmaar but there was no other way of getting our equipment in less than three days. The yard owner, Dr. Conijn (himself a keen yachtsman who has sailed his "CUFPT#3TI" to Finland without engine) would take us to his ho.age and give us our charts for the IJsselmeer, then bring us to a restaurant for lunch where, said Herr Burger, "I can recommend the rijstafel - fantastic!" agree: no inquiring appetite should miss it - but prepare for it with a twelve hour fast!) Herr Burger could be free for the afternoon and since his Volkswagen was too small to accommodate our crate, dinghy and pair of oars, as well as fire extinguishers and our bed-roll, he would hire a car with a larger boot, drive us to Rotterdam, negotiate for our gear, and deliver us with it at Den Helder - 40 km. north of Alkmaar, Meanwhile, the yard would take KAZakha up the Noord Hollandsche Kanaal to await us at Den Helder. Next morning (they concluded happily) we could get our clearance papers for England, put out to sea, “but, of course, you might find it necessary to return to port...IJmuiden, for
instance...the wind forecast is good for going there up till tomorrow morning...you will be a British ship...no trouble at all."

5.

-

- Thus about 20.00 hrs. (still raining or sleeting) we went aboard AuZatka at Den Helder; our gear was with us but technically in bond. Herr Burger shook hands with us in the cabin as if all this were part of a normal day's business. We owe thanks indeed both to him, for driving us over 20 km., and to his delightful wife who gave us coffee (and lent Maggie a pair of warm slippers) on our second transit through Alkmaar. "I am sorry my English is not as good as my husband's," she said, "I was a schipper's (sailor's) daughter and did not go to school so much." Before we left Herr Burger gave the children their bedtime kiss. His wife called him back, “Sweetie you've forgotten something." He looked startled, checked his brief case. “You've forgotten onma." We decided Holland was charming.

Fittings out. April 4th/6th

Our bedding was in a sack separate from the rest of our gear and we used it — in bond or not. Nevertheless, the mate got up next morning at 06.00 because she was too cold to sleep. at 06.30 the B.B.C. Light programme reported the coldest April night for sixty years did we know it! was wind For German Bight the forecast Ns 6/7 with rain and sleet: direction fine, but Maggie assured herself no one could expect a new crew and new boat to go out in a near gale.

At 07.50 I went to get “clearance” (we wanted our pans for a hot meal! — we had drunk the remains of our flask of coffee from Maldon and eaten the last battered sandwiches for breakfast). Explanations were difficult since the Customs officer had not much English and I less Dutch, but he had a moped and he came down to the ship, myself on the pillion. Then he went off to fetch a colleague and eventually after much discussion as to which regulations could best be applied, they drew up our crew list and provisioning list, which one of them presented to us with the comment, “You are now free to go to sea", while ‘the other said, "I go to make paper."

f2.

We were moored alongside “Casfun", a barge converted into a clubhouse for the sailing club of the Royal Netherlands Navy. They were surprised but interested to see us and wde us free of the place while we fitted out. Our mast had yet to be stepped (in a tabernacle on the coachroof). Herr Burger had said the two of us would be able to do this easily, but this was hard to believe, for it is full of full “Offshore" weight. By rigging a tackle on the jib halliard, and assisted by one small boy from a nearby cruiser, we did raise it. Offshore passage to IJmuiden — April 7th

On Tuesday, April 7th, the forecast was wind force 3-5, NW at first, backing SW later - i.e. in 12-24 hours. This was a clear “sailing order" as this might be the last of the fair winds for IJmuiden. The distance from Den Helder to IJmuiden is about 36 Nautical miles; once through the Marsdiep and in the North Sea we could expect a fair wind, The tide should be under us from 16.00 to 22.00 hrs.; and might carry us about 4 miles (peak rate 1 knot at neaps); the stream in and out of IJmuiden beings fairly small. Sunset would be about 19.25, and the moon - last quarter — would not rise till 03.00. However, entry in the dark should be practicable a general coastal chart (2322) and the IJmuiden/North sea Canal large scale chart (124) were clipped to the chart board in readiness, along with arawiny instruments (tied on for security). after lunch we locked into the outer harbour, warned by our Navy friends that it was blowing force 7 outside. we motored and sailed round the harbour for some tine to get the feel of her, and then, plucking up courage, beat out with 5 rolls in the mainsail, and working jib... Force 5 or 6 perhaps, NW. she sails all right: But comforting to have the island of Texel giving some shelter until could bear away a bit. Both of us were wearing Haward safety belts, a great comfort in bouncy seas.

It was nearly 17.00 when we started the run down the coast. Navigation could be mostly visual, a good thing as we had had no chance to swing the compass. Doing an exhilarating 6 knots at first, but the wind was easing: and after two hours we were down to 4 knots. The coast, rather featureless by day, was easier to identify at night. %gnond and IJmuiden (main) lighthouses appeared at dusk -- both unmistakable — but the IJmuiden light is remarkably difficult to pinpoint on the large-scale chart among a mass of lesser lights all represented by the same size of symbol. (It is actually on the south side of the channel, and 7 cables inland.)

Because of her geographical position, Great Britain has always had close ties with the sea and ships. a large number of British folk and traditional songs are concerned with these subjects, With the “folk-song revival", many singers have shown much interest in sea shanties, but the average folk club audience seeks to Know little about them.

There is wide disagreement over the derivation of the word shanty. The Oxford Dictionary suggests the French word “chanter" (to sing) might be the source, as does Grove's Dictionary of Music.
R.R. Terry, in his "The shanty Book" suggests that the word is derived from the West Indian huts called shanties. These were moved from place to place by gangs of men pulling on ropes attached to the hut. They worked in time with the singing of a man sitting on the hut.

/4,

there is a difference between sea songs and sea ghanties. ine songs were usually long, roszantic ballads telling of great sea battles, famous ships and captains, ane of faithful Cor, in any cases, untalthruts ) sailor's sweethearts waiting patiently on the Shore, but shanties were essentially work-songs. They were sung by merehant seamen as they performed their everyday tasks on board ship, such as weighing working the pumps, or setting sails.
One nan, called a shantyman sang out the verse to the sailors, who were perhaps hauling on a rope. The sailors sang the chorus and altogether on certain words, for example, in the well-known shanty slow the than Lown, the shearyaeers first line was sung solo by the

“way-ay, blow the man down..."

Various kinds of work needed their own particular shanty forzs. ihere were two main types: capstan or windlass shanties and halliard shanties. Capstan shanties were used for capstan work, as when weighing anchor, such work required a steady, sustained pull. rg ens these shanties had fairly long verses and are sung in a steady rhythm., sSanty inna and shenandoch are two fine capstan shanties. These shanties were also used for puzping opoMatieaa, ire Down Below was used exclusively for this purpose. Halliard (or “haul the yard") shanties mav be divided into two groups e called lone haul and short paul shanties. Long-haul were used for such tasks as setting the sails. They usually had two choruses with two pulls in each chorus. Reuben hanzo is a long haul shanty, and in the chorus:

Short haul shanties replaced the long haul when an extra—strong pull was needed to tighten everything up. ‘these usually had a short chorus with the pull on the last word, or as in Haul away, Joe.

The development of shanty tunes over long periods of time follows the same pattern as for English folk-song tunes - the oldest being nodal in nature. Many of the later ones are in a ninor key and some, probably corrupted, are in a major key. It is the shanty tunes other than the words that are interesting. The Pete Comton Orchestra have had many successful engagements and appearances at the Cafe de Paris, Colony and Pigalle Restaurants. In addition they have been resident at the Dorchester Hotel. Last June they were honoured to play at the Osterley Park Music Festival alongside Ted Heath and his Band.

Pete Comton and pianist Colin Parnell were recently commissioned by the Admiralty to write and compose the musical background for a film. In addition they have together written a Jazz Ballet, when the orchestra had occasion to play the score, accompanied by a troupe of the Royal Ballet, on several occasions at Art Festivals promoted by the Boroughs of London.

Please order your tickets early as we expect a 'Sell Out'. Tickets can be obtained from any Committee member or from the Bar at Stansgate.

Part IV

Durgerdam to Hoorn - April 11th

At 09.15 we met Alan Pratt outside the Central Station, wisely equipped with ski-trousers and mitts for warmth on watch, and an ample sleeping bag against cold nights. Actually, spring had broken out in the previous two days, and he had a warmer introduction to the country than we had. There was time for coffee "met slagroom" (whipped cream), a Dutch speciality, at the Dam Hotel (sic), while drawing up a programme for the next week. It was agreed that we could spare a few days for cruising on the IJsselmeer, but should be ready for the North Sea crossing on the first "slant" after Tuesday. If necessary, the crossing could be started as late as Friday.

At Durgerdam the new A.B. was signed on. He expressed willingness to navigate, and the master accepted the offer with alacrity; for this was the first time since the War that he had not had to do his own! We made a quick run over the charts and instruments: later there would be plenty of opportunity for practising.

After provisioning and watering ship, we declared for either Hoorn (19 sea miles) or Enkhuizen (24 sea miles). The decision need not be made until Marken Island, which had to be rounded in either case. About 15.45 we motored out of the lagoon, switched off engine almost at once and ghosted away under mainsail and Genoa in a bare force 2, W.

At 17.31, Marken lighthouse was close abeam. Up to this point, navigation could be mainly visual, though a compass course was a help in identifying Marken, which takes you farther from the shore than would be suggested by a casual glance at the chart.

The wind was never more than force 2 and sometimes fell away altogether. Clearly, Hoorn should be our goal: as well as being farther, Enkhuizen had a more difficult entrance, and on such a lovely evening it would have been a pity to press on under engine, as would be necessary to reach Enkhuizen in daylight.

EDITORIAL

You will no doubt notice that I have taken over the reins (or should it be helm?) of editorship (an unintentional and rather weak pun) of this magazine from John Perrin as from this issue.

Having, for the first time, really read the top of this page I realise that this is a monthly magazine but owing to circumstances - beyond my control (work!) and the fact that I shall be on holiday in — July I felt it better to make this issue cover June and july. In any = case, it probably will be July by the time you read this!

Arthur adams MAMGU Trophy Log finishes with this issue and available material is rather short so if you feel like seeing yourself in print on any subject associated with our particular interest do not hesitate to contact me at

T.I.G. Baddow Tel. Int. 436 Ext. 260

or

46, [redacted], Chelmsford Tel. [redacted]

I promise you will get no "The Editor regrets"! Would you please note that anything for inclusion in the August issue should reach me by Monday August 9th.

To turn to another subject, forming part of this issue is a complete Boat Register showing moorings and dinghy park spaces. So you should know where your boat is or where it should be.

In conclusion I would like to thank the retiring Editor, John Perrin, for the assistance in producing this issue.

J. G. Reeve,
Editor.

SAILING CLUB GOSSIP COLUMN

The first news received this month was, the engagement of Juliette Lindars and Rick Jones.
Later this summer the Lindars family are moving from Chelmsford but it looks as though one will soon be back.

Congratulations Juliette and Rick. The participants of the Norfolk Broads holiday seemed to enjoy themselves and were back in force for the Enterprise Open Meeting although the Triple K Cup and prizes went to other clubs.

2

Brian Partridge did some rapid developing and printing and showed us some of his photographs of the Broads at the Open Meeting Party.
Excellent food was provided and the raffle prizes were won by Mrs Derek Baker from Stone Sailing Club and by our Commodore Terry Hallam.

Open Day was not as well supported as last year although it was a superbly sunny day. We had a laugh when a motor boat towing a water skier capsized.

NORFOLD BROADS 1965
A great M.S.C. reunion took place at Horning Ferry one Saturday afternoon after eight Blakes boats had been hired and one privately owned Felicity had been towed to Wroxham.

Evening meals were cooked and eaten at varying speeds and later, in the pub, the singing started.

There wasn't much wind on Whit Sunday. We crept along the river to Ranworth Broad for lunch and moved even more slowly out of the Broad to Thurne for the night.

The first bridge was encountered at Potter Heigham the following day. Only minor incidents were reported. The sail up to Hickling Broad was quite pleasant.

Due either to shallow water, a deep draught boat or bad luck, David and Eleanor ran hard aground and were helped off by another crowd of sailors. The majority of the fleet were happily drinking tea in the middle of the Broad, supposedly moored with a mud weight. Mooring that night was quite complicated due to the shallow water inshore and we used a motor cruise as a bridge.

During the singsong in the Pleasure Boat, Sarah and Peter Jennings, who sail a tiny Catamaran and who were camping at Ludham Bridge, joined the party.

The following morning it rained - bucketfuls. We didn't start
sailing and/or motoring until after lunch. The starters said - up
to Horsey Mere, then on to Potter Heigham and Thurne. When the tail-encders reached Horsey there was no sign of the leaders but a nice bit of wind got up and we had a good sail. After an hour or more of tacking up a narrow river it's really nice to get out to some open water.

The leaders got to Thurne and the tail enders got to Potter Heigham which proved slightly awkward for Linda whose clothes and bed were at Potter while she was at Thurne. All ships cooks went on strike that evening and had meals out.

The Potter party awoke to John Hutchings dulcet tones. He'd spent the night in huts and under bridges. His birthday (18th) breakfast was provided by Leonie, Dave (Young) and John (Witter) and by midmorning he was united with his parents at Thume.

A gentle breeze took us to South Walsham Broad where several boats took part in a hilariéus balloon chase on the Inner Broad. The spectators on land looked very shocked at yachts being treated like dinghies.

The mouth of the River Ant was chaotic. The cruisers had seemed to be under control the day before but on Wednesday it was awful. Admittedly a couple of dozen yachts, several of which had no auxiliary or outboard engines or motors, were trying to tack up one of the narrowest of rivers but everybody sorted them-selves out and passed through Ludham Bridge for the night.

-3-

John's birthday was duly celebrated at the local hostelry.

More tacking on Thursday morning took us to Barton Broad for some more open water sailings. Sarah and Peter were spotted afloat at Barton Turf and we met them again in the evening at Ludham Bridge.

John Witter aided by Dave and Leonie and others wrote ‘'On the Norfolk Broads'' to the tune of Quartermasters Stores. One of a group of young people from Hoddesdon provided the piano accompani-ment :-

There was Con, Con, with her apron on

There was Jack, Jack, motoring at the back

There was Mike, Mike (Sissons) quanting up the dyke,

There were boats, boats, nine Marconi Boats

etc.

Brian Partridge remembered the chorus from previous years.
Young Sue Palmer's head poked through open windows on several even-ings wnile she learned the words of ''Oh Sir Jasper''.

What should have been a run out of the Ant and a reach to Horning and Wroxham turned out to be a beat nearly all the way - the wind shifted through 180° overnight. Don Freeman and Joyce had spent the night at Stalham instead of Ludham bridge and did very well to beat to Horning in one day.

The final night was spent in various boatyards and some people travelled home on Friday for the Enterprise open meeting the following
day.

Damage and repairs:-

Replacement parts for John Witter's outboard.

A new halyard for Norman Palmer.
A bowsprit found Jack Bigden's porthole and one of the dinghy oars snapped.

Mike Sisson had the misfortune to acquire a crack in his hull after a collision.

Stan Allerton grabbed at the boom crutches and fell in the river at Horning; Julian and Dave Young both got half wet.

For twenty adults and seven children this wasn't bad.

Organising stopping places for nine unmatched boats seemed a little tricky but was managed most evenings. Holiday to be repeated?
Probably!

Signed,
Eleanor C, Aldividge.

MAMGU Trophy - Winning Log
by A. Adam

Part V .

IJmuiden to Felixstowe - April 16th/17th

The 06.45 forecast was reasonable: Humber, Thames and Dover - wind S. to SE, force 3 to 4, and no deep depressions coming our way. Galloper L.V. confirmed wind 5-4 at 05.00 ship's time. We posted a letter advising our agents of our departure (they would be responsible for paying import duties), topped up the petrol tank, made up two flasks of coffee for use on the voyage, and locked through into the outer harbour, This time we did mean to go to Felixstowe!

The tide, almost of spring range, was due to flow SW from
09.00 hrs. and should give us a good start. Actually it was 10.09 as
we passed IJW 1 outer buoy, under mainsail and Genoa, doing 41/4 knots by log in a calm sea, wind SEE force 2-3. Weather fair, visibility
moderate. A course of 253° was drawn on the chart (No. 1408) as the
basic rhumb line for the Outer Gabbard L.V., distant 921/2 miles. At 4 knots (say) we should get there at 09.00 on Friday.

Up to 16.30 the wind stayed nearly South, usually about force 2; we were steering on or slightly to windward of the rhumb line and doing 31/2 to 4 knots. The log was satisfactory but needed two operators which obviously would not be possible at all times; however, it did allow us to "calibrate our guesses' fairly well.

Alan went below about 16.00 for shut-eye, leaving me on watch.
In IJmuiden we had carelessly over-filled the tank and a little of the spillage had remained on deck; we hadn't bothered unduly as there were no smokers aboard, but evidently it had seeped through at one of the stanchion fixings. The amount was probably very small and all possible ventilation was done but the smell persisted and Maggie was rather ‘knocked out' by it.

From 16.30 the wind faded; after a few breaths from different directions, we were completely becalmed at 17.40, with the sails slatting as we rolled. I fitted the boom guy to steady things, but the sails continued to flap noisily. Not until 19.10 was there any detectable wind; then it came up very light from dead aft. With the Genoa goosewinged (on the spinnaker pole) we were making 1.5 knots.

Alan relieved me at 20,10 hrs., dinner being taken at the change-over, The wind slowly improved, but also veered a little, forcing us to the right of our course, though not enough to justify a gybe. At 23.30 I came up again; we were creaming along at 6 knots. We gybed at the changeover and I put the wind on the quarter. No sooner had Alan gone below than the wind increased from force 5 to a good 6, At any rate he didn't have time to undress! We changed over from Genoa to working jib, but even then the strength was out of the wind. By 00.40 we were becalmed again, and rolling like the town drunk.

This calm did not last so long as the previous one, but the direction did not settle down until 02.00; for an hour or more I was setting the spinnaker pole and boom guy for one gybe, only to have to gybe them over for a 30 degree change of wind. At last it settled down in the SE to give 3.5 knots on a broad reach. I should have been very cross if Alan had come up to relieve me as soon as we got a decent wind: In fact, he came at 04.10, by which time f had had some reward for my labours.

We held the SE breeze until 08.00, when it started to veer slowly and increased a little: by 10.00 we were nearly close-hauled on the port tack and KAZARKA would steer herself with the tiller in the rack. Alan worked up a D.R. position for 10.00 hrs; 18.5 miles short of the Outer Gabbard and a little to the right of the rhumb line.

I brought up the D/F and took bearings on Outer Gabbard, Noord Hinder end Smith's Knall while Alan plotted them. Meanwhile KAZARKA looked after herself very capably, doing 5 knots almost close-hauled in force 4-5. The position lines from Noord Hinder and Smith's Knoll did not help much; they intersected at rather an acute angle, and the beacons were 30 and 40 miles away. However, the run of the bearings on Outer Gabbard showed that we left it to port by about 5 miles. At 12.55, by way of corroboration, we picked up a 6-fathom bank with the echo-sounder, evidently the northern continuation of Inner Gabbard; this, crossed with an Outer Gabbard radio bearing, was a fix that could be relied upon.

Coming hard on the wind, we started the long tramp down to the South Shipwash, The Sunk L.V. radio beacon, nominally only 5 miles range, gave good signals at least 15 miles away and was a useful check, Although we could bring it no nearer than 15° on our port bow, the tide was going on SAW until 16.00 hrs. and would help to keep us off the Shipwash. As a precaution, we kept the echo-sounder going.

At 15.30 a careful search for seamarks showed the W.Shipwash buoy about 2 miles away to the NW (across the shoal). At 16.00 we took a fix on the SE and SW Shipwash buoys. Now the breeze was failing and the south-going tide was ended, seeing that it was high water and the sea had gone down, a short cut across the tail of the Shipwash would be in order. In fact the lowest depth was 5 fathoms.

6

It was a beautiful afternoon, and all hands were feeling very relaxed in-the sun. We changed over to Genoa, but had left it rather late and progress over the ebb was slow, At 17.25 we started the engine, wishing to enter Felixstowe before dark, in hope of clearing Customs the same night. "Radio Caroline" was humming to herself but looking very dingy... And so to Felixstowe Dock where we berthed alongside a grain barge at 19.45.

We had no direct access to the shore, so Alan and I inflated the "Redcrest" while Maggie prepared supper. Presently there was a hail from the Customs (Waterguerd) officer; he had seen us but couldn't reach us. Alan went off in the “Redcrest" and made a complete tour of the dock before he found a place where the Customs man could come down. Clearance was effected in half an hour, and he made it very clear that as far as his department was concerned, we were free to go on to Maldon whenever
we wished, The point of this emphasis did not strike home until next morning.

Felixstowe is one of tho noisiest harbours I know, but we all slept like logs.

Felixstowe to Maldon April 18th

At 09.00 hrs. I went ashore to contact the shipping agent. He was surprised to see me: our notice-of-departure letter was still on some- body else's desk, perhaps even unopened, The import formalities would take time; we should be able to leave by Tuesday...

Blunt words passed: my delivery crew would not be available much
longer, and I had a tide to catch to Maldon - today! A taxi whisked
us up to the office at Ipswich half an hour before closing time for
the weekend, and a rush job was done. Back at Felixstowe by noon...
The Customs (Import) officer checked that the name and description of the ship were correct, Now all departments were satisfied!

While I had been in Ipswich, fog had come down and at one stage it
had been impossible to see across the dock. Now it was lifting - good!
I have sailed off Harwich in fog, but I don't do it for choice. We were already a little late on the tide as we motored out about 12.40, setting mainsail and Genoa as we went.

Leaving the main channel at Cliff Foot buoy, we set a compass course
for Stone Banks buoy, not yet visible - visibility being about half a mile. Halfway to Stone Banks, estimating that we were now clear of the flood stream into Harwich, we switched off engine and were making 3 knots close-hauled on the port tack, Later the wind backed and for a time wo were on a dead run down the Wallet, with the land just visible a mile away but no identifiable marks. At 16.10 I saw a black conical buoy ahead and the navigator verbally, patted himself on the back, "Priory Spit, right on the D.R. position." A light SE breeze brought us past N. Eagle, Bar and Bench Head while we experimented with the sheet leads of the Genoa to get the best out of it. A large spinnaker appeared astern; gradually we were overhauled by "Cavalier of Kent", Philip Hays' fine ocean racer. Appendix I - Note on charts, etc. for Holland

For the Dutch inland waterways, only Dutch charts are adequate. Yhey are, of course, printed in Dutch, but translation of the key is not too arduous a task,

The best are:

IJsselmeer charts for yachtsmen

Nos. 1810, 1815, 1816, 1817, 1618.

The complete set in plastic envelope costs about 15/-; because of the reclamation works in progress, en up-to-date chart is indispensible.

ANAB weterkaarten

These cover the canals and "grote rivieren" (Rhine and Maas systems) and give details of every navigable waterway, however small; mostly on a scale of l1/4 inches to the mile. Depths, over-head clearances and the dimensions of lock basins are given.

These charts are available at about half price to members of AT- affiliated bodies, of which the is one.

born's Schippcrskeaart van Nederland
A good general-coverage map showing the whole area from the Schelde to the sns, suitable for route-planning, etc.

Also useful:

List of opening times of railway bridges (issued free).
All the above are obtaineble from the

Bureau voor watertoecrisne,
Muscemplein 5,
Amsterdam.

British Admiralty charts are satisfactory for the coast, but in the Delta areas particularly, reclamation works may be in progress and the chart must be corrected right-up-to-date

- 8 -

We did not have a copy of the Admiralty North Sea Pilot, part IV, because a new edition was imminent at the time of the cruise. It would be helpful when using the large ports.

Not recommended

The Inland Waterways of Holland (Imray, Laurie, et al.)

Not very convenient to use and out of date. Incomplete - the Oranjesluizen are not even mentioned.

Appendix II - Lights and seamarks for IJmuiden (Brit. Ad. chart No. 124)

As stated in the log, the surfeit of lights at a major port can baffle a stranger. It is not usual to portray different "magnitudes" on a chart, so the mariner has to search through a mass of light symbols of the same size, reading their descriptions. The following is a list of the most helpful lights.

"Magnitude" - Description - Position
1 - Main lighthouse, fl. 5 sec., 171 ft. high. - 7 cables inland, to S. of channel.
2 - Steel and electricity works; tall chimneys carrying red aircraft-warning lights at vertical intervals; very characteristic. - 1-2 miles inland, to N. of channel.
2 - Signal pattern of fixed white, red and green lights ("tidal sigs." on chart), making a leading line with the main lighthouse into the Zuider Buitenkanaal. - On short pier inside breakwaters, to S. of Channel.
2 - 2 lights occulting 3 sec., switched together (distinctive), making a leading line into Noorder Buitenkanaal. N.B. These lights may only be visible over a narrow sector. - On "Fort eiland" between channels.
3 - Fixed red light, 40 ft. (lower than the other lights mentioned). - End of N. breakwater.

N.B. There are unlit buoys in parts of the outer harbour, so it is advisable to keep in the channel.

THE ATTENTION OF ALL MEMBERS IS DRAWN TO THE RISK OF FIRE BEING CAUSED BY
DISCARDED CIGARETTE ENDS, MATCHES AND COMBUSTIBLE MATERIAL ALONG THE ROAD
TO THE CLUB AND ALSO ON THE CLUB AREA.
AS HARVEST TIME APPROACHES THIS RISK BECOMES EVEN GREATER AS ALSO IS THE

EDITORIAL

Having returned from holiday in a flush of enthusiasm and with a new mast on Torch 162 (Moral:- never tow a boat with the mast up, even for 100 yards, someone's sure to throw a power cable in the way) I now embark on the August issue of NAVIGANS.

One of my friends(?) remarked recently that he expected the next issue I produced would be the bumper Christmas number, so I had to do something! To turn to a more serious topic you will note that the front page of the issue is devoted to a FIRE warning. The risk of fire, particularly on the
road to the Club is a very real thing so please read, mark, learn and inwardly digest the warning.

The anonymous contributor who writes the Gossip Column is unfortunately not with us this month so the column has been written by several anonymous writers among them Rosaleen Farthing.

In conclusion, thanks for the contributions I found on my desk when I returned from holiday.

J.G. Reeve

SATLING CLUB GOSSIP Column

Arthur and Maggie Adam have been to Holland again with KAZARKi, covering Texel to Breskens in a 3-week cruise. They had a roughish passage home, entering Brightlingsea at the same time as Fleetwind masts were breaking off Stansgate. We may hear the highlights of this cruise but they are not trying to repossess the MAMGU Trophy. How about hearing from you other cruising types?

John Perrin has received a very pleasant and chatty letter from Rosaleen Farthing from Vancour B.C. extracts from which are given below.

'This is a beautiful place by anyone's standards, but to a sailor it is something approaching paradise. There are beautiful sailing conditions both in Vancouver and in the straits between here and Vancouver Island. Vancouver is built around an inlet and there is a large bay to provide plenty of sheltered dinghy sailing. We have joined Kitsilano Yacht Club which is one of the five clubs in the city, and is the one most concerned with dinghy sailing.

We decided not to buy a boat this year but to spend at least some of our weekends exploring the countryside. We have spent several long weekends travelling hundreds of miles, but the country is so vast that we haven't seen very much. There is a limit on just how far you can explore. as there are very few roads. We have bought ourselves a small tent and we make good use of the campsites that can be found everywhere. They have a very high standard at these sites and they always provide free firewood! We have managed to do some sailing though. Both of us have been crewing in Enterprises from time to time. We have managed to combine sailing and exploring as last weekend we drove 300 miles so that Dave could crew in the Western Canada Championships. Although most of the sailing is on the coast - it is growing quite rapidly on the interior lakes too and people are keen enough to trail their boats 300 or so miles just for a regatta.

Oddly enough, organised small boat sailing is relatively recent here. The larger boats, such as Lightnings and Stars and a few Dragons, have been around for quite a while, but Flying Dutchmen, Enterprises and 505's are only just building up large enough fleets to have good racing. The most popular boats around are small, 8' 'Sabots'. They are used for just about everything from novice instruction to keen Winter racing known as Frostbiting.

-3-

We regarded them es 'bathtubs' at first, but are slowly being convinced that there must be more in them than meets the eye.

We came here with the fond idea that in this land of timber boats would be cheap. This has not proved to be the case as a new Enterprise here would cost us $1000 or over Three hundred pounds! They do not make 5/16" plywood locally and it has to be imported from Japan! There are one or two English built boats around and the difference in finish is tremendous. There are quite a few; English people to, but there is also a good mixture of Canadians, Australians, New Zealanders and other Europeans. Most of the Flying Dutchmen in the club are sailed by Dutchmen. Sailing people seem to be the same the world over though. Most of our friends are in the sailing club and we have been to quite a few good parties! The liquor lews here are rather primitive in some respects and even for a semi-official party one has to supply one's own drink. It seems kind of strange to walk along the street in a cocktail dress carrying a case of beer:

Of course we have found lots of things that are different here - some
we like and some we don't. On the whole we are very happy and like Vancouver very much. We are both enjoying our jobs and are managing to save rather more money that we could have hoped to back in England. I don't know how long that happy situation will last as there are so many lovely things to spend money on! We hope to have a boat next year and we want to learn to ski this winter so - there goes quite a proportion of our savings!

Well - I hope I get round to posting this letter. I started writing it
once before but did not get too far! Please give our regards to everyone in the club.

Incidentally congratulationsto John and his wife on producing an 83/4 lb. boy!

SAILING NOTES

I would like to thank all those who have turned out to help get the dinghy park and surroundings cleared up. Your help was greatly appreciated and I hope that everyone will do their bit to keep it tidy from now on.

In trying to sort cut the dinghy park, I was greatly handicapped by the number of boats that have no means of identification. In order to ease matters for the future we are g»ing to make available a standard size brass plate which will be painted and sign written with the boats name and/or number. These plates will be available at a small charge of approx. 2/6d, and ~.:rs owners of unnamed boats are asked to co-operate by supplying details of boats to me as soon as possible. A sample plate will be on view in the bar at Stansgate. This will also be very useful, as a means of identification, to the river authorities should a boat go adrift or missing for any reason. This applies particularly to tenders and non-class boats.

The Club has now purchased some copies of the 1965 RYA racing rules and they are available either from me or at the bar at Stansgate at 3/-d. per copy Your Committee feel that for reasons of safety and to provide the best possible service No.2 rescue launch should be manned on all occasions when there is likely to be general Club sailing (i.e. when an 0.0.D. has been appointed). To do this we must have volunteers but if they are not forthcoming some of you will be receiving notices asking you to be at Stansgate on certain occasions to help with these services.

No.l Rescue Launch

It is also necessary to build up a register of members who are willing to Cox No.1 launch on a rota basis for all occasions when it is required. It is very important that this is done and that they receive proper instruction in the use of the launch as in less than half a season's use it has deteriorated so much that it has proved necessary to have a major engine overhaul carried out for which we are greatly indebted to one of our members.

-4-

I suspect that the main reason for this is ignorance of the proper operating conditions of the engine and until I can familiarise those who have legitimate cause to use it, the use of.No.1 launch by any Club member is forbidden. The operating instructions are in the course of being prepared.

Brazil

When Brazil was presented to the Club one of her main functions was to be for novice instructions. She has not so far been used for this purpose as much as I would have liked and as an experiment I am going to make it possible for any member to use her for instruction purposes at anytime provided the book kept at Stansgate is filled in.

It is inevitable that a certain amount of damage and breakages will occur but as long as details are entered in the book it will be possible to get things repaired with the minimum delay.

The only other conditions attached to this and which are of great importance are that personal buoyancy be worn by those aboard and that some other Club member who is competent to act in an emergency shall remain on the shore while the boat is in use.

As I said this is an experiment which I hope will prove successful.
It must of course be understood that if the boat is being used but a member having made an advanced booking turns up then the boat must be surrendered immediately and no charge will be made for periods of less than complete hours.

The hiring fee is 1/-d per hour.

Elsewhere in this issue you will find a summary of race results to date and the current position regarding the various points championships. Also appear brief reports on some of the sailing meetings at which the Club hes been represented.

FLAGS AND BURGEES

The use of ideographic symbols to express ideas is almost as old as mankind itself. Certainly it is older than the written word, indeed some
languages in their written form even to-day are ideorgraphic in their form e.g. Chinese. The use of flags to indicate ownership, or membership of a corporate body, still widely used, is together with heraldry and continental road signs a modern derivative of this ancient practice,

As far as the yachtsman is concerned the use of flag symbols descends directly from Naval Lore, The country of registry or ownership is indicated by the Ensign. For most yacht clubs, as for the British Merchant Navy, this is the Red Ensign, a red flag with the Union Flag, or as it is usually called the Union Jack, in the upper quarters nearest the hoist,

One club only is allowed to wear the White Ensign, sacred to the Royal Navy; that is the Royal Yacht Squadron, the senior of all yacht clubs within the Commonwealth, The Blue Ensign, the flag of the Royal Naval Reserve is worn by the members of certain other clubs who possess an Admiralty Warrant to do so. The ship must be of British registration and the owners a British Subject. The Warrant is personal to the owner who must be onboard or in effective command whilst the ensign is worn. Incidentally, whilst other flags may be 'flown' an ensign is always ‘worn'. This Blue ensign is defaced by a symbol, usually the badge of the club concerned. The Royal Corinthian Yacht Club and the Little Ship Club are examples seen in our area,

Lastly there is the defaced Red Ensign, perhaps less commonly seen although the West Mersea Yacht have psrmission to wear it,

-11-

A yacht club is regarded by the pwoers-that-be as a vessel, so the same laws apply. The Ensign is worn whenever the Club is in commission, The Union Jack is never flown by any vessel or shore establishment counting as a vessel unless, I believe, an Admiral of the Fleet is aboard, the use of this flag at sea being his perogative only. On land of course it is the flag proper for all loyal citizens of the United Kingdom to fly on those occasions when there is cause for celebration.

The penalties for the improper use of the Ensign or Union Flag are severe, It may be seized by any officer of Her Majestys Armed Services on full pay or any Customs Officer and confiscated. In addition the offender is liable to a fine not exceeding £500.

It is probable that the Burgee of a recognised yacht club is an essential part of the legal colours of any yacht, for it is only by showing that
she is owned by a member of a recognised club that she is readily recognised as a 'pleasure yacht' and the only way of doing this in a ready and convenient manner is by wearing a burgee.

In addition to these two flags the owners of a yacht may also fly a
House Flag, Distinguishing Flag. There is no law defining this.

The Ensign and Burgee should be worn by the ship when under way whilst there is light by which to distinguish them, when at anchor, the colours are made at O800 and hauled down at sunset, the time being taken from the senior yacht present, In addition a vessel is required by law to wear the Ensign when entering or leaving a foreign port,

The traditional position for wearing the Ensign under way is at the peak of the aftermost gaff sail, and on an ensign sta f at the stern at anchor, “ith the introduction of Bermician rig a diffics . arose, At first it was hoisted to a cringle about two thirds uv the cv of the sail, but the effect was not too pleasing, smacking rather of a nasted. effect, Nowadays it is usual to wear it on the ensign staff a ie stern, -

Sunday was a beautiful sunny day and having arrived about non

at the launching site - a sandy bay facing NW with a concrete ete slip,
caravan site and restaurant - we provi alone d and water ed the ship and
fitted all the gear aboard, ‘je found the surro unding hills beckoned, st hill to gaze down on the so instead of launching we climbed the neareislan Firth of Lorne sparkling blue, dotted with ds, with the blue shoreline of ijvll as a backcloth.

a k=

We launched early Monday morning and. were Jucky enough t have an almost calm day, A quick decision had-t>s be made which waz to go. As there was no wind and only two hours of south going tide left we decided to cross ‘the Firth of Lorne and head northwards up the Sound of lull, We were not going to pass the Lism re Light and its adjacent rocks without help from the engine so downed sail. Once past the dangerous area the engine was sto:;ped and the resulting silence was
intense, Sudden heavy breathing made me jump - a couple of vorpoises
were gambling about + mile away making n: sound as they surfaced except this. snorting. The seagulis on the rocky shore about two miles away s unded like occasional human voices and the sun shone from a cloudless sky. ‘fe ghosted on hearing more breathing but unable t- see the porpoises because of the distance, The wind increased gradually to force 2 so enabling us t* avoid the rocks and shoals and by mid after- noon it was apparent that an anchorage must so:n be fund before the tide turned, It was obvious from the charts and Clyde Cruising Club's Sailing Directions that anchorages had to-be chosen with greater care than on the East Coast due to steeply shelving rocky shores, poor holding ground and greater incidence of strong winds,

Loch Aline half way along the Sound of Mull on the mainland shore proved a delightful quiet and picturesque anchorage with wooded shores and the usual castle, The anchor with warp stretching down to it could be seen in two fathoms the water was so‘clear. The wind here though, as in most lochs, was fickle blowing from first one way then the other, A visit to the small store next morning proved that provisions were much more expensive in the Highlands, The shopkeeper's ‘‘what beautiful weather we are having" was an echo of the words of every other Scot to whom we had spoken, which sounded ominously as though it was usually grey and cold in this part of the world. The morning passed pleasantly in warm sunshine running the rest of the distance up the Sound of Mull in force 5 gradually decreasing, ith plenty of fair tide left, a course up Loch Sunart, which is over 20 miles long, was planned, The wind suddenly changed to Ni Force 4 and we went careering to.ards what appeared to be a solid rocky shore, The opening showed up between island and headland and the rocks were smooth and rouned worn by the pounding of the waves over centuries, Once in the Loch the wind was again fickle with no appreciable tide because of the great depth and towards late afternoon the mist began rolling in from the west blotting out first the mountain tops then moving lower, Fortunately there was a handy bay on the north shore which we reached as the mist became a solid drizzle. An immaculate motor fisherman yacht also came in for the night, which is very short at this time of the year in Scotland and never becomes really dark,

Next morning it was still drizzling with poor visibility so we did not hurry to start and went ashore to provision and have a look at the village of Salen, Just a few cottages straggling round the . head of the bay but an excellent store and the ubiquitous sheep nibbling the grass, Returning to Aurora we found three workmen admiring her who asked. the inevitable questions, "Have you an engine?" and "Is it reliable?" We were asked this several times and thought at the tine that the Scots yachtsmen were too engine conscious but upon reflection an engine is essential in these waters unless you have a strong pair of arms and oars as it is not easy to anchor and wait for a tide because of the great depths.

The afternoon passed tacking back down Loch Sunart in thick mist against a fresh headwind, Although the sailing directions said Loch Teacndais entrance should only: be attempted under power because of the shallow devious route necessitated by rock stremm channel we entered under sculling sar and popped safely into the loch at great speed because of the current. This loch looked desolate with just a couple of houses on the shore and the low cloud and drizzle did not

help to show it off. we hastily rigged the awning after anchoring near the head of the loch and watched the off lorry Lump its way over the track which served as a road,

Next morning we sculled out the other entrance (which was even less recommended in the Sailing Directions) and saw a colony of seals on the seaweed covered rocks, ‘The adults all slid into the water leaving the pups undefended and presently a ring of faces circled the boat, They soon started playing once we were past. bright sunshine brought us to ithe next smell loch - na Droma Buidhe,

and
sea, we were tempted to bathe im the trystal clear water showing a bottom of white sand, ‘adding out waist deep through the seaweed forests and half a dozen strokes back was all the temperature of th water allowed, It was breath-takingly cold. Loch Feochan should be our next target decided, not far along the coast but the entrance prohibitively difficult according to the sailing directions. Being on the mainland and

We are now reaching the end of our third year at Stansgate- three years in which the Club has made some fivefold growth, This rapid increase in membership of all types, in boats, and equipment, has created a demand for an organisation capable of administering and operating the facilities
required by some 600 members rather than 420, Inevitably the rapid growth
has resulted in the building in of stresses which have been evident at times in the creaks and groans of the present administrative system,

This year too has had another and especial significance to the Marconi Sailing Club, It is the last year of our present lease, and it has been a year of waiting for the result of the Marina Scheme appeal. This last is now happily resolved, The Ministry of Housing and Local Government has allowed the appeal, and Outline Planning permission has been granted to Mr. Sparrow, Nevertheless this does not signal the end of negotiations; on the contrary the next year is of even more importance in that respect, if we are to achieve in the long term a stable permanent Club.

All these things and many more besides have been very much in the minds of your i"lag Officers and Committee during the past year, The result has been a number of propositions that it is intended the Committee shall put to the Annual General Meeting,

In order to publicise these and to give members time to chew them over it was decided to devote a whole issue of 'Navigans' to these questions,

Terence Hallam

This special edition of 'Navigans' has been produced so that various decisions taken in Committee may be brought to the notice of Club members well in advance of the A,G.M, One of the decisions requires suspension of a part of certain Club rule (rule &) and rather than just making a bald proposal on the A,G.M, Agenda Notice it was felt that the reasoning should be laid before the whole Club, and support asked for, in advance,

THE THIRD RACING CLASS (ORCLASSES?) by the Sailing Secretar

At a recent Sailing Committee Meeting the question of the Club supporting more pure racing classes was discussed, This resulted in the proposals which will be detailed later,

To put you all in the picture let me give you some of the background which led to the final decisions,

I started the ball rolling by sending to all members of the Sailing Commit’.ee a document laying.out my thoughts on this subject which I hoped could be used ior a basis for discussion, These ideas and suggestions stemmed from comments I had heard from various people from time to time and a feeling which I think had been present in some parts of the Club for a while, that the handicap class did not give the sort of racing most people wanted,

My own feelings were that it was not one more racing class that we needed but several, together with the facility to include even more, if sufficient support and demand were forthcoming, ‘ith this in mind I went through the boat register and listed all the boats we had which were either potential racing classes as far as the Club was concerned, or of which we might have. sufficient to run races, It was this list which was finally whittled down some two hours later to a manageabl
size
e’ when the following course of action was agreed,

Torches and Mirrors would also have their own races as there are a reasonable number of each in the Club but they would not be encouraged as racing classes,

A handicap series would still be run for other classes and all the above mentioned classes would be eligible if at any one time there were not sufficient boats of one class to run a class race,

Various Committee members had enquired from certain Club members, whom it was known were considering changing classes what they wanted to change to and whether they would be prepared to support new classes which were not exactly the ones of their choice, In general their comments were favourable, In the above choice some classes may be noticeably absent but it was felt by your Sailing Committee that there would either be insufficient sup ort or that they overlapped too much with existing classes, However, provision has been made to overcome this if the Committee are shown to be mistaken,

It was felt that this problem should be tackled at this time of the year when people were beginning to lay plans for next year and were considering changing boats, It was also important to do it before it was toe late for those who have made tentative plans to reconsider,

The adoption of these classes also gives the potential new boat owner and newcomer to racing a chance to choose the boat most suitable to his needs, It will also make it easier for Club members to advise people seeking guidance about trying boats, as the choice for class racing is now wider.

In making these suggestions we have not lost sight of the aims of the Club one of which is to provide sailing for all, but at the same time we are trying to improve the opportunities and standards for those that want to take advantage of the racing facilities offered,

The organisation of the classes will be considered in detail later by the Committee but tentative suggestions are that these new classes still be represented by th. handicap class representative on the Sailing Committee but have their own class captain responsible to the handicap class rep. until such time as a class grows sufficiently large to require its ow representative, John Witter.

YORK OR | FAY? by the Commodore

The thought of 600 members all descending upon Stansgate one fine day in the surmer, demanding their rights in the way of lebensraum in the Clubhouse, not to mention toilets, rescue launch, car park, bar and other facilities we supposedly offer them, is indeed sufficient to cause the stoutest and crustiest Flag Officer to blench, At the present time these services and all others are provided by courtesy of those members, few alas in number, who are prepared to work, Indeed they not only work, but in addition pay, subsidising the Club by expending money on petrol for special journeys, sometimes several times a week, in order that the facilities shall be maintained, albeit in a rather attenuated way. These devoted and long suffering members are about the same in number, indeed to a large extent in person as well, as were operating in the old days when our membership was
under 120,

It is true that at times we call for a working party, and we are seldom disappointed with the response, Those however are for very special occasions, It is the day to day, and week to week work which is carried out so regularly by the faithful band, It is patently obvious that in spite of the continued efforts of these chaps there are times when the facilities break down, and giving as they do all of their available time there is no spare effort to meet these occasions, .

For the whole of the existence of the Club, some fourteen years, the bas’ subscription has remained at ten shillings, notwithstanding the considerable rise in the cost of living and therefore running costs, During this period the subscription rates of other clubs have risen two, three, and in some cases, over fourfold.

The time, I am sure, has now come for a realistic look at the way we run things, and the services we offer,
The choice in simple terms is the selection of the better of two alternatives: to work or to pay. In other:
words are we prepared to continue as a "do it yourself" club but with very much more "do" by the individual member, or are we to employ the services of a full or part time servant,

The former choice would entail a drastic change to the way of Club life on the part of all members, lfore real time spent in maintaining and improving the facilities; many more helpers spending more man-hours working at Stansgate, Greater participation in the essential Committee work, Less time in which to enjoy ourselves sailing our boats, putting in everyones' interest the Club first and our own entertainment second, ed

Choosing the second of the two alternatives would hit where it tends w to hurt most, in our pockets, The subscription would rise, perhaps to. double, treble, or even more, the present sum, It would also necessitate changes in the administration, although these are inevitable anyway. The operation of a club of our size is a business and requires the application of proper management principles, It would also be necessary to modify our present forms of membership and to streamline the financial side of the club,

The choice is ours, Shall it be the first or the second alternative, Work or pay. .

Your Flag Officers and Committee have debated these at length, and
decided to propose to the A,G.M, that the choice shall be the second one:
to pay. They therefore as detailed elsewhere in this journal propose that the next Committee be instructed to take such steps as may be necessary

-/7-

within as short a time as possible to put before the Club proposals to employ a part or full time professional; to raise subscriptions to the economic level; to introduce a new form of membership to cater for the crew of a vessel who may not be marconi employee, a non voting, non privileged type of membership. In conjunction with the last to clarify the position of the Associate Member,

ANNUAL GENERAL MEETING 1965:
Herewith report on the Annual General Meeting as promised last month. The meeting, was held at the M.A.S.C., Beehive Lane on Wednesday 2th November at 7.30 p.m. The chair was taken pro tem by the Commodore.
The attendance was a record one of 120 Full and Associate members.

The minutes of the previous A.G.M. and matters arising were dealt with fairly rapidly and were followed by the Secretary's, Treasurer's and Sailing Secretary's Reports. These were all passed unanimously.

In his report the Commodore included a run-down on the events leading up to the Committee's proposals. The first was a proposal to employ a paid steward for the Club. The Club was expanding rapidly but also the work load on the comparatively few willing helpers was increasing. The proposed stewards' duties would be the cleaning and maintenance of the Club premises, site and care of the Club boats, i.e. rescue launches and Brazil.

In reply to question from the floor it was stated that one person only would be responsible for the supervision of the steward. The steward would not be expected to run the galley.

It was pointed out that to cater for this extra expenditure, changes would have to be made to the existing subscription rates and fees.

A vote was then taken on the proposal to employ a steward, 69 members voted for it, none against, with four abstentions.

The next proposal, that of suspending parts of rule 8(e), was then put before the meeting. The proposal covered that part of the rule concerned with the three year term of Flag Officers and its suspension for one year.

3

Many comments were made on this proposal, one being that a Sub-committee. should be formed to negotiate the new lease and that the Commodore should not carry out these negotiations. It was pointed out by the Sailing Secretary that the proposal had been formulated before the Marina proposition had been made public, also the Committee had a difficult task this year in deciding the normal succession to Commodore.

Comment was then made from the floor on the history of Rule 8(e). It was felt that the Committee did not understand the purpose of this rule which was to prevent any one person staying in office. The task of Commodore was an onerous one and that three years was the limit of anyone's efficiency...

In answer to this another comment was made from the floor that all viable organisations find it necessary to and do change rules that are found restrictive.

Another suggestion was that if the Committee's proposal was defeated the present Commodore could lead the previously mentioned Sub-committee as a Vice-President of the Club.

MAMGU TROPHY PRIZE WINNING LOG by C. S. Molyneux

Part I

This an account of a single handed cruise made in the yacht ‘Samuel Pepys' this summer, by the owner. Details are taken from the log kept during the cruise.

The cruise started I suppose in the 'Black Buoy’ at Wivenhoe, as I was ready to cast off well before High Water. Winds were from the S.W., about Force 6, being, I hoped, the tail end of the gales which had been sweeping up the Channel for the previous couple of weeks.

At high water, about 22.15 hours, I cast off, and set sail - full mainsail and intermediate jib, for E. Mersea where I intended to spend the night. All went well, and by midnight I was drinking a cup of cocoa before turning in.

The ocean racing I have participated in this year has removed
completely two of my previous aversions - cocoa and porridge. I am
now a believer that there is nothing more welcome during the dogwatches than this combination.

E. Mersea toward Ramsgate

The next morning turned out bright and sunny, and completely windless. I got under way at 06.16, hoping to make the Spitway before high water and carry the last of the flood up the Swin, However, progress during the first half hour was barely 50 yards, and I spent a leisurely time watching the intricate and lengthy operations of getting the schooner Valeda under way. At 07.15 a breeze developed from W.S.W as as I was starting to make progress I streamed the log. 09.08 log 8.4. Wallet Spitway buoy, wind W.S.W. force 5, visibility about 3 miles - making fine progress under largest genoa and full mainsail.

I left the boat sailing herself with the tiller held by the pegboard - as used by the Leigh cockles, and cooked my second breakfast.

Had to beat up Swin, but made W.Barrow bouy at 12.35 hours, 1.5 hours after high water, but leaving plenty of ebb to clear N. Foreland.

Lay course for the Shivering Sands Towers, and prepared a picnic lunch of luncheon meat sandwiches, bananas, and a bottle of beer.

After passing the N.E. Tongue, at 14.30 hours, the wind died away. Brought the log in as progress was too slow for it to record. Dial showed 32 miles. 15.45 - Queens’ buoy about half mile ahead. Wind freshened from the South, and had to beat down from N. Foreland to Ramsgate, entered Remsgate Harbour at 17.45 hours. By 16.15 I was tied up alongside a Baltic schooner, all stowed and made Bristol fashion.

The wind had increased to Force 7, and there was a heavy swell entering the harbour. In spite of this I slept soundly through the
night - fatigued after a splendid days sailing.

Ramsgate toward Calais

I awoke early next morning, and with great difficulty prepared breakfast whilst the boat heaved and tossed on the swell coming in round the moles into the outer harbour. I chatted with the owners of the schooner whilst awaiting the right state of tide for leaving. They had bought the vessel out of service on the Baltic 'for a song', and were taking her up to Gravesend to convert into a hotel ship for use on the
Mediterranean - all 100 tons of her.

5

The wind was blowing about Force 6 W. by S. when I set sail under intermediate jib and with about 5 rolls in the mainsail. Negotiation of the harbour entrance went off successfully, with a strong flood running, and fairly heavy seas. Having cleared the Queen bouy I started beating up the Downs. The wind seemed to have increased, and offshore heavy seas were running making progress extremely hard work, so much so that the log is rather vague at this stage as to times and positions. After clearing S. Foreland, and losing its lee the seas became just ridiculous in size -- or so I thought at the time. The ship for'ard of the mast was permanently under water, and spray from water breaking up for'ard was being thrown clear. of the after pulpit. At this stage I started thinking of putting back to Ramsgate. I gave the bilge a pump and found she had made an unprecedented amount of water. I hove to and made an inspection to find the leak. Two seams up for'ward were leaking badly. Those same seams had forced ny retirement from the R.ORC. West Mersea - Ostend race, which was sailed under gale conditions. They had been re-caulked and stopped since then, and the fact that they leaking again suggested that the trouble might be serious, so I decided to put back to Ramsgate. On returning to the cockpit I saw two spent rocket cases floating near the boat. This was the last straw. The run back to Ramsgate was covered in what seemed nearly zero time. The boat was almost planing.

Off the harbour entrance I hove-to and took in the log line, and then entered harbour, Once inside I dropped the mainsail, and sailed up. the harbour about 18 inches from the wall, under foresail, until she touched. I quickly lowered the foresail, put out fenders, lines ashore, also a masthead line, and canted her into the sea wall. Because of the swell that was running she was pounding rather heavily, so I opened a seacock ard flooded the bilges while the tide went away from her.

Once the tide had dropped sufficiently for her to not pound with empty bilges I pumped them dry, and then went ashore to acquire materials for all possible repairs that might be necessary.

I had decided to batten the seams. Although this might slow the boat down a bit, at least it should keep the water out even if she worked a bit. Being Sunday, the only place open was a chandlers near the inner harbour Messrs. R. H.--------. The assistant, in name alone, was not really in full command of the situation, and offered me as battens sturdy pieces of 4" x 2" English oak! Rejecting his offer I decided to use a spare sail batten. Having fitted out with stopping, fibreglass, tacks, screws etc. I returned to the boat. There I met up with another yachtsman, holidaying in a bilge keel cruiser from the Crouch, who was bored to tears waiting for the right weather to 'get across’.

I am indebted to him for his help in carrying out the repairs. In the three hours around low water we managed to find and rectify the
trouble - so well in fact that those temporary repairs have lasted to
the end of the season with no leakage.

We celebrated with a meal and drinks ashore in the evening, when we also learnt from the Harbour Officials that they had been récording a steady Force 7 in the harbour for most of the day. Of the three boats that had left the harbour that day, two had come back, and the third was brought back by the lifeboat.
