MAMGU TROPHY PRIZE WIKNING LOG , by C.S. Molyneux

Part II

Ramsgate towards Belgium

Next morning the wind was still strong, Force 6 - 7, and from the S.W. Whilst walking along the harbour wall meditating on possibilities for the day's sailing I saw the schooner VALEDA and chatted with the owner. He had come round to Ramsgate on the same day as I had but being later had not saved his tide so there was insufficient water for him to enter harbour. He had anchored in the fiowns and came into Ramsgate on the Sunday.

I decided to sail for Belgium, using trade wind rig, and make for Zeebrugge, Blankenberg or Ostend, whichever was the nearer, on fetching the Belgian coast. For trade wind rig I carry two large genoas, each about 300 sq. ft., set either side of the boat, shackled to rings about 18 ins.

~3-

apart on the deck, and not hanked to the forestay. This leaves a gap for airflow between them thus enabling them to fill and act properly. The sheets are led aft and made fast to the tiller. The extra weight of wind in one sail as she veers off course causes the sheet to move the tiller and control the course. Normally, twin booms are used but I prefer in these waters, when on a closed run, not to boom them out. If one course that is not a dead run then the windward jib is, of course, boomed out.

Preparing for this I laid out the two genoas on deck and led their sheets through the appropriate blocks and fairleads to the tiller. I used just the intermediate jib and no mainsail for leaving harbour. This turned out to be a "touch-and-go" incident. At the harbour entrance, clearing the moles, I was close-hauled. There was a heavy sea which tended to stop her dead with each wave and there was also a strong cross tide.

Entering the gap between the moles at the up-tide end I cleared the other mole by about 3 ft. before I was in clear water. This made me re.: le never again to try and leave harbour in similar circumstances under foresail alone. I waited until I cleared the North Goodwin bouy before hoisting trade wind rig, by which time the wind had gone S& I was too far off a run to use the rig, so I had to hoist the mainsail in any case and then stow the twin genoas. The log had been streamed at the Queen bouy at 1130 hrs., reading 38.4 miles. The North Goodwin was passed at 12235 hre.; Sd log 42.6. At this stage the seas coming round South Foreland were felt and it was extremely bouncy. The log again becomes vague at this stage.

At about 1800 hrs. the wind, which had been increasing slowly but steadily, was up to about gale force. Nothing could be seen for spray and the boat was "surf-riding" each wave for as long as 30 seconds at a time before dropping down into a trough and trying to head to. Steering her on the course I'd set (100 deg.) became a physical impossibility so I scandalised the mainsail and ran before the wind until it eased off. The "surfing" was really exhilarating and would have been really enjoyable had it not been for the worry of preventing her from "broaching-to" every time she dropped down into a trough.

During the hour 1800 to 1900 the log recorded an increase of 10.4d. miles but at 1900 hrs. the line »sarted and the spinner was lost. at 200) hrs. the Wind eased off and the seas reduced in size a fact that worried me as it "smelt" of shoaling water. I trimmed the boat to sail herself on a course roughly due E. and went below to determine ny position on a with the radio direction-finder. I did not believe the first position obtained but when I repeated it to within a mile, I realised that perhaps I really was on Thornton Ridge. I plotted course for Blankenberg, prepared some food and then went back to the cockpit. Sure enough, about a mile away on the port bow was the black spar buoy that I expected to see - this confirmed my radio fix.

As I closed the Belgian coast the seas lessened and the Wind seemed to as well. At 2100 hrs., just as darkness was closing in, I sighted Blankenberg and Zeebrugge. The Admiralty Pilot gave directions for entering the harbour but I wasn't too happy about the description of the starboard mole remains - the mole having been destroyed during the war.

The entrance is very deceptive and it looks as though one would leave the one remaining to starboard in order to enter I'd learnt later that many boats are wrecked here as this mistake is regularly made. I hove to upstream of the entrance and partly fore-reached and partly drifted past the entrance at a distance of about half a cable. This gave ne a chance to examine it through the glasses, I decided the Admiralty were right, paid off and sailed in.

|

The time was just 2200 hrs. The quiet in the harbour was so weélcouc after the constant noise of wind, waves and spray. In fact the lack of noise was such that it was almost as if some ethereal body had come con and slipped a couple of plugs in my ears.

I tied up alongside the quay and was greeted by a couple of local fisherman, one of whom was English and had returned to Belgiun after the war.

In spite of being tired I found the energy to slip ashore for a bowl of "potage", French bread, a beer and a packet of "St. Michel!” before turning in.

Next morning the English fisherman returned and we talked for quite a while. He took me up to Zeebrugge in his car to try and obtain a replacement log-spinner. The price was so exhorbitant that I decided to manage without. He then took me home for a tea of fresh shrimps, home- made "confiture" and Belgian cream cheeses, I was also given lessons in
coffee-making,.

Blankenberg towards Vlessingen

I spent a very pleasant three days in Blankenberg, the weather being genuine old-fashioned holiday weather - the sun shone the whole time: I later learnt that Blankenberg is not recommended as a port to visit in the book used by many yachtsmen as a cruising bible - the Cruising Association Handbook. Their information is very much out of date in that they state that the harbour dries out and the town is expensive. In actual fact I had more than 6 ft. of water at low water and I found that living was far cheaper than Ostend. The harbour entrance should be negotiated with care end note taken of the state of the tide as there is a bar with 4 ft. 6 ins. of water over it at L.W.S.

I left Blankenberg at 1500 hrs., carrying the ebb up the coast. The wind was N.E. Force 4, visibility about 5 miles with the sun shining pleasantly through the haze. I made a long board about 4 miles out to sea, in order to carry one tack right up to the mouth of the West Schelde. Zeebrugge was abeam at 1600 hours. A gaff cutter, flying the red Ensign, could be seen ahead following a parallel course close inshore. Passed same off Knocks.

The coastline from Knocke right round to Breskens is completely desolate, the thin line of coast being broken only by the wreck of the Dutch radio ship VERONICA which was driven ashore last winter during bad weather.

On entering the Scheldé estuary big shipping was encountered. It was rather e hair-raising experience sharing a narrow channel with three or four 20,000 toppers. Vlessingen is fairly easy to enter, but yachts lock through into the inland waterways in order to moor up in the Yacht Haven. This is a tricky business single-handed with no auxiliary engine. The Yacht Club extends hospitality to all visiting craft and the charges are very reasonable.

By 1900 hrs. I was tied up Mediterranean fashion - stern to quay - alongside the AILSA, the gaff cutter mentioned earlier, which had come over from Pin Mill. The one disadvantage of Vlessingen is the distance of the Yacht Club from the town. However, the two mile walk was very much relieved by the jovial company and the Chinese meal at the end. We were rather intrigued to find that Dutch Chinese food is very different from English Chinese food.

Because of the lamentedly short duration of industrial leave I did not have the time I would have liked to cruise around Holland. Thus I spent a couple of days travelling around by train, visiting Amsterdam, Rotterdam, Der Hague, liordrecht an Middleburgh - a very quaint, typically Dutch town.

I left the Yacht Haven at 1700 hours on the Saturday evening. Winds felt light and + heir direction was a bit vague being inland. Difficulty was encountered at the locks as one of them had broken down so it was not until 1840 hours that I cleared the harbour mole. I had a soldier's wind - Force 4, N.N.I. - and the miles soon tramped by.

By 2035 hours Zeebrugge was abeam and 38 minutes later Blankenberg. Darkness was just beginning to fall and I was tempted to go into Blankenberg again to visit my friends once more, but decided to keep to my plans and continue to Ostend.

The Ostend lighthouse could be seen clearly as night drew in and soon the lights on the end of the harbour moles could be distinguised. Keeping the red light to the left of the green one I was sure of being far enough off-shore and also of clearing the near mole. By 2235 hours I was tied up to the North Sea Yacht Club pontoon along the Car Ferry Quay.

A meal ashore, a few drinks and a look at the night life, followed next morning by a visit to the yacht club and a very welcome hot shower heralded the beginning of three deys holidaymaking. No thoughts of hard work and sailing but just occasional consideration of the state of the tide to make sure this did not interrupt one's sun-bathing on the beach.

This could not last indefinitely, of course, and on the Wednesday I had to leave on the next leg of the cruise.

Ostend towards Dunkerque

Moored close to and alongside me was a group of seven Dutch yachts, of varying size but all larger than SAMUEL PEPYS and the oldest not two years old. These boats were all moving on to Dunkerque at the same time as me so we decided to make a race of it.

We : in the harbour started at 0915 hours and just as we were about to leave the bea ‘in the light, warning of shipping movement in the moles, & started flashing Realising that this leaves a certain amount of leeway to enable people to get clear I pressed on. I was, in fact, well clear of the moles and *. heading for the Ostend Banks buoy when the packet entered. The other seven boats, who had gone about in the harbour to wait for the entrance to clear, were held up for about ten minutes and this gave ne a a good head start.

At 1100 hours I cleared the Ostend Bank buoy and lay a course of 490 deg. inal by S. wind of no more than Force 2.

For close hauled working single-handed I normally carry the inter- mediate jib, as the short foot facilitates going about but a larger foresail tends [co back the luff of the mainsail and in my opinion gives no greater spec’: -
Astern I could see the other vessels in the t..ce, most of them carryir; large genoas. The wind was gradually increasin; all the time and I was ‘making excellent progress. ,

Before ma. ‘ing a single-handed passage I always swot up beforehand
on the chart, = - I know from memory at any time where there is Water or
where to go to “and it and where long boards over sandbanks, if “he tide is right, can i. made. At this time this practice proved invaiu:ble, as at 1220 hours + ie starboard running backstay parted. Knowing I had plenty of water I went about and made a board out to sea while carrying out temporary repa: Se

The channel from Nieuport to Dunkerque as buoyed is extremely narrow, necessi:ating very short tac’-s if one stays within the buoys. With the right state of the tide however, one can use the flats on either side and this I did. The competition from astern had reduced considerably
- all but two beats had retired and were motoring. One of the tivo
remaining still carried a large genoa but appeared to be making more leeway than head.way and had great difficulty going about with it despite the crew of six or seven people.

I entered Dunkerque harbour at 1530 hours, the second bat in (a large ketch rigj;ed boat, which had retired and motored in, had passed me). The next «wo boats in were those still under sail. They were closely followe«. by the other four motoring. We all went up the long creek to the yacht club in convoy. They were all motoring at this stage and I thought it was rather mean of them in that not one offered me a tow, although they all knew I carried no auxiliary. We were all in for a nasty shock a+ the yacht club when they came to collect the mooring fees. Iwas asked for £1 to stay overnight ami nearly put straight to sea again. However, I decided to shrink the boat a bit and, blaming my bad French, got away with twelve shillings.

SNIPE! SNIPE: SNIPE:

"FOR ANYONE WHC IS INTERESTED IN INTENNATIONAL 2-MAN RACING, THE SNIPE
IS EASILY THE BEST CLASS TO OBTAIN TOP COMPETION'

These are the words of Paul Elvstrom, the greatest Dinghy Sailor ever (4 Olympic Gold Medals and 6 World Championships).

When considering the purchase of a Snipe Sailing dinghy (as every perceptive and intelligent dinghy sailor will surely do at some time or other), the following questions will probably be asked.

1. What type of boat is the Snipe?

The Snipe is the largest one-design class with world-wide distribu- tion. Snipe racing is particularly active in Europe, North America and South America.

The Snipe is a sleek yet soundly constructed boat with a L.0.A. of 15ft. 7 in. and a beam of 5ft. It has an eMficient Bermuda rig of 110 sq. ft. The jib is large, giving the crew added importance. ‘Modern Snipes are constructed in 3" marine ply or fibreglass, have rolled decks and many have a self draining cockpit.

The Snipe is not a flimsy boat having the nautical lines of a flat dish designed to slam across the Water when the conditions of wind and waves are suitable, but a real little yacht with a high performance.

The Snipe has neither a clumsy sliding seat or awkward trapeze to pamper to unfit stomach muscles but is a fast stable boat which calls for fitness to sail at top speed and yet is undemanding physically when Sailing for pleasure.

The Snipe has a high boom which eliminates diving face down in the bilge to avoid decapitation by to boom on going about or gybing.

The Snipe has an adjustable wire or nylon horse which carries a freely sliding pulley which elininates easing the mainsheet when going
about.

The Snipe is strictly a one-design class which makes it stand out way and above many other so-called one-design classes where minor changes, turning, sails, etc., contribute so significantly to disparities in boat speed, all of which tends to minimise racing skill and tactics.

Ze How does the Snipe perform under various conditions of wind, sea and point of sailing?

The Snipe has a fair turn of speed ani with e Portsmouth number of 97 is rated faster than the Ynterprise. The performance t0 windward is
particularly satisfying; being comparable to almost all other dinghy and better than most.

The Snipe, with its good stability performs well under all condi- tions of sea. It is particularly free from yawing motion in rough water.

Due to the high boom and adjustable rope horse, the downhaul is easily adjusted (even while racing) to give optimm sail shape to suit the weight of crew and wind strength.

A spectacular demonstration of the performance of the Snipe in adverse conditions occured when 2 Cubans escaped from Havana to the U.S.A. by sailing a Snipe across the treachorous 100 mile stretch of water
between Cuba and Floride in winds of 20 - 25 knots! The trip was
accomplished in 16 hours. This feat amazed yachting experts in Florida Who are well acquainted with the rough, turbulent waters and strong currents of the Gulf Stream. Many a 30-footer has struggled to get across the same dangerous course in 30 hours.

36 How much does a Snipe cost, new or second hand?

A new fibreglass Snipe complete with Terylene sails, aluminium mast and boon would cost approx. £230.

4. good second-hand boat would probably cost between £100 and £150
complete with boat cover and launching trolley or road trailer.: (sec % Boats for Sale). ng

Le Will the Snipe hold its value?

There are two main factors which affect the value of a sailing dinghy, apart from the soundness of construction of the boat: firstly, the activity and rate of expansion within the class and secondly, the strictness with which the one-design principle is adhered to.

These points can be answered together. The Snipe Class association (S.C.I.R.A.) is a very active international organisation which publishes a monthly bulletin to keep Snipe sailors abreast of events throughout the world. strictly enforees the one-design principle to protect the class and ensure that older boats may compete on equal terms with new boats. The qualities of the Snipe and remarkable class o. ganisation is
responsible for the explosive growth of the class - currently an average
increase of 2 boats per day with the sail numbers now over the 16,000
mark.

5. Is the Snipe suitable for the Blackwater estuary and in particular, Sad
the Marconi Sailing Club?

As you probably know, the club is introducing Snipe racing within the Handicap Class this season and if the numbers are sufficient there will be separate Bmipe races. Currently, 5 members own Snipes, two of which Will certainly be actively racing and several other members have shown interest in purchasing a Snipe.

There are many open meetings each year on the Blackwater which include Snipe class racing (8 this year) and with 4 active Snipe fleets on the river there is no lack of competition. Also, the South-East Snipe Championships will be held at Stansgate for the second year running.

Details of these events and other national and international events will be posted on the Club notice board and published in next month's issue of Navigans.

A GUIDE FOR. RACE OFFICERS

le The Race Officer and his assistant are responsible for ensuring that the racing arrangements are properly carried out. They should be ready to consult the 0.0.D. ora Sailing Committee member when necessary. They should be familiar with the R.Y.A. racing rules and the Club sailing
instructions.

The Race Officer should be present one hour before the start of the race,

The jobs to be done before the start of the race can conveniently be shared as follows:—

RACE OFFICER,

1, Choose course, in consultation with the 0.0.D. or a Sailing committee member,

2. Mark up the sailing board accordingly, ensuring that
there are sufficient entry sheets and sailing instructions. Spares are in the Race Officer's
box-file,

3. Establish radio link with the rescue launch, and
instruct them as to laying special marks etc,

4. Arrange collection of entry sheets 10 mins before
the start.

5. Collect visitor's entry fees.

N.B, Ghoose the course in regard to wind strength, tide etc., and display the course letter, number of rounds and"direction of start" arrow, if possible, half an hour before the start of the race, or at least before the 10 minute signal, otherwise the start must be postponed as provided in the R.Y.A. Rules, If there is a large entry, or at low water, the lengthened starting line may have to be used, in which case the letter 'L! must be displayed after the course boards, Courses above Mundon Point may not be usable at low water,

ASSISTANT RACE OFFICER (Time Keeping).

1. Start the clock (as near as possible B.B.C. time),

2. Prepare the flags and sound signals (cannon for open
races, hooter for closed),

3. Display the course sign at the race box.

Signals.

The normal racing signals are explained in the R.Y.A. Racing Rules 4-8, The Club use class flags, not shapes (See Rule 4.4. (A) (1), and varies Rule 8 as provided in the Sailing Instructions, Wen several races are starting at intervals of 5 or 10 minutes the start signal for one race will be the 5 or 10 minutes signal for the succeeding race,

Starting the Races,

From the 10 minute signal, until the last class has started, the R.O. should station himself on the line, and watch for any breach of sailing rules. He will make the sound signals at the times indicated by the timekeeper, Both guns should

be loaded ready for a recall or a misfire. He will have radio link with the launch which may, if the entry is large, be stationed at the opposite end of the line to help spot false starters. The timekeeper will break out and lower the flags in the correct sequence, and in order to synchronise the start, the sound signals and flags, he should count dow the last minute before each signal, e.g. "one minute to Enterprise start
and Fleetwind warning......30 seconds....e..15 seconds.....10 seconds to

NOW",

6 Recalls.

If any identified boats are over the line at the start, the R.O.should shout "RECALL" and sound the other gun. The timekeepeyShould put the class flag at the dip. Competitors over the line are themselves responsible for coming back and starting to the satisfaction of the R.0., but the R.O. should use the loud hailer to attract the attention of boats that have started too soon. When premature starters have recrossed the line and started properly, their class flag is lowered, Those who do not do so shall be disqualified, and should be informed of this as soon as they come in after the race. It. despite the recall: signal some boats continue to sail the course, it is enough for the R.O. to keep their class flag flying for three minutes, at the dip after which it can be lowered.

Should there by a number of unidentified premature starters or an error in starting procedure, the R.O. should make a general recall and the lst substitute flag should be hoisted. The R.O. will reload the first cannon and sound two guns, The first- substitute should be flow for three minutes, after which it should be lowered. The class flag should be left flying if the false start is to be the ten minutes warning signal for the resrtarted

PRIZE WINNING LOG

Part IV a

Dunkerque towards Calais

Next morning a bright and early breakfast ready for an early start back to civilisation. I cast off at 09.40 hours under reefed main and intermediate jib and cleared the har»our at 09.55 hours. The wind was still W by S and blowing about Force 6, visibility 3 or 4 miles. I was making good progress and passed the Dunkirk D. C. buoy at 12.00 hours.

The Dutch boats had left after me and I could see them astern, all motoring, one carrying storm canvas and all making heavy weather, pitching
violently.

Approaching Calais T am always wary of the bar which runs down to Cap Blanc Wez and only cross it just before high water. It not being high water I kept well out to sea down to Cap Blanc Nez and then came up the coast inside the sandban .

I anchored in Calais harbour at 16.15 hours. The Dutchmen were already in, having gone straight across the bar using their echo-sounders.

In the inner harbour I saw the TANCOSCA with some friends of mine
aboard,
so we spent the eveing ashore sampling the night-life. “lost of the frgdends 1 had made there the previous years had gone back to Paris so the evening was relatively quiet. JI turned in early as I was feeling rather knocked up. I could feel a dose of 'flu or something coming on, so I decided that if I was going to be ill it may as well be in England and Would sail home the next day, Friday.

Calais towards Brightlingsea

Next morning 7 was up and about by 07.00 hours as I wanted to do some shopping before leaving. Apart from bread and crassants I could not
buy anything - French shops just don't open that early.

I sailed eat 09.00 hours under full mainsail and large genoa, with a wind by S Force 6 to 7 and visibility less than 1 wile.

From the harbour I steered 290 deg. to cross the bar (being nearly
high water), which I cleared by 09.25 hours, then lay 335 deg. for the
Bast Goodwin light vessel.

On a broad reach with this amount of canvas and wind the boat was almost planing. I passed the Bast Goodwin at 11.55 hours and the North Goodwin at 13.00 hours. Clear of the Goodwinds I hove to and changed down
4
foresail to intermediate jib..

At 14.30 hours, past the N.E. Spit buoy, I hove to again ami took in three rolls in the mainsail as the going was getting just'a bit too heavy. This, of course, was.a signal for the wind to stop, which it did completely and I was left wallowing in heavy seas.

For the next 13 hours there was no consistent wind, just occasional vague breezes from various vague directions. At 16.00 hours a really strong wind came up from the I reckoned at the tine that it was nearly gale force and 1 later learned that during the afternoon and even- ing they were recording a steady Force 7 in Brightlingsea harbour. This Wind continued with me right into Brightlingsea. The log becomes very vague again, in fact the only entry being a scrawled "very hard going".

ily course was through the S. sdinburgh Channel, across Knock John and down the Barrow Deep. I had extreme difficulty with navigation at
this stage - buoys were not where they should be. I found out later,
that whilst I was away, the sdinburgh Channels, Barrow and Spitway had all been re-buoyed.

I was feeling quite ill at this stage, being tired and with a ‘flu fever coming on. I was also very sore and bruised from being knocked
about.

In the Barrow, on a dead run, I accidentally gybed all standing and the port runner parted. I didn't feel up to replacing it there and then and it was all I could do to belay the ends to prevent flogging Hoping that the standing backstay would hold the mast up.

After clearing the N.E. end of the Barrow Sands + could see no sign of the Spitway buoys. The black W. Cunfleet buoy was 2 miles N.E. of me. As I couldn't face et this stage a thrash to windward to look for the Spitway buoys, being just on high water / laid course for Clacton and crossed the Gunfleet Sands.

I had plenty of water across at this point and was pleased to reach the smoother waters of the Yallet. The beat to windward up the Wallet.against the tide was relatively easy compared with the previous four hours.

I anchored in Brightlingsea, in the dark, at 22.15 hours, absolutely fatigued. It took ie over an hour to straighten out on deci, I then cooked a meal and fell asleep without eating it.

Last Leg

I had hoisted the Q-flag before turning in so the Customs would see it in daylight and come and clear me. They woke me at 05.30 hours; I was still fully clothed from where I had fallen asleep the night
before - ny dinner still there, cold and untouched.

My only comment about the next hour is that only a Customs Officer can fall out of bed at 5.30 in the morning and start drinking neat run!

I weighed anchor at 07.00 hours and by 08.00 hours I was safely
tied up in my berth at Wivenhoe’, happy after an excellent, if tiring, holiday and feeling extremely pleased with my little ship.

Other reasons for the disqualifications were not returning i far enough after being over the line at the start and not declaring (signing out) after each race.

John Barnard as Beach Officer organised the car and dinghy parking, the visitors being in a field loaned by Hr. Sparrow.

Actually in the Clubhouse a number of people helped in the awkward task of setting helmsuen to sign in and out and in preparing results sheets. Jack Bigden was in charge of the prizes.

There were breakages and capsizes of course but the majority of boats finished in one piece and the final race. result determined the over- all placing in several classes.

A lot of hard work was required apart from the basic sailing organi- sation. The dinghy park had to be tidied up and the grass cut to make room for the extra boats and cars. iiuch gravel was moved from the hard to the muddier parts of the dinghy and car park. The Clubhouse was cleaned daily.

The resave boats were maintained and manned. The galley and bar staffs were overworked,
BUT IT WAS A GRAND WEEKEND?

C E.C.W.

GOSSIP COLUMN

Over the past few weeks the Clubhouse and its surrounds have become noticeably tidier thanks to the efforts of Mr. Underdown, our new Steward. Let's help him. keep it that way.

We were pleased to see some old friends back for the Fleetwind Team Championships (which Marconi's won) end for the Designers Trophy. With Alan and Coleen Pratt was Andrew, aged three months. Another old ‘un back with us is Stan Adamson now crewing the Partridge Enterprise. Amongst the Cruisers we've seen a lot more of Geoff Wardell and his wife and family this year.

If a certain Dragon owner had a dinghy he and his good lady wouldn't risk being stranded on his mooring.

“we

Well done’ the’ cruisers “who actually sailed & Spoon race but ie is rungured that Mike Sisson arid Derek Welsford had soue ‘trouble finding the right pe

The G.P.14's have been to Maldon, the !nterprises to Southend, the Hornets to Stone and all three plus a Fleetwind to the Blackwater and Colne Dinghy Championships at Stone. Simon Darney was 4th in the Cock of the River race after winning the Fleetwind class.

At the "Roman Scandal" held at Stone t::e same weekend John Hutchings
very successfully changed sex - it wasn't until he referred to "my girl frien
that one Marconi member realised he wasn't a girl! George Nicholson as a gladiator with "conker" and net was another prizewinner,.

EDITORIAL

Spent an interesting Saturday at Stone recently where the E.S.5.A.
Regatta was held. It's nice to see so many enthusiastic kids taking to the water and being actively encouraged by their respective schools and the L.E, A. I believe there were 54 boats in “the last race and you should have heard the galls for water! According to the local paper, though, there seems to have been sone doubt about the results. Still it was a good day and there's a nice bar at Stone.

Not much to say about the Club but the grass seems to be groWing well on some of the dinghy park spaces. must be a good year?
So long!

Jack Reeve

CADET WEEK

It has been decided by the Main Committee, with the approval of Mr.
Sparrow, to run a camp under canvas for the Cadets during the Cadet week at Stansgate, i.e. from 10 a.m. Monday 8th August until 6 p.m. Friday 12th ‘wy
August.

There will be, in fact, two separate camps, one for the girls and another for the lads. These: will be at‘all tines under the charge of a member of the Main Committee.

The whole camp will be run on Navy lines, the Cadets being divided into messes of eight to ten youngsters. These messes will be self-catering but will be able to draw bulk cooked basic food from a central: galley staffed by mums. Any trimmings Will be sorted out among the members of the individual
MESSES«

An Executive, consisting of Senior Cadets and junior members of the Club, is being formed to run the show and the intention is to provide an active "adventure" type of experience for boys and girls between the ages of
11 and 18, based on sailing.

The Main Committee has voted a sum of money to help things aLOng and this Will be largely devoted to rewards to encourage self-reliance.

A charge of 30/~- per head will be made to cover the cost of the basic food supplied.

At present plans are a little vague and any suggestions or ideas will be welcome. We would also be grateful fbr the loan of Calor gas equipment, to cook the bulk food, if any is available.

Tom Gaskell
Cadet Officer

VISITING THE PIRATES by Fred Partlett

PART I

At 0910 hours on Thursday 7th July my son Mick and myself set off downriver in our Wayfarer sailing dinghy "Sobraon" for a short cruise, short because tie had to be back on the Saturday. We took the boat cover to sleep under, two air beds, sleeping beg, blankets, a change of clothing, fres water food, Primus stove, a coastal chart and radio. The latter was intended for weather forecasts but it spent most of its time churning out the "pops".

A light and variable westerly wind was blowing and the sky overcast as we headed towards Bradwell. There were two other craft, cruisers, under way, one rounded St. Peters Flats and the other headed up the Colne. —

We made for the wreck buoy on ‘the Cocum Hills and from there kept a straight course towards no.
2 buoy at the entrance to the Colne. I estimated our speed as 5 knots. Soon after leaving Colne Point behind Mick went ashore for supplies (chocolate) before proceeding along the coast about half mile
offshore.

We-had caught the last of the ebb tide out of the Blackwater am the tidal stream chart showed slack water close inshore at all states of the tide. It was a pleasant run with little to do except avoid sailing by the lee in the varying Wind. At1250 hours we rounded Clacton Pier and our estimated speed from no. 2 buoy was about 34 knots.

At 1400 hours, with Frinton ahead, we could make out the radio ships on the horizon and Wwe made toward them. The wind, although still light seemed more variable than ever, and with our burgee swinging through 180 deg. we were caught with two accidental gybes. Deciding that discretion was the better part of valour we returned nearer the shore and continued toward Frinton.

4500 hours with walton Pier abeam and allowing for the dog-leg seawards, I estimated our speed since Clacton Pier as 24 knots. In spite of giving what I considered to be generous clearance the fishermen on Walton Pier greeted our passing with shouts of "Get the **** out of it" and "Clear off, you Our reply was much shorter and more to the point. Relating this incident since to a regular pier fisherman he informed me that he would expect all boats to keep at least mile away.

We scanned the beaches beyond the pier for possible landing places.
Only two spots seemed obviously to be uncovered at high tide am we selected one for our attempt at a “soft landing". The beach was rather steep and the waves were breaking, apparently quite fiercely, on the sand. I realised that our stern might be swamped as we went in but we would be into wind the risk appeared to be small. Some water did come over as I took the mainsail down. Mick, of course, was holdings the bow and holidaymakers came forward to pukl us clear of the surf and up to high vater mark. The time was 1515 hours and high tide was at 150 hours.

One of our helpers introduced himself as Brian and offered to put a kettle on, in fact his wife made us a cup of tea which we downed after bailing the boat and stowing the sails.

It was our original intention to sail further up the. coast and after a council of war, more war than council, “Mick and I agreed to stay overnight. ve would float "Sabraon" off on-the early morning tide and after finishing our sleep, head further up the coast.

In preparation for this we eased the boat farther down the beach. After a meal of cold chicken, potatoes and peas we walked up to the cliffs above the Naze before turning in. The sound of maroons going off and the sight of flares fired from the Coastguard Station indicated that the lifeboat was being called out. In the half Light we could see a cruiser flashing SOS. The sea was.calm and the boat was anchored so we assumed engine failure to be the cause. The lifeboat put out after about 15 minutes and the. cruiser was :towed to Harwich,

We returned to the beach and having already put the boom up and the cover on we inflated our air beds and.got down for the night. Mick slept soundiy but I cat-napped in case We missed the tide and at 0330 hours Friday morning we were outside in swimming trunks ready to launch omemore. Dawn was just breaking but it was still dark on the beach and the waves as they broke on the shore seemed enormous. ‘e were, I think, both relieved when we. realised that the tide ha: turnedwell short and we were not going for an wy early morning dip. We lost no time getting back to bed and finishing our
sleep.

SAILING NOTES

Attached to this copy of. "Navigans" will be found a list of members boats giving their allocated dinghy park spare or mooring. If you have a boat at Stansgate (or want. to bring one) which is not included on the list please get in touch With me as soon as possible.

Also attached is a summary sheet for the points series races which have taken place so far this year. As you will see only three classes have raced this year, namely Enterprise, Hornets and G. P.'s. ‘Races are also scheduled for Fleetwinds, Snipes, Cadets and Torches and Mirrors as well ow Handicap points races which are open to all classes with the exception of
| Enterprises, Hornets and G.P.'s. There are also Spoon and Scratch races for
dinghies and cruisers which are mainly for enjoyment and as a good introduc— tion to racing.

There seems to be a feeling that racing is all cut and thrust sailing but this: is iia’? far from true. Racing in a small way is an excellent method of improving one's ability to handle a boat. Only by using the yardstick of someone else sailing under the same conditions will you find out. why your boat does not go as well as an identical one. Nine times out of ten it will turn out not to be the boat but the person at the "blunt end" who is at fault.

The very full and detailed programme produced this year was the result of a lot of very hard work by your Sailing Comsittee in an endeavour to give ample. opportunity for all-types of competitive and informative sailing. This was based on a belief that this was what the Club wanted.

So far the Committee are very disappointed with the results of their endavours as there have been more races cancelled through lack of support than have actually taken place. It is therefore probable that unless more enthusiasm is shown for these events between now and the end of the season very few extra races will be scheduled for next year.

Possibly it is not realised that for each extra race a Race Officer and rescue launch facilities have to be provided. Therefore it is unfair to ask people to make a special journey to Stansgate to undertake these duties and then find their services unwanted.

To most of you this will read like a good old moan, which it is, but if these activities are not wanted there is not point in arranging then. It appears that the majority of the Club do not want these events, even though there are more boats in the dinghy perk than ever before.

Memo To: All Members of the Marconi Sailing Club.
1st August, 1966.
From: The Officers & Committee of the marconi Sailing Club.

Subject:- Club Discipline.

At the General Meeting of the executive Committee held this evening opinions were voiced from all quarters in relation to the general lack of discipline, disregard of Bye-laws, instructions and carelessness in relation to Club property exercised by Members throughout the Club.

Although in the majority of cases the Committee are sure that such careless disregard and indiscipline is unintentional there are cases of blatant wrong-doing and disregard.

Members are reminded that the Club exists‘for their pleasure and enjoy- ment providing they comply with the rules made on their behalf by the Committee who in turn are the servants of the Club freely elected ina
democratic manner. We also owe allegiance to our parent body - The hiarconi
Athletic & Social Club and to the rules and conditions applicable to some. Other interests from whom we must accept conditions are the l.aldon Borough Council and the Essex Rivers Board, but possibly the most important of all is the obedience we must give to the conditions laid down by our Landlord which have been freely accepted by the Club in relation to the use of and access to our Club Site. These conditions must be upheld as abuse by any member could endanger out existence as a Club at Stansgate.

It was also felt that your Officers and Conmmittec had of recent months become lax to some degree in upholding and imposing the conditions of Club Rules and Bye-laws and it was decided that if this were so such laxity would cease forthwith. It was agreed that all future offenders would be warned and corrected and should misbehaviour continue they would be disciplined in accordance with the rules of both the lharconi Sailing Club and the Marconi Athletic & Social Club. The Duty Officers log shall be used to record all incidents of misbehaviour or other offences against the Club and will be inspected at each General Meeting of the Sailing Club when the Club Secretary will be instructed to take the action decided upon arising from the reported incident.

Among the more commonly broken regulations which will be watched in future are the following.

a) All guest's names to be entered in the visitors book. One member
may only introduce two guests at any one time, the same guests may only be introduced a reasonable number of times per year and must always be accompanied by the member.

b) Many non-members are habitually using the Club site and will be
turned away. Members are strongly advised to carry membership cards when visiting Stansgate to avoid embarrassment.

c) The use to which Club boats, launching trollies and trailers
are put.

a) The use by unauthorised persons of the record player and radio gear.

e) The use of No. 1 rescue launch and gear from Rescue locker by:
urn:uthorised persons is forbidden.

f) It is not permitted to climb the seawall or to reach the beach by
climbing through fence (this is a River Board regulation to combat
erosion).

of 30 minutes on some years). it was obvious “Jithin a few minutes that all was not well. The number of people present exceeded the number of suppers that had been prepared and several people did not partake of the prescribed menu.

John Barnard has a good voice for an M.C and after a toast to the Queen and permission to smoke, he bade Terry Hallam introduce and toast the guests. ilir.F.N.Sutherland , Chairman of the marconi Group of Companies and President of the M.A.S.C. ANNUAL GENERAL MEETING HELD AT THE M.A.S.C.
ON 22nd NOVEMBER 19.30. HRS,
Commodore's Report 1966
Ladies and Gentlemen,
This year has been a full one, if a little disappointing in some ways. I had hoped to be able to report to you at this A.G.M. that a longer term lease had been secured. This has not been possible however, Due to events - over which we as a Club have no control, e.g. the financial climate, leading — as it has to restrictions in private capital works, the marina scheme, to which our future is in many ways tied, had not gone as far as we had hoped. We have indeed continued our cordial relationships with our landlord, Mr.Sparrow, the result of which has been an extension until the end of next year and it is to be hoped that before our lease runs out the situation will be such that we shall be successful in negotiating for a longer term.

On the Social Side we have been partially successful in spite of the quite strenuous efforts on the part of the Social Secretary, Our highlight was undoubtedly the Barbecue, although in spite of the enormous crowd attending we still did not make such a large profit. The same applied to the other social events, good attendance but financially only just about breaking even.

On this subject of Social events I would at this time point out that the Social Secretary and his small band of helpers received little support when it came to the work and they are to be congratulated for the success they did achieve.

As far as the Sailing is concerned perhaps the most noticeable feature was the lack of interest of the Cadets. I cannot stress too highly the importance of a good strong and enthusiastic Cadet section and I trust that next year we shall see a change in attitude and performance, The rest of the sailing was patchy. We had some first class open events; the Whitsun Regatta was undoubtedly a success, but Club support for racing in spite of the removal of entry fees,is still rather poor. The high spot was probably the enthusiasm of our new class, the Hornets.

The cruisers look as though they might be coalescing into a class, and we hope that next season will see some enthusiastic cruiser racing,

On the clubhouse Side you will all have noticed a change in the condition of the Club this year. The employment of a Steward/Handyman although beset by problems at first, has proved to be a first class thing. Mr.Underdown is without doubt a most valuable acquisition. Members I am sure, are not aware of the amount of real hard work he does, at times when the ordinary member is not around to see, For example, he was at the Club at three o'clock in the morning last week when a gale was blowing to make sure all was well. This is not an isolated case either.

Still on the theme of buildings, we have been fortunate to obtain from the English Electric Valve Company, at a very reasonable charge, a building which is destined to be our new Clubhouse when the lease situation is clearer, For this I would like to express all our thanks to the Valve Company.

At the present time a smaller structure, also obtained from the English Electric Company is in processs of being erected at Stansgate for a boat shelter, I am sure that Jack Bigden, Jack Bates, and all the others of that small but willing band of helpers would be only too grateful for your assistance at the working parties each Sunday for the next few weeks.

Another acquisition, so recent as not to be collected yet, is another larger rescue launch, some twenty feet long.

It is intended that a crew's shelter be erected on this during the winter so that the rescuers next year will be in rather more comfort under

heavy wind and raid conditions.

Those ladies and gentlemen, are the hichlights of last season.
I now come to a more personal matter. Tonight I am retiring from the “o1t as Commodore.

As some of the older members know I have had the honour of being your first Commodore, and in the fifteen years or so of the Club's existence I have been in that office some nine or ten times and only for one year have I been out of any office. Fourteen almost continuous years filled with events, always with the Club going forward, During that time the Club has grown from a handful of enthusiasts to over 500 men and women. This, ladies and gentlemen is an enormous achievement, one of which w2 should all be proud.

Although I have been privileged to lead the Club for so much of its life it is to the officers and committees that we must address our thanks. But for the support given, and the personal time and money spent, by them, and that of many other ordinary members of the Club we would not be in the very enviable position we are in today, So may I on behalf of you all offer to 211 who have helped my very sincere thanks.

Tony Hallam,

VISITING THE PIRATES

On July 7th, Fred Partlett with his son Mick, sailed from Stansgate in their Wayfarer dinghy "SOBRAON" to Frinton.

We left them asleep in their boat which they had pulled up
the beach above the high water mark...ccovcsee

Friday morning was still overcast with a fresh wind. Brian
and his family came down to the beach surprised that we wore still high and dry, After breakfast of sausage, bacon and egg we discussed the Situation and Brian thought he could persuade fellow holidaymakers to assist in putting Sobraon into the water, In fact nobody needed persuading, there was a rush of willing helpers, of all ages. We used the warp from our spare anchor (borrowed from Mike Sissons! "Valkyrie") and slung this under the boat abeam the mast and with two lifting at this point, two on the handles and four or five either side aft Sobraon (350 lbs) was lifted bodily and taken in three stages down the beach and into the water which by now was just past low tide. liick and I thought there was little to be gained going further up the coast at this late hour (11.00 hrs) so after giving Brian a sail up to The Naze and back we set course for Radio London.

The wind was still variable, force 1-2 and we had an uneventful sail coming up to Radio London slightly upstream. We ran against the tide in order to round her, a supply ship had just gone alongside flying the Netherlands flag. Mick recognised one disc jockcy who had visited Danbury, and after taking some photographs we headed south west to "Caroline", Rounding Caroline we headed back to ‘walton arriving there about 30 mins before high water, Remembering our previous landing and swamping over the stern I released the tiller pin and rudder strap before we beached and as Mick went over the foredeck to fend off I had the tiller and rudder in on board quicker than it takes to write about it, the mainsail down, then over the side to swing the boat round putting her bows to the breakers, No water came over into the boat and a few pulls put us high and dry once more. The round trip had taken approximately 5 hours. ‘Once again our landing was followed by a cup of tea made by Brian's wife who had watched us sail in. Brian enthused by his morning trip had Sone to the boating lake to have a go on his own, We did not fancy shopping for food so dinner consisted of sausages, potatoes, peas and runner beans (ex tin). After washing up and preparing our "tent" we caught a bus into Clacton and spent the rest of the evening at the cinema, arriving back at Walton soon after
2300 hours.

Not intending to catch the early tide we slept soundly and awoke at 07.00 hours when a few people made their early morning excursions to the beach, After breakfast we prepared for the homeward trip. Mick packed some biscuits and cheese and orange squash for having whilst under way and soon after 10.00 hours we had the boat in the water once again with the assistance of holidaymakers.

10.20 hrs set course round WaIton Pier’ (no fishermen), the wind appeared to be straight up the coast (westerly) and very light, the sun was breaking through and we seemed all set for a gentle sail home. TI had checked the weather forecast with the coastguard station, wind force westerly barometer rising.’ As we tacked: down the coast the waves became more pronounced and there was a gentle swell. ‘The wind was increasing and it needed constant attention to ease the boat over the waves. She responded well and at no time did we feel under undue stress. On one occasion we were brought up short and twice we took it green over the foredeck, one of these skimmed the foot of our jib which is set high on Sobraon. From around Frinton we could see the barge race in progress off the Blackwater, just dim shapes on the horizon but there was no doubt about their identity. Around 13.30 hours we were in calmer waters and took the opportunity to refresh ourselves, it was not long before the sailing, once again

* 8 =

needed our undivided attention. The kicking strap came undone at the mast fittings and at a suitable moment we luffed up whilst Mick made a running repair and pulled it down hand.

As we wanted to see something of the barge race we held our course further off shore than on the outward run, and by the time Colne Pt. was abeam to Starboard we were heading across the estuary towards a Sloop anchored between the Bench Hd bouy and Sales Pt, whom we assumed to be an official boat concerned with the race, We joined the cavalcade ahead of the last barge and during the beat up to Stansgate managed to pass four more, At 16.20 hours we beached at Stansgate, 6 hours after leaving Walton and with three enjoyable days of dinghy cruising behind us.

After two days rest we set off again, this time to sail round to Burnham—-on-—Crouch, but that is another story.

Fred Partlett.

This month's log is tke Mamgu Trophy Prizewinners log of a trip to
France
by Geoffrey Bond, Derek. and Eric, sailing Geoffrey's 'Vivacity'.

Beginner's Luck

Sailing a dinghy for a few seasons I developed a yearning for the open sea, especially after sailing with tide and wind to Clacton and Colne Point, and having to beat home again.

It was then my thoughts turned to cruisers, and having purchased a secondhand Vivacity, in October, I launched her when everybody else was laying up for the winter. I registered at night school for a course in navigation, and learnt but only the rudiments, as the course proved abortive owing to lack of support.

Came June -— and we were ready to spend a week away from Stansgate; but a week before departure the rudder broke -— it had been made of plywood and
painted white - we had to beach her at Stone, whilst a new one was quickly
made by Charfleet marine carpenters. We then found we could not match the transom fittings, and it was only on the eve of our holiday that we fitted new gudgeon and pintle to "Calypso's" stern.

However - Friday June 10th arrived, and complete with new Crescent©
outboard engine, and a company of wives, children and well wishers, we drove to Stansgate, —

Imagine our embarrasswent however when we arrived 5 minutes too late to prevent the boat from going aground! We all three pushed and dug but without success, therefore took out time in completing the stowage and éxperiencing our first nigit afloat on safe moorings.

We remained up until fidnight for the weather forecast, but as the time passed realised we had tuned into the wrong station! It ‘turnedout fortunate that we hadn't sailed, for there was a severe storm at 03.00 hrs.

Saturday June llth We floa! at again at 04.00 hrs. Derek made a light
breakfast at 04.30 hrs and there being no wind, we started the outboard engines on fitting the, rudder however, we fouled the prepeytee and, this made a short delay whilst a new shearpin was fitted. ain inatenaiaie

We motored to Bradwell power station at high water, and off St.Peter' 8
point steered 104° passing Bench Head buoy at.07.30 hrs. A course of 115°
took us to the Knowle buoy, then 156° to the Wallet spit. We passed Buxey sands at 08.30 hrs the weather remaining clear and sunny. but Wwindless.
At 08.45 hrs we changed course at No.l.w Swin to 9 Barrow and. picked |
up the S.idinburgh channel. :

The tide was then against us and we took a considerable time to keep east of ‘and beyond Margate sands; nevertheless the wind was now blowing blusteringly and the sky became overcast, the rain descended and continued whilst we passed North Foreland and into Ramsgate harbour at 20.30 hrs. We tied up in the outer harbour and made for the nearest fish and chip shop! and we were in our bunks at 23.00 hrs.

Sunday June 12th We went ashore again to find petrol‘ and waited until
a garage opened at 09.15 hys; we did-not leave Ramsgate until 09.45 hrs.

The weather was again windless but foggy, visibility being less than© Ir mile, we made a bearing for the Quern buoy and altered course down the Goodwin channel via the Brake buoy. We saw several small fishing vessels in the channel and two large vessels were noticeable more by their.foghorn than their appearance! One motor cruiser came over to us in his Pog to ask if we were alright as we had no sail up at the time.

We did not see the S.Goodwin light vessel but by its foghorn, could determine our position. At this time Eric collected an exhausted pigeon which he regarded as his special pet and fed it whilst it was with us until we reached land, he nicknamed it 'Sammy going South'.

-3-

We made a bearing of 158° towards Cape Criz Nez, and then sailed off shore to Boulogne, we arrived off Boulogne harbour at 20.00 hrs but had to lay off for + hr whilst a large ship was towed into the southern harbour. We were then given the green light by the traffic light on the pier and we sailed passed the interested French onlookers, including six nuns, who gave us a friendly wave. We passed the car ferry bays and, on instruction from the harbour official, tied up alongside a fishing smack in the Port de Narée, Sammy our pigeon then flew away towards other pigeons, whilst we were left to clear up all his mess!

As the customs official did not arrive we made our way to the town and a welcome restaurant. We tried unsuccessfully to ring home but had to make do purchasing picture postcards.

Monday June 13th. We went to sleep on board at midnight, but were awakened
at 02.45 hrs by the fishermen talking and banging boxes, and also swilling
their evil smelling.decks down - the water coming into our cockpit.
Many boats left at 04.00 hrs but luckily the one against which we were tied remained until later. However, we were unable to sleep much owing to the excessive swell as the traffic in the port became heavier, so we arose at
06.30 and left Derek - who was now an excellent cook -— preparing breakfast
whilst Eric and myself again bought petrol and bread. We returned to find a shady looking character offering cheap cigarettes etc. He turned out to be the custom's runner and took our order for duty free goods and returned with the cigarettes and brandy and the custom's officer, who (perhaps because of the fishy smell) declined to come aboard. ‘ie then lowered the Q flag from the cross trees and cleaned up our decks. .

We set sail for the open sea again and left harbour at 10.00 hrs and had a delightful mornings' sail southwards, with a fresh tacking breeze and sunshine. Visibility was very good and the beaches were clearly visible, we could see expanse of mud and sand of the river Canche at low tide, and
admired the sand - yachts racing on Le Touquet beach. Wie anchored off Le
Touquet and after lunch swam ashore, and we felt the trip had been worth it for this.

We spoke to the skipper of a small fishing boat. and he told us we could not travel up the Canche river until 18.30 hrs at high water. We waited until then and followed him between the markers and then over the bar under power.

The channel was very tortuous and we occasionally went aground — our draught is eft 3 ins and his was 95 cms. However it was a flooding tide and we were the second in the queue of about 6 vessels all going to Etaples, their village. We passed the Le Touquet Yacht Club where we saw many small yachts but only one had twin keels, the rest were all lying on neee Side until they floated at high tide.

We anchored just before the village harbour and used the dinghy for the once and only time on the whole journey — merely to step on to prevent us from Sinking into the mud, as the water receded with the tide. We changed our clothes, battened dawn, and went into the village for a beer — which
Eric reminded me afterwards we never did get -— but we found that Etaples | 7

was on the main line to Paris. The village itself was very ordinary, although the villagers were very friendly.

Tuesday June 14th We overslept and awoke 07.00 hrs, we put on our city
clothes and dashed, without breakfast, through the town to catch the 07.26 - train to Paris. ‘We spent a happy day in brilliant sunshine and visited Montmatre in the morning. Eric took us to the Paris branch of his firm and treated us to lunch on the premises. HORWET MATNSHEET

How not to Capsize!

Centrifugal helming's the pass word. What is it? Briefly it is this. If you put the helm down at speed, in a fast boat such as a Hornet, the boat luffs up on an arc and heels sharply to leeward. Conversly if you up the helm you will heel to’ windward. Thus in a rough sea or during gybing, when all else fails, you can force your boat level with the tiller. Make every effort to gybe when your mast is plumb-vertical and if, as your boom crashes over, you heel to leeward, yank hard on that tiller.

Some hints and tips on Spinnaker Work .

L. As a general rule the spinnaker pole should be horizontal and at
right angles to the apparent wind. It should be well up on the mast, except when the spinnaker sags badly in light airs.

Ze Contrary to popular belief, a spinnaker will develop more forward thrust in a lean wind if the pole is kept high.

3 ‘Most of the trimming should be done on the leeward sheet with the object of keeping the sail pulling forwards and not sideways. ase the sheet until the luff shows signs of wanting to fall in, then harden slightly. Take every advantage of every free puff by easing on the sheet again and harden as the sail starts to fall again. Trim constantly as the wind shifts. lajor shifts have to be allowed for by altering the trim of the pole.

What are the special implications of these in connection with Hornets?

ne Since the Hornet's spinnaker pole is a stowable five feet in length it does not project far forward of the forestay on a close reach. Therefore, the pole should clip onto the mast about as high as your crew can manage — say two feet above the gooseneck. It will then project into fresh air and this distance will be maximised if the pole is at right angles to the stay.

Ze You can prevent the pole from pointing below the horizontal by tying a piece of terylene in parallel with the shock cord of your up haul. Make your down—haul adjustable,

Se Most keen helmsmen use a continuous sheet for their spinnaker and more and more helmsmen leave their spinnaker permanently clipped onto the halyard. The halyard comes down from its Sheave to the bottom of a shroud outside and then under the job sheet and then to the spinnaker.

NATIONAL ENTERPRISE CLASS RULE CHANGES

The National Enterprise Class Rules have been amended to include 2 fibreglass form of construction as well as the traditional wooden hull. A fibreglass bo2t, known as the "404" has been designed to comply fairly closely with the Enterprise specification and performance. Following the
rule changes that became effective on 1st November, 1966, the "404" now
ranks as an Enterprise.

Other changes authorise certain optional alterations to wooden boats and the use of metal spars.

There are now three optional versions of the Enterprise, each 'One Design', as follows:-

1, The glass fibre boat.
2. The wooden boat, as at present.
3. The wooden boat with Built in buoyancy.

Permutations or combinations of the three will not be permitted, A glass fibre hull may not h2ve wooden decks, and a tanked wooden boat must have all the tanks as shown on the plans. The minimum weight of the glass fibre boat and the wooden boat with built in buoyancy is 220 lbs.

Glass Fibre Boats

The position on the construction of glass fibre hulls is:

a) Construction will be permitted only under licence from the
R.YeAo It will be a condition of the issue of the licence
that the shells are made available to the trade and to individuals for finishing.

b) Houlding must be done from moulds made from a master plug.
Glass fibre boats will be measured in the same way as wooden boats.

Existing 404's

Minor modifications have been made to the 404 during its development but it is the intention that all existing 404's shall be brought into the [Enterprise class subject only to measurement of the hull dimensions etc. It is understood that the R.Y.A. is setting aside a block of Enterprise sail numbers for issue to existing 404's,

Wooden Boats

Built in Buoyancy. The tanking in wooden boats takes the form of a forw2zrd bulkhead, giving a bow tank, together with side tanks extending from the transom, under the side benches to the forward end of the side benches. The tanking has been designed for ease of installation in existing boats.

Optional Variations

1‘ an optional wider rubbing bead.

An optional position for the forward thwart (only the position shown in the plans are permitted).
3. An optional higher tiller port.

Metal Spars

The following sections, tapered or untapered may be used,

Masts. Booms

Holt Allen Enterprise section. Enterprise section.
International M35 section M35 section.
Proctor B section C section.

The rules authorise these specific sections and specify a minimum mast weight of 17 lbs excluding rigging and all normally removable fittings on a

centre of gravity at a minimum of 9*6" from the heel. - The weight and
7

cof g are to be stamped on the mast by the maker.

SOCIAL NES
A 'Brains Trust’ evening was held at M.AS.C. Social Club, Beehive Lane on Friday 20th January. The panel were Commander C.H.Fricker, Jack Kennewell - of the Blackwater S.C.Geoff “ardell and Terry Hallam of the M.S.C. About fifty people came dong to ask questions on a wide range of subjects connected with the sea, and there were some interesting discussions between members of the panel and the audience.

Commander Fricker told us about the sailing of square riggers to Australia, and Francis Chichester's attempt to sail back from Australia was criticised.

A question
on the bare essentials necessary when going to sea sparked off a discussion on navigation, leading to instructions from the panel on how to work out the deviation of a compass. There were some interesting reminiscences from Terry Hallam on navigating the Blackwater in dark and
fog.

Some interesting tips were given on how to find a good cruiser if you
intend to race it - this involved water line lengths, theoretical lengths,
and the ratio of one to the other.

-9-

Olympic dinghy racing set everyone arguing in favour of their preferred class, and an interesting discussion developed on the skills of dinghy racing, and how these should best be tried. To plane or not to plane, that is the question. Terry considered skill in sailing to windward was more important.

Mike Sissons had a knotty problem -— what does a knot in the Ensign mean? Answer -— you have dutiable goods on board and wish to see
the Customs Officer, Moral - don't fly your flags “ith knots in them -
it might mean something important.

The discussions ranged far and wide on everything from glassfibre to flags, with several jokes and amusing stories thrown in, and %f course plenty of lubrication was available at the bar. Everyone enjoyed themselves, I am sure, and thanks are due to Chairman Jack Bigden and the
Panel,

One important question put during the evening that I have not mentioned was on the changing shape of the Blackwater. The answer to that one -— come along on 17th February and you will learn all about the river . that we sail on, in a talk entitled ‘Ecology of the Blackwater', See you there at 7.30.pm.

SOCIAL REPORT

The second winter meeting of the M.S.C. took place at the Social Club, Beehive Lane, on Friday 17th February. Mr.Roy Masefield of Marconi College gave a very interesting talk on the ecology and geology of the Blackwater,

He started by showing us a film about beaches - stones and
shells, where they come from and how. Then, illustrating his points with diagrams, he showed us how the British coastline, the local hills and valleys, and the local rivers gradually took shape, influenced to a large extend by the advance and retreat of the ice-age glaciers, It was with great interest that we learnt that the river Thames at one time flowed through the valley where our Clubhouse now stands. (Stansgate-on-Thames, indeed!).

After a short interval Kr. Masefield went on to show how marshes build up, different plants growing on them according to how long the tide covers that area of land. This was illustrated by some very nice colour slides.

Slides were also used to illustrate the formation of spits, how they are broken and build up again, and how the marshes form behind them.

The talk was rounded off with a short film entitled 'The River' which followed the course of the river from its small beginning right down to the sea, passing under willow trees, over weirs, through locks, past cricket fields, towns and, of course, the sailing clubs.

Leonie Carlisle.

DOCTOR AFLOAT! A BOOK REVIEW FROM A MAGAZINE, sent to us by Jack Bigden.

All Dr. Roger Pilkington wanted was to claim the rights, guaranteed by Parliament, that included the passage of the Kennet and Avon Navigation. But when he arrived at the Bridge of Serpents, Reading, the boat wouldn't go under, He rang the Town Hall and sluices were raised down stream and closed farther up river. The water dropped four inches, He removed the mast, the windscreen, the ventilators, opened the sea-cocks and partially flooded the ship. It still wouldn't go under.

The deputy borough engineer then gave orders to close down the pumps of the sewage works that serviced 100,000 people. The river went down, but still not far enough. The early evening rush-hour had now started. It was half past five, and the Town Hall said could Dr.Pilkington wait till next day ds they usually stopped work at six o'clock? He obligingly
opened the sea-cocks again, took off another inch - in - vain and cordially
declined. The borough engineer came up with a back room brainwaves 2 mobile crane to be brought from a nearby RAF station next days; the road to be closed, traffic diverted, while the crane loaded the boat with steel girders until it was low enough. But Dr.Pilkington countered with an even better idea, ‘hy not a ton or more of people? The municipal employees with brief-cases and bowler hats arrived in cars, and Dr.Pilkington began cramming them aboard, He shut them in the hold. He squeezed them into the fore cabin. Five hours after reaching the bridge, the boat passed under with a quarter of an inch to spare,

Certainly, Dr.Pilkington is stubborn. Freedom to roam is worth being awkward about, I recommend his "Small Best on the Thames" (Macmillan £1.10.). All Dr.P's aneedotes are certainly lively.

~HE MAMGU TROPHY

A reminder to all dinghy and cruiser owners of the principle of the
Mamgu Trophy.

Several people recently have said how interesting the accounts of sea trips are. I can't invent these but there must be several ‘people who during the summer will make one or two-day excursions up the coast, which, while not perhaps long enough for entry for the hiamgu Trophy, would make extremely interesting reading in Navigans and encourage the new Cruiser owners to venture out of the Blackwater Estuary.

I have noticed that a number of Cadets have parents with cruisers.
There are other cruising prizes as well as the main Trophy -— cruise to a neighbouring estuary or abroad or a weeks cruise away from home water. what about the Cadets entering 2 log or sending one to Navigans?

The MAMGU Trophy is a 12 ft to one inch model of Mamgu presented by Mr and Mrs, A.M,Adam to the Marconi Sailing Club for two purposes:

first, to commemorate the ship which for five vital years of the Club's growth served as our Clubhouse,

second, to promote a wider interest in the sea and seamanship by encouraging members to go cruising and to share their experiences for the benefit of others.

The Trophy is to be awarded annually, and held by the winner for one year, for the best log and account of a cruise made in the preceding twelve months,

The cruise must be in a sailing or auxiliary yacht or dinghy, and should be generally of at least three days! duration, though a shorter passage of particular interest may be considered, Use of engine, if any, must be stated. The log may usefully include details of the yacht and any other interesting and relevant matter.

The author of the log must be a member or associate member of the Clubs he/she must have taken an active part in sailing the yacht, but need not have been the owner, charterer or skipper.

A small panel shall be appointed by the Committee to judge the entries, the decision of the panel to be final. The panel need not consist entirely of club members.

Logs are to be judged on their interest and value for others who may attempt similar cruises, and on the seamanship and enterprise implied by the whole undertaking. Thus the riding out of a gale or a passage in heavy weather, conducted in a safe and proper manner and described well enough to assist another mariner in a like situation, should score highly, whereas a colourful account of escapades arising out of gross ignorance or neglect of seamanlike prudence or out of sheer foolnardiness, may be placed lower than a cruise in which hazardous conditions were avoided by good planninh,. A copy of each log entered for the MAMGU shall be presented to the Club if the judges deem it worthy, to be kept for members to read, and to be published, if required, in "Navigans".

The award of the MAMGU Trophy may be withheld in any year if the judges consider that no entries of sufficient merit have been received; but only after giving notice in "Navigans" at least two weeks before the closing date,
