RULES

1., NAME.
The name of the Club shall be "Marconi Athletic and Social Club".

2. DEFINITIONS.
"The Club" means the "Marconi Athletic and Social Club".
"The Club House" means the Club House at Beehive Lane, Chelmsford or such other club house as may from time to time be occupied by the Club. "The Company" means The Marconi Company Limited. "The Associated Companies” means The Marconi International Marine Company Limited and English Electric Valve Company Limited.
"The General Committee” shall mean the committee elected in accordance with Rule 9(A).
The expressions “Ordinary Member", "Family Member", “Associate Member" and "Honorary Life Member" shall bear the meanings assigned to them by Rule 6.
The expressions "Outside Section Member” and "Junior Family Member" shall bear the meanings assigned to them by Rule 7.
"Section" shall mean a section formed in accordance with Rule 25(A) and Section Committee shall mean in relation to any Section the Com- mittee elected or formed thereunder,

3. COLOURS.
The Club colours shall be Royal Blue and White.

4. CONSTITUTION.
The Club shall be a members’ club and shall

1

consist of Ordinary Members, together with such other classes of members as are hereinafter
mentioned.

5. OBJECTS.
The objects of the Club shall be to promote social fellowship, physical fitness and mutual helpfulness among employeesof The Marconi Company Limited and employees of the Associated Companies employed in the Chelmsford area by organising and providing the means for such employees to meet, to engage in sports and recreations of all kinds and to pursue other activities of a social, edu- cational and charitable nature.

6. MEMBERSHIP OF THE CLUB.
(A) The Club shall consist of
(i) Ordinary Members
(ii) | Family Members
Associate Members
(iv) Honorary Life Members

(B) Ordinary Membership.
All employees of the Company and employees of the Associated Companies + e ford—ezea- shall be eligible to become Ordinary Members of the Club.

(C) Family Membership.
A person may become a Family Member of the Club at the discretion of the General Committee if such person is the wife, husband, father, mother, son, daughter, brother or sister of an Ordinary Member or an Honorary Life Member and such person is sixteen years of age or over.
Application for Family Membership shall be made on the applicant’s behalf by such Ordinary Member or Honorary Life Member (hereinafter referred to
2

as "the Sponsor*) and shall be submitted to the General Committee. The Sponsor shall be liable for the subscription payable in respect of a Family Member of which he is Sponsor. Such sub- scription ‘shall be paid by deduction from the wages or salary of the Sponsor if such Sponsor is an Ordinary Member and shall be paid direct to the Treasurer of the Club by the Sponsor if such Sponsor is an Honorary Life Member.
A Family Member shall cease to be a member of the Club forthwith if the Sponsor ceases to be an Deanery, Member or Honorary Life Member of the
Club.
A Family Member shall be entitled to all the privileges of Club membership except the right to introduce guests and the right to vote at any election or general meeting of the Club:

(D) Associate Membership.
Associate Membership of the Club may be granted to any person of sixteen years of age or over not being an employee of the Company or an employee of the Associated Companies employed in the Chelmsford area who has first applied for member- ship of a Section and whom the Section Committee is willing to accept as a member of that Section. No application for Associate Membership shall be granted, if the granting of such ‘Associate Membership shall cause the aggregate numbers of Associate Members of the Club to exceed three per cent. of the total Ordinary Membership of the Club provided that the General Committee shall have discretion in exceptional circumstances to exceed this limit where the General Committee has reasonable cause to believe that the limit will be restored by the normal turnover of membership within a period of twelve months.
A candidate for Associate Membership shall first apply for membership of a Section. The Committee of that Section, if willing to accept his application, shall before so doing recommend to the General Committee in writing that he be granted Associate Membership of the Club. If the

3

recommendation be not eppzowed by the General Committee the candidate shall not be admitted to membership of the Section but shall be free to make fresh application to the same or some other Bee than after the lapse of not less than six
months.
An Associate Member shall be eligible to apply for membership of more than one Section.
An Associate Membér shall be entitled to all the privileges of Club membership except the right to introduce guests and the right to vote at any election or general meeting of the Club.

(E) Honorary Life Membership.
Any person who has left the service of the Company or of one of the Associated Companies on retirement and who at the date of such retirement has been an Ordinary Member of the Club for a period of not less than ten years or periods totalling not less than ten years in the aggre- gate shall, provided he has been an Ordinary Member of the Club for a continuous period of two years ending on the date of such retirement be entitled to become an Honorary Life Member of the Club on making an application to the General Committee for Honorary Life Membership. Such application may be made at any time provided that in the case of a person who has not already retired at the date of his application, such application shall not be made more than three months before the date of his retirement and stele only take effect on the date of his retire-
ment.
The General Committee shall have the power to elect any Ordinary Member who is about to retire from the service of the Company or the Associated Companies or any former Ordinary Member who has so retired to Honorary Life Membership if such Ordinary Member or former Ordinary Member has been or was an Ordinary Member for a period of not less than five years or periods totalling not less than five years in the aggregate.

4

An Honorary Life Member shall be entitled to all the privileges of Club membership except the right to vote at any election or general meeting of the Club.

(F) Election to Membership.
No person shall become a member of the Club unless he shall have been elected to membership by the General Committee. Application for member- ship shall be made in writing in the appropriate form prescribed by the General Committee, by the applicant or in the case of applications for Family Membership by the applicant’s Sponsor. The name and address of any applicant for member- ship shall be prominently displayed in the Club House in a part of the Club House frequented by the Club members not less than two clear days before the election of such applicant as a member.

(G) Cessation of Membership.
A member shall cease to be a member in the following events: -
(a) if he resigns his membership by giving not
less than one week’s notice in writing to the Chief Executive; such resignation shall take effect at the expiry of the said period of notice
(b) if being an Ordinary Member -he cancels the
authority to his Company to deduct his subscrip- tion from his wages or salary, he shall cease to be a memberon the expiry of the period in respect of which his subscription has been paid.
(c) if being an Ordinary Member he shall cease to
be employed by the Company or to be employed by one of the Associated Companies in the Chelmsford area unless immediately on ceasing to be so em- ployed he shall become an Honorary Life Member
(d) if he shall have failed to pay his subscrip-
tion or in the case of a Family Member his sub- scription shall not have been paid by him or by his Sponsor within thirty days after the same shall have become due and the General Committee
5

shall resolve to terminate his membership on the grounds of nonpayment of his subscription
(e) if being a Family Member his Sponsor ceases
to be an Ordinary Member or Honorary Life Member
(f) if his membership shall be terminated in
accordance with Rule 23.

(H) Membership Cards.
The membership cards issued to members shall remain the property of the Club and shall be surrendered to the Chief Executive upon the ter- mination of membership for whatever cause.

7. MEMBERSHIP OF SECTIONS OF THE CLUB.
(A) A Section of the Club shall consist of
(i) Ordinary Members
(ii) Family Members,
Associate Members
(iv) Honorary Life Members
(vy) Outside Section Members
(vi) Junior Family Members
(B) Ordinary Members, Family Members and Honorary
Life Members shall be entitled to become members of any Section of the Club upon making application for membership of that Section to the Section
Committee.

(C) Associate Members
An Associate Member of the Club may become a member of a Section on making application and being elected by the Section Committee. The election as a member of a Section of a person applying for Associate Membership under Rule 6(D) shall not become effective unless and until such person shall have been electedan Associate Member by the General Committee.
6

A decision of a Section Committee not to permit an Associate Member to Section Membership shall be final.

(D) Outside Section Members
The Committee of any Section, the normal activities of which take place on premises other than those of the Club or of the Company or the Associated Companies, may grant Outside Section Membership to persons of sixteen years of age or over, not being employees of the Company or the Associated Companies nor qualified for Family Membership provided that the grant of Outside Section Membership to any person will not cause the number of Outside Section Members of that Section to be more than twenty five per cent. of the total number of Ordinary Members who are members of the Section. An Outside Section Member shall not be admitted to membership of more than two Sections and may participate only in the activities of his Section or Sections which are held on premises other than those of the Club or of the Company or the Associated Companies.
The name of every person admitted to Outside Section Membership shall be notified forthwith by the Section Committee to the General Committee. An Outside Section Member shall be subject) to these Rules and the decisions and control of the General Committee in all matters affecting his
membership.

(E) Junior Family Membership of Sections.
The Committee of any Section the Rules of which so allow may grant Junior Family Membership to any son or daughter (being fifteen years of age or under) of any member of the section other than an Qutside Section Member. The parent of a Junior Family Member shall be responsible for his child strictly observing the Rules of the Section and the Rules and Bye-Laws of the Club.

7

The subscription, if any, charged by the Section for anton Family Membership shall be paid by the
parent.
Upon attaining the age of sixteen years, a Junior Family Member shall cease to be a member of his Section or Sections unless within one month from the date of his sixteenth birthday he is admitted to Family or Associate Membership of the Club or Outside Section Membership.
A Junior Family Member may participate only in the activities of his Section or Sections and shall not use the premises of the Club otherwise than for the purpose of such activities.
The name of every person admitted to Junior Family Membership of a Section shall be notified forthwith by the Section Committee to the General
Committee.

(F) Election to Section Membership
A person other than an Ordinary Member, Family Member or Honorary Life Member applying for membership of a Section shall only become a member of that Section upon making application to the Section Committee in accordance with the Rules of the Section and being elected a Section Member by the Section Committee provided that in the case of a person applying for Associate Membership of the Club such person shall not become a memberof the Section until he is elected an Associate Member of the Club by the General
Committee.

8. SUBSCRIPTIONS
The subscriptions payable by the President, Vice Presidents, Ordinary Members, Family Members and Associate Members shall be fixed and may from time to time be varied by resolution of a general meeting of the Club passed in accordance with Rule 11(C).

Particulars of the subscriptions for the time being payable shall at all times be posted in a prominent position in the Club House.
The subscriptions payable for membership of a Section including the subscriptions (if any) payable by Outside Section Members and Junior Family Members shall be those fixed by or in accordance with the Rules of the Section or Sections of which they are members.
Subscriptions shall be payable in advance and in the case of annual subscriptions shall be due and payable on the anniversary of the date the member became a President, Vice President or Associate Member as the case may
The subscription payable by an Honorary Life Member in respect of a Family Member of which he is Sponsor shall be paid by such Honorary Life Member to the Club Treasurer,
The subscriptionofan Ordinary Member including the subscriptions payable by him in respect of Family Members of which he is Sponsor shall be paid by deductions from his wages or salary and authority to his Company to make such deductions shall be given. in his form of Application for Membership. An Ordinary Member who cancels such authority shall be deemed to have resigned his membership from the date his subscription ceases. The subscription of an Associate Member shall be paid to the Section which sponsored his applied- tion for Associate Membership and shall be re- wave by such Section to the Treasurer of the
Club.

9. MANAGEMENT
(A) General Committee
The affairs of the Club, in all matters not in these Rules reserved for the Club in General Meeting, shall be managed by a General Committee consisting of twelve Ordinary Members elected to serve for a term of two years.

9

At its first meeting after each Annual Election the General Committee shall elect a Chairman and a Vice-Chairman for the ensuing year.
The General Committee shall meet at least once a month. Seven members shall constitute a quorum. Each member shall be entitled to one vote except that in the case of an equality of votes, the Chairman of the Meeting shall have a second or casting vote. Any member of the. General Committee who absents himself from three consecutive meetings without reasonable excuse shall upon the resolu- tion of the other members thereof cease to be a member of the General Committee and his position may thereupon be filled as a casual vacancy. The members of the General Committee shall have power to appoint any Ordinary Member of the Club to fill a casual vacancy.
The proceedings of the General Committee shall be recorded ina Minute Book kept for that purpose, which shall be available for inspection by any member of the General Committee.

(B) Bar Sub-Committee
At its first meeting after each election, the General Committee shall appoint a Bar Sub- Committee which shall consist solely of the Chairman and four or more other members of the General Committee.
The Bar Sub-Committee shall be responsible for the orderly conductof the Club Bars in accordance with the licensing laws for the time being in force and for the purchase for the Club and the supply by the Club of intoxicating liquor.
The Bar Sub-Committee shall meet at least once a month. Three members shall constitute a quorum.

(C) Other Sub-Committees.
The General Committee may appoint one or more Sub-Committees in addition to the Bar Sub- Committee for such purposes and with such

10

responsibilities as it may deem appropriate. Such Sub-Committee shall at all times be responsible to the General Committee which may direct that particular matters shall be referred to it for approval or decision and shall have the right where circumstances permit to over-ride decisions taken by a Sub-Committee. Unless otherwise de- cided by the General Committee, the proceedings of a Sub-Committee shall be recorded in a Minute Book kept for that purpose, which shall be available for inspection by any member of the General Committee.

10. ELECTION OF GENERAL COMMITTEE
In every year, six members of the General Committee shall retire from office and shall be eligible for re-election. The members so re- tiring shall be those who have been longest in office since their last election. A member appointed to fill a casual vacancy on the General Committee shall be deemed to have taken office on the date on which the membet in whose place he is appointed was last elected.
Notices inviting the nomination of candidates to serve on the General Committee shall be posted by the Chief Executive in the Club House and in such other places as the General Committee may determine on the First day of October in every year. Nominations shall be in writing signed by two Ordinary Members, countersigned by the candi- date to signify his consent and deposited with the Chief Executive within a period of fourteen days from the date of such notices. Only Ordinary Members who are over the age of twenty- one shall be eligible for nomination.
The election shall take place during the first complete week of November on dates determined by the General Committee, which shall make all necessary arrangements in connection therewith, including the appointment of three scrutineers who shall not be members of nor candidates for election to the General Committee. The result

11

shall be declared by the posting in the Club House of notices signed by the scrutineers re- cording the number of votes polled by each candi- ave. it indicating which candidates have been
elected.
The election shall be by ballot. Each Ordinary Member shall have six votes but shall not be entitled to cast more than one vote for a parti- cular candidate and shall not be obliged to cast all the votes to which he is entitled.
Should the ballot result in two or more candi- dates receiving an equal number of votes, being the lowest number cast which is sufficient to secure election, the scrutineers shall draw lots to determine which of such candidates shall fill the vacancy.

11. GENERAL MEETINGS
(A) Annual General Meetings.
An Annual General Meeting of the Club shall be held in every year not later than the Thirtieth day of April and not more than fifteen months shall elapse between the date of one Annual General Meeting and that of the next. Notice of the date and time of the Annual General Meeting shall be posted by the Chief Executive in the Club House and in such other places as the General Committee may determine at least fourteen clear days before such date.
The business of an Annual General Meeting shall be to receive and consider the Balance Sheet and the reports of the General Committee, Officers and Auditors; to elect the President and Vice Presidents; to appoint Auditors and to transact any other business which may be determined by the President or the General Committee and stated in the notice of the meeting or of which notice signed by at least two Ordinary Members has been given to the Chief Executive at least seven clear days before the date fixed for the Meeting.

12

(B) Special General Meetings.
A Special General Meeting may be called by the President or the General Committee on not less than seven days notice at the time and place specified in the notice of such Special General Meeting or upon the written requisition of at least thirty Ordinary Members or one fifth of the total number of Ordinary Members whichever is ‘the less and shall, if so requisitioned, be held not less than seven clear days nor more than twenty one clear days from the date of the receipt by the Chief Executive of such requisition. Notice of the date and time of a Special General Meeting shall be posted by the Chief Executive in the Club House at least seven clear days before the date of such meeting.

(C) Voting at General Meetings.
At any General Meeting a resolution put to the yote of the meeting shall be decided on a show of membership cards unless a poll is (before or on the declaration of the show of membership cards)
demanded;
(a) by the Chairman of the Meeting; or
(b) by ten Ordinary Members.
Unless a poll be so demanded a declaration by the Chairman that a resolution has on a show of membership cards been carried or carried unani- mously or by a particular majority or lost and an entry to that effect in the book containing the minutes of the proceedings of the meeting shall be conclusive evidence of the fact without proof of the number or proportion of the votes recorded for or against such resolution.
A demand for a poll may be withdrawn.
If a poll is duly demanded it shall be taken
forthwith.
On a show of membership cards or on a poll every Ordinary Member present at the meeting shall have one vote.
13

Except in the case of resolutions to alter the rules resolutions shall be passed if voted for by a majority of the Ordinary Members present in person at the meeting and voting. In the case of an equality of votes, the resolutions shall be treated as not passed and in such case the Chair- man shall not have a second or casting vote.
cD)
12. ACCOUNTS
The General Committee shall cause proper books of account to be kept with respect to all sums of money received and expended by the Club, all sales and purchases. by the Club and the assets and liabilities of the Club. At every Annual General Meeting, the General Committee shall lay before the Club a Balance Sheet made up to the Thirty-first day of December in the previous year, duly audited and signed by the Auditors. A copy of the Balance Sheet shall be posted in the Club House and in such other places as the General Committee may determine at least fourteen clear days before the date of the Annual General Meeting.

13. VICE-PRESIDENTS
The Club shall have such number of Vice- Presidents as may from time to time be determined by the General Committee. A Vice-President shall be elected at the Annual General Meeting and shall hold office for life unless he shall resign from the office of Vice-President by giving not less than one weeks notice in writing to the Chief Executive or shall fail to pay his sub- scription within thirty days after the same shall have become due and the General Committee shall resolve to remove him from the office of Vice- President. No person shall be nominated for election as a Vice-President unless such nomina- tion shall have been made or approved by the General Committee. The General Committee shall have power to appoint any person as an additional Vice-President or to fill a casual vacancy in the office of Vice-President until the next following Annual General Meeting.
14

The Vice-Presidents shall be entitled to all the privileges of Ordinary Membership and shall have the right to attend and speak at meetings of the General Committee but not to vote thereat.

14. PRESIDENT
The Club shall have a President who shall be elected annually at the Annual General Meeting. No person shall be nominated for election as President unless he is a Vice-President and un- less such nomination shall have been made or approved by the General Committee. Upon the conclusion of his term of office, a retiring President, if not re-elected, shall resume the office of Vice-President. The General Committee shall have power to appoint any Vice-President to fill a casual vacancy in the office of President until the next following Annual General Meeting. The President shall be entitled to all the privileges of Ordinary Membership and shall have the right to attend and speak at meetings of the General Committee but not to vote thereat.

15. TRUSTEES
The Club shall have not less than two nor more than three Trustees who shall be appointed by the Company acting in consultation with the General Committee and may be removed from office by the Company. A Trustee shall be entitled to resign his office by giving not less than one month’s notice in writing to the Company. All property of the Club, including land and investments but excluding the Club’s bank account or accounts, shall be vested in the Trustees for the time being in their own names so far as necessary and practicable for the use and benefit of the Club. The Trustees shall have the right to attend and speak at meetings of the General Committee but shall not have a vote.

15

16. OFFICERS
(A) Chief Executive
The Chief Executive of the Club shall be appointed by the Company acting in consultation with the General Committee and shall be an employee of the Company.
The Chief Executive shall have such duties and responsibilities relating to the organisation of the Club and its activities as shall from time to time be assigned to him by the General Committee in agreement with the Company.

(B) Executive Officer
The Executive Officer of the Club shall be appointed by the Company acting in consultation with the General Committee and shall be an em- ployee of the Company.
The Executive Officer shall carry out under the directions of the Chief Executive such duties and responsibilities as may from time to time be assigned to him.

(C) Treasurer
The Treasurer of the Club shall be appointed by the Company acting in consultation with the General Committee and shall be an employee of the
Company.
The Treasurer shall carry out under the direc- tions of the Chief Executive such duties and responsibilities as may from time to time be assigned to him.

17. AUDITORS
Two Auditors, not being members of the General Committee nor Officers of the Club, shall be appointed annually at the Annual General Meeting. No person shall be nominated for appointment as an Auditor unless he shall have consented to such nomination and such nomination shall have been
16

made or approved by the General Committee. The General Committee shall have power to appoint any person to fill a casual vacancy in the office of Auditor until the next Annual General Meeting. The Auditors shall have access to all the books, accounts, vouchers, deeds, securities, minute books and other documents of the Club, including those of the Sections.

18. BYE-LAWS:
The General Committee shall have power from time to time to make, vary and revoke Bye-laws (not inconsistent with these Rules) for the regu- lation of the internal affairsof the Club and the conduct of the members. The Bye-laws for the time being in force shall be binding on all members, and a copy thereof shall at all times be posted in a prominent position in the Club House.

21. INTRODUCTION OF VISITORS
(A) Members’ Guests
Ordinary Members and Honorary Life Members may introduce and entertain guests at the premises of the Club. The maximum number of guests which an Ordinary Member or Honorary Life Member may in- troduce on any one occasion shall be stated in the Bye-laws and a notice of any decision by the General Committee to reduce such maximum number shall be prominently displayed in the Club House at least seven clear days before the reduction takes effect.
There shall be kept at all premises of the Club a Visitors’ Book which shall be signed by every guest and by the Ordinary Member or Honorary Life Member effecting the introduction, The General Committee shall have power by Bye-law to deter- mine the fee, if any, which shall be payable by an Ordinary Member or Honorary Life Member in respect of each guest introduced by him.

19

No guest of an Ordinary Member or Honorary Life Member shall be permitted to make payment, direct- ly or indirectly for any intoxicating liquor pro- vided on the Club premises. Any guest found or reasonably suspected to be in breach of this sub- rule shall be required to leave the Club premises immediately and the Ordinary Member or Honorary Life Member by whom such guest was introduced shall be liable to suspension upon the breach being duly proved.

(B) Visitors from other Clubs
Officers and members of other Clubs visiting premises of the Club by official invitation shall during the period of their stay be permitted to buy intoxicating liquor for consumption on the Club premises.
A Section shall not issue such an invitation except with the authorityof the General Committee and advance notice of any such visit shall be given by the Section concerned to the Chief
Executive.

22. BETTING, LOTTERIES AND GAMING
No betting shall be allowed on any premises of the Club. No lottery shall be promoted by any member or Officer on behalf of or in any way con- nected with the Club or with any entertainment or event held by or in connection with the Club without the previous authority of the General Committee. Gaming shall be permitted on the pre- mises of the Club so, however, as not to con- travene any of the provisions of the Betting, Gaming and Lotteries Act, 1963 or any statutory modification thereof for the time being in force.

23. MISCONDUCT OF MEMBERS
(A) Misconduct _on Club premises
Any Officer of the Club, any member of the General Committee or any person authorised by the
20

General Committee may require any person to leave any premises of the Club forthwith for the re- mainder of that day if in the opinion of such Officer, Committee member or person so authorised such person’s behaviour is detrimental to the proper conduct of the Club or any Section thereof or causes annoyance to other members.

(B) Suspension and Termination of Membership
(i) Suspension by Chief Executive
The Chief Executive (or other Officer deputising for him) with the consent of not less than two members of the General Committee may suspend the membership of any member of the Club whose con- duct, whether on the premises of the Club or elsewhere, is or has been in their opinion con~- trary to the interests of the Club or injurious to its reputation. Such suspension shall take effect until the next following meeting of the General Committee.
A member so suspended shall be given written notice of his suspension and of the date and place of the next following meetingof the General Committee at which the suspension will be con- sidered and shall be informed that if he desires he may appear before the General Committee to answer any allegation made against him or make written representations to the General Committee. of Geet meeting the General Committee shall
either: -
(a) re-instate the suspended member; or
(b) extend the suspension for a specified
period not exceeding three months; or
(c) subject as hereinafter provided, resolve
to terminate the membership of the suspended member.
(ii) Suspension or termination of Membership by
General Committee
If in the opinion of the General Committee the conduct of a member of the Club, whether on the

21

premises of the Club or elsewhere is or has been contrary to the interests of the Club or in- jurious to its reputation the General Committee may resolve to suspend the membership of such member for a specified period not exceeding three months or subject as hereinafter provided may resolve to terminate such member’s membership. If practicable not less than 24 hours written notice shall be given to such member informing him of the date and place of the General Committee Meeting at which the suspension or termination of his membership will be considered and informing him that if he desires he may appear before the meeting to answer any allegation made against him or make written representations to the General Committee. If such notice is not given and the General Committee at such meeting resolves to suspend or terminate his membership, he shall be given written notice of such suspension or ter- mination and of the date and place of the next following meeting of the General Committee at which if such member so desires such suspension or termination will be reconsidered and shall be informed that if he desires he may appear before the General Committee or submit written repre- sentations in answer to any allegation. If the member appears at such meeting or makes such ropreseteartone the General Committee shall
either:-
(a) re-instate such member as a member; or
(b) reduce the period of suspension; or
(c) confirm the suspension or termination of
his membership subject in the case of termination to the member’s right of appeal to the Club in General Meeting.

If the member shall not appear at such meeting or make such representations the decision of the General Committee shall stand subject in the case of termination of membership to the member’s right of appeal to the Club in General Meeting.

22

(C) Appeal against Termination of Membership
A member whose membership the General Committee has resolved to terminate shall (unless there shall still be available to such member the right to have the decision of the General Committee re- considered by the General Committee under sub- section (B) of this Rule), be informed (by letter, if he did not appear before the Committee) that he has the right within seven days to give written notice of his desire to appeal to the Club in General Meeting (his membership meanwhile being suspended) and that failing such notice of appeal his membership will terminate and his name will be removed from the list of members at the expiration of the said period of seven days.
In the event of a notice of appeal being duly received, the General Committee shall call a Special General Meeting of the Club for a day not more than twenty-one clear days after the date of receipt of the notice of appeal. The suspended member shall be given written notice of the date of such Special General Meeting and shall be in- formed that if he so desires he may be present.

At any such Special General Meeting any allega- tions against the suspended member shall be re- lated (in his presence, ifhe attends) by a member of the General Committee and the suspended member shall (if he desires) be heard in answer. A decision whether to re-instate the suspended member or to terminate his membership shall be taken by vote ina ballot conducted by scrutineers appointed for the purposeby the General Committee and shall be conclusive.

(D) Re-admission after Expulsion for Misconduct
A member whose membership has been terminated on grounds of misconduct may at the discretion of the General Committee be re-admitted to member- ship after a period of not. less than six months from the date of such termination.
23

24. DISPUTES AND COMPLAINTS
(A) Disputes between Members and Officers and
complaints about or by Officers
Any dispute between a member and an Officer of the Club and any complaint by a member concerning an Officer of the Club or by an Officer of the Club concerning a member shall, unless settled amicably, be referred by the member or Officer concerned to the General Committee. The General Committee shall take such action as may be appro- priate including the suspension or termination of membership under Rule 23(B)(ii) if the conduct of the member concerned justifies it. If the member or Officer concerned is dissatisfied with the
decision of the General Committee, either party may request that the matter be referred for arbi- tration by one or more of the Trustees, appointed under Rule 15, whose decision shall be final provided always that if such decision of the General Committee involves the termination of a person’s membership the matter shall not be re- ferred to the Trustees but such person shall have a right of appeal to the Club in general meeting pursuant to Rule 23.

(B) Disputes between Members and other complaints
Any dispute: between members which cannot be settled amicably and any complaint by a member other than a complaint concerning an Officer of the Club shall be referred by the member or members concerned to the Chief Executive (or other officer deputising for him) who, if unable to settle the matter to the satisfaction of such member or members, shall refer it at the request of any such member to the General Committee whose decision shall be final provided always that if in the opinion of the Chief Executive (or other Officer deputising for him) the dispute or com- plaint concerns conduct by a member whether on the premises of the Club or elsewhere, which is or has been in the opinion of the Chief Executive (or such other Officer) contrary to the interests of the Club or injurious to its reputation, the
24

Chief Executive (or other officer deputising for him) shall refer the matter immediately to the General Committee and the matter shall be dealt with under the provisions of Rule 23(B) (ii).

(C) Right to attend meeting of General Committee
Any member or Officer about whom a complaint is made or who makes a complaint or who is a party to a dispute may attend the meetingof the General Committee at which such complaint or dispute is considered or if the matter is referred to the arbitration of oneormore of the Trustees, before the Trusteejor Trustees, to state his case or answer any allegations made against him,

25. EXCLUSION OF LIABILITY AND _INDEMNITIES
(A) Exclusion of Liability
Neither the Club not any member acting on behalf of the Club nor any Officer thereof nor the Trustees shall be liable to any member or guest of a member or visitor for any loss of or damage to any property occurring, from whatever cause, in or about any premises of the Club; nor for any injury sustained by a member or guest or visitor whilst on or entering or leaving any premises of the Club.

(B) Indemnity of Officers, Employees and the
Company
The Officers and employees of the Club and the Company shall be entitled to be indemnified out of the assets of the Club against all expenses, costs, claims and liabilities arising out of or in the course of the Officers’ or employees’ duties or acts as Officers or employees which the Officers or employees or their predecessors may incur, except such (if any) as they may incur through their own wilful neglect or default. If the assets of the Club shall be insufficient, the Officers, the employees and the Company shall be entitled to be indemnified to the extend of such

25

deficiency by the Ordinary’ Members of the Club and those persons who were Ordinary Members at the date the liability was incurred but have subsequently ceased to be Ordinary Members. The liability of the Ordinary Members and such past Ordinary Members shall be joint and several.

(C). Indemnity of General Committee and the
Trustees
The members of the General Committee and the Trustees shall be entitled to be indemnified out of the assets of the Club against all expenses, costs, claims and liabilities arising our of or in the course of their duties or acts as members of the General Committee or Trustees as the case may be which they or their predecessors in title may incur, except such (if any) as they may incur through their own wilful neglect or default. If the assets of the Club shall be insufficient the members of the General Committee or the Trustees as the case may be shall be entitled to be in- demnified to the extent of the deficiency by the Ordinary Members of the Club and those persons who were Ordinary Members of the Club at the date the liability was incurred but have subsequently ceased to be Ordinary Members. The liability of the Ordinary Members and such past Ordinary Members shall be joint and several.

26. SECTIONS
(A) Formation and control
Any group of ten or more Ordinary Members having a common sporting, social or cultural interest may with the previous approval of the General Committee form a Section. No person who has not first been elected a member of the Club shall be admitted to membership of a Section except as an Outside Section Member or a Junior Family Member.
Each Section shall be under the control of a Section Committee elected annually by and con- sisting of members of the Section other than

26

Associate Members, Outside Section Members and Junior Family Members. Upon a Section being formed the Members thereof shall forthwith elect a Section Committee. The Section Committee shall be responsible to the General Committee for the conduct of its Section. The first Section Committee shall be elected as soon as practicable after the approval of the General Committee to the formation of the Section shall have been given, at a meeting of the Section convened for that purpose by the General Committee.
The Section Committee of a newly-formed Section shall, as soon as possible after taking office, prepare and submit to the General Committee Rules for the operation and conduct of the Section. Such Rules shall not come into force until approved with or without amendment by the General Committee and thereafter shall not be amended without the previous approval of the General
Committee.
Each Section shall submit a written report on its activities to the General Committee at such jntervals as the General Committee may decide.

(B) Subscriptions to Sections
The additional subscriptions, if any, charged for membership of a Section shall be fixed and may from time to time be varied by the Section Committee subject, in the case of Outside Section Members, to the approval of the General Committee.

(C) Section Accounts
Each Section shall appoint a Section Treasurer who shall keep a true record of the financial transactions of that Section in accordance with such directions as may from time to time be given to him by the General Committee or laid down in the Bye-laws.
(D) Dissolution of Sections
Upon the dissolution of a Section all funds, equipment and other property of the Section shall

27

be checked and recorded by the Auditors who shall submit an inventory thereof to the General Com- mittee. Such property shall thereafter be used and applied for the benefit of the general body of Club members and the members of the Section shall have no claim against any person for the distribution of the said property or its equiva- lent in money among the members of the Section that has been dissolved.

27. ALTERATION OF RULES
These Rules may be revoked, added to or altered by resolution of a General Meeting of the Club passed by a majority comprising at least two- thirds of the Ordinary Members present and voting. So long as the Club is registered in respect of any premises under Part II of the Licensing Act, 1964 or any statutory amendment or re-enactment thereof for the time being in force the Chief Executive shall give written notice of any alteration of these Rules to the Chief Officer of Police and the Clerk of the Local Authority in each area in which such premises are situated within twenty eight days of such alteration and no alteration of these Rules so as to authorise sales of intoxicating liquor not authorised at the time of the application or last application by the Club for the issue or renewal of a regi- stration certificate shall be effective until such written notice shall have been given.

BRAZIL

Fitting out the club dinghy 'Brazil' has been my labour of love for two seasons now and on each occasion I have endeavoured to add some improvement or refinement that would make her better and/or safer for would be helmsmen.

This year drainage holes have been fitted, the bungs being of the screw type, inserted from inside the boat and attached by a lanyard to prevent loss. The cover has been repaired and draw lines attached that pass under the hull and enable the cover to be tied sufficiently tight so as to prevent sagging. A "boom" has been provided to support the cover, please note how it is fitted and replace it correctly when you have finished, also please see that it is not left lying where it can be damaged whilst you are out
sailing.

"Brazil" is not fitted with banding to her keel or bilge strakes, I hope to remedy this for next year. In the meantime please remember that she lacks protection in these vital parts, and refrain from grounding her
unnecessarily.

Finally please report any damage to the 0.0.D. who will note it in his report, and I should be able to sort it out from there.

Good luck, good sailing and thank you in anticipation of your careful use of "Brazil".

Fred Partlett (iwayfarer 181).

SOCIAL EVENING
Se

The last winter meeting of the Sailing Club was held at the - Beehive Lane Clubhouse on I'riday, 21st April. About fifty people were . present to enjoy the usual bar facilities, exchange of news, and talks by three very good speakers,

The first speaker was Mr. Alan Hill, who won the Bronze Medal with his craft at the last Boat Show.

Mr, Hill told us a lot about the designing and building of boats, his special interest being fibreglass boats, which he believes will become much more popular in the next few years, one of his reasons being the speed of this type of manufacture as opposed to the traditional methods, He explained the system of Lloyd's certificates and recommended that any prospective buyer should ask to see the hull or series certificate.

Ve were given tips on the purchase of new and secondhand cruisers; the small points to watch for in the building and current condition of the boat. Alsn, we were told how.to maintain a fibreglass boat by buffing he surface to keep it polished and clean, Point to note: once the fibreglass boat goes svongy and has to be painted it requires -the same amount of maintenance as any wooden or metal boat.

If you ever need to repair your fibreglass boat we discovered that the name of the builder should be found, so that ne can thereby ascertain
which type of resin was used in the. original construction - it is always
advisable to stick to the same type.

Mr, Hall also discussed the fitting out of the boats, including the fitting of gas appliances and engines,

Altogether he gave us a great deal of useful and helpful advice and information, illustrated with stories and.examples from his own experience.

Mr, Sam Peulton of Maldon was the next speaker and he kept the audience laughing with tales ef his early sailing days, from the first boat he had, to the times when he beat Buster Payne in many a race by
using the 'hard boiled egg' technique - guaranteed to succeed,

He also gave helpful hints on navigating "then you shin up the mast with your binoculars and have a look round", and told us of the advantages and disadvantages ef amming a Thames barge,

Since most of his tales need “the Sam Poulton” touch to Give them full flavour none of them is repeated here, but any reader who did not attend the meeting is advised to make the mast of his ar her opportunity next time they have a chance to hear him speak, -

The third speaker of the evening was Keith Musto, who, of course, needs no introduction.
He came along prepared to answer any questions on sailing. However, before getting don to technicalities, he showed us some very interesting and entertaining colour’slides oi Tolcyo taken during the Olympic'Games, and told us about the incidents, people and places illustrated, This was most enjoyable, although it was not all
about sailing but included tales such as that of the Japanese god whose huge stone statue survived two earthquakes and a tidal.wave, and now has gifts brought to him by many pilgrims, one of whoifmade him a giant pair of sandals, which will come in handy should he ever want to take a walk,

The evening passed very quickly indeed, and thanks were expressed to all three speakers for the excellent advice and entertainment they gave us,

FALLING IN THE WATER

Compared with the high accident rate of road users, sailing is a relatively safe pastime. However, accidents do occur, and when they do are usually more ‘Serious as often rescue is either a long way away or more difficult.to obtain. It is therefore more important to take precautions and also to know what to do when an accident does occur.

According to the Registrar General's Statistical Review for 1962, there were 898 deaths in the waters around England and ‘ales, including 72 deaths due to submersion of the occupant of 2 small boat and 40 due to other water-transport injury by submersion. Total tragedies are not that infrequent in our own Blackwater which compared with many sailing areas, is sheltered, and potential rescuers not far away.

Why do people die when they fall in the water? Other than attack by sharks or mechanical injury there are three main causes of death.

l. Hypothermia, i.e. lowering ofbody temperature due to the cold’ environment,

a Drowning, i.e. filling of the lungs with water

and

3s Vaso-vagal shock, i.e. the shock of water entering the lower pharynx or upper respiratory passages causing a nervous reflex which stops the heart.

To deal with these in turn, the first is by far the commonest cause of death as to immersion. In the unfortunate Lakonia disaster,
.of the 124 deaths, there is strong evidence to show that apart from 11 deaths due to injury, most of the
remaining
113 were due to hypothermia leading to helplessness unconciousness and then drowning only as a terminal event. when you consider that the.water temperaturé
was
64°R, a temperature never obtained around.England, and that help was relatively quickly obtained, you will realise how important is heat loss,

Tt has been shown that few people survive for more than seven hours in water at 59 F, again much higher than British sea temperatures, and the survival time in water at 32°F is only a matter of a few minutes.

As on land, the best way of keeping warm in the water is to wear warm clothing, Into this category come"was suits" of which I have no personal experience, but which should be the best of all. If you can get out of the water and sit on your dinghy so much the better as unless the wind is particularly cold your heat loss is slower, Contrary to what might be expected, movement in the water accelerates heat loss as the extra heat generated by muscular effort is more than offset by the removal of the warmer layer of water around, and heated by, the body. Therefore, unless it is to swim a short distance to a rescue boat or the shore it is much better to lie as still possible in the water supported by a life-jacket. As the time of immersion is obviously an important factor, one should.stay as near as possible to the point where rescue might be expected. This usually means strying near the boat.

There is no evidence to show that alcohol in normal quantities accelerates heat loss, which may be of some comfort to those if us who imbibe.

In the Lakonia disaster it is known that 15 people died from hypothermia after being picked up so it is important, should you rescue someone who has been immersed for some time, to warm them up as quickly as possible. This is really only important if the rescued is “unconscious as conscious people are unlikely to be in danger,
The quickest method of warming someone is a warm bath — temperature 97°F - 100 F,
but this is onlyof use if they can be bathed within 20 minutes and is seldom feasible. A warm atmosphere, hot water bottles, the close proximity of another human body ‘and warm blankets after removal of the cold wet clothing are the usual methods. So if you cannot rescue yourself, wear warm clothing, keep still and make it as easy as possible for your rescuers by staying near the boat or where they expect you to be.

To pass on to the last two headings, prevention is - wear a good life jacket and
hold your breath as you go in. Once a person has ceased to breath, irreversible brain damage occurs within 3-5 mins so that any attempt to revive them must be made immediately. If drowning is complicated by hypothermia the chance of successful revival is very small however,

Before considering how to revive a person let us consider briefly what happens when lungs fll with water. The water may be fresh or sea water, In the former case the osmotic pressure of the blood causes a rapid absorption of water from the lungs

4 -

into the blood stream which so lowers the osmotic pressure of the blood that the red cells burst, releasing a large amount of potassium which the heart cannot tolerate and it stops. This takes place very rapidly, as roughly speaking the minute sacs in the lungs, if all spread out would cover a tennis court and they are designed specially to absorb,

In the latter case the reverse occurs as the osmotic pressure of sea water is higher than that of the blood and this causes an outflow of fluid from the blood stream, flooding the lungs and preventing oxygen getting into the blood. The heart can keep beating for 2 few minutes after this occurs, so the chances of successful revival are much higher.

The treatment of drowning and also of vaso-vagal shock is the same, namely artificual respirationl I am sure that the simplest and most effective method
is mouth to mouth respiration - perhaps better known as the kiss of life. As with
all unconscious people, including unconsciousness due to hypothermia, the first essential is to maintain a clear airway. This is done by hooking the forefingers of each hand behind the angle of the jaw of the rescued and lifting the jaw, and thereby the tongue, forward, If possible the lower teeth can be hooked over the upper teeth.

It is a waste of time attempting th empty water from the lungs of the rescued. It is much better to attempt to inflate that part of the lung which is not filled
with water - usually a considerable proportion, If you kneel facing the feet it
is possible to lift the jaw forward, hold the lips together in an airtight joint and breathe gently down the nose. In this position one can watch the chest to see it inflate. Remarkably little effort is required and adequate time should be allowed for the chest to deflate, ahout three times as long as the inflation period. If the sirway is clear, i.e. the tongue is not blocking the back of the throat, the movement of the chest should be gentle and easy.

I don't know how long one should continue this as jit is mainly a moral question. If one considers that the brain is dead after five minutes and quadruples this time, I think this is reasonable and is the criterion I have taken on the few occasions I have had to do it.

It is important to realise that if the rescued is breathing it is positively dangerous to give artificial respiration. This will only hinder their own respiratory efforts and possibly inflate the stomach, blowing vomit into their air passages and killing then. It is only necessary to keep a clear airway and keep them warm,

One last point which I must mention is the question of vomiting, In a conscious person they will get rid of their own vomit but in an unconscious person they may well inhale it with fatal results, Turn them on their side with the head lower than their waist, and no fluid can possibly enter the lungs,

This article has turned out to be much longer than I anticipated but even so is only an outline of what happens when one "falls in the water",

Greater pens than mine have said "prevention is better than cure" and it is never more true than of sailing accidents,

4,DOCTOR.

PILOT'S CUP 1967

We gulped when the Pilot's cup course was announced. Fifteen miles with the wind getting stronger, Up to Southey (close hauled) down to West Mersea S.C.
No.5 (close - broad reach) back to Stansgate (close haul/beat. The entries
included the Dragons of Terry and Mike, Hornets of Richard, GP14's of Howard,
Norman and Ken, Enterprises of Julian and Norman and ourselves. Tide going out, keep out of tide going up through the narrows. Bit choppy up to Osea Pier, in fact very glad of self-balers. Notice in sailing instruction "observe channel marks", Thinks, what are the twins, Julian and Howard doing leaving the Doctor to Porte Oh! well, the Dragons are leaving it to starboard and so ill we. Leave Southey to starboard as instructed. Get on plane after a couple of hundred yards. Stay on plane for miles except for brief rests. Pass Dragons. ixhausted but know that those in front will be disqualified. Norman, Ken etc stop before Stone and go home. Still planing. whoops, there go Howard and Jane. Several cruisers (including the Dragons) around and quite honestly we're not in sufficient control of our own boat to be able to help then. Approach Bradwell Power station, still on plane. Just deciding to go between large metal "breakwater thing" and Bradwell shore when whoops there we go. "Phew it's cold", Boat upright, then over the other way. I get the sails down. John gets the boat up. I hang onto bows as John tries to steer. ‘Jind has taken us to leeward of breakwater, Several cruisers moored. Grab the first one, After a lot of bother the boat is lying head to wind, John is on board, and I'm being hauled in like a sack of potatoes, Estimated water temperature low. Have read A-Doctor's article and know I have only a few minutes to live. My legs feel like jelly.and I can hardly stand, John seems in better shape and returns to dinghy to bale out, Meanwhile the cruiser owners have supplied hot tea, The Dragons go past, The twins, Julian and the Dragons come back. Mr and krs, Tibby volunteer the information that they were about to trawl up to Stansgate but will give us a tow.
Their son gets out wind speed indicator - 30 mp.h.+ Gradually legs become
stronger, John sits in Spree to steer, Mast got spiked by bowsprit and praise/ compression crease is main reason for not sailing back, Very grateful for tow.

Dragons noted that Richard and Julian went wrong side of Doctor. So
victory to Dragons but well done H1073 (and Charles) and 21563 (and Jill).

Course (15 miles remember) was completed in 1 hour 52 minutes by the Hornet which isn't bad going,

Bleanor.

remember,

shortening to 1 lap. The clouds on the horizon began to cover the sky and the wind got up and up. tee

HORNET MAINSHEBT

Marconi 5.C. wins at Saltcote

The first leg of our annual team race against Saltcote S.C. took place on
Saturday 13th May in very hot weather and rather light airs. The Marconi team
had a resounding success winning both races. The Marconi team consisted of Peter Darney and Jane Cottam, Peter Jennings and Geoff “white and Richard and Charles Houlding.

The start was the usual running start and the Marconi team got away well with spinnakers up as the gun went except for Peter Darney who pulled down his centre plate instead not being conversant with the Hornet rigging, but he soon found the right rope to pull! Saltcote spotted this and ganged up on him pinching
his wind from astern. But some good sailing soon saw Marconi lst, 2nd and 3rd and the finishing order was Jennings, Houlding, Darney.

The second race proved more interesting with some unusual wind changes.
Saltcote brought in their reserve boat and vigourously swopped sails around from boat to boat, but larconi's once again held the first three positions at the last but one buoy with only a beat left} to complete to the finish against a strong tide, Unfortunately just prior to this the Houldings lost their spinny pole overboard which was kindly picked up by one of.the .trailing Saltcote boats,

The wind then completely dropped and boats began drifting stern first away from the finishing line. The wind then changed direction through 180 degrees to a run and slowly began to puff again, Peter Darney was quick to spot this and hoisted spinny much to Saltcote's amazement and soon built up a small but useful lead on the three Saltcote boats, Sailing right up the middle of the river against the tide he managed to tempt the Saltcote boats into mid-stream leaving the Houldings and Jennings on the lea shore out of the tide. Here the Houldings soon began to loose ground not being able to hoist their spinny. Peter Jennings then moved over to attack from the leeward side luffing and eventually sitting on the windward side of the second Saltcote boat. By now the Houlding brothers had also moved into mid-stream behind the fleet and had the nerve to ask for their Spinny pole back from the Saltcote boat. Surprisingly they thravit in the water and the Houldings sailed up and picked it. up.

Peter Darney was just ahead of the first Saltcote boat and to windward covering him well with only inches between them at times, Peter Jennings was using similar tactics on Saltcote's second boat slowing it down by Geoff “hite alternatively filling the spinny and then letting it flap, allowing. the Houldings to catch up, eventually drawing alongside Peter and Geoff tO windward, As soon as they were level Peter drew away from the Saltcote boat and the finishing order was Ist Peter Darney, 2nd Saltcote, 3rd Peter Jennings and 4th Houldings.

The return race will take place at liarconi's later in the year.
H.Ornet.

A SHORT DINGHY CRUISE

Dave Polley (GP14) and Fred Partlett (Wayfarer) arrived early at Stansgate on Saturday the lst July for their planned cruise to Clacton, and at 0830 hours both boats were apparently ready to sail, Dave, with his wife and daughter was soon off on his way down river but Fred's mainsail jammed and, mindful of his capsize the previous week end, he lowered his mast and found the luff groove choked with Blackwater mud, By this time Dave had come about to see what the hold up was but, re-assured he set off down river once more. Fred and Linda with Alan Polley as the third crew member left the hard at 0900 hours confident that they would overhaul the GP14 before very long. However, it was soon apparent that Dave was continuing to draw ahead, and nearing Bradwell he came about once more and asked Fred if.he had been fishing!!

Once out of the Blackwater howeverthe Wayfarer surged ahead past the wreck buoys off Mersea and on to the Inner Bench Head, The wind was S.5, about force 2 although the forecast was force 3 and it made for very pleasant sailing all the way up the coast, Fred 'hove to' in the Wayfarer when he was getting out of touch with the GP14 and finally ‘rounded Clacton Pier at approximately 1230 hours shortly followed by Dave, who found himself gicing with a Shearwater whose helmsman showed a lack of courtesy by sailing too close,

With the oe bagscads the party had lunch and lazed for a while in the sun. As the tide turned, the boats swung broadside on and it was decided to put them on anchor, it would have been wiser to have anchored on arrival as by this .time both’ centre boards were jammed with ania) Snune=4 and it was quite a task to free them,

Although there was an. onshore wind, getting off was no problem and the boats were soon away watched by a large number of holiday makers lining the promenade above. Running and reaching, the trip back lasted 2 hours 40 mins, and was very enjoyable. All voted it a successful ‘day cruise and hoped for another like it.

P,o, Subject to weather and suitable tides ‘this trip could ‘be repeated, If anyone is interested would they please contact Dave Polley or Fred Partlett both of whom would be pleased to go again,

Fred Partlett.

HALLAM TROPHY JULY 8TH and 9TH
The Marconi Sailing Club held its first open meeting for 16 ft National Hornet Class dinghies last week—end., The meeting was a resounding success With 25 entries from all over the South Bast, including entries from Deal, Kent, Pinner, Middlesex, Dunstable, Beds and Addlestone, Surrey.

The programme consisted of four races with any three to count, two races on the Saturday and two on the Sunday,

Saturday proved disastrous for some, with a force 6 wind blowing only
seven boats managed to finish and the rescue launches were kept busy.

The second race on Saturday was postponed until the following day in order to eliminate any further damage’ to boats. E,Styles, DownsS,C. Kent finished first and this win eventually clinched for him the overall championship, even though his next best position on the Sunday was 3rd place.

Sunday was promised force 3-4 winds becoming lighter towards the end of the
day. This proved to be the biggest understatement of the week, for half way through the third race on Sunday the wind completely died and only 14 boats managed to finish-against.a strong tide. . In this last race Simon Darney, who only needed a place in the first 4 to become the overall winner, was caught out in the light airs and eventually finished 5th, which, although it made him equal on pointsto the eventual winner, actually gave him second place when the discarded race was taken into account to decide the tie.

No dinghy .won more than one race out of the four and only two points|
separated the first 5 boats,

The ex~Commodore T.W.Hallam, gave the Trophy, and eight other prizes in stainless steel were presented by the Commodore's wife, Mrs. J, Bigden. Results: Ist &, Styles Downs S.C.

LAYING-UP SUPPUR AND DANCE

Wednesday 8th November 1967. 7.0.pm for 7.30.pm at The Heybridge
Country Club.

Owing to the fact that the Company can no longer accommodate Dinner and Dance functions at their Canteens, we have been forced to find an alternative venue for this year's Laying-Up Supper and Dance. Places in the Chelmsford area which can cope with large numbers sare very few, but by personal contact we have been able to go to the Heybridge Country
Club,

For those who do not know, this club is very attractive, and the Manager has personally assured me that he intends to do his utmost to make it an excellent evening. It is realised that Wednesday is not the most popular day of the week but we had no choice of date and were very fortunate to get any booking -— even when booking November last year, They hope, if we wish to go there again in 1968,to be able to give us 2
Friday booking,

This brings me to a vital point -— as we are now moving away from our own Canteens we will be unable to fit in any people who "decide to come at the last minute". The tickets will be on sale from approximately
lst October and the last day of sale will be Friday 3rd November - we are
sorry but there can be no exceptions to this as we are committed to the Caterers on that date for our final total. There is also.a definite table plan to be drawn and it will not be possible to alter the seating
after that day, so will you please let your Ticket Agent know with whom you wish to sit.

Last point - the price will be 32/6. I know this is more than
we have charged in the past but then we were helped by the very low charges made by the Company Canteens — for which we were all most grateful. We are still trying to keep the price as low as possible "at the same time giving value for money" and we look forward to seeing as many of our members as possible on that night.

The number will be strictly limited to 230 - so please do get
your tickets early - (pay days are 4th October and lst November).

John Barnard.

FROM THE R.Y.A. The Use of Flares and Rockets—

30th June.

We have learnt from the rescue services, which do so much for yachtsmen, that a great and growing number of unnecessary sorties have been caused owing to the misuse of flares and other distress signals.

It must be borne in mind that although a white flare is not an official distress signal, even such a flare may cause alarm for two reasons. Firstly, Some white flares which have been stored for some time give off a pinkish glow, Secondly, there are a great many occasions when a boat in distress, which has no official signals, burns petrol soaked rags or Similar material. For these and other reasons even "white" flares cannot be ignored by the rescue services.

There have been many instances where sorties have been made and either no vessel found, or information has been received that the flare was a private signal to a wife or friends.

Yachtsmen are also reminded that a fire-arms certificate is required for 2a Verey pistol,

It is earnestly hoped that you will discourage your members from using any flares or other signals except when in distress. If, however, flares are to be fired as finishing.signals at the end of a night race it is earnestly hoped that prior warning of this possibility will be given to any distress and rescue control centre which might be alerted by the coastguards, the police or members of the public.

Donald and Barbara Woods wrote this interesting log a few weeks after their trip to Holland earlier this year and earned themselves a "runner-up"
award, :
APRIL IN HOLLAND

The aim was to open the 1967 season with a cruise in company to Rotterdam, through the Dutch waterways and back via Flushing. The craft are "Jayess", a Snapdragon 23, skippered by Dr. McKendrick Marconi 58.C., and "Ruadh Sgeir", Content 29 skippered by Ramond Sutton of Creeksea Y.C. Barbara and I shipped with Raymond, Ingrid and their 17 year old son, Ian.

We left moorings at Creeksea 1030 hrs, April 5th. just before high water and with a N.E., Force 6-8 romped up to Harwich under working jib only, averaging 6 knots. A beautiful sail marred only by the tragic loss of 4 gallons of home brewed beer, This split from an inalequately chocked off polythene cask which fell and split. Even in a G.R.P boat you can't reclaim it from the bilges! We picked up a mooring just below Pin Mills this is an error inaN,E. gale as it was damnably uncomfortable all night. We Should have anchored down river ‘bélow thé big Left hand bend to get shelter.

April 6th was a very: rough day redeemed by getting two "pinlets"
7 pint containers) of beer at the Butt and Oyster. These keep seven weeks unopened and three days after opening. They travelled well. There was no Sign of our consort in Harwich harbour. By 1800 hrs although the forecast was gales,-local conditions were still and calm. It seemed possible we were in the centre of a depression; however the 0200 hrs. forecast was N.f 5-6, We still had a flat calm so off we went under motor leaving moorings 0310 hrs. April 7th. Time being short it had been agreed to ‘motor/sail if speed fell below 4 knots.- By ‘0600 hrs all bar two of the crew were incapacitated by sea sickness and remained so for the duration of the crossing, the main trouble being a peculiar lumpy sea left over from the gale.
The wind came up just before 0600 hrs and at 0845 we put in eight rolls to
the main and sailed thus until the next day. By 1000 hrs. the Galloper L.V
was abeam, log 32.2 wind NE 3-4, 090 Magnetic 4 knots. -At- 2050 hrs. the
loom of the Goeree L.V. was detected log 78.6, 086 M, wind :NE 3-4. At this
point I had expected to see only the Goeree light, but the coastal lights also were clearly visible, in particular the 3 sec. ela of Neauimapelte light house. ne Red

A slight brush, with a — was solved by ating ihe spreader lights to the navigation and masthead lights. This worked very well but apparently means "I am fishing but my green light has gone out", About the same time I was puzzled by searchlights on two small vessels to starboard. These kept sweeping the sea in a random fashion.. In.fact they were probably fishing boats indicating that they had gear. lying out on-the side to which the lights were directed,

At 2150 hrs April 7th the wind fell lights; attempts to use the engine were unsuccessful: it would run for a few minutes then stop sounding like a petrol fault. Petrol was appearing at the carburettor and water was circulatings further than that-we.could not go in the dark. The wind remained variable and light-but the tide was north going early flood and we had been set to the south of. the intended course. About midnight we picked up the whistle buoy of the Schouwen Bank so knew exactly our position. Later we had a transit of the L.V and: the Bollen wreck. buoy as we travelled slowly up the coast mainly with the tide. There is an overall general .N.i. tidal set up the Dutch and Belgian coasts. By 0230 hrs the Goeree L.V. was abeam and by 0400 we were off the Hook. 7 ‘ “=

The chart shows 3 buoys about 5 miles offshore plus a cryptic light on the northern mole end "Fl W.R, 3sec'"' None of us had been there before. We had about 33 assorted lights plus plenty of traffic. Vihat do you make of a stationary, close cluster of four yellow lights, two vertical fixed, and two horizontal flashing? Or of a flashing white light, the size ge frequency of a buoy light but which appears and disappears with no recognisable periodicity and possibly in a slightly different place?

io Bm

There was a cluster of five huge white arc lamps over-lying a just discernible
long darkness - a steamer's lights came out from shore towards this,
disappeared behind the arc lights and reappeared as she stood out to sea. The end of the mole? Meanwhile a steady stream of shipping was passing astern of us and sailing straight for the shore. The absence of crashes and bangs indicated they knew what they were doings: we didn't so stood off until dawn. This plus the turn of the tide revealed that the cluster of white arc lights were distribited along the 10,000 ton freighter in the anchoring area N.W. 5 miles of the Hook mole, The yellow lights were attached to a small vessel moored a mile further north and doing goodness knows what, That hide and seek white flashing buoy is a manually operated light on the pilot boat. The key and virtually only light to the Hook is on the end of the northern mole and flashes 5 times white followed by a
3 second red light, The North Sea Pilot 1963, P.194 line 20 does not
state this, and the chart is not explicit.

With daylight the engine problem was tackled, as it turned out very wisely, The petrol tank of stainless steel in the cockpit locker had never been given petrol except through a fine filter funnel. None the less the filter chamber at the base of the tank was choked with corroded filth very difficult to remove. Once this was done the engine ran well and none too soon, The North-Sea Pilot recommends caution attempting the Hook in an onshore wind and I can endorse this. The wind had fallen light, the tide was ebbing and the seas were something better experienced by daylight. For two miles offshore and between the mole ends they would have been most alarming to have met abruptly in the dark. Indeed on the southern mole was a 7-8,000 ton Greek freighter plus its tug where they had clearly been cast a day or so earlier, A chastening sights; without the engine we Should never have got in against the ebb with only a light following wind.

At 0900 hrs April 8th we entered Berghaven 119 miles and 29 hrs out
of darwich. This little harbour on the port hand just inshore is easily found, but, being an official herbous for lifeboat etc only yachts in transit are permitted to use it. ve Stayed to breakfast and tidy up, everybody having rapidly revived from seasickness. Customs came and cleared us and told us we were the first of the season.

Leaving Berghaven we motored up the Nieuwe Waterweg leaving Eurpoort and its new canal over to starboard. It is a fascinating if dirty trip; so much industry and so many ships and barges. Here we made our first acquaintance with the extraordinary fact that a°1,000 ton barge lightly laden or decks awash could pass 20 ft away at 8-10 knots. and yet the disturbance to our yacht would be less than that from many an. outboard motor boat on the Blackwater. This is just as well with the colossal amount of traffic otherwise the canal walls would suffer and life on a cruising yacht would be intolerable. How it is achieved with blunt blows, slab sides and much power I do not understand,

We passed the Schiedam Y.C to port, ctlearly identifiable and looking very attractive, and went on to the Royal Yacht Club de Maas arriving
1200 hrs., log 133.7, This lies on the port hand soon after sighting
the bridges of Rotterdan, We were made welcome and had we thought to pack white ties could have joined in their Fitting Out Party that evening, We shopped and admired Rotterdam, especially the traffic free shopping precinct and grand multi-halled arts centre.’ (Memo to lady crew members: the Y.C lies in the heart of the seaman's mission areas, Don't do ag oyrs did and go ashore alone unless prepared to handle unusual situations!). After 22 hrs on my feet qT Slept well,

Sunday April 9th. Still no sign of our consort. We looked at
T.S. Mercator, a Belgian barquentine’ some 40 years old with more than
140, 657 sea miles of training voyages behind her. - Following local
knowledge we-left for Willemstad. The major bridges open only at fixed times on weekdays and often not at all on Sundays. So instead of going on through Rotterdam to Dordrecht we turned to take the Oude Maas. Traffic on the canals keeps to the right, so when turning left you make a good wide circle to avoid. getting a ispee portside amidships, as it comes out of the branch canal. The bridges lift in response to 3 hefty toots on the horn; they rise just far enough to permit your passage and

25 Be

and a bit more, The journey from Rotterdam to Willemstad can be accomplished by 3 routes, Attention should be paid to the bridge opening times and the state of the tide. We followed the Oude Maas under three bridges, ignoring the Spui and skirting Dordrecht on the west side by the Dordsche Kil. Even on Sunday we met barges six abreast in the canal including a phenomenal monster of at least 3000 tons capacity, consisting of a square box propelled from the rear by an articulated power unit. Heaven knows how it steers in a cross wind! However there is absolutely no cause for alarm in amongst all this traffic such is the perfect discipline. ‘Je then came out on to the Hollandsche Diep and had a gentle down wind, down tide evening sail, on a vast deserted sheet of water, with negligible evidence of civilisation, which brought us to
Willemstad at 1620 hrs, log 167.2

The Pilot says Willemstad has only 4 ft of waters; we drew 4% ft.
However, at the Royal Maas a member had told us he regularly took his 40 ft long 54 ft draft motor sailer in. In fact against the quay there is only 3 ft L.W.S. but six feet away from the bank there is enough water at all states of the tide. The harbour is tiny: so is the town and it is. charming. There are several boats concerned with dyke works using the harbour and it is possible to tie up to one of these, We walked round the town's ancient stellate moat, practically stepping over sleeping ducks and swans, who pay scant heed to humans, We then adjourned to "Het Wapen van Willemstad" on the quay and enjoyed what the skipper described, with massive meiosis, as a "memorable steak" highly to be recommended and extremely reasonable, We slept well that night tool.
