Security
and Clubhouse Keys

Many of you will have noticed that the Clubhouse now has a large safe installed and that a general tightening up of security is taking
place.

In future members will not have access to many pieces of Club property or to Store Houses except through the Officer of the Day. Access to the Store Shed (Pete's Palace) is now strictly forbidden and any members with property in that shed should remove it immediately. Members requiring storage for oars should contact Terry Hallam at Baddow for details of arrangements. The boatshed is about to be cleaned up and members are asked to remove their property to prevent its loss.

As from 15th July the door by the bar in the Clubhouse will be bolted on the inside so that keys for that door will be useless. The new back door by the Gents changing room has a new Yale lock and is openable with new Yale keys. You may hire a key for the new door for 5/- or exchange your old key plus 1/6 for a new key. New keys must be applied for personally at the Clubhouse on 22nd, 23rd June or at 7 [redacted], Chelmsford (evenings). John Witter holds the key book and members will be required to sign an undertaking that the key is for their own personal use only. The 5/- is a hiring fee and the key must be returned if you leave the Club. The loss of a key should be roper- ted to John Witter immediately.

These actions to make the Club and its property more secure result from the findings of a Working Committee and the co-operation of all members is requested to make the scheme work. Please ensure that the Club is secure when you leave and that no unauthorized persons have entry to the premises. If in doubt of a person's right to be at Stansgate do not hesitate to challenge, and then report the details to any Club Officer or Committee Member.

Members are also reminded that there is a limit to the number of guests they may introduce to Stansgate and that guests may only arrive accompanied by the members introducing them. Visitors names etc. should be entered in the Visitors book with the member's signature, whether or not they enter the Clubhouse. Employees of the Marconi Group of Companies should not be introduced as guests but should be enrolled as members of the M.S.C. and M.A.S.C.

Sailing Club Main Committee.

Associate Member Fees

A chance remark made in the Club house recently, has prompted me to 'clear up' the misconception by some of our Associate Members that the club should be in a better financial position since according to our application form Associates pay 300% more in Membership Fees than #'ull iiarconi Members.

This is just not so, and should one have studied our Balance Sheet, it would have shown that 2 gns. of every Assoc. Fee (excluding moorings, Dinghy Park etc.) is paid into our parent body the M.A.S.C. whereas the full member pays 9d weekly. Thus the Full Facilities of the M.A.S.C. are available to every Associate member. The only difference between FULL members and Associates is that an Associate member cannot have voting powers or introduce Guests to the Club.

An Associate can join any other section of the M.A.S.C. by paying the appropriate section fee and there are 24. sections to -choose from, to name a few:-

Dramatics, Tennis, Bowls, Squash, Jilliards, Dancing, Auto and
Archery.

In addition there is a very good discount scheme and compre- hensive lists of shops are available. A visit to the Main Club in Beehive Lane, Chelmsford, could prove worthwhile should you wish to dance in the evening or just sit and relax in the lounge.

J- Bigden.

‘Team Race with Osea Sailing Club - 8th June, 1968

On being awakened on Saturday morning by a steady drip-drip as rain overflowed the gutter outside my bedroom window, I began to wish I had not so gallantly accepted Julian's invitation (if you can call it that) to crew for him in the team race against Osea Sailing Club. However, by the time the two teams had arrived at Stansgate at about 10 o'ciock, the rain had eased off and we were to have a very pleasant afternoon's sail.

Osea team with their Commodore Alf Lepper as team captain, had been able to bring only one Enterprise with then, borrowing two Enterprises from the Marconi Sailing Club members. Nothing daunted, they ventured to inform us, in the nicest possible way of course, that they would ‘beat us hollow’. Nothing like giving an air of confidence!

At the first gun all six boats were off to a very good start and it soon became obvious that competition would be very keen. One beat up towards E mark off Osea Island, boats kept well spaced apart, keeping a wary eye on each other with crews (especially me!) not daring to say a word lest we disturb the concentration of our helmsmen:

Having rounded the first mark successfully with Eric Pike of
0.5.C.
in the lead, it was felt that some team action was in order, and Julian decided to indulge in a luffing match, forcing Eric Pike (in his own boat) and Gordon Cooper (in John Witter's boat) in towards the Osea shore, thus causing them to lose the advantage of the tide. Terry Roper (M.S.C.) with Timny Bigden as crew seized this opportunity to shoot up to first position which he retained for the remainder of the race. Also along this stretch of water between E mark and No.1, A. Lepper (in Bob Miller's boat) and Norman Beadle with Charles Hewlett as crew. changed positions, with A. Lepper coming up to fifth position.

8
The second lap of this race saw Terry Roper of in the lead with Eric Pike and ourselves following; close together. It was not until I found myself being drenched that I realised we were planing through to leeward to overtake Eric Pike on the reach past
the club. By this time the wind had changed direction slig:tly - in
fact it seemed to be very changeable during the whole race.

So the first race finished with Terry Roper (1i.5.C.) in first position, Julian (.S.C.) second, Gordon Cooper (0.5S.C.) third, Eric Pike (0.S.C.) fourth, Norman Beadle (M.S.C.}) fifth, and Alf
Lepper (0.S.C.) sixth, giving Osea 13 points and Marconi 7S.

The next race was not to be so successful for the Marconi boats. Alf Lepper sailing Bob Miller's boat got away to a very good start, keenly followed by ourselves with Osea boats in third and fourth positions. At the first mark A. Lepper was one boat's length in front of us so we immediately tacked away on to a port tack. As A Lepper did not tack to cover, this left us with clear air and on the next tack we were able to catch A. Lepper who was then on port. Positions changed frequently amonyz the rest of the fleet with the final result for the second race being ourselves first, A1f Lepper second, Gordon Cooper third, Terry Roper fourth, Norman Beadle fifth, and Eric Pike sixth. This gave Osea 1l points to M.S.C's 9%.

These results give Marconi Sailing Club a small lead of 63 points, but it will be interesting to see the final result after the return meeting at Osea on Saturday, 14th September.

On behalf of the club, we would like to thank all those who took part at this meeting and John Witter and Bob Miller for kindly lending their boats. Thanks also go to Peter Batey who joined in the good humoured spirit of the afternoon as Race Officer.

Jill Godwin.

Stan Campbell (Gallant 53) was surprised to find very little water two hours after low water (the earliest recommended time for a
boat like the Gallant). His chart gave 1 - 2 ft. of water at low
tide. However, Stan has checked the latest chart, No.1975 and the channel now dries out from 1-4 ft. He suggests that another two hours of flood should be allowed by anyone else making the passage.

The Trans-Atlantic Race

At the time of writing this article, we ‘land-dubbers' in the southern half of the country are enjoying bright sunshine and very warm weather. Meanwhile close to the Azores we have lone yachtsman Alec Rose nearing the last stage of his solo trip around the world, and I hope we shall see him safely in harbour during the next few weeks. However, he too at the moment is enjoying fine sailing conditions due to an anti-cyclone centred around the Azores.

Much further North in Mjd Atlantic there is a low depression causing
storms and gale force winds of Force 8 - 9, which at this moment are
venting their fury upon the competitors of the Single Handed Trans- Atlantic Race, news of which most of us follow closely through the medium of the Press and B.B.C.

2
One of the competitors undergoing this trial of pure guts, determination and skill is Noél Bevan of Elliott Automation, a member of the hiarconi Group of Companies.

Noel Bevan has taken seven weeks leave in order to compete; he is, in fact, the oldest competitor in the race and has the oldest boat 'iiyth of Malham', that famous old Lady of many ocean races. She was designed by L. Giles soon after the war as a "flat out" Class II Ocean Racer and as she was a conspicuous success, her design had a profound effect on the design and appearance of many yachts that followed her. She has an excessively blunted bow and a chopped off stern. She is not (it is said) a pretty.boat, but a workman-like boat that will stand up to any amount of hard sailing.

'Myth of Malham', rigged as a Bermudan Cutter, goes 14 tons TM. ,
is 59.7 ft. long with a beam of 9.2 ft. and draws 7.00 ft.

Noel Bevan has odds of 10 to 1 against winning the race, but the mere completion of the passage will be, I am sure, a wonderful Sense of achievement. I think he intends to complete the course, "go about' and come straight home again in order to meet his seven week deadline. I.sincerely hope he is successful. and that you receive this article in time to follow the race at its conclusion.

Perhaps one day you may have the opportunity to meet Noel .. Bevan and hear of his experiences first hand.

Jack Bigden.

DINGHY CRUISE

1968

Dinghy cruising can be very rewarding and this is a short account of one such cruise.

From Stansgate we set off in a 'Wayfarer' to make our way round to Burnham via the Ray Sand Channel. As already reported in Navigans the water in this channel is now conspicuous by its absence at low tide and although we went through some two hours beforehand we became uneasy of the situation. Close hauled on port tack with the channel marker bouys to starboard the centre-board touched bottom and we sounded our way through using the jibstick as a sounding pole. The centre-—board had to come fully up with only 12" under the boat, -and our leeward drift became pronounced, however we slipped past the southern buoy and the depth rapidly increased to 4 feet as we headed for the "Outer Crouch".

Admirals Hard (Near Enterprise Sailing School) at Burnham is a public hard, freshwater and toilets are available nearby and the soft mud gives a good berth for dinghies, we spent two nights there, With the boom set up in a crutch the boat cover made a good tent, open at the transom. The Wayfarer has room for an air bed each side of the centre—board case and these plus sleeping bags ensured that we were snug and warm.

From the Crouch we sailed up to the Colne in poor visibility and having to rely on our compass most of the way. The wind was easterly force 4 plus but in the shelter of Colne Point the water was calm and we beached, baled out, dried out and then set up camp for the night. The wind had not abated by next morning and we headed for Brightlingsea rather than risk the east coast.

Brightlingsea, for those who have not visited there has an excellent public hard and causeway both of which are tended by a hardmaster, Freshwater is available from tap on the hard and there is "The George" nearby for those who prefer something stronger. Unless you have a heavy anchor don't drop your hook off the hard and expect it to hold, you will need a pick-axe to penetrate the bottom, Don't be misled by the local fisherman's dinghies that appear to be safely at anchor there. At low water it can be seen that all their anchors are "on" the bottom and not "in" it, they rely on the weight
only.

Our next port of call was Wivenhoe not a readily accessible frontage and the sailing club hard is not very wide. The river is very narrow and large vessels navigate the Colne beyond, particularly up to Hythe Quay and it is tricky dicing with these comparitive monsters in narrow waters, However, we spent a pleasant day in and around Wivenhoe but returned to the estuary and camped once more near Colne Point before our return home to Stansgate.

The trip lasted seven days and all six nights were spent aboard and throughout the week only two of our meals were purchased ashore in a cafe, We had no newspapers and used the radio for weather forecasts only. The cost of the holiday was virtually the cost of the food and we both spent less in additional items than during a normal week at home.

If you feel like trying your hand at cruising don't forget the Club cruise on July 20th,

Happy sailing.
Fred Partlett.

I recently sent = letter to a well known Norfolk sailmaker for a quotation and delivery promise for a boat cover for my Mirror Dinghy. Back came the reply and a delivery promise pe {--10 days. sag Gives

to tie the cover on temporarily’ to~protect my boat, to write a letter to the makers to complain of their omission, and to offer to put the eyelets in myself, if they would send me enough to do the job. Back came a gem of a letter which I quote word for word

"whilst we thank you for your letter received today, we regret most sincerely to note that we have omitted to insert eyelets to this cover. THE OVER FORTIES RACE

In some trepidation I got ready for the race and donned the horrible Mae West. It was a lovely day with only light winds so I wore only sun top and shorts, little knowing how I was going to suffer the next day with a very burnt back.

Never having raced before in any kind of race I hoped we wouldn't capsize or get stuck.in the mud as Jack is famed for doing.

Marjorie Allerton and Joan Gaskell were also racing for the first time and Marjorie said "Oh Con, what happens if we capsize", I said hang on to the boat and she said "which part", I replied the nearest and don't let go. Joan also had butterflies in her tum, I won't tell you how I felt as with Jack anything can happen.

Well we seemed to make a fair start what I saw of it, what with grabbing the jib sheets and falling over the = at ailloeaie “Seushe a glimpse of Norman in front and Dave Polley about level. We had a pleasant and uneventful sail to Heybridge (all dying for a drink at the "Jolly Sailor") which of course was the target. Norman beached on fairly solid ground but Stan, Tom and we got as near to the "Sailor" as possible. Knowing Heybridge mud of old I stayed put and told Marjorie to do the same until the men had pulled the boats in, Tom asked Joan to bring the anchor and she gaily got out of the boat and went into the mud up to her knees, It was quite a revelation to hear the crew telling the helmsman off in no uncertain terms, it's usually the reverses but anyway Tom and Joan washed their legs in the river and over a drink and sandwiches sitting on the sea wall good temper was restored.

After a short rest we started back with a starting signal from the rescue launch manned by Gordon Golding (coxswain) and Jack Reeves as race officer. By this time the wind had freshened somewhat and there were several boats moored and sailing. Of course Jack and I had to - get tangled up with a bow-sprit (fatal things for Jack). Anyway he managed to free us without ripping the mainsail and as the boat gave a hefty lurch I either leapt or fell onto the other side which righted the boat and Jack actually said "Well done".

ie all got away without further incident with John Hurrel in the lead in a Hornet and Norman next in a GP and believe it or not we kept third place all the way back and I believe came in second on handicap. ‘I think we all enjoyed it. Since then Marjorie has enjoyed several _ Sails with Stan in " Roxy Lou" so perhaps it might be a good idea to

have a few more events for us near middle age sailors!

Connie Bigtten.

Having had no experience of pursuit races, it was with some trepidation that I agreed to organise the dinghy pursuit rage which was held on Saturday 24th August.. For those who have not heard of this type of race, it can best be described as a dinghy handicap race in which ' the starting times of boats are staggered, so that all boats have an equal chance of being first across the finishing line. Therefore, with Peter Batey's advice and the help of a slide rule, the starting times for all dinghy classes that might possibly enter the race were calculated for various "corrected times” (to time thata GP would take to complete the course). Conditions on the day were fairly easy, with a light easterly wind and a strong ebb tide. A corrected time of 75 minutes was therefore set for the nine boats which wore entered for the race, As the starting times had been calculated on the basis that Mirrors would be the slowest competitors, the race officer ensured the presence of some Mirrors by pursuading three to enter (two had never raced before and had to be shown the positions of the marks!), Also entered were 2 GPs and four Interprises. There was quite a lot of crew swapping with Nick Bevins crewing for Ken, Sheila Crick for Charlie Hewlett (in Julian's boat) and Ken Stevens for Peter Crick. John Smith eventually managed to pursuade his wife Ann that she should try her hand at crewing in a race.

Since the staggered starts would present problems if the usual type of start was used a "Le Mans" start was introduced. Thus at 1500 hrs, three lNirror helmsmen were seen sprinting from the starting line at the top of the hard towards their boats, which were being held in the water by the respective crews. (The race officer declined to consider any additional handicap for age or infirmity unless birth or medical certificates could be produced in evidence). Course G was set, but starting by leaving mark A to starboard. It became obvious that some of the Mirrors needed to know more about the racing rules when John Smith was prevented from rounding A mark, at the first attempt due to an "outside" boat forcing him out of the way. ‘‘hen the GPs were due to start 15.5 minutes later, Nurray Todd in his Mirror had already rounded Breezy Point mark and was over half-way to Goldhanger Creek with his spinnaker helping him to puil away from the other Mirrors who were also well on their way to Goldhanger Creek. Of all three starts, that of the Enterprises was the most energetic, but Bob liller found, as he slipped and dived head first into his boat, that it does not pay to run too fast on seaweed. The Enterprises started 1.5 minutes after the GPs,

Once all the boats were on their way towards Goldhanger Creek, “Charlie and Sheila were already overtaking Joyce Reeve's GP (from where does Julian's boat get all its "go"?). By the end of the first lap, Murray's liirror was still leading but with Nick's GP hot in pursuit, leaving the other Mirrors being rapidly overhauled by the remainder of the fleet. When the Enterprises had round No.l conical buoy, it was noticed that some of them seemed to be creeping along the Osea foreshore before heading across to A mark. This was however apparently not crafty tactics, but because they thought that they were supposed to round E mark. Just before Goldhanger Creek was reached for the second time, Nick overtook Murray, but the rest of the fleet were now a long way behind, With the other Mirrors forming a rearguard,

In order to ensure that the race actually finished as near as possible to the set time (1631.30 hours for a 75 minute corrected time), it was agreed that the finishing line would be between a committee boat and a nearby mark, The mark so chosen would be the one to which the leader would be closest at the finishing time. It was fortunate that this mark happened to be A mark, as none of the rescue launches would start and the Fisherman had to be rowed out by the race officer and Stan Allerton, Due to a little trouble in anchoring, the committee boat (flying flag S from Do-Yot's whisker pole) ended up rather close to A mark, but the two "committee" members decided that the small gap would make the finish more interesting. ‘ith only three minutes to go before the agreed finishing time, Nick's GP crossed the line, with Murray's Mirror finishing not far behind. As Nick crossed the line, the race officer remembered that he had left his writing implements behind, and so he asked Ken to tell the assistant race officer, Edna Cooper to record the finishing order, There was an exciting moment when all the Enterprises seemed to be coming in together, but Charlie and Bob processed across the line in that order and only Arthur Hodges and Peter Crick carein neck-and-neck with Arthur squeezing through first. Joyce Reeve's GP followed the Enterprises and John Smith and S.Randal in their liirrors following quite a way behind her.

I think that I would be correct in saying that the competitors enjoyed the race as much as the race officer enjoyed organising it and so perhaps we might-have more pursuit and other novelty races in the future. How about holding them on those Sundays when there is no other racing arranged?
C.K. Cooper.

BARBECUE - Saturday 3lst August.

"Yell, there are beefburgers, sausages, lamb chops or a slice off
the lamb - with or without onion". I explained once more as I took the
proffered ticket,

"Ere... 2 beefburger, please — with onion"

I repeated the order to Chris allerton, who quickly filled the roll I held out with a sizzling beefburger and topped it with onions. Yes, our barbecue was under way once again.

Vie had spent-.the day making preparations, and now it was all happening -— the crowds had arrived, the band was playing, the bar was doing a roaring trade, and so were we, serving food to our eager customers. They were all hungrily eyeing the lamb, which after four hours on the spit was cooked to perfection. This was being expertly carved by Arthur, our butcher, who had come armed with a wonderful array of knives, aprons and hats, and a very solid chopping
block. ,

He had arrived early in the afternoon and promptly set up his block and started to prepare the chops, Around him the electricians
festooned the hard with an assortment of cables....Rod shinned up the
temporary "mast" of Number One rescue launch to fix a string of coloured lights and his assistant Jack and various members of the working party waited until he reached the "On to tell him that the "mast" was rotten.

Over by the barbecue Roger and black got the spit working, and in the band tent the girls, having recovered from their onion peeling session, were cutting the seven hundred rolls in halves, And then, there we were, filling and serving them as fast as we could, nearly roasting ourselves, as well as the meat, for Jack Bates kept the charcoal fires well stoked and glowing eel hot.
Everything went with a swing, for after a heavy shower in the afternoon the evening turned out fine and warn, though for those who were chilly there was a large bonfire on the beach,

After filling themselves with a large quantity of meat, washed down with plenty of beer, dancing to the Trad Jazz Band and toasting their toes round the fire, our two hundred and fifty suests finally departed, leaving the workers to pack up and revive themselves with a cup of coffee before going hone.

All except Chris Allerton, that is, who sank down exhausted behind the shed, and awoke the next morning to find himself still dressed in his apron and hat!

Roll on the next Barbecue!

Noreen Douce.

The Industrial Recreation Clubs of the U.K are having their second Annual Team Race on September 2lst.This year Marconi are sending a team comprising two Enterprises and one Hornet, helmed by Julian Bigden, Peter Jennings (Capt) and Terry Rope respectively.

Last year ten clubs accepted the challenger to compete for the Silver cup presented by Sir Bernard liiller, the Chzirman of the John Lewis Partnership. Gach club was allowed to enter two teams of three
sailing dinghies - any class was allowed. In the event, about thirty-six
lined up for the event. These cane from twelve different classes. By uSing the authorised handicap tables, they started at different times - the slowest first.

It was a beach start, the beach being the private one adjoining Brownsea Castle, the holidy club belonging to the John Lewis Partnership on Brownsea Island, The Castle's dining room was used for tea and prize giving at the end of the day.

To decide the winners, two identical races were held, one before and one after lunch. Each team only had to record the results of two boats, the results of.the two races combined giving the final placings. The contestants came from the sailing clubs of BBC, BlA, Decca, Laings JLP, Mullards, Smiths Industries, Vickers and Walls (Gloucester). Lloyds Bank were unable to make it at the last minute.

At lunch which was t.iken as a picnic on the beach, BEA 'A!' were leading with eight points, with JLP 'A' second with ten points and BEA 'B! third with seventeen points. The afternoon's race confirmed this form.

The teams of Decca, Mullard, Vickers and Walls not having two boats finishing in both races were unplaced.

We can't let BEA fly around with a sailing trophy for ever so Marconi will be after tracking it down.

INTERFLIRG RACE MonTING aT POOLE

The Marconi team arrived lnte Friday evening at Poole and made an early start on Saturday morning. We had to sail from the Royal Motor Y.C across to Brownsea Island,

The wind was around force 5-6 and several boats capsized. before reaching the island, The race officer then decided to postpone the race for 1 hour. Having travelled so far we were determined that the race should be held. Hence Terry Roper and Tim Bigden sailed round the course without any mishaps and the Race Officer was at last convinced that we could race,

There were 12 teams of three boats. Some teams threw all thejr eggs in one basket and brought 3 Fireflys or 3 unterprises or 3 Riveroats, whilst others split their team to cover all conditions such as the Cjvil Service whoswteam consisted of a Swift Catamaran, an Albacore and an Enterprise. The Marconi team consisted of Julian Bigden and Jill Godwin, Terry Roper and Tim Bigden both in Enterprises and Peter Jennings and Mick Turner in a Hornet.

The triangular course was badly sited as the first buoy was a fetch on starboard, the second buoy was a fetch on port and the dead run back to the start. The course was very short, about 3 miles, and this does not allow for any capsizing or mistakes in handicap racing.

A good start was made by Narconis and at the first buoy the only boat ahead of our team was an albacore. The next leg, the Swift Catamaran of the Civil Service began to catch us as the wind verred to a close reach,

The turn down to the finish was a nightmare with boats jibing, rolling from side to side and eventually capsizing, mainly due to running onto he sand around Brownsea Island. Julian was 2longside Peter after the first lap and on handle2p was well placed. Terry Roper capsized at the jibe mark which lost him very little time with transom flaps wide open he reached off at enormous speed and emptied the boat in next to no time
to finish 10th with Peter 12th and Julian 3rd,

The second race proved disastrous to Marconis with a similar course to the first race except that the tide was on the way out. Julian, once again in a very favourable position, broke his mast on the run but only had about 300 yards to go to the finish a commendable 10th. Terry broke his tiller and with only 6 inches left to steer with managed to finish also. Peter capsized when he planed full speed onto the sand which by now seemed to be just below the surface on all legs of the course and in places even above the surface. marconi finished 5th overall, despite the mishaps, with the Civil Service overall winners and BEA (last year's winners) second.
WA

The reception, tea and prize giving was in Brownsea Castle. The event was well worth while, and we hope next year to come back with the trophy.

SOME THOUGHTS ON TRAM RACING

This season we were "fortunate" in being accepted for the Wraysbury Lake S.C, Autumn Leaf Trophy. Sixteen teams were split into two groups
and within the group everyone sailed against everyone else - seven
races spread over one and a half days. At Stansgate that would be very grueiling. The shape of the gravel pit is such that the start and finish lines can be some way apart and in fact the lines are served by two separate race boxes so there is never a problem in finishing one group while the other group's starting.

Gravel pit sailing can be fun but there was too little wind for the liking of the Marconi team and their efforts on the Saturday were little short of disastrous. It should however be borne in mind that most Clubs we sailed against, regularly took part in team racing -— as often as once a fortnight -— and our team had not sailed together, as. a team, before. By Sunday there was more wind and the team were much more at home. They found that they could initiate instead of being governed solely by what little wind was available on Saturday.

wD

Their final race with Staines S.C. provided the first win of the .week-end.
While other peoples protests were being heard the wind got up a treat but by 3 o'clock when the lst semi final was due, the wind had lightened again. Beeston S.C. were beaten by Horning, and then Wraysbury Lake beat Hayling Island. Wraysbury beat Horning in the final in hardly any wind at all.

It is significant to note that both these Clubs are lake sailors and Wraysbury were on their home ground,

What should we do to get better results? lkntering Open Meetings wakes one up to the standard in other Clubs. It's all too easy to assume that the best Marconi people are "good". It's painfully obvious that in the company of others we are very mediocre, secondly for team racing practice is essential. At Stansgate the fleet spreads out very quickly and often there isn't anyone very close at a buoy. In team racing on inland waters there are always other people very close by and one has to know all the Rules. Putting other people out is a very important part of team racing. his sometimes leads to protest meetings. Our team were rather disturbed about the unpleasant attitude of some
of their opponents in this respect - it should always be done in a keen
but friendly manner. So .

As a Club we need to be more sure of our rights on the water and be prepared to stick to our guns and assert our rights. If this leads to protests so much the better, We'd all learn much more quickly, It's not just a case of who gets the points for that race but just as much it clears up some of the more obscure interpretations of the rules that enable the next race to be sailed without incident.

We came to the conclusion that enclosed water team-racing was a different sport altogether from the sailing we enjoy!

Jackie & Brian Bowsher's Summer Cruise to Holland

28th June to 14th July, 1968

PART 1 — PREPARATIONS

We decided on a sailing holiday in Holland around the beginning of the year, though the idea had been in the back of my mind ever since buying the boat four years azo. The Roger Pilkington Small Boat books, and articles in Navizans and the yachting press. had painted such an interesting picture of Duropean waterways that we decided it was really time to see for ourselves, We were interested in Holland largely due to the reports from friends telling of the excellent sailing facilities there, and of the friendliness of the sailing fraternity.

First thoughts were to sail to the Hook and make our way up the canals to Amsterdam, spending sometime in the Lake of de Kaag north of Leiden, which is a popular sailing area, and is reported to be the Holland of one's imagination, However, the prospect of the North Sea crossing from Imuiden was somewhat daunting, and so we decided to explore the esturies of Zeeland, and to make our landfall in Belgiun.

AS previously our longest trip had been to Pin Mill, and ny navigation had never had a real test, I started reading navigation books to more purpose. For a North Sea chart, we chose the Imray, Laurie, Norie and Wilson chart No, %30, which covers Harwich to the Hook and Dover to Calais, and has large scale plans of the main ports. I drew magnetic north iines acro7s the chert, so that I could use a Douglas protractor, as this method or course plotting seems to me the most convenient in 4 small boat with ro fixed navigation table,

A suitable p’ lot book proved to he a big problem, as the Admiralty books do not give approach and harbour information in yachtsman's terms, and it was a fortnight to our holiday before I discovered a book newly published by Adland Coles entitles ‘North Sea Harlbcurs and Pilotage —

Calais to Den Helder! by FE,
th.
Delmar-Morfan.

Undoubtedly, the single most importaus factor in a sex crossing is the weather, and in ozder to try to urderstand how it changes, I received 2 Daily Yeather Report from the Met, Office for the three months before our holidszy. This is an exsellent service and cost 15/- for one month and for three months. each report consists of four sequential weather -harts, drawn at six hour intervals and covers up to 06,00 the previous day.

Our boat ‘Natasha' is a 20 foot fibre-glass Vivacity, which is moored at Stansgate, To prepare for the trip, i fitted the boat with electric navigation lights to be can from the car battery and provided two independent sources of ligh* for the compacs, After a good deal of metal—bashing a 14 inch radaz reflectér was produced, which could be shackled between the shrouds and hauled up to the spreader. I ran a life-line along each side ieck and made some plywood covers that could be fitted over the ports, as 1 felt these to be weakness of the design, We bought a barometer, and life belt light, and changed the Seagull Centry Plus for a Penta 5 h.p. outboard. Although the Seagull had always performed faithfully, the small tank was very inconvenient, and the high noise level extremely unpleasant, particularly as we might have to use the engine for a long period. In addition, the Penta has has a lighting output that can be used for battery charging.

We already had a pack of mini-flares, but decided to get some more powerful rocket-flares, and a couple of white hand flares to be used as ship scarers. By this time we had used up 211 our holiday money, and therefore had to eat baked benns for a ronth,

Jackie and I were to spend the holiday by ourselves, but we thought that it would be sensible to have two men for the crossings, and we were lucky in having a friend Denn:s Taylor who was very willing to help.

On one of our sailing weekend, we checked the steering compass against the hand bearing compass on various courses, and found no disagreement, It was as well to check this, as we had found that
‘ ; to 0
the outboard in certain positions could cause an error of 20°.

As we had no real experience of night sailing, particularly in traffic, we decided to have a night run down to the hiedway, but unfortunately a complete lack of wind meant that we only reached the Whitaker Buoy. However, some lessons were learnt, as it was an extremely black night and impossible to see the unlit buoys, which became quite a hazard when entering the Colne later on. I therefore determined to get a much more powerful spctiight, which additionally, would be a good ship scarer,.

A week before our holiday I telephoned the Customs Officer at Maldon, who noted that we were going foreign, and said that if we would ring hin on our return, he would gladly come down to Stansgate to give us clearance, However, he suggested that we might get 2 quicker clearance at Brightlingsea as there are more men on duty there.

We planned to sail at 09.30 on Friday 21st June, and with Stansgate high tide at 10,30 would have the best of the tide out of the Thames Istuary: We decided to make for Ostend, as Dennis could easily fly back from there to his home in Southend. Allowing twenty hours for the crossing, we would make our landfall at down, and having the advantage of being able to see the powerful Ostend light, and also be able to enter the harbour in daylight. The only disadvantage being that we would have to cross the shipping lanes at night.

Although the week started well, the weather gradually deteriorated until the forecast at 06.40 on Friday was S.W. 4-6, due largely to a depression north of Scotland. I rang the London Yeather Centre who told me that the situation was likely to get rapidly worse due to a depression forming west of Ireland, and that gale force winds were likely on Saturday. ve waited until Saturday, which produced the promised weather, and as Dennis had to be at work on Monday, we realised that we muss postpone our trip. ve were bitterly disappointed, but fortunate in being able to delay our holidays for a week, though we felt somewhat sheepish in going back to work on the Monday, as in the eyes of non-sailing people, it kad beéa a fine sailing week-end,

I used a Met Pad for recording the radio forecast information, and using this, was abi to construct a rouga and ready weather map, which was particularly us.cul when telephoning the Weather Centre. During the following week I listened to the 14.00 forecast each day, and found them extremely gloomy, with high pressure over the Continent and a procession of wave depressions crossing the country. .Friday was a day of torrential rain ard high winds, and I felt the depressions were crossing me as I rang the Weather Centre after work. Much to our
amazement,
the forecaster was optimistic, and said that the present depression would be clear by late evening, and that we should have at least 24 hours of light southerly winds, before a deep depression of 984 millibars started to effect western districts. Not able to believe my ears, I wang the Mildenhall Weather Office for a second Opinion, and they confirmed the situation and said that the cold front was crossing them et the moment,

I phoned Dennis, and we were all down on the boat by 21.00, the wind having died completely. ie deflated the bow section of the Avon dinghy and tied down the dinghy securely on to the coachroof, not realising that it would remain there for the rest of the holiday. As high tide at Stansgate was not until 03.30 we decided to have 2 short sleep, and I set the alarm for the 02.00 weather report.

COMMODORE'S REPORT 1968

The Marconi Sailing Club'is now one of the largest Clubs on the River Blackwater and possibly the cheapest, taking into consideration the facilities available to members.

The Club membership is ever increasing, in fact by 80 in 1968.
Consequently it is inevitable that the duties of the Officers and Committee become rather demanding,

It is envisaged that there must be changes in our outlook and administration for next year and with the much needed co-operation of members it is hoped that we can ease the situation by delegating some of their duties. For instance, a Dinghy Park Secretary will be appointed thus relieving our over-worked Sailing Secretary of allocation problems and an Hquipment Officer will be required to administer Club property. Member volunteers will be required to undertake the maintenance of Club Boats, trollies and radio equipment. Further help will be required in the bar, With race marks and on the rescue launches and Club Houge, A rota of Race Officers will be included in the 1969 programme,

tx

There must be many of you, who though not prepared to stand for Committee, would be pleased to-undertake some small task on behalf of the Club, To ensure that we can all sail without that 'guilt' complex, I appeal to those members who would like to offer their services to put your names forward to any Officer or Committee member please.

Early in the season we were able to complete the work on the approach roaé and although the cost exceeded our original estimate, it must be agreed that it was money well spent, The response for donations was good,
but we did not reach our target figure. Many members, gave far above the minimum figure but there were far more who gave the bare 10/-.
However, in order to start the 1969 season with a clean sheet your Committee have decided to 'clear' the balance from Club funds.

The social- account and aspect of the Club has declined during the season. I did however receive’ some encouraging reports on the Laying—Up Supper. I would like to take this opportunity of thanking Robbie Simms for the help he gave me in the organisation at such short notice.

We have no nomination for the Office of Social Secretary for 1969, . consequently our #o¢ial programme will have to be severely curtailed, unbess of course we have a member who is prepared to take office. Should anyone be interested I wovld -be delighted to hear from him — or (since preparing this report the post-has now been filled).

Mr. Underdown has continued to give sterling service in his 20 hours a week.to the Club. I am sure he is one of the Club's greatest assets.

Regarding our Security of Tenure at Stansgate I cannot at the moment Say any more than you already.know, You can rest assured, however, that as soon as I know of any major developmerts, steps will be taken to inform you all,

In conclusion I would like to say that in 1969 with the much needed help and ¢o-operation of our members, we shell together continue to seek security, sunshine and sailing for 211 at Stansgate in a happy family environment.

I thank you .
Jack Bigden — Commodore.

SECRETARY'S 3REPORT
Committee meetings have in general been held on the first Monday of each month and committee members attendance have been fairly good.

Sub-committees were formed to deal with the various activities of the club. ‘In some instances it was hoped that these would have been more successful. In particular the Clubhouse sub-committee was restricted in its activities due to lack of finances; early in the year it was hoped that we could purchase a wooden building for a new gent's changing room. However, the response to the "road fund" did not meet expectations, so this and other proposals for Clubhouse facilities had to be shelved. SATLING SECRETARY'S REPORT 1968

1968 has seen an increase in the number of boats in the Club, 166 dinghy
and 44 cruiser registrations were made compared with 114 dinghies and 44 cruisers last year. Among the dinghy classes there are 30 Enterprises,
30 GP14's, 19 Mirrors and 13 Hornets. A few more helmsmen have entered
races but not regularly, so that in the points series the number of entries is nearly the same as last year, However, inclusion of the reorganised Helmsman of the Year series brings the total number of race entries in 7 closed events 10% above last years figure.

The Cruisers have not been able to run any of the Barnacle Series and the only races were those in the Regatta including a fairly successful race for the Maldon Yacht Club Silhouette Trophy.

The Open Hornet Meeting, ably organised by our fleet, was again a successful occasion and appears to be established in the Hornet Association's programme. The timing of this event one week before the Regatta was an aid in securing Hornet entries in our Regatta.

The Regatta during the Spring Bank Holiday was an excellent dinghy event, but the Cruiser side was disappointing (It is thought that the Cruiser Cup would be better held at an ordinary week-end). Trophies raced for were the Enterprise Triple K Cup, the GP14 Commodore Cup, The Fleetwind Designer's Trophy and a new Gem Trophy for Graduates and there were good entries in the Hornet, Finn, Snipe and Mirror classes. My thanks go to John Witter who undertook the secretarial work of the Regatta,

We were successful in the Hornet Team races with Saltcote S.C and also the Enterprise team race with Osea S.C. The Hornet Invite Series with Stone S.C. got off to a good start but interest slackened towards the end of the year,

Only one week-end (14th-15th Sept) had such bad weather as to prevent Sailing but a midweek gale in July damaged several moored boats.

-5-

The reorganised Helmsman of the Year series went well but it seems that 8 weekends may be too many and next year the 8 races could be kept to 4 days. The dinghy cruise in company wnd the pursuit race were both enjoyed.

The two main rescue launches have been used for many rescues — some
from serious situations - but neither boat has been completely satisfactory
and on occasion the 14' with outboard has had to be used.

Brazil has been used less this year possibly because there are other boats Suitable for tuition including one owned by the Apprentice Association,

In general the mooring situation has been satisfactory but there have been 2 few mishaps particularly when the gales in July and September revealed one or two inadequate moorings, My thanks go to Pat Black for dealing with the allocation and positioning of moorings.

Several race marks were lost this season and a new set will be BES Some materials have been purchased but were not used this year,

I should like to thank Richard Benwell for being Race Officer on 2 number of days and to others who undertook the job at short notice on other occasions, It has not been easy to get race officers and rescue boat crews this year and we were recommending that a rota of members prepared to do these duties should be included in next seasons programme.

I have enjoyed much of the sailing secretary's work but have not had time at work at E.E,V to contact people (through the external phones) and confirm arrangements for each weekend. Hence I have come to face the fact that something or someone Will be missing at Stansgate and as the season progressed it became something of a chore to make the visit. In these circumstances I do not wish to continue as Sailing Secretary and I hope we can all try to make my sucessor's job as smooth and pleasant as possible.

P.H. Batey.

PART 2 of BRIAN BOWSHER'S SUMMER CRUISE

THE CROSSING

The forecast was 5.1-3. The barometer had risen to 1013, and by 03,00
we were on our way, with the genoa and main pulling gently on a faint breeze from the At the Bench Head we ran out the log, and as the wind had died completely started the outboard, which was to run till noon. The Spring Tide was now ebbing at it's peak, and by 06.00 we were at -the Wallet Spitway, and 07.00 saw us at the Sunk Beacon, having set a course via the
N.E. Middle and Barrow No.3. buoys.

For tidal information on the Thames Estuary I used an Admiralty Tidal Atlas, in which I marked in advance the actual times of use for each page. I kept an hourly log of the barometer, wind and log reading, and on the chart I marked the time, log and new course-at each significant point, be it actual or dead-reckoning. I found it convenient to keep the hourly log time in terms of the tidal reference time, and could then quickly tell the tidal set to allow when plotting a position.

From the Sunk Beacon, which is on the N.B&. edge of a drying section on the Sunk Sand, wé set a course to take us midway between two drying sections on the Long Sand. This seemed to me the most direct course to take to Ostend, but at low tide there is very little water, and I would not have attempted it in bad weather. While crossing the Sunk Sand we monitored the echo-sounder, partly to avoid running aground, but also alias to note when we had reached the Black Deep. This appeared with a sudden jump of 40 feet and we found ourselves crossing in front of two large tankers coming out of the Thames, I checked their bearing against the rigging and noted that we would comfortably pass ahead, but the bone in their teeth could be seen distinctly, The Black Deep was marked by buoys, but as our chart was not, they were of little use navigationally.

At 08,10 the echo-sounder made another dramatic leap, and we were crossing the Long Sand. It was now near low tide, and being the peak of a Spring Tide, we were down to Chart Datum. However, in crossing the sands we never recorded anything less than 10 feet, although there were several 5 foot depths on the course line. When the echo-sounder showed deep water again, we had réached Knock Deep, and we set a course to take us between the Middle Knock and South Knock buoys, which are about 2 miles apart, At 10.10 wé picked out the South Knock, and declared ourselves in the North Sea.

We changed over from the Thames Estuary to the North Sea Chart, and set a course to the Fairy Bank Buoy, using the tidal diagrams incorporated hr in the chart. The buoy was 26 miles on, and although the vishbility was good I must confess I had little confidence in picking it up. However, the West Hinder Light Ship was 8 miles beyond the buoy, and would be easier to find. ;

Since leaving the Bench Head, we had found no wind at all, and the sea was a glassy calm, but around noon a good sailing breeze came up from the South, and thankfully we were able to stop the outboard motor. Until then the sky had been overcast, but suddenly the clouds dispersed, and we had a perfect afternoon, Jackie made some lunch, and being well fed and content, we basked in the sunshine, while the boat furrowed on, rising and falling on a gentle swell. All weather symptoms were good. The barometer had risen steadily to 1020 and was still rising, and the weather. forecast suggested that the S.E. of lngland was coming under the influence of the high pressure over the Continent, while the deep Atlantic depression was taking a more northerly course. At 15.00 we were crossing the South bound shipping lane, and an hour later the North bound traffic appeared. Luckily the traffic was light, and we never found ourselves in the embarrassing position of being run down. Much to my amazement at 16.10 we sighted a buoy to starboard, It was very indistinct, and a running fix put us 2 miles to the North. Assuming this to be the Fairy Bank Buoy we set a.course for the West Hinder, which we passed at 17.45, giving and receiving a wave from the crew, From the lightship it was a three mile hop to the East Dyck buoy, and a further eight miles to the Middelkerk buoy. The wind now began to lighten until none remained and we were forced to start the outboard again.

a) -7-

The tidal current off the Belgian Coast behaves very stangely, as the tidal set makes a complete circle every 12 hours, and I found it useful to refer to the tidal diagram in Delmar—Morgan's Pilot Book.

From the Middelkerk, the buoys are spaced at about 2 mile intervals, and it was just a case of buoy hopping into Ostend. However, it seemed the longest part.of the trip, as the coast was in view for about three hours, and until the last hour, never seemed to get closer. Approaching the Binnen Stroombank buoy just outside Ostend, we pulled in the log line which had recorded 87 miles from the Bench Head.

It was just getting dark as we approached Ostend and I switched on the navigation lights, There were quite a few fishing boats about, and a couple of ferries came in, which were the first we had seen, I would have worried about entering Ostend at night had it not been for theexcellent Pilot Book, — which gave such good pictures and information, that I had no doubts, The incoming ferries turn round half a mile outside the entrance, and then enter stern first, and it is important not to try to squeeze in ahead of then, There are traffic signals on the end of the N.E, breakwater and it is advisable to obey these if there are any ferries about, though the local fishing boats do not seem to worry.

Just as we came up to the entrance we received the go ahead signal, and we ran along the S.i/. breakwater, until we reached the first break to 2=starboard which is the entrance to MontZomery Dock. Turning to starboard inside the dock, we found ourselves at the North Sea Yacht Club pontoon, and were lucky enough to find a vacant berth there. The time was 23.15 and we moored with our bow to a buoy and our stern to the pontoon, and then stepped ashore for a quick stroll round the harbour to get our land-legs, before climbing very contentedly into our sleeping bags.

On Sunday morning we woke up to a clear blue sky, with the nine o'clock
sun already quite warm. We flew our courtesy Belgian ensign, and, in common
With several other yachts, raised the yellow Customs flag, only to find that
Sunday is a Customs day off.

The North Sea Yacht Club overlooks the yacht basin, and we were made very welcome there, We had a drink on the verandah and watched the ferries docking just passed the entrance to Montgomery Dock, and noted the flashing light that warns those in the harbour not to venture out when a ferry is on the move. The harbour at Ostend is delightful, with ocean racers and day boars huddling together with gin palances in the deep well of the dock, while the fishing boats bustle about feeding the market in the main street
above.

Later that morning we took a walk around the town, and were fortunate in seeing 'The Procession of the Blessing of the Sea’, This is a most interesting and colourful procession, involving perhaps 400 people, many of them wearing the most elaborate costumes, 'Kach year the various groups recall the gratitude of the fisherman to God, the Almightly, Creator of the Sea, their struggle for their livelihood and their hope of returning safe and sound to harbour!

By now it was so hot that we were glad to escape into the cool shade of a restaurant on the seafront. This was a mistake however, because, ajthough the food was good, the price made us thankful that we had brought so much food with us. Dennis had to fly back in the afternoon, and Jackie and I spent the rest of the day lazing on the beach and swimming to keep cool. That evening we ate on the boat, and just sat in the cockpit watching the harbour.

To the Mediterranean - Dr, Donald iicKm@mdrick

les Iles d'Hyeres (the Golden Isles) lie about 25 miles east of Toulon, We had previously taken our five topper there and decided to repeat these highly successful holidays in 1968, The 'Jayess' is a 23 foot bilge keel Gnapdragon in which we have cruised widely during our four years of ownership, On this occasion our i. consisted of myseli, my wife Evelyn, Sally (daught er?
and Sally (friend) - two pretty (sic) inexperienced but keen 15 year olds,

To reduce the driving in lrance we cross Newhaven- Dieppe. Tovwing with a 2.2 litre Ensign estate has proved no problem in the past but on the way home this year we boiled excessively on some of the hills (the car had done 80,000 miles!) so it has now been replaced by a Land Rover for future trips.

We left Arkley (Herts) at 1400 hours on Thursday August 8th. With a large tow one gets very favourable treatment on ferries and is among the first both on and off, jrriving in Dieppe about midnight we pulled off the road on to the ample parking space on the front, climbed into our sleeping bags and slept in comfort until the morning. At midday on Sunday (24 days latex we drove into Toulon where unfortunately we were met by the police with a message from home which meant Evelyn had to fly home imnacdiately.

£%-0800 hours on iionday morning we were expertly craned into the water in a matter of minutes. There was a strong mistral blowing so after getting the mast up we motored to a more protected berth at the Societe des Regattes where we lay in comfort head on to the pontoon. On Tuesday the mistral still blew. This is a favourable wind for the Golden Isles so the Sallys and I set off with the working jib end 8 rolls, bathing costumes instead of oilies -in the force 5 plus, a not unusual combination in this part of the world, We were in fact over-reefed so after five miles I shoook out the reefs and we
made better progress, ie had a good run to Porquerolle - the main’island
in the group - where we turned into a small sheltered bay. There we dropped
the hook, took a stern line ashore to a convenient tree in the accepted manner and all thankfa dived overboard to get cool,

We spent three weeks in this delightful cruising ground. If you like hot sun’ and warm bathing in deep blue crystal-clear water with the bottom visible at-ten fathoms quite often and three fathoms always, if you like watching the wondrous ways of the French dropping their anchors at full
speed ahead - always done bt the wife with the husband at the tiller giving
advice at twenty to the dozen, if you like
1 and quiet
in idyllic
scenery, then come to the Golden isles, ic visited the mainland occasionally but always were thankful to get back to the tranquillity of the Islands. Porquerolle has numerous beaches and even more simall rocky bays most of which can only be reached b3 boat. Fort Cros is the pretticst of the three islands where the gold of the rocks is really striking in certain lights. It has
two main bays - Port Cros and Port hian - one of which will amost certainly
give protection against the prevalent vands of the summer, although during this holiday they were each to give us their measure of excitement, There
are no stores at Port itan but the third island - Levant - is only a mile
away. This-‘is the island famous because it favours nudism, where indeed one feels rather overdressed in the grocers if one is wearing more than a G-string. ut the nudists attract the tourists and’we only visit Levant Tor shopping.

We had a lot of wind this year. {Two nights stand out. The first was in Fort Man which is a deep bay where we were sheltering from a strong notrth-westerly which nevertheless bounced off Levant and appeared to blow straight in. During a very restless night nearly all of the 40 odd boats dragged. The Jayess, an Atalanta and a Hillyard did not, no doubt because English yachts tend to carry much heavier ground tackle than most of the French boats in the iicditcrranean,. The other night was one we will long remember and occurred soon after Evelyn had rejoincd us in Porquerollc. We were back in Port Cioss end at anchor on a rater dull évening. Evelyn and the Sallyshad gone ashore with friends from another boat and I stayed on board because I did not much like the look ci the sky. The storm began dramatically just as the shore party were returning and this very crowded anchorage turned into chaos in séconds. age.n we were protected, this time

=o

from the 'Levant' which is the notorious casterly of this reri of the world, so there was really nothing of séa. Yet the gusts laid us well over and this is the only time in my sailing career I have renoved while at anchor well lashed down foresails, boarding ladder and everything else possible from deck in order to reduce windage. During the next four hours the ventimeter repeatedly registered force ten, and this of course in a sheltered anchorage. The storm took its toll of at least one boat in the area and I believe there was another also with loss of life, We were safe enough in Port man although we dragged at first like everyone else, We ended up well secure with 25 fathoms of chain on the main, 20 fathoms on the kedge and a 100 fathoin line to a bollard ashore. One of the many interesting features of this exciting evening was the sudden appearance of f'rogmen who dived repeatedly in 30 feet of water leading boats to better holding ground and finally apparently hooking anchors on to rocks on the sea bed.

We love the sun and the bathing from the boat. the sailing is mixed - plenty of wind at times but the engine is often required for passage making
as there is no help from tides - a deficiency more than compensated for by
the pleasure of anchoring in three feet of water on any sandy beach. A Snapdragon is an ideal type of yacht for the Mediterranean with its large cockpit and airy cabin. There is always plenty of room for sunbathing and a lilo aft of the mast is a favourite spot whether sailing or at anchor, Whatever the wind it is always possible to get shelter and there is now a good harbour in Porquerolle for those who like to be in port at night. We don't too many people, too much noise but worst of all no pro-breakfast swin, Except when the wind is from the Mast, which is rare, there is almost continuous
sun, .

The Mistral blew hard at the end of our holiday as it had at the beginning. It usually eases off a bit at night so we sailed for Toulon at 2300 -hours on September Ist. It was a pitch dark moonless overcast night and we had a fairly wet: beat back so I was glad I had been persuaded to put in our oilics byEvelyn ('just in case') as I had wanted to leave them at home. The Jayess was on her trailer by lunchtime on Monday and we were home in our beds in Arkley in the carly hours of Friday 6th, The journey is no problem, indeed it is very much part of the holiday (once we came home vis Paris to the constermation of the camp sité in the Bois de Boulogne). We would be very happy to supply details of the practicalities to anyone considering a similar holiday.
We will certainly be there again next summer.

One of the Merlin-Rocket class's carly classics was a Sussex coast meeting when a race was started before the first mark was laid. The boat carrying the buoy could not overtake the fleet and the leaders set sail for the only speck on the horizon, a fisherman snoozing over his rod,

After the first six ierlins had roared round his lonely outpost the fisherman decided to up anchor and row to a niore peaceable spot.
Pursued by the lierlin fleet, now buzzing like a horde of angry bees, the worthy angler rowed fast. Meanwhile the confusion and rapid changes of course among the dinghies allowed the boat carrying the first buoy to make progress and soon the tail-enders espied it laying the mark,

That the last shall be first was again »vroven as the back-markers peeled off from the fishermman-chasing contingent to round the buoy. Like So many nautical orienteers, the various Sailors, by now scattered around the horizon, pursued their chosen turning marks. 411 were ultimately reunited ashore in a fierce argument quelled only when the sailing committee belatedly. declared the race avahdoned,.

PAR? 111 of Jackie & Brian Bowsher's Summer Cruise
Ostende to the Veersemeer

On Monday the Customs men appeared, but when approached they seemed more concerned about any bonded stores that might be needed. I made a mistake here, because I decided to wait until later, and in fact Ostend was the only place we visited where it was possible to buy bonded drink for a yacht,

We left for Blankenberg at Midday, thereby having the best of the tide along the coast. “We had wondered whether to go inland on the canals to Terneuzen, but it was so hot again, that we felt it would be cooler at sea. ‘The breeze was very erratic, but it was only eight miles along the coast, and we sailed along leisurely, reaching Blankenberg in three hours. We will always remember the blast of heat at the harbour entrance, It was quite withering. Looking back at the dreadful weather of the summer, we realise our good fortune in having the two hottest days of the summer during our holiday.

Slankenberg has a very attractive little harbour behind the sea front, and it is hard to imagine that 18 years ago it was completely silted up. The entrance is still shallow, but once inside there is a reasonable depth of water by the pontoons, The town is a fairly large seaside resort, and appeared rather uninteresting during the day, but in the evening everyone was “gut- strolling along the streets and gazing in the busy shops, and we were content to~spend a couple of hours walking to and fro with the crowd.

Tuesday .came with a slightly overcast sky, which soon cleared, giving
us another hot day. The wind was $8.2 and we set sail at 11.00 for Breskens, 20 miles along the coast. We kept close to the shorc, apart from giving the Zeebrugge iuole a wide clearance as suggested in the Filot. The wind coming off the shore gradually increased, and presented our travelling Compansion, a Westerly 22, with e FIND plastic canoe, and shortly afterwards gave us an enormous beach bail.

4s we approached Holland we come under the influence of the flood-tide into the Wester Scheldc, and with the wind now 8.4 we made good progress reaching Breskens just after 16.00, Soon after we arrived a violent thunderstorm loomed up and we were thankful not to be sailing, but the rain soon passed, leaving a pleasantly cool and refreshing evening.

The yacht basin is new and most impressive, holding perhaps 390 boats on pontoons, but possibly due to being nationally run, it seemed a cold and uninteresting place to us. There were plenty of people about, but everyone kept themselves to themselves, and I do not think that we spoke to a soul. There was a toilet, shower and a couple of men's stand-ups in @ block house overlooking the basin, and we could only think that the harbour was for men only, as there appeared to be no other facilities
about.

We noticed that our yellow flag was the only one flying, and after three hours we took it down again, Having become somewhat relaxed by the Customs! approach in Belgium, we felt that we had done our bit in entering Holland, but learnt later from friends in Rotterdam, that the Dutch view things differently, and that immigration clearance is essential. Had we entered Flusing we would have been cleared quickly, but «8s breskens has no Customs Office we should have reported to the local Police Station.

In the evening we walked around the quiet fishing town and it seemed a thousand miles from Blankenberg. All the streets were incredibly neat and tidy and the living rooms of the houses, with their lights on and curtains undrawn, almost forced you to look in at the tidy rooms full of flowers and pot plants,

That night the wind blew hard from the west, causing a tremendous din in 500 masts.In the morning thewind was Wi, from a clear sky, and there appeared to be quite a séa ruming with the wind against tide. We donned waterproofs and with working jib and four rolls in the main we stood out of the harbour. Directly outside a wave shot up and broke across our

se
er

shoulders, which shook us considerably and added safety harnesses to our attire. It was only a three mile hop across the Schelde to Flushing, but with a three knot tide rushing out, it took us over an hour in a séa that did not break on us again, but was extremely lumpy.

The Pilot book gave an excellent description of Flushing, and we had no difficulty in finding our way to the lock and to the Walcheren Canal
beyond.
a The eight
& mile journey
J up the canal was beautifullyiv calm and peaceful after the torment on the Schelde, At Middelburg a couple of lads in . a canoe, looking as if they had stepped out of Dickens, asked for a tow to Veere, We took good care of them, but along came a gin palace with wash in tow and completely ssturated the chap in front, inmuch to the other's
amusement,

We reached Veere at Midday, having passed through a lockitay I thought to be crammed to capacity before we arrived, but the Lock-keeper thought differently and somehow we were squeezed in. There is a small marina in the canal, but we went round to the town quay, where the Harbour haster put us alongside a 22 foot Dutch yacht.

Once a flourishing port, and now cut off from the see, Veere has become a yachtsman's paradise. The still waters of the tiny harbour, no longer troubled by tide and current, allow the friendliness of boat to boat mooring, and up above the tree lined ausy the old merchants' houses look out over the Veersemeer, and to the life beyond the seca wall that once was theirs, Above all stands the delicate Carillon tower of the Town Hall, and for two hours each day the iiunicipal Carilloneur plays for those with time to listen, Not only are the buildings picturesque, put the inhabitants also, with a number of women still wearing traditional Zecland costumes, and lending an air of unreality to the scene. It really is a lovely town, and quite free from the comnercialisation of the tourist tra On the quay near the entrance to the harbour stands the old fisn i” which has now become the town yacht club, where the atmosphere was particularly friendly and we were made to feel very welcon:,

We were fortunate in where we moored as the Dutch couple alongside spoke excellent Unglish, end we found that we had much in common. We arranged to spend long weekends with each other next year, and hope to visit them at bulb time.

With the good company, werm weather and the chama of the town, we were content to stay there for the rest of our holiday, but we knew we met ? meet Dennis in Ostend or Kotterdam, and therefore reluctantly set sail again late on Friday afternoon. Not wishing to back-—t-wreck we decided to head for Rotterdam, and so we sailed to Zandkreck at the far end of the Veersemeer, This was only a short hot of nine miles and we pulled up for the night at the Deita Marina about a mile from the lock.

This was one of four lexrgc marinas that we saw on the Veersemeer, and being in non-tidal water, was able to use staging instead of pontoons, The Marina building not only had the usual toilets, showers, bar and restaurant, but also a launderette and an afternoon 'Kinder Creche‘ A far cry from the world of Veere,

Reviews Three Boys in a Boat by David Brook

Do not be misled by the title, to expect a new Jerome K Jerome; the book owes nothing to that style, though it is written with a light and humourous hand, It could as well have been entitled "Peter Pan on the Bast Coast" or "How I brought up three boys and became a yachtsman", and any of these titles would have been incomplete,

David Brook tells how he was faced with the job of raising three sons who lost their mother, without foregoing his own life and leisure if he could avoid it. Living on Mersea Island, he owned, and occasionally sailed, a "tore-out" 20-footer, and was a casual member of the W.M.Y.C., but would never have called himself a keen yachtsman, Indeed, he admits that he felt no affinity for the offshore-racing crowd that piled into the clubhouse when there was a big race, However, he took the boys on a cruise in a chartered boat up to the Deben, decided they would take to the water’ but wanted a handier yacht, and presently bought Kim Holman's prototype "26" fresh from a successful Burnham Week.

"Nymphet" showed her paces from the beginnings after reading of the chilly reception he got from winning his first major race in spite of a monumental (and public) bloomer, one may well feel there should be a handicap penalty on any Holman designed boat, to be doubled if it was Holman - tuned! I am sure the crack Class 1 crews must have felt so when they were pipped by a few minutes in that race,

There are some fine pieces of descriptive writing of heavy weather in the North Seas of ‘the inevitable squabbles of a family together (never sail close to leeward of a light vessel about 12 o'clock; the boys'. tongues will hang out agonisingly as you pass by the galley ventilation); of cruising in the Netherlands and the Channel Isless of EAORA races in calms and near-gales and blind-man's buff navigation of the Rays'n channel.

After "Nymphet" came "Bandit", Brook did not have the benefit of the magic touch of Kim Holman's tuning (only the design this time) and he obviously felt he was slow in getting her to sail to her ratings but <—~~4

offshore his growing williness made up for 2 good deal. No more would he be seen keeping out of the tide after it had turned in favour, (unless there was a deeper game to play). Though he does not admit as much, I seem to recall that it took Holman himself to put "Bandit" out of the money in any of the 1964-65 offshore races.

As for the "happy ending" you must read the book for that.
Anyone who sails the East Coast will surely eajoy it.

Jackie & Brian Bowsher's Sumner Cruise to Holland.

PART 1V
— Delta Marina to Rotterdam

Beyond the lock we would be in the tidal waters of the Easter Schelde, and it was important to judge the time of departure for the next day. We decided to leave at 06.00 in order to have the best of the tide up to Zijpe and Willemstad, but we would have to battle against the Easter Scheie for about four miles,

A friend lent us some recent Dutch estuary charts, and we supplemented these where necessary, and also bought some tidal charts, For general information we borrowed 'Inlend Waterways of Holland' and 'Thorpe's Yachtsman's Guide to Dutch Waterways' from Chelmsford Library, though these are rather out of date now.

We set off on Saturday in e steady drizzle, which soon developed into a continuous downpour. We passed through the lock with two motor yachts, end then battled into the wind and tide, The rain continued to get heavier until visibility was very poor, and it became increasingly difficult to pick out the navigation buoys. With several sandbanks around to worry us, we decided to call it a day, and so we ran back to the iuarina,. However, on this occasion the Lock-keeper did not seem inclined to let us in, and we cruised around for about three-quarters of an hour in the lock entrance, unable to moor due to the swell, until eventually a ferry appeared and took us through.

It rained solidly until 6 o'clock that evening, and we were cold, wet and miserable, but Sunday arrived bright and clear, and so we set off again in the early inorning. This time we could just hold a course for Zierikzee, and so fighting the tide was not such a problem, Due to the estuaries being inter-connected, the tides have unfamiliar ways, and at this time the Easter Schelde was flooding strongly while the Keeten Channel to. Zijpe was just on the turn, Just before the Oosterscheldebrug connecting Noord-Beveland to Schouwen Duiveland, we turned up the Keeten Channel, and joined the heavy barge traffic to and from the Zuid-Leéveland Canal. This is one of the main waterways of Europe and the air was full of the rythmic thud of diesels «S an unending procession of international barges passed us on their way to Antwerp or Rotterdam, These barges are also homes and have window boxes and washing lines, play-yens and swings, and to the children this is the normal way of life,

The wind slackened to a gentle breeze from the west, but with the tide building up its strength beneath us, we soon reached Zijpe, and turning into the Volkerak Channel, we ran gently on our way to Willemstad, The sun was shining, and seeing all the barges with their washing lines full, Jackie proceeded to fill the backstays with towels and tea cloths, and yesterday's wet clothing.

Just before Willemstad we went through an enormous new lock, which could swallow perhaps a 1000 Vivacities, and yet we were through in no time at all. It was interesting to compare this lock with the large lock at Veere, which took half an hour's hard labour by the Llock-keeper and his mate to bring a boat through. luckily, it is only the larger barges that use this lock,

Out of the lock, we turned into the Hollandsch Diep, and soon to starboard saw Willemstad hiding behind its fortifications, Running in beside the nole, and through the narrow entrance in the walls, we were presented with an unforgetable picture of this little harbour, jostling with boats, and overlooked by the newly-restored windmill standing four square at the end of the quay. The time was 14.00 and we were 50 miles from the impersonaility of the Marina and back into the world of Veere.

The Harbour liaster put us five boats out from the shore and added another two to us, leaving room further along the quay for the bigger boats that might come later, Scrambling ashore, we climbed up on tb the carthen walls, and watched the boats come and go, and noted the new marina being built outside. _ That evening it rained quite heavily and though the weather on the whole was good for the rest of our holiday, the heat-wave had finally passed.

that had to be judged carefully, so that we would reach Dordrecht at high tide, and thereby have the tide with us to Rotterdam. Just before the Moerdijk railway and road bridges we turned off to port into the River Kil, finally leaving behind us the broad estuaries,

and crossed t; - gunter-balanced bridges, looked full of interest. However,
