CRUISE TO THE SCILLY ISLES
by JOHN TODDS

Mor-An-—“Ira is an attractive 18'6" glassfibre sloop of the Hurley 18 class. During the summer of 1968 she was moored on the Helford River in Cornwall and I had sailed in her there a few times with Robbie, her owner. Friends of his had offered to lay the boat up in the Scillies, so when September came we made our plans for sailing her there. For both of us this was to be our first real cruise, since 311 our previous sailing experience had been gained in racing dinghies.

The channel pilot, when talking of the Scillies, speaks darkly of not approaching them without local knowledge or a pilot, but we decided that the warning was intended for larger ships than Mor-—An—Yra and made our pians accordingly. In order to arrive in daylight we would have to sail part of the journey by night, since we had a distance of about 55 miles to cover. ‘We'd decided to attempt the trip in one hop, since Penzance, the nearest good harbour to the Scillies, was still 40 miles from them, and about 30 from the Helford, It seemed that the navigation would be fairly straightforward, provided the visibility remained good, since these waters are well provided with light and bouys.

The weather forecast on Thursday, the 12th September, was for winds S to SW, force 3 to 4, with a slight chance of some fog early the following morning, we decided that this was a good enough forecast to enable us to leave that evening, so, after moving the boat from her mooring to Helford quay to load our gear, we finally got away at 19.30 hours under the power of the Seagull Century. As we motored down the river we hoisted the sails and heated some water which was put in the thermos for coffee later in the night. The outboard was then stopped, taken up from its well and stowed away, and the Compari dinghy was deflated and stowed in the stern locker. The evening seemed very quiet and the wind fairly light as we sailed out into the open sea. It was dark perhaps an hour after we had left, but our first mark, the Manacles bouy, was easily seen, flashing in the distance over our starboard bow. To the north of us lay the lights of Falmouth, with the lighthouse on St Anthony's Head nearby. One light out to sea puzzled us for a time. It was flashing red, but our charts Showed no bouys in that direction. Eventually we realised that we had been taking bearings on 2 helicopter from the Culdrose Naval Air Station, hovering out at sea on night exercises! At about 22.15 we came upon another yacht idling around. Having no fixed navigation lights we shone a red-shaded torch over our port side at then. This drew forth a startled oath, followed by the sound of a motor starting. The yacht sailed round ahead of us and then headed back towards Falmouth. During the interlude the moon had risen so that we could see her quite clearly.
She carried self-steering gear on her stern. Shortly after this encounter I took the helm from the skipper and continued what was by now a slow beat down the coast. I could see the dark outline of the land by the loon of the Lizard light beyond.

Slowly we passed the Manacles and then the light of Coverack. We had intended to pass close to the Manacles bouy, but because of the wind direction we went well outside it, in the eastern white sector of St. Anthony's light, As we tacked to the south we frequently passed from this white sector back into the red sector, which gave us a good position line, .

Eventually the Lizard Lighthouse came into view, yet we were Still not quite abeam of it when Robbie took the helm again at 02.00. The signal station flashed us, but the skipper couldn't make out the message, so we made no reply. Later we saw the station talking to other ships in the vicinity, and we watched them answer. ‘We had informed the coastguard of our plans, so the signal station probably knew who we were.

It was low tide when we reached the Lizard, and we were anxious to keep clear of the many rocks which lie off the shore. Ye finally decided we had enough water when we found ourselves passing rather close. to a couple of small coasters, which smelied warmly of diesel engines. From there we were able to set course, due west magnetic, for the scillies, about 40 miles out into the Atlantic. There had been quite a

TS

lot of shipping about just off the Lizard, but once past the point we were able to relax. The wind had gone southerly and freshened a little, So we were making quite good speed. I went below to try to get some sleep, but the movement of the boat made it impossible. I lay listening to the rush of water past the hull, and wondering if I felt seasick, till eventually I was dozing fitfully.

At about 0500 the skipper raised both the Longships Lighthouse, off Land's End, and the Wolf Rock lighthouse, Our course lay a mile or two south of the ‘iolf.

Day was beginning to break when I took the helm at 0600, and we were Still reaching merrily along with the wind from the south. Robbie went below and managed to sleep for an hour, which was no mean achievement as the seas were building up. The existing wave p2ttern had built up with the previous few days westerly winds, so the sea was getting lumpy. At about 0730 abeam of the ‘olf Rock, I said that I thought we should change the jib as I was having to spill wind. In a calm sea the wind ifgself would have been perfect, but with the waves rolling us the boat was becoming overpowered, so the skipper, encased in waterproofs and life jacket, went forward to set the storm jib. He had to do this sitting on the fore-deck with his back supported against the pulpit because of the movements. (Mor-An-"ra is also fitted with a taffrail and guard-lines, and these were certrinly essential out on the open sea), A little later, after watching a large liner head nobth between us and the mainland, we wound 2 couple of rolls down on the main to balance the boat better, Mor-—An-vra was still tramping xzlong, but she proved 2S very dry. We shipping nothing but a couple of dollops of spray on the whole trip, so there was no chance to test the efficiency of the self- draining cockpit. Considering the state of the sea this was a very reassuring performance from a pretty small boat.

The weather had been cloudy for some hours, but now the sky to the west began to look black and ominous as the Wolf Rock lighthouse slid past our starboard bean, The skipper wondered if a storm was brewing. To me the clouds seemed more like rain than wind, and as there had been no gale warning on the radio we decided to press on. Cornwall was gradually fading from view, and so our only landmark was the lighthouse astern. With no sign of our landfall, the dark sky and heaving Atlantic combined to produce a slightly frightening atmosphere.

We were constantly checking our compasses, for now we had nothing to aim for. From the cockpit the horizon was only a couple of miles away. Suddenly I saw a sleek blue grey shape leap clear of the water dead ahead - a porpoise. I c2lled Robbie, who fetched his camera, and soon a whole
school
of these creatures was playing around the boat. They were leaping and in twos and threes on all sides of us, and sometimes a group would play at cutting right across the bows as if to see which could get closest without being hit. ‘We could plainly hear them calling to each other in high pitched squeaks. It seems they were a good omen, in best maritime tradition, for by the time they left the sky had brightened a little, and very shortly afterwards we sighted the Scillices.

With our destination in sight and the wind still fresh on the beam our spirits rose, and we were able to enjoy the experience of Sailing at speed in rough water. Mor-—An-W/ra was a pleasure to handle. In the hard puff of wind just a quick pull on the tiller would be sufficient to hold her on course.

We saw one or two fishing craft, and one of the BHA helicopters on the Scillies run from Penzance flew close past us. We gave. him a wave, as he had come a few miles south of his course to look at us. A friend of the skipper works at the Scillies Heliport, and he watched our final twelve miles in through binoculars from the control tower. He later told us that a large submarine had surfaced fairly close astern of us, but neither of us had seen anything of it. We had, however, noticed a strange cloud formation ahead of us over the Scillies, which we jokingly called a waterspout. Only after our arrival did we find that it had been one.

We were making very good time, and we began to wonder whether we would beat the mail ship, "the Scillonion" into St. Mary's harbour, as she was due in at about 1130 hours. However, just a few miles from the islands we saw her corning up fast on our starboard quarter, and she passed us just before the Spanish Lodge bouy, the first of two red can bouys marking St. Mary's Sound. This Sound is the channel to the south-west of St. Mary's, and here we met 3 patch of the roughest water we'd encountered, probably a combination of wind, tide race, and wash from the Scillonien. We were only in it for a minute of two, and then things were much easier, The sun was by then shining brightly, and the wind had eased a little. I prepnzred the anchor in case we had to use it, and then took the reef out of the main. We sailed north past the Garrison, the westernmost point of St. Mary's and then east to the harbour, which faces north west and is normally fairly sheltered. Feeling rather pleased with ourselves at our first successful cruise, wo picked up a vacant mooring at 12.50, less than 17% hours after our departure from Helford quay. Robbie went ashore in the dinghy while I took off the sails and did a bit of tidying up down below. Having found the Harbourmaster, who pointed out an unused mooring closer to the quay, the skipper returned and we moved the boat under the outboard to the new mooring. After the continual movement and cloudy skies of our Atlantic crossing, it was very peaceful to be moored on calm clear water on that bright late-summer's day. It seemed unlike a Friday the
13th.

We'd eaten very little during our trip, so we went ashore for lunch in the "Mermaid", where we realized that we'd have to find our land legs again, The whole bar seemed to be swaying, even before we'd drunk our beer, ‘We spent a few days on the ishand, and had a really great time. The people were very friendly and the scenery was fascinating, especially to anyone who loves boats and water. On return trip, on "The Scillonion"
was a less pleasant experience - a force 8 northerly gale built up huge
seas which rolled the ship violently, and she was over an hour late getting back to Penzance.

SAILING 1969 WHAT'S HAPPENING

The Sailing Programme (Year Book) for 1969 has been revised to include more information about the Club and to make the programme itself more readable,

In the Programme the name of the Race Organiser (R.O.) is now included, This means that the named individual is responsible for the provision of (for example) race officers for an event, The idea is to relieve the Sailing Secretary of some of his responsibilities and to share the duties more equally between members,

The Sailing activities provided differ from last year. There are now two Points series, Spring and Main, for each class except the Hornets who retain their Invitation Points with Stone S.C and just one Points
series, - The people who are not ready by Easter will be able to compete
on equal terms later in the Season with those who have more time during the winter to prepare their boats. Sunday Points racing will be for Enterprise, Hornet, GP14, Mirror and Handicap fleets.

Another new Series is the Saturday Points, This replaces the individual Spoon Races previously held and is designed to make it more interesting and enjoyable as well as to encourage Handicap racing in which all Fleets may participate, If the turn out for this series is good, there is nothing to stop it being divided into two to provide Suitable sailing for both the faster and slower boats,

Sailing is scheduled to start on Easter Sunday with a Tuning-Up Race
and a Pennant Race. This is all dependant on all the facilities being ready by then and at the present rate of progress it is going to be very difficult to guarantee this.

The programme is at present with the printers and if we are not-- -- able to circulate it to Paid Up menibers with this Navigans then it will follow fairly soon,

LETTERS

Dear Mrs, Witter

As a relatively recent convert to sailing, I thought some of my - last season's experiences may be of some interest to other beginners. It is easy to be put off when hearing old hands discussing racing rules, navigation and so on, and this is a pity, for there is a vast amount of enjoyment to be had from sailing,

I bought ‘Quackers! -— Mirror 3284 last February, when I was still working and living at my home in Coventry. I joined the Mid Warwickshire Y.C and thus started out as a reservoir sailor. le sailed all year round ‘ there, weather permitting, and on one or two occasions, the rescue boat had to go out first to break the ice up!

Easter saw my friend John and myself in Torquay for a few days.
The harbourmaster was very helpful, although the harbour and slipway fee was a bit steep. The weather remained fine throughout our stay, but the wind tended to be rather blustery. On 2 relatively calm day we crossed Torbay to Brixham, where several people came down to the slipway and said they had watchéd our passage. I didn'r think anybody had noticed! The average speed was about 4 knots over the five miles or so across the bay, and outward bound on a beat it was a good trip. However, on the return journey, ‘the combination of a following wind and sea made poor John feel ill, I think he said he wanted to die or something! On the last day but one in Devon, I was sailing solo in the harbour when a gust caught me on the hop, and I had my‘first (and so far, only) ducking, I inadvertently let the boat get upside down due to my own incompetence. After tying the painter to a handy buoy I righted the boat quite easily. My plimsolls were in the little open fronted locker, and they were still dry. Fortunately, being Baster time, there were not too many people watching, but even so, at least two strangers had a joke on me the following day.

At the beginning of July I moved south to Marconi and within a week had joined MSC and brought the boat down. From this point on, all ny sailing from Stansgate has been single—handed, as I have not yet taken up racing, but more of that later,

4&n early sortie was the dinghy cruise to Brightlingsea, Although the
wind was light we averaged 34 - 4 knots if my memory serves me correctly.
‘The return trip almost developed into a race, and by taking a short cut through sone very shallow shallows, I found myself temporarily in the lead, I would point out here that this was not a bad risk to take since the tide was rising and the boat was only making a few inches draught with the centreboard up and the rudder about 2/34 up (the wind was following). A very friendly and interesting cruise ended with rain just es I reached the

the slipway.

In the summer John and I had 2 week at Teignmouth, and here I was soundly taught a lesson: carry a compass when on the séa, -One day I sailed along the coast to Torquay, which is about: ten miles, We stayed there the night with my relatives, and the next day I elected to sail back again while John went by road in ny car. It started off a fine day
but-
as I reached the furthest point from land, fog clamped down tightly and the wind dropped, The rolling motion and some apprehension caused me to have my only bout of sea-sickness -_it was horrible. <Anyway, I took ny bearings from the wind, turned 45° to port, and rowed most of the way home. I was never more pleased to see those towering cliffs of Teignmouth. So you see, even on such a short coastal hop, a compass would have:been useful, If the wind direction had changed, I might have been in trouble as the fog stayed down at sea level until about 9.pn.

The second week of our holiday was at Lyme Regis on the south coast, The fee for using the dinghy park and picturesque little harbour was 30/-. At low tide, the harbour dries out as far as the eritranee, and the wind direction made it difficult to get out of the narrow opening. However, once on the sea, the sailing was exhilarating. About a mile and a half to the east is Charmouth, where the offshore wind funnelled down between the hills, rippling the sea over 2 large-area at about force 5. The thrill obtained from beating up past this area and then planing back on a broad reach has never been paralleled in my experience, The boat became alive, and the centreboard hummed merrily in its. case,..This is sailing at its best. This is what it is all about. Jo sail.a small dinghy*in fair weather is fine, but in.a blow, and. on the sea, it is a tremendously exciting experience, It is a once 9 but one which must be tempered with prudence, for the sea may be a tranquill friend one minute, and it can turn sour on you the next. The wind too is a fickle ally, as the next episode illustrates.

One pleasant Saturday morning I left Stansgate at 8.30.am on “the falling ‘tide, crossed the Colne estuary and beached near Clacton for lunch Returning in the afternoon was peaceful in light airs, until it got tighter and lighter. By the time I had made Mersea it was almost non-existant.
Progress
was so slow that I had barely reached the estuary as the ebb tide began, so I was slowed even more instead of being carried upstream on the previous flood, The sun went down the light began to fade, and as.
Quackers passed Bradwell, darkness reigncd. The lights on three Bites anchored near the power atetion gave soac comfort, but as they receded astcrmn only a few tiny pin-pricks of light remained ahead. I judged thesc to be at Stone, and I was right. There was a pale moon highlighting the water to leeward, and from this I was able to fix my position in the river. Thus I had two approximatc bearings from which to-navigate. Stansgate was found without having collided with anything, and I felt almost guilty about coming home so late. Hauling the boat up the wet slipway on that heavy. trolley and in the dark was a trying job, as I was getting a bit tired after fourteen ‘hours in the saddle. Anyway it was accomplished by attacking the slope at an angle, and as I drove home ina: Saale to Writtle, there was time to ponder on the day's happenings. '

So, that was the season that was, very full and quite eventful.
There were many other trips both up and down the river, other than those I have related; following the Barge race, and Old Gaffers Race for example. The boat is back at Coventry waiting to be repainted and this coming Easter, with a bit of luck, the two of us will be back at Torquay.

The best way to learn is by experiéncc, although it is sometimes the hard ways Mistakes are bound to occur but so long as no-one is harmed, nothing is lost. Nothing ventured, nothing gained, after all.

Next season I shall break newground (for myself) by starting to race. So if anyone requires a crew in a dinghy or cruiser carly in the season, I shall be glad to oblige (Baddow extn.97).

I have no doubt that an experienced sailor would have made light

of my difficult situations, but I also feel that a beginner such as myself should not bc too tinid about cxperinenting and finding out his limitations. Sailing is a great pastimc, ané@ one which is becoming open to more and more people. And if any person has learned anything from reading this, then I am pleased, for I have achieved my objective.

Brian S Lidstonc.

CONTINUING JACKIE & BRIAN BOWSHUR'S SUMMER CRUISE
TO HOLLAND

PART 5 ROTTERDAM — HOLib

On Friday we picked Dennis up from the airport and prepared to leave for home at 08.00 on Saturday, 13th July. The time was chosen with reference to the Pilot Book which suggested leaving at three hours after Hook H.W. Before leaving England Demis rang Mildenhall Weather Office and this information, together with the radio forecasts, gave a weather picture of high pressure, areas over Germany and to the of Iceland, and a shallow depression of 1004 millibars moving slowly towards the Southwest Approaches, For more local. information I could have themed the Weather Centre at the Hook but the situation seemed fairly stable.

The 06.40 weather forecast gave S.E. 1-2 and by 08.00 we were on our
way with hardly enough wind to fill the sails, but with 25 knot tide thrusting.us along, we motored rapidly pest mile after mile of docks. We passed..a.tanker burnt and twistcd, with a gaping hole.in its side, and noticed the roofs missing from several houses nearby. Early the previous morning, Rotterdam had been shaken by a tremendous explosion which occurred when the ship's tanks were being cleaned.

In Rotterdam the river traffic had been light but as we approached the Europoort the shipping built up, and so we kept well over and left the super-tankers to themselves. Rotterdam's position as the premier port of Europe is quite possibly due to the small tidal range of only seven feet, but this does not mean that the currents are any the less. Twenty foot below the surface the currents can be twice the surface speed, which means of course, the ships can be affected by a five knot tide,

We reached the end of the Hook breakwater at 10.350 and noticed the turbulenec as this great mass of water met the sea, Et must be a terrifying place for yachtsmen in bad weather,

We reached the Goeree Lightship at 13.20 having by now cscaped the great mass of shipping surrounding the Hook, and with the wind non-cxistcnt we motored on a course due East, heading ultimately for a point midway between the Galloper and Outer Gabbard Lightships. These would be the first navigation marks we would sec in sixty miles, but during the day we were reminded that our course was correct by the occasional Hook to Harwich Ferry or by running into the waste thrown overboard from them, «at one stage the outboard came to a stop wedged firmly into a cardboard box filled with packing wool, and later, with the outboard running normally, imagine our surprise at coming to a gentle but complete stop, only to find a great wicker basket caught between the bilge keels.

By the evening there was still no wind and not the slightest movement in the sea, The weather report said that the depression off Ircland had dcepened slightly, but was still slow moving, and they forecast S.W. 4-5 in the Thamcs area on Sunday. With our 24 hour supply of fuel now half finished, it looked as if wo would need this wind to get us hone,

With night approaching, Jackie snuggled into the warmth of her sleeping bag, while Demis and I put on extra clothing and donned our Pitt. regalia of watcrproofs, life jackets and safety harnesses. Vié raised the radar reflector and prepared to switch on the navigation lights whenever a ship was sighted.

Bias

_ dust as night fell Fred the racing pidgcon, aiming for the mast head, hit the slack mainsail,.
and came tumbling down to the side deck. Recovering his self~possession, and: after a quick look through the port at Jackie sleeping down below, he settled down to wait patiently for dam,

Several times ships passed us at a distance, and we found it very difficult to judge their direction from the lights, but hopefully, I had visions of Officers of the Watch straining their eyes for the 5000 ton boat that showed so clearly on their radar screens.

At 03.10
we picked up the Outer Gabbard light but visibility was not good enough to catch it dipping, and thercforcewc did not get an immediate fix. Taking a running fix over an hour put us almost exactly midway
between
the two lightships, and soon afterwards we picked up the Galloper light. We then set a course for the Sunk Lightship, and wondered whether the, wind would come before: the petrol ran out.

At day-break Fred stretched, came down to the cockpit, checked the- COMPASS, and pen. flew ahtaigne off without so much as a nod.

! sus. keene 08.00 we felt a breath of wind and by 09.15 we were at
the Sunk Lightship and sailing. hard on the wind, with working jib and five rolls in the main, ive were doubly fortunate that soon afterwards the wind. backed :slightly enabling us to head down the Wallet,:and in addition we: just caught the start of the flood tide. It rained heavily© and blew:hard, but. the rain soon passed and we had an exhilarating sail in home waters again, 14.30 we ran into Brightlingsea to pick up the Customs having logged 119 miles from the Hook, and it only remained to “" pick up our’mooring at Stansgate to complete a really enjoyable holiday.

LONDON DINGHY EXHIBITION

8th - 9th MARCH

On Fred Partlett's recommendation John and I drove to the Crystal Bilace Recreation Centre (getting lost on the way) and joined several hundred, if not several thousand, other dinghy types. number of familiar Stone and Maylandsea Bay faces were seen on the stands and about half a dozen hiarconi faces were wandering around.

We started by listening and watching Keith Musto setting the sails of a Flying Dutchman for light and heavy weather, The bends of the mast and boom had to be seen to be believed. I'm still not sure how to implement his advice
on our gadget - free Enterprise,

. The film 'Sail to Win' is one that we nearly had at a Winter programme meeting last year. Four F.D's with different coloured sails are filmed having a race. The start was filmed several times with different wind strengths and tide sects to show what can happen to boats in apparently the same starting position. CRUISE TO CHRISTCHURCH IN 'HULLAB4LOO
by L.A. Payne.

MAY/ JUNE 1968

Having a son, Roger, et the Signals Resesrch and Development Establishment (S.R.D.TM) Christchurch, I was anxious to accept his long- standing invit ition to visit him by sea, so made enquiries about. finding a crew. I knew that Walter Standing from the Marconi Sailing Club -had
disposed of his Kingfisher cruiser and was without a boat and that he had frequently given me a hand in the race box at Stansgate so I approached him and was dcelightcd to find that not only did he accept, but that he was able to supply a further hand, Colin Edmund, whose father is the skipper of the famous gaff-cutter Theodora, belonging to the Ocean Youth Club.

It was decided to make the cruise to Christchurch during the Spring Bank holiday, which gave us three clear days as both Walter and Colin had to return to their duties on the Tuesday, and a few days beforé the start were occupied with loading up the Atalanta cruiser ‘Hullabaloo with water, petrol, stores and generally checking the boat and her gear, although as she had been afloat for only about a month there was not much doubt about this. The great day arrived: the Walton Coast Guard was advised of our sail number, time of departure and destination; the crew turned up in good time so that we were able to make our first entry in the log:-

155C hrs. Left mooring at Blackwater Sailing Club: Wind S.E. force 3, -, Colin had already obtained the weather report, by telephone, which was
- favourable and the weather was fine and clear; but as the wind was dead
_ against us and we were anxious to cross as much of the Thames as possible “in daylight, we proceeded under engine, hoping to set sail after rounding --Osea pier, However, it was not before Stone that we sect sail and then only just managed to weather Thirsle: spit beacon and as the next board would have taken us into St. Lawrence Say and out of the tide, we decided to hand sails and continue under engine.

1/3C hrs: Passed Cradwell Nuclear Pewer Station: Wind nowE.3. It was not until we were well past Bradwell that we were able to set sail and then, with the tide under us, we soon passed the Bench Head, New. Knoll, Eagle and Knoll; but with wind against tide, there was by now quite a choppy sea which was not quite so pleasant for those down below poring over the charts planning our course over the sands, and it was not long before both my crew succumbed, It speaks well for their fortitude and strength of will that they were both Soon able to carry on with theiz duties despite the discomfort.

1915 hrs, Passed the Wallet Spitway, sailing fast.
As it was nov’ half tide we found there was plenty of water through the Spitway, and we passed in grand style the Whitaker and Heaps and we soon saw the light from the Barrow Deep light vessel, as it was now dusk.

2100 hrs. Barrow Deep left to port: Wind Eb force 3 and twentyfive miles of our journey completed; average speed 5 kt. Here we nearly had a major ‘disaster. A sheet fouled the compass supporting ring which sprung and allowed the compass to fall from its gimbals on to the deck. Fortunately the compass appeared to be undamaged and it was soon sprungback into its gimbals: This time we tock the precaution of securing it by a thin nylon
line,

With visibility excellent and the wind holding, we decided to go through Fisherman's Gat so bore away, and leaving the Sunk Beacon to. starboard, picked up the Black Deep 8 where, although now about low water, we found plenty of depth ard after leaving No.10 to port soon saw the welcome light from the Tonguc L.V as by now it was quite dark. I was unable to persuade
either of my crew to partake of any refreshment not even a cup of Bovril - so
being fairly confident of our course, I sent them both below for a well earned rest, Being now alone on deck and having been at the helm since’ leaving the mooriugs, I soon realised that I was ravanously hungry. I had taken the precaution of stowing vast quantities of food in the cockpit - locker, so now treated myself to a considerable meal, at.‘the same time realising how wonderfully my crew had carried on in spite of their disability

and without a grumble, i ;

2400 hrs, Leaving Tongue L.V to starboard. Flood started; wind dying. After my ample repast I was feeling that so far we had not done too badly when my complacency was rapidly brought to an end by the presence of the Thames traffic, and as the beam from the Tonguc L.V. swung round, it was evident that there was a considerable amount of shipping about. However, the North Foreland lighthouse red sector was picked up and, after what seemed an interminable time, the white sector. This we held for some time but with the wirji dying and the flood carrying us up the Thames, we were again back in the red sector. The shipping was now causing anxiety and I reluctantly decided to call Walter and together we decided to drop sail and continue under engine and with navigation, most head light and stern lights all switched on we were soon.on our way again and back in the white sector. The shipping seemed to we very kind to us and on several occasions vessels which seemed to be heading straight for us eventually bore away and although we were doing only two to three knots against the tide, we were nevertheless able to take avoiding action. As I could still not prevail on Walter to partake of any refreshment and as he seemed to be quite happy at the helm, I went below and turned in,

N.Goodwin L.V. was seen to port in the distance during the night,
and the sea was confused while rounding N.Foreland, but by dawn Broadstairs Knoll buoy was passed followed by the Gull Stream and South Black off Deal. Although there was very little wind we set sail in order to show our number to the Coastguard, the Walton-station of which had been informed of our departure and route.

0835 hrs, Dover abeam; Wind light variable: Weather overcast. Possibly owing to the port strike, no traffic was entering or leaving the harbour at either entrance, so we passed without incident. The Harbourmaster had very obligingly hoisted his black ball allowing us to enter, but we continued doggedly on our way and passed the Hythe buoy. Here we saw the iialdon cutter Rikki-Tikki-Tavi, much to Colin's joy; as he knew the crew.

11.30 hrs. Dungeness abeam, Wind still light cariable; sails not doing much good so engine left running at tick-over., The engine, although a 16 hsp. Coventry Victor, ran so smoothly and started so readily at the press of a button, ‘that Colin named it "the sewing machine"and throughout the cruise it was thus referred to. On passing Dungeness I went below and made a brew-up and then turned in, the long haul of some 50 miles across the bay being too much for my patience. When I came on deck again we were approaching Beachy Head and I found that Colin had set the Spinnaker and was having a great time trying to get it to draw. However, it was not doing us much good and again we had to resort to "the sewing machine".

We were now well-over the half-way mark on our outward cruise. By this time I was anxiously measuring the petrol depth in the tank and making ‘calculations about our ability to reach out destination should there still be no wind, As Newhaven was so very little off our course we decided to call in to re~fuel and strétch our legs and we reached the harbour at 20,15 hrs. We tied up at the petrol float and unhappily the attendants had gone home, so Walter and Colin very nobly agreed to go ashore with the spare cans and find a garage. By now the Harbourmaster had followed us down from his office and told us that we might not stay without paying harbour dues but that’ if we could get away by 2100 hrs he would let us off. I invited him on board and plied hin with sherry and cigarettes, but in the end I had to pay up as the crew did not get back in time, The Harbourmaster was at some pains to explain that this would entitle us to tie up in harbour for the night, but as Walter and Colin had had to walk quite a long way before finding a petrol station, they took advantage of the occasion to refresh themselves at the same tine and on returning would not hear of staying for the night, so we left, with a' wave from the Harbourmaster from the top of the pier.

It was dusk with en off-shore breeze, and we sped along happily with large. genoa set. I sent tis Grow below For a snooze. It seemed an interminable time passing the lights of Brighton and towards widnight I found myself dozing so was obliged to call Colin to do a spell, and didn't he need some wakening: When I came on deck again at 0400 hrs, Littlthanptmwas ‘faintly visible astern, and what there was of it, the wind was back to the East.

(i Phere were a lot of fishing boats about and big ships were passing towards

on

KY
a Goes

‘ Portsmouth, but after 56 1.4.46 of drifting we were rather worried about our position and could find neither the Nab tower nor the Owers L.V and could get wireless signals from neither. Walter therefore got busy with the wireless and with bearings from Le Havre, Cape Barfleur and St. Catherine's Point obtained a series of error triangles which showed that we were, in fact, too much South, Our course was duly corrected and to our relief, Dunnose Head on the Isle of Wight appears through the murk on our starboard bow,

1640 hrs. St. Catherine's Point abeam wand light from E, sea calm, After the prolonged spdl of easterly winds, quite a swell of very long wave- length had developed and it was fascinating to sve that when in the trough nothing but sea could be secn on the horizon, whilst on a crest the Isle of Wight and all the shipping came into view. We crossed Freshwater Bay with wind dying and the Needles were soon picked up. As we passed the Needles a large steamer was clearing the Shingles ani it stopped to pat her pilot off on to the boat which had been following, Having passed astern of this boat, we set course for Christchurch Bay, the last lap of our outward passage. Hengistbury Head was seen on our port bow, and the white inflated rubber dome cnclosing Roger's satellite dish aerial at S.R.D.E was soon spotted on the clifs right ahead, «As we approached the buoys at the entrance to the harbour several yachts and fishing boats were anchored waiting for the flood, as the pilot handbook warns sailors that the ebb (known as ‘the Run') may reach as much as 9 knots and there is very little depth over the bar. However, as it would have meant waiting two hours for the flood, by which time it would have been dark, we decided to make a dash for it. This is where the great advantage of the Atalanta, with its adjustable keels and powerful engine, became apparent. We therefore raised the keels to 2.5 ft and got the anchor ready, while Colin stood by with the lead line, We got safely over the bar, although the rudder did touch, it was qickly lifted and then wemet the full force of the cbb. "The Sewing Machine" was opencé out to give its full 16 hp and although it still ran very quietly there was a dintinctly healthy burble heard from the stern of the boat, There was a look of concern on the faces of the fishermen who lined the quay watching our hazardous entry as we made about 1 kt over the torrent; but once in the harbour we made for the only mooring buoy which was vacant, which, in fact, turned out to be the mooring which Roger had arranged for us in collaboration with the local Cruising Association boatmen,

Within a very host time Walter end Colin were getting themselves ready to go ashore whilst I launshed the rubber dinghy which had been carried fully inflated on the stern. and they set off for the quay to telephone Roger to come to see us and to the Coastgoard to inform Walton of our safe arrival.

After Roger's visit we had a splendid meal on board and turned in, Needless to say, none oF us needed any rocking that night: The distance was
just about 200 miles and it had taken us 52 hours, the average speed being 3.85 kt,
The mooring which we used was on the edge of the channel up to Christchurch and with certain conditions of wind and tide we took the ground, but as it was
beautiful soft golden sand this did not mtter at all - in fact - it was an
advantage, for during my daily swimming I was sable to scrub down and touch up the mull and topsides, so that by the end of our stay all were in perfect condition, During our stay in Christchurch I was able to visit Roger's satellite communications establishment where, as a retired harconi engineer, I was very gratified to note that the equipment was largely liarconi,

There was a very popular pub on the quay where the local boatmen assembled and they were always very helpful in obtaining petrol and stores and providing local knowledge. Provisions and newspapers we got from the cafe on the beach, and there were several standpipes from which drinking water could be obtained. As my crew were not available the following week-end, I had to stay two weeks in harbour, but this was not a bit too long and with spendid weather and plenty of yachts coming and going, there was never a dull moment. I took the opportunity of running over the whole ship and engine in preparation for the return journey but found everything was in first class order and apart from cleaning up, there was nothing to be done,

REGATTA 1969

The Marconi Regatta is again taking place at Whitsun and the arrangements are well in hand for the event. The formula is much the same as previous years, minor changes have been incorporated to try to provide more enjoyment and better facilities.

The racing programe is little changed except that there will be two Pennant Races for Dinghies on the Saturday. These will be divided such that boats with speed figures of up to 100 will sail in one race and those having a figure above 100 in the second race,

The only difference in the Points Series is that this year the Hornet races will be for the Hallam Trophy which in the past has been held on a different week-end.

At slack water I cast off the mooring which had served us so well whilst in harbour and brought Hullabaloo alongside the quay, where our friends the fishermen took our lines, All our fenders were needed to keep us off the quay and as by this time the flood had started, and being stern on, it was almost impossible to move the rudder, such was the force of the tide. Also whilst awaiting my crew, the wind which had been off-shore, now started to veer and increase in force which added to my difficulty in fending off, However, the wind eventually died and by this time ‘alter and Colin arrived with Roger who had collected them from the station. Within minutes, they had donned their sailing garb and we were soon away from the quay. The wind was now light and dead against us and as there was still quite a lot of the flood left we decided to make use of it and make the passage inside the Isle of Wight thus giving ourselves the satisfaction of having made the trip round the island.

1920 hrs, Cast off moorings from Christchurch quay. wind &, Light vars course 120° for North, Channel buoy to avoid the shingles sands and Hurst Castle abeam at 2045 hrs. Passed close to Hurst Point with overfalls rather ominous; heavy shower, Wind now completely gone so proceeded under engine. As visibility was not too good we decided to cross at once to the Isle of ‘right where we picked up the Albert Fort on the cliffs and proceeded up the Solent in great style with the tide still under us. The rain had now ceased and

the night was fine although still overcast. By now it was dusk and by |
2100 hrs we had the ilghts of Yarmouth abeam. The Hamstead buoys off Newtown and eventually Egypt Point off Cowes were passed. It was now quite dark and we were obliged to use our searchlight as the numerous unlighted buoys caused us some anxiety.

2200 hrs. Gurnard buoys and lights off Cowes passed — no traffic about. Towards midnight we sew the lights of Ryde with what we thought was its brilliantly—-lighted pavilion looking resplendent in the pitch—black darkness, We had been at the helm for quite a spell and both “alter and I thought we must have been dowing for it seemed the pavilion was moving out to seas of course we soon realised that it was the Southampton Ferry boat which was then moving away from the pier, which we were seeing! As we approached the forts off the shipping from Southampton down the Spithead became considerable and we prudentiy kept our course well to the south of the channel. The France, brilliantly illuminated an’ with her name under the bridge, passed us at an incredibly high speed and was soon out of sight. Having set course for the Looe channel with the light of the Nab on our starboard bow, I turned in — not without some misgiving as conditions were suggesting that we might encounter fog. I had not been asleep for long before I was quickly brought back to my senses by Colin rushing down into the Cabin calling for the foghorn. I at once came on deck and was alarmed to find dense fog and to ry horror the towering stern of a large cargo boat passing ahead of us. The distance
looked like 100 ft but in all probability it was nearer 100 yards but still
unfomfortably close. We blew our horn frequently but it would probably have been of no avail and I expect that the cargo boat had not even seen us, Fog horns were ahead from all directions and we spent an anxious half hour on deck with our eyes skinned until, to our great relief, at dawn the fog began to lift. As we possessed no proper radar reflector, Colin had most enterprisingly hoisted an aluminium saucepan in the rigging in the hope of giving an improved radar response to that due only to our rigging. ‘Is it possible that the cargo boat we had so narrowly missed had actually got a response and, in fact, taken avoiding action?

We had altered our course to get us clear of the main deep water shipping channel, and as daylight came we found ourselves amongst numerous boats which were fishing off Selsey Bill. We had quite a time and went considerably off course in avoiding their nets. However, fog came down again and we passed rather close to a large yacht and we heard the Nab blowing his fog horn but the coast was not visible. Nevertheless, we were able to pick up the Pullar and Street buoys marking the Looe passage.

it was bright and clear with a little breeze - albeit ahead -— we were able to
set sail and with our course set for Beachy ahead, Brighton and Newhaven were picked up, the chimneys of Shoreham Power station also, and bearings were taken on then. A high-speed R.A.F. rescue launch came out from Newhaven and circled us, but as we appeared to be doing no harm and proceeding nicely, they left us unmolested,

1830 hrs. Passed Beachy ilead: Wind astern, light variable, so set spinnaker but did no good so resorted to "the sewing machine". We now started the long haul of about 30 miles to Dungeness, coming well into Pevensey Bay to avoid the worst of the tide. Although we could have done with 2 good breeze to enable us to sail we also thought of the consequences of getting caught out in a storm in the middle of the bay with very long distances to ports of shelter — Newhaven to the west and Folkestone to the east.

Dungeness was passed at 0215 with the new power station plainly visible and another long haul to Dover in prospect. Fortunately: there was now no fog, but the wind, what there was of it, still right ahead. The Hoyal Sovereign L.V was. just visible on our starboard beam and we realised that this would probably be the last time we should see it because it is to be replaced by an unmanned automatic lighthouse now being assembled in an engineering works in Grays -— the firm which made a similar lighthouse for Dun Laoghaire in Dublin Bay The lights of Hastings.
and Fairlight were visible in the distance and we : VY wondered whether we should be able to find our way into Rye harbour in the event of trouble for it was a long way to any other ports of shelter.

Passed Dover at 0645 hrs and were not inconvenienced by traffic entering or leaving: Misty morning but still very little wind and what there was of it, dead ahead,

Set sail to Deal to show our number to the Coastguard and tacked for:quite a while with little progress and tiring ourselves in the process, Had the wind held from the East we should have sailed very well after rounding South Foreland but luck was against us, for as we turned northwards, the wind backed and headed us. By this time we had run the engine quite a lot and I made calculations as to whether our fuel supply would hold out. Ramsgate was dead ahead and I considered it prudent to call in and replenish our supplies. As we approached we got the signal from the Harbourmaster that we might enter the harbour, but as we did so, we noticed a Hovercraft coming towards us at great speed and throwing off huge clouds of spray and evidently also wishing
to enters so although he appeared to wish to give way to us, we considered it |
more prudent to let him enter first and we therefore made a wide turn and follow in his wake. In the harbour we soon spotted to the south a floating petrol station and tied up alongside when a hose was passed aboard and we filled om tanks to our heart's content with the precious liquid. We were asked to move away as soon as possible so were not able to stretch our legs ashore. It soon became obvious that the urgency was due to the Putney—Calais—Putney speedboat..race, and high speed motor boats were coming and going in great numbers, some to take petrol. It was fantastic to see the way they shot into the air with engines roaring when they hit the waves and it speaks well for the fibreglass hulls that they withstood the impact when they came down on the water again with great force.

1300-hrs, Left Ramsgate, ‘and N. Force 2/3. Overcast. sea agitated. We. soon passed Broadstairs and by 1400 hrs we were with North Foreland lighthouse abeam, At this moment we thought we saw Colin's father's boat Theodora proceeding towards Edinburgh Channel. As the wind was now blowing quite strongly we considered how best we could use it to our advantage and although it entailed some careful navigation, we decided to take a northwesterly course to the Swin. We therefore tacked first to the Margate Sand beacon, the Pan Sand beacon and the Shivvering Sands tower, where the illicit broadcasting station was situated, and so into the West Swin. Here at dusk, it was tantalising to see the wireless towers on Foulness, so near yet so far!

By now, although the wind held, it had veered and was now blowing at force 3 from the N.i, so that it was necessary to tack past the Maplin buoys and the Whitaker, which called for considerable concentration and we were very relieved when we eventually picked up the welcome flashing of the Swin Spitway, We were now able to bear away and sailed through the Spitway without once touching the bottom although our keels were lowered to their full 5'6" and it was nearly low water, One boat had not been so successful and was aground about half way across gwaiting the flood to carry her off:
had we not been so occupied with our own safety and beamed our searchlight on her we should have discovered that it was Theodora, which we had previously seen coming up the Edinburgh channel.

The wind had almost gone and was anyway dead against us so we pressed the button and proceeded under engine, Leaving “alter at the helm, I went below to sleep. When I came on deck at dawn we were passing Bradwell nuclear power station and before going below Walter related how during the night he had mistaken the lights of the power station for an anchored fishing boat and had sought to take avoiding actions he had been with the charts almost continuously since leaving Margate and was doubtless very tired. I took over the helm and proceeded up the river and eventually picked up my mooring at the Blackwater Sailing Club at 0500 hours.

The dinghy was launched and Walter and Colin were soon ashore and were able to get to Colin's house at Maldon in time for breakfast and to report that Theodora would probably be back on the evening tide. Neither was late for his duties that morning but after their strenuous night I don't know how they managed to see the day through.

The total time taken for the trip was 57 hours including the stop at Ramsgate. This gave an average speed of abour 3.5 kt. The amount of petrol used was 15 gallons. ,

The cruise was very successful. ‘Ye were favoured with good weather and calm seas but owing to the lack of time the crew was able to allow, it was necessary to use the’ engine more than I should have liked.

The Atalanta gave every satisfaction and never any cause for anxiety; it proved very comfortable and the galley was most efficient. The engine behaved remarkably well and its reputation as "the Sewing Machine" was well justified, its petrol consumption being in the region of 0.3 gall/hr and it was generally run at quarter throttle.

It would have been nice to have made the trip under sail alone, but there are not places like the Pyfleet where one can put in should the weather turn bad along the south coast and with a climate such as ours there is a lot to be said for motor sailing. Great credit is due to ny crew who carried out their duties without ever a grumble and those who have sailed with me know how fussy I can be! I hope, however, that this would be put down to my age!

B.A. Payne.

The General Purpose 1h ft dinghy. commonly known as the G.P.1h

This is one of the oldest classes sailed on our river, fee first one having been introduced in the mid cighteenth century sailing under the name of 'Victory'. In 1805 her helmsman, one Horatio Melson was Killed during a rather notted up protest in a regatta off Cape Trafalger. Although this class has been greatly modified in size and sail area, its weight has remained largely unchanged.

The International fiornet Class,

The fly in the ointment. This boat was designed especially for the helmsman who doesn't like his crew. It is equipped with many anti-crew devices such as ejector seat(Sliding board )or hanging noose (trapeze).

late last year, One “ireball accounted for....three Mirrors
sunk, ecight protested out and one swamped in his wash. Yet the Mirrors still won the race outright.

EDITORIAL

The editorial this month concerns messages I've had from several people about swimming,

Firstly, in the last three weeks two little girls have found themselves out of their depths when only a few feet from the water's edge. Fortunately their respective Mums were close at hand and it was they and not their daughters who were scared. Parents — please be careful to watch the children, especially the non-—swimmers. The beach does slope very steeply and the children should be encouraged to swim or paddle parallel to the shore. The strength of the tide shouldn't be under estimated either.

Secondly, boats sometimes approach the hard very fast and with a flick of the helmsman's wrist they are almost stationary, head—to-—wind and completely under control. Although I quite agree that swimmers have as much right to use the water as the sailors, boats are bigger than a Swimmer's head and it would seem sensible if swimmers would not swim from the hard when dinghies are-coming in. The gravel at the Stone end of the hard really is a safer place to swim. Hedmsmen please try to come in slowly if you think its swimming weather,

Thirdly, for Cadets (and those under 10) who like Swimming, why not make a point of going swimming with your friends in the summer holidays at a particular time. For Mum's benefit I'm suggesting Wednesdays, Thursdays and Fridays. Now that the Market is right beside the swimming pool, park in the short stay car park, have a swim with the kids, do your shopping and then go home, duty and pleasure combined, Already several families with under 10's are making arrangements, now what about some of the over 10's getting themselves organised.

FIRST TIME OUT.

From the shore, the water sparkled invitingly in the spring sun and a light breeze fluttered through the red, white and blue sails of the waiting boats. It was a gay colourful scene. Happy laughing sailors in yellow anoraks and bright yachting caps busied themselves about their craft, setting sails and adjusting strange gadgets
to
their satisfaction. My helmsman and boat appeared calm and serene
on the shore-line as they waited for me - the all important crew,
to climb aboard. 0, it was all such fun!! At last, at last, I was going for a real live sail!

Ten minutes later, I was perched uncomfortably on top of a jambing cleat with strict instructions to "pull the jib sheet hard in". I nobly tried to please by pulling hard on a jib sheet, but unfortunately it was the wrong one. This brought forth a stream of incomprehensible commands from my helmsman in the stern, who had suddently turned into a fearsome ogre speaking a strange language.

-5-

I could understand the adjectives, which were rather distressing, but the rest was couched in obscure technical terms.

For the next hour or so, I bounced gaily from deck to centre- board box to shroud, collecting more bruises at every tack, and frequently landing on my posterior in two inches of water in the bottom of the boat, feet flailing uselessly in the air. WNotsuch fun after all. I was rapidly learning about the dastardly crew- traps in an Enterprise -— that kicking strap, highly tensed and waiting to slice off an unsuspecting ear, that centreboard box with special knobs to give extra special bruises and those toe-straps specially designed to trip up the crew when tacking, And how was I supposed to look out for boats on starboard tack when my field of vision was totally obscured by a massive wall of blue sail??

When it actually happened, I was just beginning to relax and enjoy myself, We were skimming along quite pleasantly on what the helmsman called a "run". The wind appeared to have dropped right off and I began to look around and take an interest in some exciting water skiing on the other side of the estuary. Sailing wasn't so bad,
after all......cuddenly the whole world tipped at an alarming angle
and I received yet another almighty blow across the head as the boom swung across. Then, slowly, but Oh so surely, we were lowered into the icy depths of Blackwater estuary. For a moment everything was splutter and choke and I dogsy—paddled around uselessly until I realised that my feet were tangled up in the mainsheet and I wasn't getting anywhere fast. The freezing water gradually seeped through layers of clothing and I couldn't breathe, it was so cold.

Helmsman righted the boat at the second attempt, the first try ending in an ignominious dive backwards off the centreboard amid gurgled curses. (This was quite the highlight of the day). Eventually the rescue launch arrived and I was heaved on board feeling very much like a freshly caught walrus. Then we were putting for home.

But the humiliation of that walk up the beach!!! As & squelched up to the clubhouse, I was surrounded by grinning faces and greeted by cheerful hearty jeers. Happy laughing DRY sailors in yellow anoraks and bright yachting caps, Fool me. They had never left the shore. Now I know what they're laughing about,

EDITORIAL

May I start by saying that the Editorial usually consists of my own thoughts on happenings at the Club and though it may be 'vetted' by John it is not necessarily the Committee's view. If anyone objects to what I write about I do wish they'd send me a stinking letter to print in
Navigans,

Although the incidents were small, the principles involved were somewhat greater, The incidents — several rowing dinghtes fairly near to the shore on a very sunny day and a dead flat calm. One thing noticed was children standing in a boat and another was that none of the youngsters were wearing lifejackets. Even on a calm day it is only common sense to make sure that Cadets do not do silly things in boats. It is one thing to go swimming voluntarily from the shore, and another to be tipped into the Blackwater unexpectedly.

There is a Club Sailing Byelaw, which was made by your elected Committee and not by a nebulous "them!" to spoil everyone's fun, that days that all Cadets under 18 shall wear personal bouyancy when sailing from Stansgate. I suspect that the "sailing" was meant to imply rowing and even outboard motoring.

I suppose that if a parent does not wish a child to wear a lifejacket the correct course would be to join a club without the rule (which seems rather a harsh solution) or approach the Committee to have the Byelaw amended,

There must be other byelaws and rules that are not adhered to and my own view is that the committee would be pleased to hear from members who wish to suggest amendments or new rules.

oe Bow

Personally I feel that the lifejacket rule for Cadets is sensible and most of the senior Cadets set a good example and wear their life- jackets everytime they go out for a sail or row.

Surely it's a good thing to encourage the youngsters to be aware of the possible hazards in boating (without frightening them) and to teach them the common sense safety rules,

As I said, my own thoughts, prompted by two or three dinghies with children but I'm not "getting" at them in particular and I beg them not to take offence — they just triggered the ideas. I hope that the remarks will cause a bit of discussion and possibly a few letters in Navigans???

Eleanor Witter.

SAPWOOD by the Gribble

The exodus to Holland seems to be greater this year than ever, among Blackwater clubs as a whole, if not the MSC in particular, and there has been a great deal of trading of charts and general information. One of our senior members has extended his knowledge of where to go aground to the non—tidal Veerse Meer, but as his yacht has since been seen on the Blackwater, his skill at Kedging off was evidently equal to the occasion!

Not all cruising types are willing to "call their shots" and no one of experience can blame them for that. I recall the owner of a sturdy, but not very weatherly, yacht planning to go to the West Country; but being faced with steady westerlies when his holiday began, did a smart about-face and went (by way of his chart-agent, we hope) to the River Schelde. However, the point of these remarks is, if you don't want to say where you intend to go, do tell us all afterwards where you have been, This summer looks the most encouraging for some years, and we ought to have a bumper crop of logs from it. Dinghy cruisers may need their oars, and larger ones their engines, more than sometimes, but it's seldom too warm for comfort in the North Sea or the Channel.

If you've been wondering why it has been so peaceful and quiet at the Club on Sundays lately it is because several members of both the Hornet and Enterprise fleets have been away at Open Meetings.

Members of the Enterprise fleet have taken to the roads with their boats and have attended several of the Open Meetings held at local clubs, including the 'East Coast Area Championships! which was held at Clacton Sailing Club. EAST SCHELDE LANDFALL
(1968):

I had heard several yachtsmen speak of the East Schelde or Roompot as the most attractive entrance to the Netherlands. Some were probably reminiscing of the days when you could sail straight into Veere, and the Patent Agent of larconi's (alias Hon. Navigation Instructor, L.S.C) may have regarded it as an intriguing problem in navigation; but in a few years' time it will be closed by a dyke in the course of the "Delta Plan", the current master-plan for the shortening of the immense length of the Dutch sea-defences, Also it would be a good exercise in D.F. navigation, for which 2 "Seafix" was available; there are few off-—lying marks, but cross—-bearings could be taken from the radio beacons on the Noord Hinder and Goeree light vessels. (There is nothing intoxicating about the Roompot, by the ways; "Room" in Dutch is cream. Delicious, or possibly "easily whipped up")?

Weather was generally anticyclonic, with actual wind about ESE force 3-4, and forecast wind NE force 3-6. We left Harwich at 1500 of 12th June under "Kazarka's" favourite cruising rig of main and No.2 Genoas a few tacks took us out past Landguard Point and over the N. tip of the Cork Sand, Still nearly close—hauled on port rack, we passed Roughs Tower at 1702. Backing wind and the North—-going tide allowed sheets to be eased as we went on towards the Sunk, indeed we were being set up towards the Shipwash. Checked the "Seafix" on the Sunk L.V and got sharp nulls and accurate alignment between radio and visual (boresight, the Americans would call it). Sensitivity was also OK on beacons at full nominal range. I laid off courses for E Schelde, W. Schelde, Zeebrugge and Ostend, but the first choice seemed to be "on" unless the wind headed us severely.

Maggie took the helm from cast-off until past the Sunk, while I worked out the navigation plan, rested and passed up hot soup. The sky was clear and it was getting cold already when I relieved her after 1900. We crossed the Galloper, well North of the light vessel; in the fairly slight sea there were strong tide-ripples, although the chart gave 2 fathoms plus, There was not very much shipping until near the N. Hinder L.V., and even there most of it was not on cross tracks and there were no close-quarters situations. Passed 1 mile North of the
N.Hinder at 0155. Thursday, and traffic soon decreased to less than one
ship per hour until we were quite near the Dutch coast, About 0230 I lashed the helm and went below, leaving "Kazarka" nearly close—hauleds; not the ideal course but good for self-steering, One day I'll make a self-steering gear! Although no-one was on deck, I could keep watch through the cabin windows, while being out of the wind and cold, and within reach of food, and charts.

I started DF's about 0400, getting N. Hinder 250 T and Goeree 066 T.3
nearly in line, a poor fix but it showed we must bear away to close the coast so I would have to take the helm again. The sea was absolutely featureless after losing N. Hinder, for we were too far out to pick up the shore lighthouses before dawn. But on a course of 124M,, later (and not wisely) 145M., the DF lines gradually opened up. To save repeated plotting, I had prepared the chart with compass roses on the two beaconss a very useful dodge suggested by Mary Blewitt in "Navigation for Yachtsmen". But hour after hour there was no visual check.

Ultimately I spied a tower, rather hazy. I hoped it would be Domburg church on the NW shore of Walcheren island, but it could also be Westkapelle lighthouse at the W. tip (it was about 8 miles away). This was about 0930. Later, and very slowly, we caméup on a green wreck-buoy nearly due W of Westkapelles I was surprised to find the tide past it nearly West-going as a result of the streams out of the E and W Scheldeg the tidal atlas gave it as more SW-going, i.e. along the main coast line, This was our first buoy since the N, Hinder group. Close-hauled now, we needed a few tacks to make Westkapelle. some large ships were in the deep Oostgat near the coast, but their channel was narrow and well marked, We had to dodge the Botkil to the W. of Westkapelle, by transits on the smaller Noorderhoofd lighthouse and the OG 1 buoy, The wind was now NNE 5 and a small but

=O=
J

lumpy sea was being set up. '"Kweerens" and "Domburger Rassen' were names on the charts "queer 'uns" we felt described the waves here.

From 1200 we could expect a fair tides we should carry it right up to Zierikzee. At 1240 we had Domburg church abeam (no doubt this time). Rather hard pressed and with the mainsail usually eased, I hoped it would be better in a mile or two when we could bear away a little. But by 1315 it was evident that we were still over-canvassed, the jib was pressing down our bows and "Kazarka" was carrying massive weather helm. Took off jib and didn't put up anothers a little later, started the engine. Some of the channels ran nearly to windward and I didn't want to miss stays in the trickier spots, with a short wind- against—-tide sea running. I reckoned it a full force 6 when taking the No.2. Genoa off.

Past the Veeregat dam the channel funnels down and is called "Schar van Onrust''s roughly "the strait of unrest', In these conditions this was good Anglo-Dutch understay¥ement, On the North Side is the Hompels shoal which dries at low water, Waves were breaking heavily on it, but were also breaking for about a mile across the Schar itself; very short and steep waves like a weather-going tide in force 7 off Stansgate, “only more so", Nothing to do but keep her going, in the channel, and hold on! That was a full-time job pspecially in the narrowest part of the channel, for the tide appears to spill over, as it were, and sets partly across the Hompels., However, we kept the transits moving the right way on the buoys, and came through with our teeth still in their sockets. After all, it was a spring flood, and wind rising force 7 against it. Another time we'll take it with Wind and tide, and see if it is a little less "onrustig".

On to Zierikzee it was just a hard punch, mostly to windwards a lot of spray flying, but we were used to it now. The difficulty was to see the buoys and their numbers through well-salted eyes, The Zierikzee entrance canal is* mile before the Oosterschelde bridge, which the most salt—blinded sailor could sees but because of the Size of the bridge, it seems much nearer, Not wishing to go down-tide of the entrance, we went up to a light-buoy to read its number! The entrance is clear when you come to its we entered at 1545, 24° hours and 105 charted miles out from Harwich.

We weren't the only yacht out that afternoons a small Dutch yacht entered with us, under jib only. But they knew better than to go through the Schar van Onrust -— they had come up close under the lee of the North shore!

A.M. Adan.

THE SATLORS DILEMMA by D.A.R. Edwards.

I suppose all sailors who aspire to owning their own boat go through the
agonics of decision - making when the time comes to buy the first or subsequent
boat. Three seasons ago the choice for me was fairly simple and was solved .. .-. mainly on financial grounds coupled with the need for something that I could manage both ashore and afloat and the need for a craft that would not dump myself and family in the water at the slightcst pretext. The draft chosen was “a Mirror dinghy which was cheap, safe and light. Having joined the Marconi Sailing Club it began to dawn on me that there were other factors to consider, The most important of these was the necessity to be able to sail against the current in a light breeze and to be able to point reasonably close to the wind. It was also irksome to be the tail end charlie in a handicap race, arriving home to find the other crews changed and having tea, The Mirror, being short hylled and gunter rigged was inclined to be slow and not terribly close winded, having a Portsmouth rating of 122. In the Autumn of this year, we said goodbye to the Mirror, banked the money, and started looking around for the next choice.

It was soon evident that certain criteria had to be ratified. Firstly we decided to go for a dinghy with a fibreglass hull, if possible, about 1),' long but not too heavy. It should have a Portsmouth rating of 90 to 100 and it should not cost more than about £250. Later we found that the dimensions. of beam and height of the hull were important in determining whether the hull would pass sideways through a door in the garden wall for winter storage behind the house. Having obtained a cheap trailer car topping was no longer a criterion but due regard needed to be paid to whether the boat should be one of the established classes at the club in order to avoid handicap racing, although quite a lot of pottering was also envisaged for the benefit of the non-racing mcembers of the family. It seemed that the choice had to be one of four boats, the GP14, the Enterprise, the Scorpion and the Lark. The first two were obvious candidates as they were well established and thriving club classés, Wie fell in love with the Scorpion at the boat show and the Lark was chucked in for good measure as the second non club class as it was a modern design,

All four boats could be purchased in stage 3 kit form or secondhand and could be used in minimum sailing trim i.e. no. spinnaker or other extras, for around £250 mark. The Scorpion was the only one of the 4 which was not available with GRP hull. Research showed that the GPl4. was purchasable from agents or builders within 20 miles radius of Chelmsford, it was a good secaboat and competitive with the genoa increasing the sail area but it was inclined to be heavy (293 lb plus) and it looked as if those door posts would have to come down in order to pass the hull through sideways, especially as the glass hull had moulded in washboards (the Mark 11 version).

The Scorpion was fairly quickly eliminated because of its non GRP hull and it seemed to have characteristics which were similar to the Enterprise or the Lark, The builders were also in Devon, although no doubt the boat could be bought more locally. The Enterprise merited a very long scrutiny indeed. It has a spacious hull, is very popular both at the Club and throughout the country, and comes very close indeed to buing an ideal’choice. However demerits were its rumoured hull weakness in glass, its need for a smaller main for pottering, especially in a blow, and its apparent desire to broach on the run if indifferently helmed. It was now the turn of the Lark. Hull very similar to the Enterprise but round bilged and reputedly easily driven, with some characteristics reminiscent of the National 12. Small wonder for it was designed by Michael Jackson and markcted by Dick Wyche, both of them having close associations with the National 12. It is claimed that this boat will easily achieve its Portsmouth Rating of 9 3 with the modest sail area of 105 square feet. It is also claimed that it will stand up to a blow without serious crew discomfort by hardening down on Cunningham hole and kicker. Shceéting can be on a centre or transom horsé and the alloy centreplate is controlled by a lanyard brought out to each side deck. My interest was sufficiently aroused that I went down to see Dick iiyche at Chichester and had a look at the real thing. Dick received me very couteously and patiently answered all my questions so that I decided that if I choose the Lark, he would supply it. As far as I could see the only problem would be that mine would be the only Lark in the club, indeed, probably on the Blackwater. However I talked myself into waiving this little difficulty and dispatched my order and cheque. I am now waiting anxiously for Dick to tell me to collect. I am looking forward to bringing the Lark to Stansgate next season and, who knows, she may generate sufficient interest to persuade others, who are undecided what to go for next, to start the nucleus of a flicet. Now that the organised Club programme has been completed and the |
Sailing Season is over, members with boats will be considering the winter's work of refitting,: repairing and modifying their craft. The Club's boats will require similar treatment. To finish even the more necessary tasks befére a new season's sailing helpers will be required each weekend from now on. The reliability of the rescue launches is in inverse proportion to the Winter's work and the amount of extra naintainance that has to be carried out during: the Sailing Season. As the amount of that work which :
can be completed in the time available depends on the assistance received Will "you" please help for a few Sundays (or Saturdays if you prefer) during the winter, A large part of the work is cleaning and preparing the bonts for re-painting for which no great skill is required, so that

‘ - 7 -

anyone can help, However, because of the limited number of tools available at the Club it would help if-you brought some for your own use. Examples of particularly useful items are scrapers, wire brushes, files, hammers, screw drivers, saws, sanding blocks and for a limited number of jobs powered sanding tools.

This year to achieve continuity and an improved organisation it is hoped to have someone with an over2ll knowledge of the work to be done and who will be in charge of the work for each working day at Stansgate. In addition it is intended to break down the projected work into a number of areas and to ask volunteers to undertake, as Task Leaders, to organise the individual tasks. It is envisaged that the job of the Task Leaders will be to organise any necessary help, tools, materials etc for his individual project, to arrange for continuity of effort on working days at Stanszete and on a rota basis to assist the overall Orcaniser.

Obviously, unless an undue burden is to be placed on a few
Willing numbers, these proposed schemes can only be implemented if sufficient people can be found willing to give up a little time in organising the work and to spend 2 few days at Stansgate during the winter, Also, even if sufficient organisers can be found, the scheme will fail unless enough numbers will sacrifice a few days to allow working parties to be formed at Stansgate each weekend.

If you ond the majority of other members adopt the attitude that sufficient people will volunteer without you yourself participating the result will be one of the following:-

(a) All the work will fall on a very sn2ll proportion of ‘the
Club members,

(b) The Rescue Launches will not be ready in time.

(c) The essential work will only be partially completed,
resulting in decreasing the. reliability of the boats during the Szason, increasing the maintainance during that period, and adding to next winter's work.

None of these situations should arise if the response to this appeal is adequate but the onus is on you.

Work has already started and all volunteers can'be gainfully employed from Sunday November 16th.
